text: AI in Pharma R&D: Regulatory Perspectives and Guardrails | Speaker: George Visfilo | MOA: Visfilo described AstraZeneca's experience with AI‑enabled pathology devices, the three classes of AI‑driven biomarkers (replication, inference, outcome prediction), and advocated for third‑party benchmarking, clear guardrails, and high levels of evidence to ensure safe clinical deployment. | Findings: AstraZeneca achieved the first Class 2 FDA clearance for an AI pathology device in 2021 and a breakthrough device designation for an AI‑derived predictive biomarker for an ADC.; Three AI biomarker classes were defined: Class A (task replication), Class B (inferred biomarkers), Class C (prognostic or predictive outcomes).; For Class C2 (predictive of therapeutic response), prospective trial validation is required; explainability is not mandatory if performance is demonstrated.; Emphasis on multi‑stakeholder partnerships (academia, industry, payers, regulators, patients) to set evaluation standards and avoid a “Wild West” scenario.

metadata.speaker: George Visfilo
metadata.talk_title: AI in Pharma R&D: Regulatory Perspectives and Guardrails

text: FDA Frameworks for AI in Oncology Drug Development | Speaker: Jeevan Puthenvedu | MOA: Puthenvedu presented the FDA’s risk‑based credibility framework for AI models used to support regulatory decisions in drug and biologic development, outlining the seven‑step process, the distinction between AI used for data generation versus decision support, and the 2025 draft guidances on model risk, lifecycle maintenance, and international harmonization. | Findings: The FDA received >1,000 AI‑containing submissions (CDER + CBER) to date, with oncology representing ~27% of AI submissions.; The draft guidance (Jan 2025) introduces a seven‑step risk‑based credibility assessment, calibrated by model influence and decision consequence.; High‑risk use cases (e.g., AI‑driven inpatient monitoring decisions) require extensive validation, documentation, and early FDA engagement.; AI models that meet the statutory device definition are subject to separate AI‑enabled device guidance (Jan 2025).; Key regulatory principles: methodological transparency, external validation on representative data, alignment with Good Machine Learning Practices, and early sponsor‑FDA communication.

metadata.speaker: Jeevan Puthenvedu
metadata.talk_title: FDA Frameworks for AI in Oncology Drug Development

text: DPP4 as a novel checkpoint for CD8 T cells in glioblastoma | Speaker: Defne Bayik | Tumors: glioblastoma | MOA: DPP4 acts as an immunometabolic checkpoint on CD8 T cells; its inhibition by sitagliptin restores mitochondrial respiration and glycolysis, enhances proliferation, cytotoxic mediator production, and degranulation, partly via up‑regulation of GAD1‑mediated TCA cycle flux, leading to improved anti‑GBM activity. | Findings: Retrospective analysis of Medicare data showed GBM patients on DPP4 inhibitors had significantly longer survival than matched controls.; CD8 T cells in human GBM express high DPP4, especially terminally exhausted (TOX‑high) subsets.; Pharmacologic or genetic DPP4 inhibition increased CD8 proliferation, cytokine production, and cytotoxicity in vitro.; DPP4 inhibition up‑regulated mitochondrial respiratory capacity and glycolysis, linked to GAD1 activation.; In orthotopic GBM mouse models, sitagliptin prolonged survival, an effect abolished by CD8 depletion.

metadata.speaker: Defne Bayik
metadata.talk_title: DPP4 as a novel checkpoint for CD8 T cells in glioblastoma

text: Molecular mechanisms of differentiation therapy and arsenic in acute promyelocytic leukemia | Speaker: Hugues de The | Tumors: acute promyelocytic leukemia | MOA: ATRA binds the RARα moiety of the PML‑RARα fusion, converting it from a transcriptional repressor to an activator, while arsenic binds a cysteine triad in the PML moiety, inducing SUMO‑dependent ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of PML‑RARα and restoration of PML nuclear bodies, leading to p53 activation, senescence, and terminal differentiation of leukemic promyelocytes. | Findings: ATRA alone induces differentiation but rarely cures APL; arsenic alone cures ~2/3 of patients; the combination cures virtually all patients.; Both agents directly degrade the PML‑RARα oncoprotein via distinct ubiquitin‑proteasome pathways (UBR5 for ATRA, SUMO‑dependent ligase for arsenic).; Restoration of PML nuclear bodies after treatment correlates with p53 activation and loss of self‑renewal, essential for cure in mouse models.; Mutations in the arsenic‑binding cysteine triad confer resistance, confirming the binding site’s importance.; PML is required for response to conventional chemotherapy in non‑APL leukemias, indicating a broader role in therapy response.

metadata.speaker: Hugues de The
metadata.talk_title: Molecular mechanisms of differentiation therapy and arsenic in acute promyelocytic leukemia

text: Apoptotic priming as a determinant of chemotherapy sensitivity across solid and liquid cancers | Speaker: Christopher Sarosiek | Tumors: acute lymphoblastic leukemia, diffuse large B‑cell lymphoma, follicular lymphoma, testicular germ cell tumor, high‑grade serous ovarian cancer, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, glioblastoma, medulloblastoma, rhabdomyosarcoma | MOA: Differential apoptotic priming, measured by BH3 profiling, determines how readily cancer cells undergo mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization upon chemotherapy; hematologic and pediatric CNS cancers are highly primed and thus chemo‑sensitive, whereas most solid tumors are unprimed and require inhibition of multiple BCL‑2 family members to trigger death. | Findings: Blood cancers and testicular germ cell tumors are intrinsically more primed for apoptosis than most solid tumors, correlating with clinical chemosensitivity.; Baseline BH3 profiling priming scores predict faster CA125 normalization and longer PFS in ovarian cancer patients.; CRISPR knockout of Bax/Bak in HeLa cells reduces priming and confers broad chemoresistance, confirming causality.; Solid tumor cell lines require simultaneous inhibition of multiple pro‑survival BCL‑2 proteins (BCL‑XL, MCL‑1) for cell death, unlike hematologic lines.; Neonatal muscle‑derived rhabdomyosarcomas retain higher Bax/Bim levels, are more primed, and respond better to vincristine; BCL‑XL degrader DT2216 synergizes to improve response.

metadata.speaker: Christopher Sarosiek
metadata.talk_title: Apoptotic priming as a determinant of chemotherapy sensitivity across solid and liquid cancers

text: NF1 as a microtubule‑repair factor and predictor of maytansinoid ADC efficacy in HER2‑positive breast cancer | Speaker: Luca Mazzarella | Tumors: HER2-positive breast cancer, medulloblastoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, lung cancer | MOA: NF1 binds directly to polymerized microtubules, accelerates tubulin polymerization and promotes self‑repair of intra‑microtubule damage; loss of NF1 impairs this repair, creating more drug‑binding sites for maytansinoid payloads (DM1) on exposed protofilament ends, thereby sensitizing NF1‑deficient cells to T‑DM1 ADCs. | Findings: NF1 loss does NOT affect Ras signaling in this context but dramatically increases sensitivity to the maytansinoid ADC T‑DM1.; Re‑expression of wild‑type NF1 rescues mitotic timing defects and reduces DM1 sensitivity, confirming specificity.; NF1 directly binds microtubules and accelerates polymerization; in vitro, NF1 counteracts DM1‑induced polymerization block.; NF1‑deficient cells display impaired microtubule self‑repair, leading to increased DM1 binding sites and heightened cytotoxicity.; Clinical cohort analysis shows NF1‑mutated HER2‑positive breast cancer patients have significantly longer PFS on T‑DM1.

metadata.speaker: Luca Mazzarella
metadata.talk_title: NF1 as a microtubule‑repair factor and predictor of maytansinoid ADC efficacy in HER2‑positive breast cancer

text: Statistical considerations for early cancer detection test performance | Speaker: Bob Smith | MOA: Bob Smith explained that sensitivity and specificity for single-cancer early detection tests differ from multi-cancer tests, highlighted the concept of program sensitivity, and argued that MCEDs have lower aggregate sensitivity but broader public health impact, emphasizing the need for contextual interpretation of performance metrics. | Findings: Program sensitivity can equalize comparisons between frequent low-cost tests and less frequent high-cost tests.; Sensitivity and specificity can move together when test quality improves, contrary to the assumed inverse relationship.; MCED aggregate sensitivity is lower than single-cancer tests, but modeling suggests annual MCED screening could prevent 17% of cancer deaths.; Stage shift is a blunt endpoint; within-stage tumor size changes can drive survival benefits.; False positive rates for MCEDs are often mischaracterized; a 1% rate reflects the complement of PPV at biopsy.

metadata.speaker: Bob Smith
metadata.session_title: Contextual Challenges in Blood-Based Early Cancer Detection Tests
metadata.talk_title: Statistical considerations for early cancer detection test performance

text: Defining target condition and cancer signal origin in MCED tests | Speaker: Nima Visvade | MOA: Nima Visvade argued that the target condition for MCEDs should be defined by clinically actionable cancer signal origin (CSO), emphasizing biologic parity and diagnostic pathway grouping to improve workup efficiency and clinical utility. | Findings: Target condition for MCEDs is inseparable from cancer signal origin, which guides diagnostic pathways.; Methylation‑based MCEDs provide accurate CSO predictions that are clinically useful for directing workup.; Biologic families (e.g., HPV‑related tumors) may be more appropriate grouping than strict organ boundaries.; Pathway‑based grouping aligns workup burden with clinical benefit, allowing a single imaging study to evaluate multiple CSOs.; High CSO accuracy transforms MCEDs from vague screening signals to actionable diagnostic starting points.

metadata.speaker: Nima Visvade
metadata.session_title: Contextual Challenges in Blood-Based Early Cancer Detection Tests
metadata.talk_title: Defining target condition and cancer signal origin in MCED tests

text: Generalizability and implementation considerations for MCED and single‑cancer tests | Speaker: Asma Shukat | MOA: Asma Shukat highlighted how trial enrichment (age, stage, risk) inflates performance metrics of early detection tests and advocated for age‑sex adjustment, detailed subgroup reporting, and likelihood ratios to improve generalizability to real‑world populations. | Findings: Trial populations often enrich for older age, higher stage, or known cancers, leading to inflated sensitivity and PPV.; Healthy‑volunteer bias can produce lower prevalence than intended use, underestimating PPV.; Age and sex standardization to the US census modestly shifts sensitivity and specificity, as shown in the PREEMPT CRC cohort.; Granular reporting of performance by cancer type, stage, lesion size, and advanced precursor lesion subcategories is needed but limited by power.; Likelihood ratios and number‑needed‑to‑screen are valuable metrics for clinicians to assess post‑test probability.

metadata.speaker: Asma Shukat
metadata.session_title: Contextual Challenges in Blood-Based Early Cancer Detection Tests
metadata.talk_title: Generalizability and implementation considerations for MCED and single‑cancer tests

text: Consumer wearable data for functional monitoring and outcome prediction in cancer patients | Speaker: Charissa | Tumors: breast cancer, pancreatic cancer, colorectal cancer, solid tumor | MOA: The study demonstrates that continuous consumer‑wearable metrics (step count, peak gait cadence, activity fragmentation) can be reliably collected during active cancer treatment and are associated with clinical outcomes such as readmission, fall risk, and overall survival, providing prognostic information beyond clinician‑rated performance status. | Findings: Patients undergoing chemotherapy wore Fitbits ≥8 h/day on 70% of study days over 90 days, with no decline over time.; Older patients showed higher adherence than younger patients; non‑white participants had significantly lower adherence.; Higher inpatient step counts after cytoreductive surgery (≈1,250 steps/day) were associated with lower 60‑day readmission versus 500 steps/day in readmitted patients.; Peak gait cadence ≥100 steps/min predicted reduced fall risk in older cancer survivors and differentiated fallers in ROC analysis.; In a 2.5‑year follow‑up of 213 chemotherapy patients, peak gait cadence and activity fragmentation remained independent predictors of overall survival after adjusting for age, stage, cancer type, ECOG, and step count.

metadata.speaker: Charissa
metadata.talk_title: Consumer wearable data for functional monitoring and outcome prediction in cancer patients

text: Wearable sensors and AI for digital trials across disease domains | Speaker: Giorgio Aquile | MOA: By leveraging large‑scale passive wearable data (resting heart rate, activity, sleep) combined with AI algorithms, the presented digital trials demonstrate early detection of infectious disease, risk stratification for pre‑diabetes, and the feasibility of fully remote, multimodal clinical studies across diverse health conditions. | Findings: A wearable‑based algorithm achieved AUC 0.8 for early COVID‑19 detection in a 40,000‑person cohort.; In the Detect Ahead trial, delivering wearable‑generated alerts did not significantly increase testing adherence, highlighting behavioral barriers to action.; A multimodal classifier integrating wearable, CGM, EHR, saliva, and stool data distinguished normoglycemic from type 2 diabetic individuals with AUC 0.96.; The same classifier generated a continuous risk score that refined risk stratification among pre‑diabetic participants beyond HbA1c alone.; Remote digital trials enrolling up to 1,000 participants were executed without in‑person visits, demonstrating scalability of fully virtual study designs.

metadata.speaker: Giorgio Aquile
metadata.talk_title: Wearable sensors and AI for digital trials across disease domains

text: Integrating wearable sensor data and AI into oncology practice | Speaker: George Niava | Tumors: lung cancer, pancreatic cancer, breast cancer, prostate cancer | MOA: Wearable‑derived continuous physiologic streams (steps, heart rate, sleep) combined with AI models can augment traditional oncology assessments, improving prediction of adverse events, treatment toxicity, and health‑care utilization, while highlighting the need for patient adherence and health‑system integration. | Findings: Only <1% of Medicare cancer patients had billed remote patient monitoring codes, indicating poor system adoption.; AI‑driven coaching achieved a 5% body‑weight reduction in breast cancer patients, but overall adherence to wearable wear time declined over study duration.; Multimodal models integrating wearable, PRO, lab, and imaging data reached AUC 0.86 for predicting urgent care visits, outperforming EHR‑only models.; Physician‑patient performance‑status assessments show high variability; AI analysis of movement videos can provide more objective scores.; Patients receiving subcutaneous PD‑1 therapy at home showed higher compliance with vital‑sign uploads than with step‑count data, underscoring task‑specific adherence challenges.

metadata.speaker: George Niava
metadata.talk_title: Integrating wearable sensor data and AI into oncology practice

text: AI‑Guided Discovery and Targeting of Plexin B2 in Circulating Tumor Cell Clusters | Speaker: Fangjia Tong | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: AI‑driven ranking (R‑score) identified plexin B2 as a top adhesion molecule driving homotypic and heterotypic CTC cluster formation; neutralizing antibodies block plexin B2, reducing cluster size and number, decreasing lung metastasis in mice, and correlating with improved patient outcomes. | Findings: R‑score prioritized plexin B2 among 30 adhesion proteins as the top CTC‑cluster driver.; Genetic knockout of plexin B2 in 4T1 cells reduces lung micro‑metastases by ~70% (p<0.001).; Anti‑plexin B2 antibodies decrease both homotypic tumor‑tumor and heterotypic tumor‑myeloid clusters in vitro.; Single‑dose anti‑plexin B2 treatment in BALB/c mice cuts metastatic burden by 60% (p<0.01).; High plexin B2 expression in patient CTC clusters associates with worse distant metastasis‑free survival.

metadata.speaker: Fangjia Tong
metadata.talk_title: AI‑Guided Discovery and Targeting of Plexin B2 in Circulating Tumor Cell Clusters

text: SWALL‑1 Controls Epigenetic Methylation, Mitochondrial Metabolism, and Antitumor Immunity in IDH‑Mutant Gliomas | Speaker: Henry Chen | Tumors: glioma | MOA: SWELL1 forms the LRRC8A‑C VRAC complex that mediates passive export of the oncometabolite D‑2HG from IDH‑mutant glioma cells; loss of SWELL1 reduces extracellular D‑2HG, enhances cGAS‑STING activation, increases CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration, and suppresses tumor proliferation via hyper‑methylation of MYC/SOX2 pathways and impaired mitochondrial respiration. | Findings: SWELL1 knockdown decreases extracellular D‑2HG release by ~40% without affecting LDH release.; LRRC8C knockdown reduces D‑2HG release ~25%; LRRC8D knockdown increases release, indicating subunit specificity.; SWELL1‑KO IDH‑mut glioma xenografts show prolonged mouse survival (median 45 vs 30 days, p=0.004).; SWELL1 loss leads to increased microglial CD86⁺ activation and CD8⁺ T‑cell IFN‑γ⁺ frequency.; SWELL1‑KO cells accumulate intracellular D‑2HG (~2‑fold) and display increased H3K27me3 and DNA hyper‑methylation, down‑regulating MYC and SOX2.

metadata.speaker: Henry Chen
metadata.talk_title: SWALL‑1 Controls Epigenetic Methylation, Mitochondrial Metabolism, and Antitumor Immunity in IDH‑Mutant Gliomas

text: Lineage Plasticity Drives Antibody‑Drug Conjugate Resistance in Bladder Cancer | Speaker: Xiao Chenluo Lu | Tumors: bladder cancer | MOA: Lineage plasticity driven by ASCL1/NEUROD1 reprogramming suppresses NECTIN‑4 expression, rendering enfortumab vedotin ineffective; variant histology tumors up‑regulate alternative surface antigens such as DL3, offering new ADC targets for combination therapy. | Findings: ASCL1/NEUROD1 overexpression in HT1376 cells reduces NECTIN‑4 mRNA by 70% and abolishes EV‑mediated cytotoxicity.; Spatial transcriptomics shows NECTIN‑4 loss confined to neuroendocrine regions, while DL3 is up‑regulated there.; Patients with NECTIN‑4‑low variant histology have significantly shorter EV treatment duration.; Proposed combination of NECTIN‑4 ADC with DL3‑targeted ADC could address heterogeneous antigen expression.

metadata.speaker: Xiao Chenluo Lu
metadata.talk_title: Lineage Plasticity Drives Antibody‑Drug Conjugate Resistance in Bladder Cancer

text: eIF4A1 Inhibition Suppresses AML via Serine Biosynthesis Blockade | Speaker: Xiaoxu Zhang | Tumors: AML | MOA: Zoledronate inhibits eIF4A1, destabilizing YB‑1‑bound mRNAs such as PHGDH, leading to reduced serine biosynthesis, impaired oxidative phosphorylation, and AML cell death; combined with MCL1 inhibition yields synergistic cytotoxicity. | Findings: eIF4A1 is the most overexpressed translation initiation factor in AML vs normal hematopoietic cells.; eIF4A1 knockout prolongs survival in immunocompetent AML mouse model (median 60 vs 38 days, p=0.003).; Zoledronate kills AML cell lines with nanomolar IC50 while sparing normal CD34⁺ cells.; PHGDH down‑regulation mediates serine depletion; overexpression rescues growth inhibition.; CRISPR screen identifies YB‑1 and MCL1 as top sensitizers; zoledronate + MCL1 inhibitor shows >2‑fold synergy (CI<0.5).

metadata.speaker: Xiaoxu Zhang
metadata.talk_title: eIF4A1 Inhibition Suppresses AML via Serine Biosynthesis Blockade

text: Targeting Rho1/2 to Overcome ADC Resistance in Triple‑Negative Breast Cancer | Speaker: Emanuela Ghia | Tumors: triple‑negative breast cancer | MOA: Anti‑RHO1/2 antibodies bind surface oncogenic embryonic proteins re‑expressed in TNBC stem‑like cells, suppressing stemness signatures, NF‑κB signaling, and NRF2‑driven antioxidant response, thereby sensitizing cells to the redox‑modulating agent APR‑246. | Findings: RHO2+ sorted TNBC cells generate tumors at 5,000 cells; RHO2‑ cells fail to engraft.; Anti‑RHO2 treatment reduces NF‑κB p‑p65 and NQO1 levels in vitro.; Combination of anti‑RHO2 antibody with APR‑246 lowers APR‑246 IC50 by 2.5‑fold in TNBC cell lines.; In vivo, anti‑RHO2 alone modestly slows tumor growth; combined with APR‑246 yields significant tumor regression (p<0.01).

metadata.speaker: Emanuela Ghia
metadata.talk_title: Targeting Rho1/2 to Overcome ADC Resistance in Triple‑Negative Breast Cancer

text: Potentiating venetoclax response in AML with the NAMPT inhibitor OT-82 | Speaker: Michelle Haber | Tumors: AML | MOA: OT-82 inhibits NAMPT, reducing NAD biosynthesis and creating a metabolic vulnerability in venetoclax‑resistant AML cells; combined with venetoclax it restores apoptotic sensitivity and yields durable tumor regressions in diverse AML PDX models. | Findings: OT-82 showed the lowest LC50 among tested AML drugs across 10 adult AML samples, with a wide therapeutic window versus normal bone marrow cells.; In pediatric AML PDXs (PRR485, AML49), OT-82 alone extended event‑free survival, and the combination with venetoclax further improved survival without added benefit from azacitidine.; Across 16 heterogeneous AML PDXs, the venetoclax + OT‑82 combination produced the most robust and durable responses, achieving maintained complete remissions.; Response was observed irrespective of adverse genomic features (TP53, FLT3, KMT2A rearrangements), suggesting broad applicability.

metadata.speaker: Michelle Haber
metadata.talk_title: Potentiating venetoclax response in AML with the NAMPT inhibitor OT-82

text: Non‑canonical CAR T cell states associated with durable responses in multiple myeloma | Speaker: Kai Wu | Tumors: multiple myeloma | MOA: Single‑cell multi‑omics of BCMA CAR T therapy revealed that durable responders harbor proliferative, early‑memory CAR T cells and a unique ‘T persistor’ state marked by AP‑1 and NF‑κB activation, low exhaustion, and bone‑marrow residency, which correlates with sustained CAR T persistence and improved clinical outcomes. | Findings: Durable responders showed enrichment of proliferating and early‑memory CAR T cells early post‑infusion, whereas transient responders displayed higher CD8 exhaustion signatures.; A novel ‘T persistor’ CAR T state emerged at later time points in durable responders, characterized by high AP‑1, NF‑κB, cytokine (IFN‑γ, TNF‑α, IL‑2) expression and CXCR4/CD69 bone‑marrow residency markers.; Clonal tracking demonstrated that T persistor cells arise from multiple early CAR T states, including both CD4 and CD8 subsets.; Effective CAR T therapy reshaped the bone‑marrow microenvironment, reducing immunosuppressive monocyte signatures in durable responders.

metadata.speaker: Kai Wu
metadata.talk_title: Non‑canonical CAR T cell states associated with durable responses in multiple myeloma

text: KatTCIP molecular glue recruiting P300/CBP to BCL6 induces death in DLBCL | Speaker: Meredith Nix | Tumors: diffuse large B‑cell lymphoma | MOA: TCIP3 is a bivalent molecular glue that simultaneously binds the BCL6 BTB domain (via BI‑3812) and the P300/CBP bromodomain (via GNE‑781), inducing a cooperative ternary complex that recruits acetyltransferase activity to BCL6 loci, leading to localized histone and BCL6 acetylation, transcriptional activation of cell‑death genes, and rapid apoptosis of BCL6‑dependent DLBCL cells. | Findings: TCIP3 forms a cooperative ternary complex between BCL6 and P300/CBP, confirmed by ITC and X‑ray crystallography.; TCIP3 induces potent GFP reporter activation and apoptosis in high‑BCL6 DLBCL lines with an IC50 of 0.8 nM, outperforming BCL6 degraders.; ChIP‑seq shows selective recruitment of p300 and increased H3K27ac at BCL6 target sites without global acetylation loss.; In vivo, TCIP3 depletes germinal‑center B cells and drives near‑complete tumor regression in a DLBCL xenograft model with minimal toxicity.

metadata.speaker: Meredith Nix
metadata.talk_title: KatTCIP molecular glue recruiting P300/CBP to BCL6 induces death in DLBCL

text: FGFR1 inhibition remodels fibroblast‑derived TGF‑β niche to enhance CAR‑T efficacy in DLBCL | Speaker: Nicolas Dicieri | Tumors: diffuse large B‑cell lymphoma | MOA: FGFR1 inhibition in cancer‑associated fibroblasts suppresses TGF‑β production and induces MCP chemokine secretion, leading to recruitment of macrophages and enhanced infiltration of CAR‑T cells; the remodeled microenvironment synergizes with anti‑CD19 CAR‑T to eradicate resistant DLBCL in vivo. | Findings: FGFR1 inhibition reduced CAF‑derived TGF‑β and simultaneously increased CCL2/7/8 expression, driving macrophage recruitment.; Macrophage depletion partially reversed the anti‑lymphoma effect of FGFR1 inhibition, indicating a contributory role of macrophages.; Combination of FGFR1 inhibitor with anti‑CD19 CAR‑T markedly increased circulating CAR‑T cells and eliminated tumor burden in a resistant DLBCL PDX model.; FGFR1 inhibition did not impair normal hematopoiesis in treated mice, suggesting a therapeutic window.

metadata.speaker: Nicolas Dicieri
metadata.talk_title: FGFR1 inhibition remodels fibroblast‑derived TGF‑β niche to enhance CAR‑T efficacy in DLBCL

text: Condensate dynamics drive adaptive METTL3 inhibitor resistance | Speaker: Xujing Yang | Tumors: acute myeloid leukemia, pancreatic cancer, melanoma | MOA: METTL3 inhibition reduces m6A on oncogenic transcripts (MYC, BCL2) but induces adaptive up‑regulation and nuclear condensate formation of the m6A reader YTHDC1; gel‑like YTHDC1 condensates sequester residual m6A‑modified RNAs, restoring translation of survival genes and conferring resistance, which can be overcome by YTHDC1 inhibition or venetoclax co‑treatment. | Findings: CRISPR screens identified YTHDC1 as a top sensitizer to METTL3 inhibition; its loss synergizes with METTL3 inhibitors in AML and melanoma.; METTL3 inhibition enlarges YTHDC1 nuclear condensates, shifting them to a less liquid, gel‑like state correlated with resistance.; Overexpression of YTHDC1 or PABPN1 disrupts condensate dynamics and confers resistance; YTHDC1 inhibition restores sensitivity.; Combining a YTHDC1 inhibitor or venetoclax with METTL3 inhibition yields strong synergistic anti‑tumor effects with minimal impact on normal CD34+ cells.

metadata.speaker: Xujing Yang
metadata.talk_title: Condensate dynamics drive adaptive METTL3 inhibitor resistance

text: Lymphotoxin‑α induces TRAF2 degradation and necroptotic death in AML | Speaker: Jost | Tumors: acute myeloid leukemia | MOA: Recombinant lymphotoxin‑α engages TNFR1 on AML cells, leading to depletion of the pro‑survival adaptor TRAF2, which shifts TNFR1 signaling toward necroptotic complex formation and cell death, while sparing normal hematopoietic progenitors that retain higher TRAF2 levels. | Findings: Genetic deletion of LTα in FLT3‑ITD AML mice accelerates disease onset, indicating a tumor‑suppressive role for LTα.; Exogenous LTα induces rapid death of primary AML blasts, including high‑risk TP53‑mutated samples, and promotes differentiation (loss of CD34, gain of CD38).; LTα treatment eradicates leukemia in both syngeneic and immunodeficient PDX models without causing cytopenia or impairing normal hematopoiesis.; TRAF2 is markedly down‑regulated in AML patient samples across genetic subtypes, rendering leukemic cells uniquely sensitive to LTα‑mediated necroptosis.

metadata.speaker: Jost
metadata.talk_title: Lymphotoxin‑α induces TRAF2 degradation and necroptotic death in AML

text: Integrating multi-omics and novel modalities to map EGFR TKI resistance in NSCLC | Speaker: Daniel S.W. Tan | Tumors: NSCLC | MOA: Tan described how sequential EGFR TKIs select for on‑target (e.g., C797S) and off‑target alterations (MET amplification, lineage plasticity) and how multi‑omics (DNA, RNA, spatial transcriptomics, proteomics) can map these states. He showed that ctDNA persistence, MET amplification, and stromal TME signatures predict resistance, and that rational combinations (e.g., EGFR TKI + MET inhibitor, EGFR TKI + chemotherapy, anti‑CD47) can be matched to specific resistance phenotypes. | Findings: EGFR TKIs achieve high initial ORR (60‑80%) but 50‑60% of patients on frontline third‑gen inhibitors lack any detectable resistance mechanism by NGS.; On‑target resistance mutations (e.g., C797S) occur in 10‑25% of resistant biopsies, while MET amplification is found in 15‑20% and predicts response to MET inhibitors (4/9 partial responses).; Persistent EGFR ctDNA after TKI therapy identifies a high‑risk subgroup with median PFS 5.2 mo vs 9.8 mo (p<0.01).; Spatial transcriptomics revealed CD47 up‑regulation in on‑treatment lesions, suggesting a combinatorial anti‑CD47 strategy.; Stromal‑rich TME signatures (activated neutrophils, CAFs) correlate with 2‑year relapse rates of 48% vs 22% (p=0.004), defining a poor‑risk population for upfront combination trials.

metadata.speaker: Daniel S.W. Tan
metadata.talk_title: Integrating multi-omics and novel modalities to map EGFR TKI resistance in NSCLC

text: Eco-evolutionary lens for understanding the tumor microenvironment | Speaker: Ken Pienta | Tumors: pan-cancer | MOA: Pienta presented an eco‑evolutionary framework in which tumors are viewed as ecosystems that undergo niche construction, creating steep fitness gradients (hypoxia, acidosis, immune pruning) that accelerate clonal selection and drive convergent lethal phenotypes such as metastasis and therapy resistance. He emphasized that cytokine‑driven “cancer swamp gas” (e.g., IL‑6, TNF‑α, MMPs) from the microenvironment underlies systemic lethal effects. | Findings: Convergent evolution in cancer leads to two lethal phenotypes: metastasis and therapy resistance.; Ecological engineering by cancer cells (allogenic and autogenic) remodels the tumor microenvironment, accelerating clonal dominance (e.g., 73% reduction in barcode diversity in vivo vs. in vitro).; Steep fitness gradients from hypoxia, acidosis, and immune pruning create rapid clonal selection, observable across precancerous lesions to metastatic disease.; Cytokine overproduction (IL‑6, TNF‑α, MMPs) from stromal and immune cells constitutes a “miasma” that drives cachexia, thrombosis, and organ failure, accounting for mortality beyond tumor mass.; Integrating evolutionary ecology principles could enable new therapeutic timing and selective pressure strategies to disrupt the tumor ecosystem.

metadata.speaker: Ken Pienta
metadata.talk_title: Eco-evolutionary lens for understanding the tumor microenvironment

text: AI‑enabled virtual patient modeling and tumor microenvironment analysis | Speaker: Hoifung Poon | Tumors: pan-cancer | MOA: Poon described three AI‑derived capabilities—microscope, crystal ball, and wind tunnel—to decode tumor microenvironment complexity. He highlighted AI‑driven virtual trial simulation (TrialScope) that reproduces KEYNOTE‑10 outcomes, a pathology foundation model (GigaPath) that predicts EGFR mutation from H&E across 41 cancer types, a modality translator (GigaTime) that synthesizes spatial proteomics from routine slides, and a large‑scale virtual patient model (Curiosity) trained on 300 M patients and 100 B medical events that matches supervised baselines on 78 clinical tasks. | Findings: TrialScope AI can simulate a virtual trial that reproduces the KEYNOTE‑10 pembrolizumab results, demonstrating feasibility of real‑world data‑driven trial emulation.; GigaPath transformer model scales to gigapixel whole‑slide images and learns a pan‑cancer signature across 41 tumor types, enabling EGFR mutation prediction directly from H&E with high accuracy.; GigaTime translates cheap H&E pathology into virtual multiplex immunofluorescence (MIF), generating over 300 000 virtual MIF maps from 14 000 patients and revealing spatial proteomic patterns linked to outcomes.; Curiosity, a 1‑billion‑parameter foundation model trained on 300 M patient journeys (100 B events), matches or exceeds 78 supervised clinical task models without task‑specific fine‑tuning.; AI can automate extraction of eligibility windows from unstructured clinical notes, reducing abstraction cost from hours to seconds and enabling 24/7 trial feasibility monitoring.

metadata.speaker: Hoifung Poon
metadata.talk_title: AI‑enabled virtual patient modeling and tumor microenvironment analysis

text: Single-cell clonal analysis of normal skin and cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma evolution | Speaker: Hunter Shane | Tumors: skin | MOA: Shane's work combines single‑cell clonal expansion and bulk sequencing to show that early loss‑of‑function NOTCH and TP53 mutations persist in normal‑appearing keratinocytes without driving overt proliferation, but they create a mutator phenotype that accelerates UV‑induced DNA damage, leading to high‑burden clones that can give rise to actinic keratosis and, when additional driver events (TERT promoter, CDKN2A loss, MAPK activation) occur, to invasive cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. | Findings: Normal‑appearing keratinocytes can harbor up to eight pathogenic driver mutations (NOTCH1/2, TP53, FAT1, PBRM1) yet remain histologically benign.; Pathogenic‑mutant keratinocytes exhibit a 40‑fold higher mutation burden than neighboring wild‑type cells, indicating a mutator phenotype.; Only ~10% of actinic keratosis lesions adjacent to SCC are genetically related; most represent collision tumors.; Progression to SCC is associated with acquisition of TERT promoter mutations, CDKN2A loss, and MAPK pathway activation (KRAS hotspot).; In a 45,000‑case national cohort, loss‑of‑function mutations in SWI/SNF (ARID2), MAPK activation, and TGF‑β pathway alterations predict metastatic outcome.

metadata.speaker: Hunter Shane
metadata.talk_title: Single-cell clonal analysis of normal skin and cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma evolution

text: Spatial and 3D atlases of breast and prostate tumor evolution and bone metastasis | Speaker: Li Ding | Tumors: breast cancer, prostate cancer | MOA: Ding's team integrates 2D and 3D spatial transcriptomics (Visium, Xenium, Codex) with computational pipelines (MORF, Calico ST, Mushroom) to map spatial subclones and their microenvironmental interactions during pre‑cancer to cancer transition in breast and prostate, and to dissect tumor‑osteoclast/osteoblast crosstalk in bone metastases, revealing FGFR2/ACKR3‑mediated homing, AR‑driven programs, and distinct immune niches that may guide combination anti‑angiogenic and macrophage‑targeted therapies. | Findings: Spatial subclones can be resolved in 2D and 3D; LDHB mutation maps to a distinct subclone in breast tissue.; Bone metastases show tumor‑specific upregulation of ACKR3 (CXCL12 receptor) in breast and AR in prostate, suggesting organ‑specific homing mechanisms.; Prostate bone metastases display increased osteoblast signatures (BMP signaling, SPP1‑CD44), while breast bone metastases show osteoclast activation (PDGF‑β, TGF‑β‑ITGB1).; Both metastasis types exhibit heightened fibroblast (MYCAF) and vascular (VEGF‑A/KDR, FGFR2, JAK1/Notch3‑4) signaling, indicating potential combinatorial anti‑angiogenic targets.; Immune profiling reveals macrophage enrichment toward tumor cores and reduced T‑cell infiltration; breast bone mets have IFN‑γ⁺ macrophages, prostate mets have SPP1⁺ immunosuppressive macrophages.

metadata.speaker: Li Ding
metadata.talk_title: Spatial and 3D atlases of breast and prostate tumor evolution and bone metastasis

text: Multi‑omic atlases of multiple myeloma precursors and early immunotherapy interventions | Speaker: Irene Ghobrial | Tumors: multiple myeloma | MOA: Ghobrial's group integrates whole‑genome, bulk RNA, and single‑cell BCR‑RNA profiling of MGUS, smoldering, and overt multiple myeloma to derive a genomic MM‑like score and a transcriptional MST score that predict progression; spatial proteomics (IMC) of decalcified bone marrow reveals cellular neighborhoods where tumor‑immune interactions (e.g., granzyme B CD8 TEMs, SPP1‑positive macrophages) correlate with outcomes and CAR‑T or bispecific therapy response, supporting early immunotherapy interception. | Findings: A 14‑gene MM‑like genomic score distinguishes MGUS‑like from myeloma‑like precursor cases.; Six transcriptional signatures, especially beta‑2M, predict progression independent of DNA alterations.; The MST transcriptional score accurately stratifies risk across MGUS, smoldering, and overt MM cohorts.; Spatial IMC identifies tumor‑immune cellular neighborhoods that predict CAR‑T efficacy and cytokine‑release syndrome risk.; Early bispecific antibody (teclistamab) treatment in high‑risk smoldering myeloma yields 100% MRD‑negative responses with favorable safety.

metadata.speaker: Irene Ghobrial
metadata.talk_title: Multi‑omic atlases of multiple myeloma precursors and early immunotherapy interventions

text: Fundamentals of Deep Learning for Digital Pathology | Speaker: Alex Pearson | MOA: Pearson described the architecture of convolutional neural networks and vision transformers applied to whole slide H&E images, and introduced foundation models that learn a language-like embedding from 1.5 million slides (120,000 patients). These embeddings can be fine‑tuned for downstream tasks such as mutation prediction, tumor detection, and segmentation, while highlighting bias sources (e.g., ancestry prediction from TCGA site effects) and mitigation strategies (color normalization, batch correction, synthetic image explainability). | Findings: Trained a pathology foundation model on 1.5 million H&E slides from 120 k patients, generating a reduced‑dimensional feature vector for each image.; Demonstrated that foundation models can achieve high accuracy on tasks such as ancestry prediction, but identified spurious site‑related biases in TCGA data.; Showed that synthetic GAN‑generated images can be used to train pathologists to recognize molecular patterns (e.g., BRAF‑like vs RAS‑like) improving human prediction performance.; Presented an FDA‑cleared breakthrough‑designated AI tool for Trop2‑ADC companion diagnostics, illustrating clinical translation of digital pathology AI.

metadata.speaker: Alex Pearson
metadata.talk_title: Fundamentals of Deep Learning for Digital Pathology

text: Implementation of AI Models for Pathology: Prospective Validation and Clinical Deployment | Speaker: Gabriele Cambiamalla | Tumors: lung adenocarcinoma | MOA: Cambiamalla presented a prospectively validated AI model that infers EGFR mutation status directly from H&E whole‑slide images, allowing the model to act as a non‑exhaustive computational biomarker; by setting high‑sensitivity or high‑specificity thresholds the workflow can safely triage patients away from rapid PCR testing, reducing unnecessary assays by 43% without loss of diagnostic performance. | Findings: Developed an end‑to‑end EGFR prediction pipeline using a foundation model fine‑tuned on >80,000 H&E slides from MSK Impact.; Internal and external validation showed no performance drop compared with the original research cohort.; Prospective silent trial demonstrated a 43% reduction in rapid EGFR PCR tests while maintaining equivalent PPV and NPV to the gold‑standard workflow.; Independent third‑party validation confirmed robust performance across institutions.; Proposed scaling the silent‑trial framework to multi‑center deployments for additional lung cancer biomarkers and low‑resource settings.

metadata.speaker: Gabriele Cambiamalla
metadata.talk_title: Implementation of AI Models for Pathology: Prospective Validation and Clinical Deployment

text: AI‑Enabled Spatial Multi‑Omics: From 2D Tissue Maps to 3D Biomarkers | Speaker: Lihua Wang | Tumors: pan-cancer | MOA: Wang described deep‑learning pipelines that align H&E images with spatial transcriptomics and proteomics at single‑cell resolution, register serial sections into 3D tumor maps, and extract spatial niches (e.g., CAF subtypes, macrophage phenotypes, vascular structures, TIS) which can be quantified and linked to clinical outcomes such as immunotherapy response. | Findings: Generated multimodal 3D maps of human tumors comprising >2 million cells, revealing spatial gradients of CXCL13 and CXCL5 signals.; Identified four distinct CAF spatial organizations that correlate with patient survival.; Discovered two macrophage phenotypes (TIM‑2⁺ immunosuppressive vs CXCL9⁺ immune‑active) with divergent spatial distributions across tumor cores and peripheries.; Developed Omni‑TIS framework that quantifies mature vs immature tumor‑infiltrating stromal niches and predicts response to checkpoint blockade in renal cell carcinoma.; Demonstrated that 3D reconstruction of TIS structures changes perceived volume and may improve biomarker robustness compared with 2D counts.

metadata.speaker: Lihua Wang
metadata.talk_title: AI‑Enabled Spatial Multi‑Omics: From 2D Tissue Maps to 3D Biomarkers

text: Transcription factor subtypes and DLL3 bispecific T‑cell engager tarlatamab resistance mechanisms in small cell lung cancer | Speaker: Dr. Osar | Tumors: small cell lung cancer | MOA: Tarlatamab is a DLL3‑CD3 bispecific T‑cell engager that induces tumor cell killing in DLL3‑high ASCL1 SCLC. Resistance emerges via a transcriptional switch to a NEUROD1 subtype, leading to DLL3 down‑regulation and impaired T‑cell activation, with NEUROD1 overexpression causally driving early resistance in mouse models. | Findings: Tarlatamab achieved a 35‑40% ORR and 7‑9 month DOR in second‑line SCLC (n=46).; ASCL1 transcriptional subtype correlated with response; 80% of ASCL1 patients responded.; NEUROD1 up‑regulation and DLL3 loss were observed at acquired resistance in both patients and mouse models.; CRISPR‑mediated DLL3 knockout abrogated tarlatamab binding and killing in syngeneic models.; NEUROD1 overexpression in tumor cells caused early resistance to tarlatamab in vivo.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Osar
metadata.talk_title: Transcription factor subtypes and DLL3 bispecific T‑cell engager tarlatamab resistance mechanisms in small cell lung cancer

text: Antibody‑drug conjugates targeting DLL3, CES6, B7H3 and other surface antigens in small cell and high‑grade neuroendocrine cancers | Speaker: Dr. Lauren Byers | Tumors: small cell lung cancer, high‑grade neuroendocrine cancers | MOA: ABBV‑706 is an ADC linking a cytotoxic Top1 payload to antibodies against surface antigens DLL3, CES6 or B7H3, delivering DNA‑damage–inducing payloads selectively to SCLC and high‑grade neuroendocrine tumors, with SLFN11 expression enhancing payload efficacy. | Findings: CES6‑targeted ADC (ABBV‑706) produced a ~60% ORR in relapsed SCLC and high‑grade neuroendocrine cancers (n=127).; Responses were rapid, often within one week of treatment initiation.; SLFN11 positivity correlated with higher response rates, suggesting a predictive biomarker for ADC payload sensitivity.; ADC activity observed across diverse neuroendocrine sites (small cell bladder, cervix, Merkel cell carcinoma).; Preclinical PDX models (≈400) recapitulated clinical efficacy and supported biomarker development.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Lauren Byers
metadata.talk_title: Antibody‑drug conjugates targeting DLL3, CES6, B7H3 and other surface antigens in small cell and high‑grade neuroendocrine cancers

text: Neuronal activity drives proliferation and plasticity of small cell lung cancer brain metastases and primary lung tumors | Speaker: Dr. Hamsa Venkatesh | Tumors: small cell lung cancer | MOA: Neuronal activity, via glutamatergic and especially depolarizing GABAergic signaling, induces depolarization of SCLC cells, promoting proliferation, invasion, and a transcriptional shift toward a neuroD1‑like phenotype; direct tumor depolarization recapitulates these effects, and anti‑seizure drug levetiracetam suppresses tumor growth in brain metastasis models. | Findings: Optogenetic activation of premotor cortical circuits increased SCLC brain tumor proliferation and invasion in mice.; SCLC cells receive depolarizing GABAergic currents due to high intracellular chloride, driving growth.; Co‑culture with GABAergic neurons boosted proliferation of all tested SCLC lines; effect blocked by gabazine or tetrodotoxin.; Direct optogenetic depolarization of SCLC cells in vivo accelerated tumor burden, confirming depolarization as the driver.; Vagotomy reduced lung tumor initiation and extended survival in a GEM SCLC model.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Hamsa Venkatesh
metadata.talk_title: Neuronal activity drives proliferation and plasticity of small cell lung cancer brain metastases and primary lung tumors

text: Quantitative fluorescence assay for HER2 and Trop-2 to guide ADC selection | Speaker: David Reim | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: Reim presented a CLIA‑validated quantitative fluorescence assay that converts HER2 and Trop‑2 protein levels on breast cancer slides into attomoles per mm², enabling continuous, low‑CV measurement. Retrospective analysis showed that higher HER2 abundance predicts longer time to next treatment with trastuzumab‑deruxtecan, while unexpectedly high Trop‑2 levels correlate with poorer response, supporting a selective biomarker approach for ADC choice. | Findings: Quantitative fluorescence assay (Troplex) achieves inter‑ and intra‑assay CV <10% and is NYS‑DOH approved.; Only ~6% of breast cancer biopsies are true HER2 negatives by the quantitative assay, versus higher rates by conventional IHC.; 71% of IHC HER2‑zero cases have measurable HER2 by the quantitative assay, indicating under‑detection by standard IHC.; Patients with HER2 levels above the median have a median time to next treatment of 12.8 months versus 7.5 months for those below median.; High Trop‑2 expression is associated with shorter time to next treatment and poorer response to T‑DXd, suggesting a negative predictive role.

metadata.speaker: David Reim
metadata.talk_title: Quantitative fluorescence assay for HER2 and Trop-2 to guide ADC selection

text: Computational pathology and multimodal AI for ADC response prediction | Speaker: Maria Bakolopoulou | Tumors: breast cancer, lung cancer | MOA: Bakolopoulou described an unsupervised deep‑learning pipeline that segments IHC or H&E slides, extracts patch representations, clusters them, and links cluster composition to ADC response, revealing that regions enriched for fibroblasts/immune cells correlate with resistance, while tumor‑cell dense regions associate with sensitivity; she also introduced counterfactual‑augmented attention mechanisms to improve interpretability of supervised models. | Findings: In the DAISY trial, an unsupervised cluster enriched for fibroblast and immune cells was linked to HER2‑ADC resistance.; Applying the same pipeline to ICARUS breast and lung trials identified clusters whose cell density and HER2/DAB intensity predicted response.; A counterfactual‑augmented attention model improved region‑level interpretability without sacrificing predictive performance on TCGA lung and breast datasets.; Integrating H&E‑derived features with IHC data enhanced response prediction compared to using either modality alone.; Foundation models pretrained on large H&E datasets can generate useful representations for ADC response prediction, even with limited trial data.

metadata.speaker: Maria Bakolopoulou
metadata.talk_title: Computational pathology and multimodal AI for ADC response prediction

text: Revisiting the neoantigen approach to cancer immunotherapy | Speaker: Yardena Samuels | Tumors: melanoma, colorectal cancer, breast cancer | MOA: Samuels demonstrated that inhibiting translation fidelity via TYW2 knockout induces programmed ribosomal frameshifts, generating abundant out‑of‑frame peptides that are presented on MHC and elicit strong CD8‑T‑cell responses; chemotherapy can further boost neoantigen presentation, and recurrent driver‑derived neoantigens can be identified through HLA‑matched population databases for vaccine or TCR‑based therapies. | Findings: Chemotherapy (lymphodepleting) synergizes with KRAS G12V‑specific TCRs by increasing neoantigen presentation.; TYW2 knockout in melanoma cells produces a programmed increase in out‑of‑frame peptides, leading to CD8‑dependent tumor rejection in mice.; Ribosome profiling revealed phenylalanine‑codon pausing and both –1 and +1 frameshifts in TYW2‑KO cells.; Identified >350,000 patients per year with recurrently presented neoantigens using a data‑driven HLA‑matched pipeline.; Bacterial‑derived peptides and translation‑infidelity peptides expand the antigenic repertoire beyond somatic mutations.

metadata.speaker: Yardena Samuels
metadata.talk_title: Revisiting the neoantigen approach to cancer immunotherapy

text: Pharmacologic inhibition of PMS2 to induce mismatch repair deficiency | Speaker: Alberto | Tumors: colorectal cancer, breast cancer | MOA: The small‑molecule 1867 covalently binds cysteine‑73 in the ATPase domain of PMS2, selectively disabling its mismatch‑repair activity; treated cells acquire MSI‑high status, high mutational burden, and become sensitive to PD‑1 blockade, recapitulating the phenotype of genetic PMS2 loss without cytotoxicity. | Findings: 1867 selectively engages PMS2 cysteine‑73 with >99% specificity among >20,000 cysteines.; Pharmacologic PMS2 inhibition phenocopies genetic knockout, abolishing 6‑guanine‑induced DNA nicks.; Dose‑dependent induction of MSI‑high and mutational signatures (SBS21, SBS15) in vitro.; 1867‑treated tumor cells reject in immunocompetent mice when combined with anti‑PD‑1, but not in immunodeficient hosts.; Combination of 1867 with FOLFOXIRI accelerates MSI conversion and can induce tumor regression without checkpoint blockade.

metadata.speaker: Alberto
metadata.talk_title: Pharmacologic inhibition of PMS2 to induce mismatch repair deficiency

text: Chemically inducing mismatch repair deficiency to sensitize tumors to PD‑1 blockade | Speaker: Luis Diaz | Tumors: colorectal cancer, non-small cell lung cancer, melanoma, head‑neck cancer, renal cell carcinoma | MOA: Temozolomide induces DNA methylation and MSH2 promoter silencing, while cisplatin adds DNA cross‑links; together they rapidly down‑regulate MSH2, generate a mismatch‑repair‑deficient mutational signature rich in frameshift indels, elevate TMB and MSI, and render tumors highly sensitive to PD‑1 blockade in preclinical models and a subset of patients. | Findings: Temozolomide alone raises TMB but not MSI; cisplatin alone modestly increases frameshifts.; The combination yields a dramatic TMB gain (~125 mut/Mb) and high MSI scores with predominantly subclonal frameshift mutations.; MSH2 promoter methylation drives loss of MSH2 expression after 4–8 weeks of combo treatment.; Combo‑treated cells implanted into immunocompetent mice show delayed growth and complete regression with anti‑PD‑1, unlike single‑agent controls.; In a clinical trial, patients who acquired both high TMB and MSI signatures after therapy had longer survival, though the primary endpoint was not met.

metadata.speaker: Luis Diaz
metadata.talk_title: Chemically inducing mismatch repair deficiency to sensitize tumors to PD‑1 blockade

text: Elucidating Broad Cell-Cell Interactions via 3D Super Cell Graphs for Prostate Cancer Risk Stratification | Speaker: Yujie Zhao | Tumors: prostate cancer | MOA: The Skell 3D framework groups phenotypically similar, spatially adjacent cells into super cells, constructs super cell graphs, and extracts interaction features that predict five-year biochemical recurrence in prostate cancer with higher AUC and reduced computational cost compared to standard cell-level graphs. | Findings: Skell 3D achieved AUC 0.8 for five-year BCR prediction in a 76-patient cohort, outperforming 3D morphology alone (AUC 0.68).; Integration of Skell 3D features increased C-index from 0.64 to 0.61 in survival analysis.; Super cell graphs reduced computation time by ~25-fold relative to standard cell-level graphs.; Ablation studies identified optimal super cell neighbor threshold (15 µm) and interaction distance (20 µm).; Super cell approach showed robustness to simulated Gaussian noise compared with cell-level graphs.

metadata.speaker: Yujie Zhao
metadata.talk_title: Elucidating Broad Cell-Cell Interactions via 3D Super Cell Graphs for Prostate Cancer Risk Stratification

text: AI-Driven Spatial Analysis of 1,100 Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma Patients' H&E Slides Uncovers Three Tumor Subtypes with Distinct Microenvironments and Survival | Speaker: Sumana Biswas | Tumors: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma | MOA: A deep learning model predicts spatial transcriptomic gene expression from H&E slides, enabling clustering of tumors into immune-activated and immune-exhausted spatiotypes; these spatiotypes robustly stratify survival and predict therapy response across multiple head and neck cancer cohorts. | Findings: Model accurately predicts spatial expression of ~2,800 genes from H&E images, capturing cancer hallmark pathways.; Clustering of predicted spatial transcriptomics identifies two spatiotypes (immune-activated vs immune-exhausted) with distinct survival outcomes.; Immune-exhausted spatiotype shows worse overall, progression-free, and disease-specific survival across TCGA, Hancock, and Taiwan cohorts.; Spatial cluster-based model predicts treatment response with AUC 0.74 and odds ratio ~5 in a 94-patient immunotherapy cohort.; Model performance correlates with number of genes robustly predicted; external validation confirms reproducibility.

metadata.speaker: Sumana Biswas
metadata.talk_title: AI-Driven Spatial Analysis of 1,100 Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma Patients' H&E Slides Uncovers Three Tumor Subtypes with Distinct Microenvironments and Survival
tumor_types: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma

text: Pan-Cancer Prediction of Response to Immune Checkpoint Blockade from Histopathology | Speaker: Dan Thai Hoang | Tumors: pan-cancer, melanoma, NSCLC, head and neck, colorectal, others | MOA: A composite tumor hotness signature (TAHMAC) derived from immune score, inflammation score, and TMB in melanoma is applied pan‑cancer to classify hot vs cold tumors; Path2Omic deep learning infers gene expression from H&E, enabling hotness and ICB response prediction directly from pathology with performance comparable to measured transcriptomics. | Findings: TAHMAC signature achieved AUC 0.98 for hot/cold classification across 11 diverse cancer cohorts despite being derived from melanoma.; TAHMAC outperformed 26 existing ICB response signatures with AUC 0.74 on 22 transcriptomic cohorts.; Path2Omic accurately inferred ~6,000 genes per cancer type, with TAM genes among the most reliably predicted.; Using inferred expression, tumor hotness prediction reached mean AUC 0.96 across eight TCGA cancers.; ICB response prediction from inferred expression achieved AUC 0.72 on nine external cohorts, surpassing direct slide‑to‑response models.

metadata.speaker: Dan Thai Hoang
metadata.talk_title: Pan-Cancer Prediction of Response to Immune Checkpoint Blockade from Histopathology

text: A Large Scale Multi-Target Deep Learning Model for Virtual Genomic Profiling in Colorectal Cancer | Speaker: Eric Bergstrom | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: A transformer-based deep learning model processes tiled H&E images to predict whole-exome sequencing mutations (including MSI, BRAF, KRAS) and infer molecular recurrence risk, demonstrating that morphological features can capture pathway-level alterations and correlate with ctDNA-defined outcomes. | Findings: Single-task models achieved AUC >0.7 for >80% of 463 genes in a 45,000-patient cohort.; Multitask training improved performance for 95% of genes, with ~40% gaining ≥5% AUC.; MSI prediction reached AUC 0.98, BRAF V600E AUC 0.90+, and KRAS AUC 0.85+.; Patients with model-predicted BRAF V600E but wild-type sequencing showed similar poor survival, suggesting pathway-level phenotype capture.; H&E‑based risk model stratified MRD‑negative patients into high/low risk, adding prognostic value beyond ctDNA alone.

metadata.speaker: Eric Bergstrom
metadata.talk_title: A Large Scale Multi-Target Deep Learning Model for Virtual Genomic Profiling in Colorectal Cancer

text: Peritumoral Collagen Microarchitecture is Differentially Prognostic of Biochemical Recurrence Across Populations in Prostate Cancer | Speaker: Ajay Rajaraman Subramanian | Tumors: prostate cancer | MOA: A deep learning collagen segmentation model extracts structural, spatial, and textural features from peritumoral regions of prostatectomy slides; African American‑specific collagen signatures strongly predict biochemical recurrence, whereas European American signatures do not, highlighting population-specific tumor microenvironment differences. | Findings: Nine collagen features derived from African American training set stratified recurrence risk in the whole test set (HR 4.09, p=0.02).; The same AA features also stratified risk within the AA test subset but failed in the EA test subset.; European American-derived features did not achieve significant prognostic power in any cohort.; Only one feature (Haralick entropy variability) overlapped between AA and EA signatures, indicating distinct collagen architectures.; Texture entropy and GLCM entropy were significantly higher in AA tumors compared to EA.

metadata.speaker: Ajay Rajaraman Subramanian
metadata.talk_title: Peritumoral Collagen Microarchitecture is Differentially Prognostic of Biochemical Recurrence Across Populations in Prostate Cancer

text: PathIO: Deep Learning Pathomics Framework for Personalized Immunotherapy Selection and Outcome Prediction in Metastatic NSCLC | Speaker: Rukmini Bandopadhyay | Tumors: non-small cell lung cancer | MOA: PathIO uses a pathologist-annotated tissue habitat map from H&E slides, aggregates multi-scale ROI embeddings, and trains a random survival forest to generate a risk score that independently predicts overall and progression-free survival in metastatic NSCLC, correlating with immune cell infiltration and guiding monotherapy versus combination immunotherapy selection. | Findings: PathIO risk score significantly stratifies OS and PFS across four independent metastatic NSCLC cohorts.; Risk score remains an independent predictor after multivariate adjustment for clinical factors.; Low-risk patients exhibit higher immune cell density and lower tumor cell density on multiplex IF.; In PD-L1‑high patients, low-risk scores predict benefit from ICI monotherapy, whereas high-risk scores suggest added chemotherapy benefit.; Combining PathIO with CT‑based radiomics and clinical variables improves prognostic performance over any single modality.

metadata.speaker: Rukmini Bandopadhyay
metadata.talk_title: PathIO: Deep Learning Pathomics Framework for Personalized Immunotherapy Selection and Outcome Prediction in Metastatic NSCLC

text: From Persistence to Relapse: Evolution of Drug Resistance in Lung Cancer | Speaker: Aaron Hata | Tumors: non-small cell lung cancer | MOA: Hata demonstrated that drug‑tolerant persister cells in EGFR‑ or ALK‑mutant NSCLC up‑regulate APOBEC3A, leading to increased APOBEC signature mutagenesis, DNA damage, and acquisition of resistance mutations such as EGFR T790M, C797S, or ALK E1210K. Knock‑down of APOBEC3A suppresses mutagenesis and prevents emergence of resistant clones in vitro and in xenografts, implicating therapy‑induced APOBEC activity as a driver of multi‑step resistance evolution. | Findings: Drug‑tolerant persister NSCLC cells up‑regulate APOBEC3A within 1‑2 days of targeted therapy exposure.; APOBEC3A induction correlates with increased APOBEC signature (SBS2/13) mutations and structural variations in persister clones.; APOBEC3A knock‑down eliminates therapy‑induced APOBEC mutations, reduces double‑strand DNA breaks, and abolishes outgrowth of resistant persister populations in vitro and in vivo.; Patient tumor sequencing reveals enrichment of APOBEC signatures in resistant lesions that were absent pre‑treatment, supporting clinical relevance.

metadata.speaker: Aaron Hata
metadata.session_title: The Next Frontier in Minimal Residual Disease: Solid Tumors
metadata.talk_title: From Persistence to Relapse: Evolution of Drug Resistance in Lung Cancer

text: Therapeutic Strategies to Address Cancer Cell Heterogeneity and Plasticity | Speaker: Chris Marine | Tumors: melanoma | MOA: Marine introduced a morphology‑based “Origami” platform that quantifies cell surface area and volume to map melanoma cell states. He showed that the trametinib + palbociclib (TP) combination drives a uniform adaptive trajectory toward high‑volume, lysosome‑rich cells; these become vulnerable to nilotinib‑induced ferroptosis. Parallel high‑surface cells can be sensitized by ER‑Golgi inhibitors (e.g., brefeldin A). The quadruple TP + nilotinib + brefeldin A (TPNB) regimen eradicates heterogeneous persister populations in vitro and yields curative responses in mouse models, also enhancing anti‑PD‑1 efficacy via immunogenic cell death. | Findings: Morphometric profiling (cell surface vs volume) distinguishes four melanoma transcriptional states without omics.; TP (trametinib + palbociclib) induces a uniform high‑volume, lysosome‑rich persister phenotype across 20 cell lines.; High‑volume persisters are selectively killed by nilotinib, a ferroptosis‑sensitizing agent; effect is rescued by ferroptosis inhibitors.; High‑surface persisters are sensitized by ER‑Golgi inhibitors (e.g., brefeldin A), which reduce surface area and enhance TP efficacy.; The quadruple combination TP + nilotinib + brefeldin A (TPNB) eliminates persisters in vitro and produces >1‑year disease control, with curative outcomes in some mouse models.

metadata.speaker: Chris Marine
metadata.session_title: The Next Frontier in Minimal Residual Disease: Solid Tumors
metadata.talk_title: Therapeutic Strategies to Address Cancer Cell Heterogeneity and Plasticity

text: The Hidden Lives of Cancer Cells: Somatic Evolution, Cellular Plasticity, and the Detection of Residual Disease | Speaker: Dan Landau | Tumors: glioblastoma, lung cancer, pan-cancer | MOA: Landau presented a phylogenetic framework that reconstructs high‑resolution tumor trees from single‑cell methylome or whole‑genome data, enabling measurement of heritability versus plasticity of cell states. By annotating leaves with transcriptomic phenotypes, he showed that stem‑like, astrocytic, and mesenchymal states in glioblastoma are heritable, while transition probabilities reveal lineage‑specific intermediates. Parallelly, he described whole‑genome ctDNA analysis using AI‑enhanced error suppression and ultra‑deep sequencing to quantify tumor burden (parts‑per‑million) and detect mutational signatures (APOBEC, tobacco) without tumor‑informed panels, providing early MRD detection and treatment monitoring. | Findings: Methylation‑derived epimutations enable reconstruction of patient‑specific phylogenies from a single tumor sample.; Stem‑like, astrocytic, and mesenchymal GBM states are heritable across cell divisions, as shown by high Moran's I values.; Transition probability analysis reveals a required astrocytic intermediate for stem‑to‑mesenchymal conversion.; In IDH‑mutant gliomas, differentiation follows a unidirectional hierarchy; IDH‑wt GBM shows bidirectional plasticity with dedifferentiation.; Smart PTA scaling to 3,500 cells allows tracing normal esophageal clones back to conception, revealing long‑lived TP53‑mutant clones without pathology.

metadata.speaker: Dan Landau
metadata.session_title: The Next Frontier in Minimal Residual Disease: Solid Tumors
metadata.talk_title: The Hidden Lives of Cancer Cells: Somatic Evolution, Cellular Plasticity, and the Detection of Residual Disease

text: MRD Directed Treatment Strategies in Colorectal Cancer | Speaker: Jeannie Tee | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: Tee reviewed how postoperative ctDNA serves as a highly sensitive MRD biomarker in colorectal cancer, stratifying patients into high‑risk (ctDNA‑positive) and low‑risk (ctDNA‑negative) groups. ctDNA‑guided trials (DYNAMIC, DYNAMIC‑3) demonstrated that chemotherapy can be safely omitted in ctDNA‑negative stage II patients without compromising 5‑yr RFS, and that ctDNA‑positive patients exhibit heterogeneous outcomes based on molecular burden. Persistent ctDNA after adjuvant therapy predicts poor RFS, highlighting a need for escalated or novel therapies, while ctDNA clearance may serve as an early surrogate endpoint for regulatory approval. | Findings: Post‑operative ctDNA positivity predicts near‑certain recurrence across all CRC stages.; In DYNAMIC (stage II), ctDNA‑guided management halved chemotherapy use (28%→15%) with non‑inferior 5‑yr RFS (88.3% vs 87.2%).; In DYNAMIC‑3 (stage III), ctDNA‑negative de‑escalation reduced oxaliplatin use (89%→35%) but missed the non‑inferiority margin (−2.8% difference, CI crossed −7.5%).; Higher ctDNA molecular burden (>0.38 mut/mL) identifies a subgroup with 3‑yr RFS of only 23% versus 77% for low burden.; Persistent ctDNA after adjuvant therapy correlates with 3‑yr RFS of 14% versus 79% for cleared patients, suggesting ctDNA clearance as a surrogate efficacy marker.

metadata.speaker: Jeannie Tee
metadata.session_title: The Next Frontier in Minimal Residual Disease: Solid Tumors
metadata.talk_title: MRD Directed Treatment Strategies in Colorectal Cancer

text: Lymphoma Transformers: Spatial Total RNA Sequencing of FFPE Tissue | Speaker: Rong Fang | Tumors: lymphoma | MOA: Fang's group developed a spatial deterministic barcoding (DIBER+) workflow that adds poly‑tails to fragmented RNA in FFPE tissue, enabling unbiased total‑RNA sequencing (coding and non‑coding species) at near single‑cell resolution. The method captures spatial gene expression, chromatin accessibility, histone marks, SNVs, and metabolic activity (via stimulated Raman imaging), allowing reconstruction of clonal phylogeny, detection of microRNA signatures (e.g., miR‑21, miR‑155) and metabolic lipid droplet patterns that correlate with lymphoma transformation. | Findings: Developed a poly‑tailing strategy that yields higher sensitivity on fragmented FFPE RNA than fresh‑frozen spatial transcriptomics.; Achieved near‑single‑cell resolution spatial maps of coding and >1,800 microRNAs in lymphoma tissue.; Detected de‑novo SNVs and copy‑number alterations from spatial total‑RNA data, enabling clonal phylogeny reconstruction within a single FFPE section.; Identified metabolic lipid‑droplet redistribution (nuclear/perinuclear) associated with transformation to diffuse large B‑cell lymphoma.; Found miR‑155 up‑regulation linked to PI3K/AKT pathway activation, suggesting a potential biomarker for PI3K‑inhibitor response.

metadata.speaker: Rong Fang
metadata.talk_title: Lymphoma Transformers: Spatial Total RNA Sequencing of FFPE Tissue

text: Spatial Multi‑omics Dissects Immune and Stromal Heterogeneity in Angioimmunoblastic T‑cell Lymphoma | Speaker: Mamiko Sakata‑Yanagimoto | Tumors: angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma | MOA: Sakata‑Yanagimoto’s team combined single‑cell RNA‑seq, Xenium spatial transcriptomics, and multiplex digital spatial profiling to map 10 blood‑endothelial cell (BEC) subclusters in AITL, revealing a novel capillary‑activated high‑endothelial venule (cHEV1) that colocalizes with follicular dendritic cells and exhausted TIM‑3⁺ T cells, forming a cHEV‑FDC niche that predicts poor therapeutic response and overall survival. | Findings: Identified 10 BEC subclusters, with chHEV2 and TIP cells significantly expanded in AITL versus normal lymph nodes.; cHEV1 (capillary‑activated HEV) localizes closest to high‑tumor‑density regions and forms a cHEV‑FDC niche enriched for exhausted TIM‑3⁺ T cells.; Peri‑vascular index of exhausted T cells around cHEV1 is higher in non‑responders to therapy, linking the niche to treatment resistance.; High expression of cHEV and HEV signatures in bulk RNA‑seq cohorts correlates with worse overall survival.; Integrin‑related genes are up‑regulated in AITL‑associated BECs, suggesting a role in niche formation.

metadata.speaker: Mamiko Sakata‑Yanagimoto
metadata.talk_title: Spatial Multi‑omics Dissects Immune and Stromal Heterogeneity in Angioimmunoblastic T‑cell Lymphoma

text: MMEJ deficiency in Ewing sarcoma creates synthetic lethality with HR inhibition | Speaker: Alan D'Andrea | Tumors: Ewing sarcoma | MOA: The EWS-FLI1 fusion protein in Ewing sarcoma disrupts splicing of POLQ exon 25 via loss of the EWSR1 splicing complex, leading to POLQ deficiency and MMEJ impairment. These MMEJ-deficient cells become hyper‑dependent on homologous recombination, rendering them exquisitely sensitive to HR inhibition by CDK12 inhibitors. | Findings: EWS-FLI1 expression causes exon 25 skipping of POLQ mRNA, abolishing POLQ protein in Ewing sarcoma.; Knockout of EWSR1 or its splicing partners (FKBP1, KHSRP) reproduces POLQ loss and MMEJ deficiency.; Restoration of POLQ rescues MMEJ activity, confirming causality.; Ewing sarcoma cell lines with POLQ deficiency are hypersensitive to CDK12 inhibition, a synthetic lethal interaction.; Exon 25 skipping of POLQ is observed in 100% (36/36) of evaluated patient tumors, providing a potential biomarker.

metadata.speaker: Alan D'Andrea
metadata.talk_title: MMEJ deficiency in Ewing sarcoma creates synthetic lethality with HR inhibition

text: Replication gap biology defines sensitivity to PARP and FEN1 inhibition | Speaker: Sharon Kantor | MOA: BRCA1 loss leads to accumulation of 53BP1 on nascent DNA, mis‑positioning FEN1 and causing persistent replication gaps. PARP1 also positions FEN1; loss of both BRCA1 and PARP1 traps FEN1 at the fork, abolishing its activity and creating synthetic lethality. 53BP1 loss removes both pathways, rendering cells resistant to PARP and FEN1 inhibitors. | Findings: BRCA1 deficiency causes 53BP1 accumulation on nascent DNA and delayed FEN1 recruitment.; PARP1 loss mimics the BRCA1 phenotype, indicating parallel pathways for FEN1 positioning.; Combined BRCA1 loss and PARP inhibition prevent FEN1 from reaching the replisome, explaining PARP inhibitor sensitivity.; 53BP1 knockout eliminates both PARP‑ and BRCA1‑dependent FEN1 positioning, conferring resistance to both PARP and FEN1 inhibitors.; Replication gap signal measured by nick translation predicts sensitivity to PARP/FEN1 inhibition across multiple models.

metadata.speaker: Sharon Kantor
metadata.talk_title: Replication gap biology defines sensitivity to PARP and FEN1 inhibition

text: Clinical landscape of PARP inhibition and combination strategies across tumor types | Speaker: Pamela Munster | Tumors: prostate cancer, breast cancer, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, endometrial cancer, non-small cell lung cancer, gastrointestinal tumors, neuroendocrine tumors, biliary cancer, bladder cancer, liver cancer, gastric cancer | MOA: PARP inhibitors exploit synthetic lethality in BRCA1/2‑deficient tumors by trapping PARP on DNA and preventing repair of single‑strand breaks, while combination with immune checkpoint blockade leverages increased mutational load and DNA‑damage‑induced immunogenicity. Emerging data show that ATM or CHEK2 mutations confer variable benefit, and ATR or CDK12 inhibition provides an alternative synthetic lethal strategy in ATM‑ or ARID1A‑deficient cancers. | Findings: PARP inhibitor plus enzalutamide improves overall survival in metastatic prostate cancer (HR 0.8).; Patients with HRD‑positive prostate cancer derive a larger OS benefit (HR 0.5) compared with HR‑proficient patients.; BRCA2‑mutated prostate cancer shows the greatest PFS and OS improvements; BRCA1 benefit is modest.; ATM‑mutated prostate cancer shows limited or no OS benefit from PARP inhibition alone.; Combination of niraparib with pembrolizumab yields a 24% ORR in platinum‑resistant ovarian cancer, including HRD‑negative patients.

metadata.speaker: Pamela Munster
metadata.talk_title: Clinical landscape of PARP inhibition and combination strategies across tumor types

text: Oral endocrine therapy adherence in hormone receptor‑positive breast cancer | Speaker: Katherine Reeder‑Hayes | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: Long‑term oral endocrine therapy reduces recurrence and mortality in HR+ breast cancer, but suboptimal adherence—especially among younger Black women—diminishes these benefits, as shown by dose‑response relationships between medication possession ratio and survival outcomes. | Findings: Only ~60% of women remained ≥80% adherent to endocrine therapy over five years in an integrated health system.; Black women under 65 showed lower initiation and lower medication possession ratios compared with White women, especially after chemotherapy.; Distinct adherence trajectories (steady decline vs early decline with recovery) were identified, suggesting heterogeneous patient experiences.; Non‑adherent patients (<95% MPR) had a two‑fold higher risk of relapse after adjusting for prognostic factors.; GETSET trial (N=1,165) accrued and demonstrated high engagement with motivational‑interviewing arms (92% attended ≥1 session).

metadata.speaker: Katherine Reeder‑Hayes
metadata.talk_title: Oral endocrine therapy adherence in hormone receptor‑positive breast cancer

text: Improving adherence to oral therapies in colorectal cancer | Speaker: Dr. Meyris | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: Oral agents such as regorafenib, encorafenib, and capecitabine provide modest survival gains in colorectal cancer but are limited by toxicity; tailoring dose intensity via patient‑reported outcomes, pharmacogenomics (DPYD), and rapid ctDNA profiling improves tolerability and enables earlier use of effective oral targeted combos, thereby enhancing adherence and outcomes. | Findings: Regorafenib 160 mg daily improved OS by 1.4 months versus placebo but caused frequent grade 3+ toxicities.; Personalized dose‑escalation of regorafenib reduced toxicity without compromising survival.; Aligning Lonserf dosing with bevacizumab reduced neutropenia and growth‑factor use while preserving OS.; Frontline encorafenib + cetuximab (BREAKWATER) doubled OS compared with standard chemotherapy in BRAF‑mutated mCRC.; Rapid (<5 days) ctDNA testing at registration enables same‑day identification of BRAF, KRAS, HER2, and DPYD alterations to guide oral therapy selection.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Meyris
metadata.talk_title: Improving adherence to oral therapies in colorectal cancer

text: Adherence to oral 6‑mercaptopurine in pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia | Speaker: Dr. Bocchi | Tumors: acute lymphoblastic leukemia | MOA: Consistent oral 6‑MP dosing maintains therapeutic leukocyte 6‑TGN levels; sub‑optimal adherence reduces systemic exposure, leading to a two‑fold increase in relapse risk in pediatric ALL, especially among adolescents and lower‑income families. | Findings: Median adherence was 95% initially but fell to ~90% over six months.; Adolescents (<12 y vs ≥12 y) and low‑income households showed significantly lower adherence.; Patients with adherence <95% had a two‑fold higher relapse risk after adjusting for prognostic factors.; Forgets were the predominant self‑reported barrier (≈80% of missed doses).; A multicomponent intervention (education + web‑based scheduling + text reminders + caregiver supervision) improved adherence by 4% overall and 9.5% among baseline non‑adherers.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Bocchi
metadata.talk_title: Adherence to oral 6‑mercaptopurine in pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia

text: Five‑year update on FDA Project Optimus implementation and case examples | Speaker: Murat Shaw | Tumors: non‑small cell lung cancer | MOA: Project Optimus reforms oncology dose selection by shifting from maximum tolerated dose to a totality‑of‑evidence approach that integrates PK/PD, safety, early efficacy, and dose‑response data, using randomized dose comparisons to identify optimized doses before approval. | Findings: Case examples in advanced lung cancer (ADC, bispecific T‑cell engager, small‑molecule kinase inhibitors) all selected lower doses as the FDA‑labeled recommended dose after randomized dose evaluations.; Randomized dose assessments were feasible even for accelerated‑approval programs, improving safety and benefit‑risk for patients.

metadata.speaker: Murat Shaw
metadata.talk_title: Five‑year update on FDA Project Optimus implementation and case examples

text: Randomization backfill and expansion cohorts to enhance Phase 1 trials | Speaker: Alexia Iossifidis | MOA: Adaptive Bayesian model‑based designs with randomization, backfill, and expansion cohorts enable more efficient dose‑finding by providing early efficacy and safety signals across multiple dose levels and disease subgroups. | Findings: Randomized dose expansion can augment data at lower dose levels without increasing overall sample size, potentially saving 3–6 patients per trial.; Probabilistic stopping rules based on posterior dose‑toxicity probabilities improve decision‑making compared with traditional 3+3 designs.

metadata.speaker: Alexia Iossifidis
metadata.talk_title: Randomization backfill and expansion cohorts to enhance Phase 1 trials

text: Incorporating patient‑reported outcomes into dose‑finding trials | Speaker: Xing Li | MOA: PRO‑CTCAE data are integrated with traditional CTCAE grading to define tolerability thresholds (e.g., 35% severe patient‑reported toxicity) and inform dose assignment using a PRO‑augmented continual reassessment method (TIDE‑CRM). | Findings: A PRO‑based dose‑selection rule (e.g., 35% severe PRO toxicity) can lead to lower recommended doses than clinician‑only DLT thresholds.; Software tools (University of Virginia PRO‑CRM and a custom web app) enable real‑time dose assignment using combined PRO and CTCAE data.

metadata.speaker: Xing Li
metadata.talk_title: Incorporating patient‑reported outcomes into dose‑finding trials

text: Industry perspective on five‑year experience with Project Optimus | Speaker: Unnamed Pfizer speaker | MOA: Industry implementation of Project Optimus emphasizes early dose optimization using adaptive designs, exposure‑response modeling, and post‑marketing studies to refine doses, aiming to reduce PMR/PMC burdens and improve long‑term tolerability. | Findings: Historical examples (e.g., gemtuzumab ozogamicin, cabazitaxel, ceritinib, sotorasib) illustrate that lower doses can achieve comparable efficacy with better safety, often after post‑marketing studies.; Project Optimus has spurred increased use of Bayesian adaptive designs, PK/PD integration, and randomized dose comparisons in early development.

metadata.speaker: Unnamed Pfizer speaker
metadata.talk_title: Industry perspective on five‑year experience with Project Optimus
