text: Epidemiology, risk factors, and therapeutic considerations in early‑onset colorectal cancer | Speaker: Kathy Yang | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: Yang highlighted the rising incidence of early‑onset colorectal cancer, the lack of distinct molecular signatures, and discussed how anatomic location influences treatment sequencing, dose intensification, and radiation decisions, emphasizing the need for fertility, psychosocial support, and research into microbiome, ctDNA‑guided intensification, and lifestyle interventions. | Findings: Early‑onset CRC incidence is rising ~3% annually, projected 159,000 new cases in 2026 with 16% occurring before age 50.; Mortality is projected at 56,000 in 2026, making early‑onset CRC a leading cause of cancer death in <50‑year-olds.; No unique somatic mutation profile distinguishes early‑onset from average‑onset CRC across four large datasets.; Sexual dysfunction affects 58% of male and 36% of female early‑onset CRC survivors; pain (31%) and anxiety/depression (70%) are also common.; Microbiome signatures (e.g., SBS88) are enriched in patients <40 y and associate with APC mutations, suggesting a potential biomarker for future studies.

metadata.speaker: Kathy Yang
metadata.talk_title: Epidemiology, risk factors, and therapeutic considerations in early‑onset colorectal cancer

text: Precision medicine framework for pediatric and young adult survivorship | Speaker: Goali Mustafi | MOA: Mustafi described how germline variants (e.g., CBR3 GG) modulate anthracycline metabolism, increasing cardiomyopathy risk, and how epigenetic age acceleration links treatment exposure to multisystem late effects, proposing precision survivorship using genetic, epigenetic, and lifestyle data to guide preventive interventions. | Findings: Anthracycline cardiotoxicity shows a dose‑response; risk escalates >100 mg/m², with CBR3 GG carriers experiencing toxicity at lower doses.; Retinoic acid receptor gamma variants up‑regulate TOP2B, heightening anthracycline susceptibility.; SULT4A1 GG genotype confers marked cardiotoxicity risk at standard anthracycline doses.; Epigenetic age acceleration is significantly higher in survivors and predicts cardiometabolic disease, frailty, and mortality.; Survivors have a >2‑fold higher diabetes incidence; abdominal radiation dose‑dependently damages pancreatic β‑cells, especially in African ancestry with alkylator exposure.

metadata.speaker: Goali Mustafi
metadata.talk_title: Precision medicine framework for pediatric and young adult survivorship

text: Institutional scale genomic profiling and basket trial strategy for young‑onset and rare cancers | Speaker: Speaker (Sloan Kettering) | Tumors: pan-cancer | MOA: The speaker described MSK Impact's large‑scale DNA/RNA profiling enabling pan‑cancer identification of actionable alterations (e.g., HER2 amplification, NTRK fusions) and the deployment of basket trials (neratinib, trastuzumab‑deruxtecan) to match rare‑tumor patients with targeted therapies, illustrating variable efficacy across lineages due to mutation type and co‑mutations. | Findings: MSK Impact has sequenced >109,000 tumors (162,000 samples), including >10,000 patients ≤40 y.; HER2‑amplified acral melanoma responded dramatically to trastuzumab‑deruxtecan, achieving a durable complete response.; Neratinib basket trial showed ~50% ORR in HER2‑mutant breast cancer but no responses in HER2‑mutant bladder cancer, highlighting lineage‑specific drug sensitivity.; RNA‑seq identified high HER2 expression in a lung cancer patient who achieved a complete response to trastuzumab‑deruxtecan, supporting RNA‑based enrollment criteria.; Somatic mosaicism (e.g., ERCC2, ATRX) was detected in young patients with multiple primary tumors, underscoring the need for comprehensive genomic profiling.

metadata.speaker: Speaker (Sloan Kettering)
metadata.talk_title: Institutional scale genomic profiling and basket trial strategy for young‑onset and rare cancers

text: Birth cohort analysis of early-onset cancer incidence across multiple tumor types | Speaker: Hyuna Sung | Tumors: colorectal cancer, breast cancer, thyroid cancer, pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor, lung cancer, cervical cancer | MOA: Using age‑period‑cohort modeling of national cancer registry data, the speaker demonstrated generational shifts in incidence, showing that cohorts born after 1955 have ~50% higher risk of colorectal cancer and similar increases for ER‑positive breast and endometrial cancers, while other cancers show period effects; disparities by education and geography were highlighted. | Findings: Over 9,000 people under age 50 are diagnosed with cancer worldwide each day, with >3,000 deaths.; People born in 1990 have ~1.5‑fold higher incidence of small intestinal, thyroid, kidney, and pancreatic cancers compared with those born in 1955.; Cohort rate ratio for colorectal cancer indicates a ~50% higher lifetime risk for those born in the 1980s versus the 1950s.; Early‑onset colorectal cancer mortality is higher among men with lower education, with the gap widening over 30 years.; In high‑income countries, early‑onset cancer rates rise while older‑adult rates fall; in Latin America and Asia, rates rise in both age groups.

metadata.speaker: Hyuna Sung
metadata.talk_title: Birth cohort analysis of early-onset cancer incidence across multiple tumor types

text: Metabolic dysfunction and early‑onset colorectal cancer: epidemiology to prevention | Speaker: Andrew Chan | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: Large prospective cohorts (NHS1, NHS2, HPFS) were leveraged to link obesity, early‑life adiposity, ultra‑processed food intake, and hyperinsulinemia to increased incidence of early‑onset colorectal adenomas and cancer, and a single‑arm tirzepatide trial is underway to test reversal of metabolic risk. | Findings: Mid‑life obesity (BMI ≥30) confers a 2‑fold higher risk of early‑onset colorectal cancer compared with non‑obese individuals.; BMI at age 18 in the overweight range is associated with a 1.6‑fold increased risk of early‑onset colorectal cancer.; Maternal weight gain >14 kg during pregnancy is linked to a ~2‑fold higher colorectal cancer risk in offspring.; Highest quintile of ultra‑processed food intake is associated with a 1.5‑fold higher incidence of colorectal adenoma.; Predicted hyperinsulinemia (C‑peptide‑based lifestyle index) shows a 1.3‑fold increased early‑onset adenoma risk, especially in later birth cohorts.

metadata.speaker: Andrew Chan
metadata.talk_title: Metabolic dysfunction and early‑onset colorectal cancer: epidemiology to prevention

text: Early‑life mutagenesis by colibactin‑producing bacteria drives early‑onset colorectal cancer | Speaker: Ludmil Alexandrov | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: Whole‑genome sequencing of 1,000 colorectal cancers revealed enrichment of colibactin‑associated signatures (SBS88, ID18) in early‑onset cases; phylogenetic timing shows these mutations arise within the first five years of life, often generating early driver events such as APC mutations, implicating early‑life exposure to pks+ bacteria as a causal factor. | Findings: Colibactin signatures (SBS88/ID18) are present in ~50% of patients <40 y versus ~17% of patients >70 y.; Early‑onset tumors show a three‑fold enrichment of colibactin signatures compared with late‑onset tumors.; Phylogenetic analysis of normal crypts indicates colibactin exposure occurs within the first 0‑5 years of life.; In >25% of colibactin‑positive early‑onset tumors, the APC driver mutation bears the colibactin signature.; pks colonization is not required to be detectable at tumor sampling, suggesting a past transient exposure.

metadata.speaker: Ludmil Alexandrov
metadata.talk_title: Early‑life mutagenesis by colibactin‑producing bacteria drives early‑onset colorectal cancer

text: Postpartum breast cancer: involution biology and liver metastasis risk | Speaker: Pepper Shedden | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: Weaning‑induced mammary gland involution creates a wound‑healing, immunosuppressive microenvironment that promotes tumor cell shedding and metastasis; concurrent liver involution generates a pre‑metastatic niche that preferentially supports colonization of ER‑positive tumor cells, explaining the high liver metastasis rate in postpartum breast cancer. | Findings: Women diagnosed with breast cancer within 5 y postpartum have a 2‑3‑fold worse overall survival than nulliparous peers, independent of ER status.; Postpartum tumors show a distinct gene expression signature matching mouse mammary involution (immune suppression, fibroblast activation, ECM deposition).; Postpartum breast cancers are enriched for liver metastases (≈30% of metastatic sites) compared with nulliparous cases.; Weaning‑induced liver involution in mice creates a fibroblast‑rich, immunosuppressive niche that enhances tumor cell engraftment after portal vein injection.; Human liver metastases from postpartum patients often display replacement growth, integrating into existing hepatic architecture without inducing new angiogenesis.

metadata.speaker: Pepper Shedden
metadata.talk_title: Postpartum breast cancer: involution biology and liver metastasis risk

text: Bridging Science and Market Access in Pediatric Oncology | Speaker: Sam Blackman | Tumors: pan-cancer | MOA: Blackman presented a macro‑level analysis of pediatric oncology drug development, comparing the 6‑8% overall success rate of drug candidates to the 6‑8% completion rate of the Camino pilgrimage, and highlighted recent acceleration in FDA approvals driven by incentives, while emphasizing the need for faster trial activation and better market‑access pathways for agents such as the DRD2 antagonist dordivaprone in diffuse midline glioma. | Findings: Pediatric oncology drug development success mirrors the 6‑8% completion rate of the Camino pilgrimage.; Exponential growth in FDA approvals over the past decade, with 8‑9 agents approved per year and 10‑14 new indications/label expansions annually.; Dordivaprone (ONC201) received FDA approval for progressive diffuse midline glioma in patients >1 year, based on a pooled analysis of 376 patients showing a 22% response rate.; Only two pediatric‑only EMA approvals and five FDA approvals were recorded for the 2025 cohort, underscoring persistent regulatory gaps.

metadata.speaker: Sam Blackman
metadata.session_title: El Camino de la Pediatria: Finding Our Way Through the Chasm of Pediatric Oncology Drug Development
metadata.talk_title: Bridging Science and Market Access in Pediatric Oncology

text: ADC Landscape and Emerging Small‑Molecule Opportunities in Pediatric Oncology | Speaker: Beth Fox | Tumors: solid tumor, hematologic malignancy | MOA: Fox outlined the current ADC pipeline for children, highlighting successful CD30‑targeted brentuximab vedotin, the limited pediatric activity of folate‑receptor‑α ADCs (e.g., SUTRO‑002 achieving 30% CRs in a small AML cohort), and the challenges of HER2‑directed ADCs in osteosarcoma where low antigen expression limited efficacy, while also introducing emerging targets such as STEAP2 and B7‑H3 for future pediatric ADC development. | Findings: Only 2 FDA pediatric‑only approvals (EMA 2, FDA 5) despite 712 registered ADC trials worldwide.; For solid‑tumor ADCs, no actively accruing pediatric trials were identified as of April 2024.; SUTRO‑002 treated 10 children with infant AML; 3 achieved complete responses, demonstrating feasibility of pediatric ADCs.; Trastuzumab deruxtecan screened 50 osteosarcoma patients, 9 enrolled; 1 DLT and 1 prolonged stable disease observed, insufficient to proceed to stage 2.; Emerging targets STEAP2 and B7‑H3 are being prioritized for future pediatric ADC programs.

metadata.speaker: Beth Fox
metadata.session_title: El Camino de la Pediatria: Finding Our Way Through the Chasm of Pediatric Oncology Drug Development
metadata.talk_title: ADC Landscape and Emerging Small‑Molecule Opportunities in Pediatric Oncology

text: Precision Immunotherapy: CAR T Cells and Bispecific Antibodies in Pediatric Cancer | Speaker: Ted Leach | Tumors: B‑cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, AML, neuroblastoma, diffuse midline glioma, osteosarcoma, solid tumor | MOA: Leach reviewed the rapid clinical impact of CD19‑directed bispecific blinatumomab and CAR‑T (tisagenlecleucel) in pediatric B‑ALL, achieving up to 96% disease‑free survival when moved to frontline, and discussed next‑generation CAR‑T strategies (humanized, dual‑target CD19/CD22, armored constructs) and bispecifics (DLL3‑targeted tarlatamab) aimed at overcoming antigen escape and extending efficacy to solid tumors such as neuroblastoma and diffuse midline glioma. | Findings: Blinatumomab achieved 27/70 CRs in relapsed/refractory pediatric ALL and improved DFS/OS in the randomized ALL 1331 trial.; Frontline blinatumomab (ALL 1731) raised 5‑year DFS to 96% versus 88% with chemotherapy alone.; Tisagenlecleucel produced an 81% remission rate and ~60% 3‑year OS in heavily pre‑treated pediatric B‑ALL.; Humanized CD19 CAR‑T showed 98% ORR in CAR‑naïve patients, suggesting reduced immunogenicity.; CD22‑CAR trials report 70‑75% ORR, supporting dual‑target strategies to prevent CD19 loss.

metadata.speaker: Ted Leach
metadata.session_title: El Camino de la Pediatria: Finding Our Way Through the Chasm of Pediatric Oncology Drug Development
metadata.talk_title: Precision Immunotherapy: CAR T Cells and Bispecific Antibodies in Pediatric Cancer

text: Signaling-to-chromatin pathways and histone phosphorylation in lymphoma | Speaker: Steven Josefowicz | Tumors: DLBCL, lymphoma | MOA: Signal‑induced phosphorylation of histone H3 at serine 28 creates a transient domain that ejects the PRC2 complex, abolishing its allosteric activation and chromatin condensation activity, thereby converting repressive H3K27me3 domains into permissive transcriptional states in germinal‑center B cells and lymphoma. | Findings: Serine 28 phosphorylation spreads across several hundred kilobase domains in stimulated macrophages and GC B cells, whereas serine 31 phosphorylation is confined to transcription units.; In ABC DLBCL, H3S28ph is constitutively high and overlaps with PRC2‑mediated H3K27me3 at the MYC locus, defining a ‘methyl‑phos switch’.; Biophysical assays show that H3S28ph‑containing nucleosome arrays are poor substrates for EZH2 and resist PRC2‑driven chromatin condensation.; Ex vivo GC B‑cell stimulation reveals progressive loss of H3K27me3 within H3S28ph domains, accompanied by increased chromatin interactivity and H3K36me2 gain.; Similar histone phosphorylation patterns are observed in T cells (TBET locus) and NK cells (IL15RA), and are constitutive in MYD88/CD79B mutant lymphoma PDX models.

metadata.speaker: Steven Josefowicz
metadata.talk_title: Signaling-to-chromatin pathways and histone phosphorylation in lymphoma

text: ELOVL1‑mediated lipid metabolism as a dependency in NRAS‑mutant IDH‑mutant AML | Speaker: Ross Levine | Tumors: AML | MOA: ELOVL1 catalyzes very‑long‑chain fatty‑acid elongation, feeding sphingolipid/ceramide synthesis that sustains lipid‑raft integrity; in NRAS‑mutant IDH‑mutant AML, loss of ELOVL1 disrupts lipid rafts, attenuates NRAS‑driven MAPK signaling, and selectively impairs leukemia cell viability. | Findings: CRISPR screens of epigenetic and metabolic libraries identified ELOVL1 as a selective dependency in Tet/IDH mutant AML cells.; ELOVL1 knock‑out depletes NRAS‑mutant AML cells in vitro and in vivo (bone marrow and peripheral blood) but not WT or RAS‑WT AML.; Pharmacologic inhibition of ELOVL1 with a Vertex compound reproduces genetic dependency, causing selective depletion of triple‑mutant cells.; Catalytic‑dead ELOVL1 fails to rescue the phenotype, confirming requirement for enzymatic activity.; Disruption of sphingolipid biosynthesis (SPTLC1, KDSR) phenocopies ELOVL1 loss, whereas peroxisomal fatty‑acid pathways do not.

metadata.speaker: Ross Levine
metadata.talk_title: ELOVL1‑mediated lipid metabolism as a dependency in NRAS‑mutant IDH‑mutant AML

text: Epigenetic priming to enhance T‑cell directed therapies in lymphoma | Speaker: Jennifer Amengual | Tumors: lymphoma | MOA: Epigenetic agents (HAT activator YF2, HDAC3 inhibitor, EZH2 inhibitor, DNMT inhibitor) remodel chromatin to up‑regulate antigen‑presentation genes (MHC‑I/II, CD20) and reverse exhaustion markers, thereby priming lymphoma cells for enhanced recognition and killing by checkpoint blockade, CAR‑T cells, and bispecific antibodies. | Findings: YF2 increases HLA‑A/B/C and antigen‑processing gene expression, boosting MHC‑I/II surface levels in lymphoma cell lines and mouse B cells.; Combination of YF2 with anti‑PD‑L1 reduces tumor growth and prolongs survival in A20‑bearing mice, with increased tumor MHC‑I and decreased PD‑1 on infiltrating T cells.; HDAC3 inhibition plus PD‑L1 blockade yields 80% CR in primary mediastinal large B‑cell lymphoma and 57–71% CR in Hodgkin lymphoma, with durable responses.; Tazemetostat priming enhances CAR‑T cell infiltration, synapse formation, and cytokine production, achieving 100% ORR and 77% CR in a 13‑patient lymphoma cohort.; Belinostat + tazemetostat restores CD20 (including epitope‑specific variants) on bispecific‑resistant lymphoma cells, increases MHC expression, and drives T‑cell mediated killing in 3‑D spheroid models.

metadata.speaker: Jennifer Amengual
metadata.talk_title: Epigenetic priming to enhance T‑cell directed therapies in lymphoma

text: Detecting and Modeling Genetic Epistasis in Cancer Using Conditional Selection | Speaker: Jaime Aranzo | Tumors: pan-cancer, low-grade glioma, endometrial cancer, colorectal cancer | MOA: Aranzo presented a statistical framework that uses synonymous mutations to build a neutral null model of mutation, compares expected vs observed non‑synonymous counts to estimate driver selection, and then quantifies conditional selection (epistasis) by stratifying tumors on a split gene and re‑estimating selection for a query gene, implemented in the R package cosalliance. | Findings: Positive and negative epistasis are pervasive, with 25‑50% of driver mutations affected by positive epistasis across cancer types.; Epistasis networks are modular: genes within a module show synergistic interactions, while modules antagonize each other.; Module‑based mutational profiles predict patient survival better than individual gene mutations.; Early mutations in a module can forecast the eventual molecular subtype of a tumor.; Asymmetric epistatic relationships reveal logical ordering of mutations, e.g., TP53 enhances the effect of RB1 in glioblastoma but not vice versa.

metadata.speaker: Jaime Aranzo
metadata.talk_title: Detecting and Modeling Genetic Epistasis in Cancer Using Conditional Selection

text: Quantifying Epistasis and Evolutionary Trajectories in Cancer | Speaker: Jorge Alfaro-Murillo | Tumors: colorectal adenocarcinoma | MOA: Alfaro-Murillo described a continuous‑time Markov chain model that estimates substitution rates for all possible mutational pathways among a set of genes, fits these rates to observed genotype frequencies, and separates mutation from selection using neutral mutation rate estimates (e.g., NDS, SigMutCel) to derive selection coefficients and epistatic interactions. | Findings: The model can infer four substitution rates for any gene pair, capturing order‑dependent effects.; In colorectal cancer, KRAS and BRAF show strong antagonistic epistasis, while APC and KRAS display weak or non‑significant interaction.; Selection coefficients derived after correcting for mutation rates reveal that many apparent co‑occurrences are driven by high mutation rates rather than true epistasis.; Statistical tests (likelihood ratio) can formally assess the presence of epistasis and compare epistatic effects across populations.

metadata.speaker: Jorge Alfaro-Murillo
metadata.talk_title: Quantifying Epistasis and Evolutionary Trajectories in Cancer

text: Tobacco Smoking and Somatic Selective Epistasis in Lung Adenocarcinoma | Speaker: Jeff | Tumors: lung adenocarcinoma | MOA: Jeff showed that smoking alters both mutation rates and selection coefficients of key lung adenocarcinoma drivers; after deconvolution, KRAS, KEAP1, STK11 and SDK11 have higher selection in ever smokers, while EGFR, PI3K and SMAD4 are stronger drivers in never smokers, and complex gene‑by‑gene‑by‑environment epistatic interactions reshape evolutionary trajectories. | Findings: Smoking increases mutation rates genome‑wide but the magnitude varies by gene (e.g., ALK, GNAS show especially high rates).; After correcting for mutation rates, KRAS selection is significantly higher in ever smokers, while EGFR selection is negligible in smokers.; Pairwise epistasis is common in ever smokers; many driver mutations (e.g., KRAS, KEAP1) antagonize early genes like TP53, indicating early clonal emergence.; Higher‑order interactions (G×G×E) were identified, e.g., KEAP1 selection strongest in smokers without EGFR mutation, weaker in EGFR‑mutant smokers.; Clinical implications: EGFR TKIs achieve higher response rates in never smokers; co‑mutations (e.g., KRAS, KEAP1) predict poorer outcomes in EGFR‑mutant disease.

metadata.speaker: Jeff
metadata.talk_title: Tobacco Smoking and Somatic Selective Epistasis in Lung Adenocarcinoma

text: Foundation model of the tumor genome for drug response prediction and evolution analysis | Speaker: Trey Ideker | Tumors: pan-cancer | MOA: Ideker presented a self‑supervised foundation model (MutationProjector) that learns embeddings of tumor genomes by masking gene alterations and predicting them using graph‑attention networks informed by protein‑protein, TF‑binding, and synthetic‑lethal networks. The low‑dimensional embeddings capture tumor type and combinatorial mutation patterns, which can be used as features for downstream supervised models (e.g., random forest) to predict drug response, including immunotherapy efficacy. | Findings: The foundation model organizes tumors by type and reveals key single‑gene and pairwise mutation interactions (e.g., RB1‑TP53, FGFR3‑CDKN2A) driving the embedding.; Embedding coordinates improve immunotherapy response prediction in NSCLC (AUC 0.78) versus traditional biomarkers.; Clonal evolution analysis shows a pseudo‑time trajectory correlating with increasing TP53, APC, and CDKN2A alterations across stages.; Scaling the model to 270,000 genomes further improves performance, indicating data‑limited learning.

metadata.speaker: Trey Ideker
metadata.talk_title: Foundation model of the tumor genome for drug response prediction and evolution analysis

text: Aneuploidy burden as a predictive biomarker for colorectal cancer risk in inflammatory bowel disease | Speaker: Trevor Graham | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: Graham demonstrated that widespread copy‑number alterations (aneuploidy) arise in inflamed colonic epithelium of IBD patients, forming large clonal expansions that precede dysplasia. Quantifying the aneuploidy burden in dysplastic lesions or in morphologically normal biopsies predicts future colorectal cancer risk, providing a mechanistic link between chronic inflammation‑driven genomic instability and cancer evolution. | Findings: Aneuploid clones can spread across the entire colon, covering meters of tissue, without visible dysplasia.; Copy‑number burden is significantly higher in lesions that later progress to cancer versus those that do not (p<0.001).; A high aneuploidy burden in low‑grade dysplasia predicts cancer development with ~85% PPV and NPV.; Aneuploidy in non‑dysplastic surveillance biopsies also predicts future cancer, suggesting a field‑effect biomarker.; Margin analysis after endoscopic resection shows that residual aneuploid clones correlate with subsequent cancer, indicating potential for molecular clearance monitoring.

metadata.speaker: Trevor Graham
metadata.talk_title: Aneuploidy burden as a predictive biomarker for colorectal cancer risk in inflammatory bowel disease

text: Evolutionary strategies to manage therapeutic resistance in cancer | Speaker: Carlo | MOA: The speaker outlined evolutionary concepts for reducing cancer evolvability (lowering mutation rate, limiting resources, reducing selection pressure) and for changing selective pressures (drug rotation, alternating opposing therapies, adaptive dosing). He highlighted adaptive therapy—dose modulation based on tumor burden—to maintain competition between sensitive and resistant clones, citing preclinical mouse work and a phase‑II adaptive trial in prostate cancer that doubled time to progression. | Findings: Maximum tolerated dose accelerates selection for resistance; lower or adaptive dosing can prolong control.; Adaptive therapy in metastatic prostate cancer increased median time to progression from 14.3 to 33.5 months and suggested a ~7‑fold fitness cost of resistance.; Preclinical models show that adding benign selective pressures (multiple drugs) slows evolution of any single resistance.; Integrated pest management heuristics (minimum effective dose, monitoring, rotating modes of action) are proposed as a framework for cancer therapy.

metadata.speaker: Carlo
metadata.talk_title: Evolutionary strategies to manage therapeutic resistance in cancer

text: Extracellular matrix regulation of metastatic dormancy via DDR1-STAT1 signaling | Speaker: Javier Bravo-Cordero | Tumors: breast cancer, head and neck cancer, pan-cancer | MOA: Dormant disseminated tumor cells secrete collagen III, creating a pro‑quiescent ECM that signals through the collagen receptor DDR1 to activate STAT1, maintaining G0 arrest. Proline hydroxylase P4HA2 stabilizes this collagen matrix; its loss reduces hydroxylated collagens, remodels the ECM, activates mitochondria and LDH4A1‑driven metabolism, thereby awakening dormant cells. | Findings: Dormant tumor cells produce collagen III‑rich ECM that induces nuclear CDK2 biosensor localization, indicating G0 arrest.; Collagen III up‑regulates DDR1 expression, activating STAT1 signaling to maintain dormancy.; P4HA2 is up‑regulated in dormant cells; knockdown restores proliferation and metastasis in lung colonization assays.; Loss of P4HA2 decreases proline‑hydroxylated collagens (III, I, V) in the tumor microenvironment.; P4HA2‑deficient ECM triggers mitochondrial enlargement, increased basal and maximal respiration, and higher ATP production.

metadata.speaker: Javier Bravo-Cordero
metadata.talk_title: Extracellular matrix regulation of metastatic dormancy via DDR1-STAT1 signaling

text: SPARC-mediated collagen regulation impacts immunity, autoimmunity and tumor progression | Speaker: Sabina Sangaletti | Tumors: breast cancer, acute myeloid leukemia, CLL, autoimmune disease models | MOA: SPARC regulates collagen I/IV deposition, shaping ECM scaffolds that control immune cell localization and activation; loss of SPARC reduces collagen barriers, enhances NETosis, alters B‑cell maturation via CD24‑P‑selectin interactions, and promotes myeloid‑derived suppressor cell expansion, thereby influencing autoimmunity, AML aggressiveness, and breast cancer metastasis. | Findings: SPARC deficiency impairs germinal center formation and B‑cell maturation due to loss of collagen scaffolding and increased CD24‑P‑selectin‑mediated apoptosis.; In SPARC‑KO mice, neutrophil NETosis is enhanced, leading to increased IL‑6 and growth factor release that drives autoimmunity and CLL‑like disease.; High SPARC expression in breast cancer (ECM3 signature) correlates with collagen‑rich, immune‑cold tumors and increased metastasis.; SPARC‑high tumors produce more GM‑CSF, IL‑6, and CXCL12, recruiting myeloid‑derived suppressor cells; COX‑2 inhibition reduces these cytokines.; Knockdown of fatty‑acid desaturase 5 reduces SPARC secretion, decreasing myeloid suppression and metastasis in a SPARC‑high clone.

metadata.speaker: Sabina Sangaletti
metadata.talk_title: SPARC-mediated collagen regulation impacts immunity, autoimmunity and tumor progression

text: CHIL1‑neutrophil axis drives ECM remodeling, myoepithelial loss and breast cancer metastasis | Speaker: Tarek Difour | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: STAT3‑driven CHIL1 expression in mammary tumor cells recruits neutrophils, inducing NETosis and neutrophil degranulation; neutrophil elastase degrades laminin and collagen IV, dismantling the myoepithelial basement membrane, permitting tumor invasion and metastasis, while NETs create an immune‑excluded niche. | Findings: CHIL1 overexpression accelerates lung metastasis in Middle T mice within six weeks.; CHIL1 knockout tumors retain an intact CK14+ myoepithelial layer and fail to metastasize.; Neutrophil depletion (anti‑Ly6G) preserves myoepithelial markers and prevents basement membrane degradation.; Pharmacologic inhibition of neutrophil elastase with Alvestat maintains CK14, calponin, and p63 expression and reduces circulating tumor cells.; CHIL1‑driven neutrophil recruitment leads to extensive laminin and collagen IV degradation, driving myoepithelial loss.

metadata.speaker: Tarek Difour
metadata.talk_title: CHIL1‑neutrophil axis drives ECM remodeling, myoepithelial loss and breast cancer metastasis

text: Fibroblast heterogeneity and therapeutic strategies in pancreatic cancer | Speaker: Stephanie Duggan | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma | MOA: Stephanie Duggan reviewed fibroblast heterogeneity in pancreatic cancer, describing myCAF and iCAF subsets driven by TGF‑β and IL‑1β, and summarized failed clinical attempts to deplete fibroblasts or ECM (Smoothened inhibition, pegylated hyaluronidase) which paradoxically worsened survival, highlighting the need for more nuanced targeting. | Findings: Smoothened inhibition combined with gemcitabine accelerated tumor progression in humans despite preclinical efficacy.; Pegylated hyaluronidase failed to improve overall survival and worsened outcomes when combined with FOLFIRINOX.; TGF‑β blockade depleted myCAFs but did not improve survival in pancreatic cancer trials.; IL‑1β blockade showed no benefit over chemotherapy in pancreatic cancer.

metadata.speaker: Stephanie Duggan
metadata.talk_title: Fibroblast heterogeneity and therapeutic strategies in pancreatic cancer

text: Stellate‑cell derived Kit ligand as a stromal tumor‑suppressive factor in pancreatic cancer | Speaker: Mara Sherman | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma | MOA: Sherman demonstrated that Kit ligand (KITLG) is expressed by normal pancreatic stellate cells and lost during tumorigenesis; loss of stromal Kit ligand increases inflammation, leukocyte infiltration, and acinar‑to‑ductal metaplasia, thereby promoting tumor initiation, whereas its presence supports normal tissue architecture and restrains tumor progression. | Findings: Kit ligand is highly expressed in normal pancreatic stellate cells but markedly reduced in pancreatic cancer stroma.; Conditional deletion of Kit ligand in mouse pancreas increases CD45+ leukocyte infiltration and perivascular mesenchymal cells.; Kit ligand loss exacerbates cerulein‑induced pancreatitis and promotes acinar‑to‑ductal metaplasia.; In implantable tumor models, stromal Kit ligand deficiency accelerates tumor growth.

metadata.speaker: Mara Sherman
metadata.talk_title: Stellate‑cell derived Kit ligand as a stromal tumor‑suppressive factor in pancreatic cancer

text: Technical implementation and early results of MedGamma fine‑tuning with QLoRA across consortium sites | Speaker: Umut Topaloglu | Tumors: lung cancer, breast cancer | MOA: Umut described the federation of MedGamma using QLoRA adapters, where each site fine‑tunes a frozen foundation model on local lung and breast cancer records, then shares low‑rank weight updates via NVIDIA FLARE to produce a more robust multimodal extractor. | Findings: Three of four sites completed local QLoRA fine‑tuning, showing improved extraction accuracy versus out‑of‑the‑box MedGamma (visualized as orange vs blue bars).; One site demonstrated a statistically significant increase in variable extraction performance after fine‑tuning; other sites reported even larger gains.; Federated aggregation of QLoRA weights is scheduled, with the hypothesis that exposure to four centers’ data will further boost model robustness.

metadata.speaker: Umut Topaloglu
metadata.talk_title: Technical implementation and early results of MedGamma fine‑tuning with QLoRA across consortium sites

text: Fine‑tuning MedGamma with QLoRA for trial‑matching in lung and breast cancer cohorts | Speaker: Ghulam Rasool | Tumors: lung cancer, breast cancer | MOA: Rasool reported that local QLoRA fine‑tuning of MedGamma on ~500 retrospective lung and breast cancer patients per site markedly improved the model’s ability to extract structured trial‑matching variables from pathology reports and clinical notes, and that a forthcoming federated run will test whether pooled updates further enhance performance. | Findings: Local fine‑tuning at one site increased extraction performance from baseline (blue) to post‑fine‑tuning (orange).; Two additional sites reported even larger improvements after local QLoRA adaptation.; Federated aggregation of QLoRA weights is planned for the week following the conference.

metadata.speaker: Ghulam Rasool
metadata.talk_title: Fine‑tuning MedGamma with QLoRA for trial‑matching in lung and breast cancer cohorts

text: Federated deep‑learning model for overall survival prediction in glioblastoma using MRIs | Speaker: Rakesh Khanna | Tumors: glioblastoma | MOA: Khanna described a federated pipeline where a pre‑trained Vision Transformer extracts 768‑dimensional embeddings from pre‑operative MRI tumor ROIs, which are pooled and fed to an MLP to predict relative overall‑survival risk; the model was trained across public GBM datasets and a real‑world Moffitt cohort (n=104) using NVIDIA FLARE with FedAvg aggregation. | Findings: Added 104 real‑world Moffitt GBM patients to three public datasets without centralizing data.; Leave‑one‑site‑out evaluation showed consistent Kaplan‑Meier separation across held‑out cohorts.; Time‑dependent 1‑year AUC and C‑index were comparable to prior centralized studies, though absolute performance was not yet sufficient for clinical decision‑making.; Future plans include incorporating an additional private NCI GBM cohort and expanding to radiology reports, other imaging modalities, and clinical markers.

metadata.speaker: Rakesh Khanna
metadata.talk_title: Federated deep‑learning model for overall survival prediction in glioblastoma using MRIs

text: Neoadjuvant pembrolizumab stratified by tumor mutation burden and high-risk stage two, three deficient mismatch repair or MSI-high colorectal cancer: The NeoPRISM-CRC study | Speaker: Yanrong Jiang | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: Neoadjuvant pembrolizumab was used in MMRd colorectal cancer to induce pathological complete response. The study integrated ultrasensitive ctDNA monitoring and TCR profiling to identify 'super molecular responders' who clear ctDNA rapidly, suggesting a potential for non-operative management. | Findings: Nine weeks of neoadjuvant pembrolizumab achieved a 59% pCR rate in high-risk stage II/III MMRd CRC (n=31).; ctDNA was detected in 100% of patients at baseline, with 24% in the ultrasensitive range (<100 ppm).; 100% of 'super molecular responders' (rapid clearance after 1 cycle) achieved pCR.; Post-operative ctDNA surveillance demonstrated 100% specificity and 100% negative predictive value for relapse over a median follow-up of 33 months.; Baseline TCR clonal expansion correlates with pCR, and a combined Bayesian model of TCR and ctDNA kinetics improves response prediction.

metadata.speaker: Yanrong Jiang
metadata.talk_title: Neoadjuvant pembrolizumab stratified by tumor mutation burden and high-risk stage two, three deficient mismatch repair or MSI-high colorectal cancer: The NeoPRISM-CRC study

text: Early findings from MONITOR-BREAST: ctDNA dynamics during neoadjuvant therapy using an ultrasensitive MRD assay | Speaker: Julia Foldy | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: The study evaluated the association between dense, ultrasensitive ctDNA sampling and pathologic response in neoadjuvant breast cancer therapy. It found that sustained MRD negativity is a strong predictor of pCR, while persistent or intermittent positivity strongly predicts residual disease. | Findings: 100% specificity: all 47 patients achieving pCR were ctDNA negative post-neoadjuvant therapy.; Sustained MRD negativity (76% of patients) resulted in a 63% pCR rate.; Persistent MRD positivity resulted in 0% pCR and 100% residual disease (all RCB2 or 3).; Frequent sampling identified 64% more patients at risk for residual disease compared to a single post-neoadjuvant time point.; Clearance timing varied by subtype: TNBC cleared within 45 days (90% of patients) vs HR+/HER2- which took 16 weeks (90% of patients).

metadata.speaker: Julia Foldy
metadata.talk_title: Early findings from MONITOR-BREAST: ctDNA dynamics during neoadjuvant therapy using an ultrasensitive MRD assay

text: Phase 2 study of adjuvant PD-1 blockade with endocrine therapy in hormone receptor-positive and inflammatory breast cancer | Speaker: Ranjan Upadhyay | Tumors: inflammatory breast cancer | MOA: The study tested the combination of pembrolizumab and endocrine therapy in HR+ inflammatory breast cancer (IBC). The hypothesis was that targeting the immunosuppressive microenvironment of IBC would improve DFS, which was observed (71% vs 60% historical). | Findings: Two-year DFS was 71%, an improvement over the historical benchmark of 60% for HR+ IBC.; ctDNA negativity at the end of treatment was associated with 100% disease-free survival at 24 months.; ctDNA positivity provided a lead time to clinical progression of up to 15 months.; Durable responders showed lower maximum variant allele frequency (VAF) in nodal tissue compared to non-responders.; Deletions in the immunoglobulin heavy locus (IGH) were found in durable responders, suggesting B-cell involvement in the response.

metadata.speaker: Ranjan Upadhyay
metadata.talk_title: Phase 2 study of adjuvant PD-1 blockade with endocrine therapy in hormone receptor-positive and inflammatory breast cancer

text: Molecular residual disease interception in local regionally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, the MERIDIAN phase two trial | Speaker: Enrique Sanz Garcia | Tumors: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma | MOA: The MERIDIAN trial tests the 'interception' hypothesis: treating MRD-positive HNSCC patients with the PD-1/TIGIT bispecific antibody rivocostimib to clear ctDNA and prevent clinical recurrence. One patient achieved persistent ctDNA clearance and remains disease-free 2 years later. | Findings: A single patient treated with rivocostimib achieved persistent ctDNA clearance and remains disease-free 2 years post-therapy.; ctDNA detection at 8-12 weeks post-therapy had 50% sensitivity for recurrence, which improved to 73% with longitudinal tracking.; HPV DNA sequencing showed higher sensitivity but lower specificity compared to the RADAR assay in OPC patients.; Combining tumor-informed assays and HPV DNA increased sensitivity to 100% in OPC patients.; The study was paused due to lower-than-expected MRD prevalence (only 6 patients eligible for interception).

metadata.speaker: Enrique Sanz Garcia
metadata.talk_title: Molecular residual disease interception in local regionally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, the MERIDIAN phase two trial
tumor_types: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma

text: Unlocking endocrine resistance, co-targeting KAT6 and ER with bifetostat and fulvestrant | Speaker: Li Lu | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: Bifetostat inhibits KAT6A/B, shifting the tumor transcriptome toward tumor suppressor programs (e.g., FOXP3, ING4) and away from cell cycle genes (TK1, CYCB1). Combining this with fulvestrant blocks both epigenetic and ER signaling, leading to robust clearance of ESR1 variants associated with endocrine resistance. | Findings: Bifetostat 5mg + fulvestrant is the recommended dose for Phase 3 based on superior ctDNA clearance and gene expression changes.; Early ctDNA clearance (within 9 weeks) strongly correlates with clinical response (PR and SD).; Patients with undetectable ctDNA at 9 weeks had a significantly longer median PFS (21.9 vs 5.3 months).; The combination effectively clears ESR1 mutations (63% clearance rate), which are key drivers of endocrine resistance.

metadata.speaker: Li Lu
metadata.talk_title: Unlocking endocrine resistance, co-targeting KAT6 and ER with bifetostat and fulvestrant

text: ctDNA Clearance as a Prognostic Biomarker in Extensive Stage Small Cell Lung Cancer: Insights from the LUMINOUS Phase 3B Study | Speaker: Gozde Kar | Tumors: small cell lung cancer | MOA: The study used a tumor-agnostic methylation-based assay to monitor ctDNA in ES-SCLC patients treated with durvalumab and platinum-etoposide. The results show that the pattern of ctDNA clearance (sustained vs late vs never) is a powerful prognostic indicator of OS and PFS. | Findings: Sustained ctDNA clearance was associated with the best outcomes (median PFS 19.3 months vs 6.2 months for non-clearers).; ctDNA re-emergence occurred 55 days before clinical progression in one representative case.; 100% of sustained clearance patients were alive at 12 months, compared to 36% of never-clearers.; The methylation-based assay is viable for SCLC due to the high shedding nature of the tumor.; ctDNA dynamics aligned closely with longitudinal RECIST assessments.

metadata.speaker: Gozde Kar
metadata.talk_title: ctDNA Clearance as a Prognostic Biomarker in Extensive Stage Small Cell Lung Cancer: Insights from the LUMINOUS Phase 3B Study

text: Virtual patients with multimodal foundation models and agents | Speaker: Charlotte Bonner | MOA: Developed multimodal foundation models that jointly encode histopathology RGB images and spatial proteomics protein panels into a shared representation, enabling virtual patient profiling, in silico treatment forecasting, and AI‑derived biomarker discovery through early‑fusion transformer architectures and reinforcement‑learning‑based sequential acquisition (EchoK). | Findings: Trained the first multimodal foundation model on 5,003 patients (4,605 publicly released) with paired H&E and spatial proteomics data across 8 cancer types.; Demonstrated that the model can virtually stain unmeasured proteins and predict optimal protein panels, achieving comparable performance to specialized single‑modality models.; Showed that model‑derived signatures stratify responders vs non‑responders in a triple‑negative breast cancer immunotherapy cohort better than existing clinical biomarkers.; Implemented EchoK, a reinforcement‑learning sequential acquisition system that selects a minimal set of proteomic markers (as few as 8) while preserving cell‑typing accuracy.

metadata.speaker: Charlotte Bonner
metadata.talk_title: Virtual patients with multimodal foundation models and agents

text: Generative image models and visual question answering for disease dynamics | Speaker: Serena Yeung Levy | MOA: Introduced CellFlux, a flow‑matching based generative framework that learns a continuous velocity field to transform distributions of control cell images into perturbed cell images, and described scaling of the model to >11 M images, joint imaging‑transcriptomics latent representations, and the MicroVQA benchmark for multimodal scientific visual question answering. | Findings: CellFlux trained on 300 k images achieved higher image‑generation quality than prior baselines; scaling to 11.6 M images further improved performance.; Demonstrated that flow‑matching in latent space (CellFlux v2) enables realistic perturbation simulations and visualizes transformation trajectories.; Created MicroVQA, a benchmark of >1 000 expert‑curated microscopy questions covering higher‑order Bloom’s taxonomy, revealing gaps in current vision‑language models.; Showed that large multimodal LLMs (e.g., Gemini 3 Pro) achieve state‑of‑the‑art scores on MicroVQA but still struggle with fine‑grained visual reasoning.

metadata.speaker: Serena Yeung Levy
metadata.talk_title: Generative image models and visual question answering for disease dynamics

text: Reliable medical AI agents that plan, evaluate, and verify reasoning | Speaker: Michael Moore | MOA: Proposed a framework for medical AI agents that integrate structured knowledge atlases (Myriad QA pairs) and process‑reward verification models to ground and audit each reasoning step, enabling reliable multimodal decision‑making for tasks such as molecular tumor boards and 3D radiology analysis. | Findings: Constructed Myriad, a 6 M QA pair knowledge base derived from peer‑reviewed literature, improving retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) performance on MedExpertQA.; Developed a process‑reward model that checks individual reasoning steps of a language model against guidelines, reducing hallucinations across multiple downstream medical tasks.; Demonstrated an agent that performs step‑wise 3D chest CT analysis with traceable reasoning, achieving higher fidelity than baseline LLMs.

metadata.speaker: Michael Moore
metadata.talk_title: Reliable medical AI agents that plan, evaluate, and verify reasoning

text: Overview of the Cancer Research Data Commons infrastructure and usage statistics | Speaker: Tania Davisson | MOA: The CRDC provides a unified, cloud-based platform that aggregates genomic, proteomic, imaging, clinical, and other data types across seven specialized data commons, enabling standardized access, harmonized metadata, and scalable analysis without requiring data download. | Findings: CRDC hosts 533 studies covering over 200,000 subjects and 17 petabytes of data.; Since inception, the cloud resource has performed over 1,600 compute years and offers more than 1,200 public analysis tools.; User engagement includes 100,000 monthly users and 47,000 PubMed citations referencing CRDC data.

metadata.speaker: Tania Davisson
metadata.talk_title: Overview of the Cancer Research Data Commons infrastructure and usage statistics

text: CCDI Data Ecosystem: resources, enrollment, and data integration | Speaker: Subhashini Jagu | MOA: CCDI aggregates pediatric cancer clinical, genomic, and imaging data through a unified data model and APIs, enabling cohort building, cross‑resource queries, and rapid molecular characterization (results returned within 21 days) for over 9,000 enrolled patients. | Findings: CCDI ecosystem currently includes 41 datasets, including Childhood Cancer Survival Study and Pediatric MATCH.; Project Every Child has enrolled >9,000 patients, delivering molecular characterization results within 21 days.; 6,000 patients' molecular data from MCI have been released in cBioPortal, with integrated SNV and methylation widgets.; Over 4,000 pathology images are available in the Imaging Data Commons, with AI‑ready processing by DOE.

metadata.speaker: Subhashini Jagu
metadata.talk_title: CCDI Data Ecosystem: resources, enrollment, and data integration

text: ARPA‑H Biomedical Data Fabric Toolbox integration with CRDC | Speaker: Erica Kim | MOA: The BDF Toolbox develops AI‑assisted tools (e.g., Netrius DataCord for metadata harmonization, Data Gatherer for literature‑linked dataset extraction, AI chatbots for data exploration) that integrate with CRDC APIs to automate data submission, curation, and discovery, reducing manual effort and improving data readiness for analysis. | Findings: Netrius DataCord AI‑driven curation platform achieved ≥90% reduction in manual curation time in pilot deployments.; Data Gatherer combines rule‑based and LLM methods to extract dataset metadata from publications, enhancing discoverability.; BioInsight AI chatbot enables plain‑language queries across CRDC genomic, proteomic, and imaging resources.

metadata.speaker: Erica Kim
metadata.talk_title: ARPA‑H Biomedical Data Fabric Toolbox integration with CRDC

text: Obesity as a modifiable risk factor for cancer incidence and outcomes | Speaker: Jennifer Ligibel | Tumors: breast cancer, colorectal cancer, pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer, endometrial cancer | MOA: Excess adiposity drives systemic metabolic dysregulation (hyperinsulinemia, hyperleptinemia, inflammation) that increases incidence and worsens outcomes across multiple malignancies; intentional weight loss via bariatric surgery or structured lifestyle programs reverses these metabolic perturbations and reduces cancer risk and recurrence, particularly in breast cancer, by lowering insulin, leptin, and inflammatory markers. | Findings: Each 5 kg/m² increase in BMI raises post‑menopausal breast cancer risk by ~10% (IARC meta‑analysis).; Obesity at cancer diagnosis is associated with >20% higher breast cancer‑specific mortality across 36 studies.; Bariatric surgery reduces overall cancer incidence by ~40% and obesity‑related cancers (breast ~50% reduction, colorectal ~60% reduction).; In the Breast Cancer Weight Loss Trial, the lifestyle intervention achieved a mean 6% weight loss at 1 yr, with 50% of participants losing ≥5% body weight versus 12% in controls.; Weight loss lowered fasting insulin by 21% and reduced HOMA‑IR by 25% at 6 mo, indicating reversal of insulin resistance.

metadata.speaker: Jennifer Ligibel
metadata.talk_title: Obesity as a modifiable risk factor for cancer incidence and outcomes

text: Preclinical mechanisms of GLP‑1/GIP dual agonist tirzepatide in obesity‑driven breast, colon and endometrial cancer | Speaker: Steve Hursting | Tumors: breast cancer, colorectal cancer, endometrial cancer | MOA: Tirzepatide induces ~20% body‑weight loss in diet‑induced obese mice, normalizing hyperglycemia, hyperinsulinemia and hyperleptinemia; this metabolic reprogramming restores CD8⁺ T‑cell activation and antigen‑presenting cell function, reverses obesity‑driven immunosuppression, and consequently reduces tumor growth in breast, colon and endometrial cancer models, an effect that is abolished by CD8⁺ T‑cell depletion, indicating a T‑cell‑dependent mechanism. | Findings: Tirzepatide achieved ~20% weight loss in obese C57BL/6 mice, matching human clinical trial outcomes.; Obesity‑driven tumor growth in EO771, MC38 and PY230 models was reduced to lean‑control levels by tirzepatide; pair‑feeding reproduced most of the effect, indicating weight‑loss as the primary driver.; In the LKB1/p53‑deficient endometrial model, tirzepatide reduced tumor burden even in non‑obese mice, suggesting additional metabolic effects.; Obesity suppressed CD8⁺ T‑cell activation (naive markers TCF7, CCR7) and antigen‑presentation gene sets (18/18); tirzepatide fully restored activated phenotypes (granzyme B, PD‑1) and antigen‑presentation scores.; CD8⁺ T‑cell depletion abolished tirzepatide’s anti‑tumor effect, confirming T‑cell dependence.

metadata.speaker: Steve Hursting
metadata.talk_title: Preclinical mechanisms of GLP‑1/GIP dual agonist tirzepatide in obesity‑driven breast, colon and endometrial cancer

text: Real‑world evidence of GLP‑1 receptor agonists on cancer risk, incidence, and survivorship | Speaker: Zhong Bian | Tumors: breast cancer, endometrial cancer, ovarian cancer, meningioma, kidney cancer, lung cancer, colorectal cancer, pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer | MOA: Observational analyses of large Medicare and EHR datasets suggest that GLP‑1 receptor agonist exposure is associated with modest reductions in overall and obesity‑related cancer incidence (notably endometrial, ovarian, meningioma) and improved survival among cancer survivors, while a potential increased risk of kidney cancer emerges in type 2 diabetes cohorts, highlighting drug‑specific effects that may be mediated by weight loss, metabolic improvement, and immune modulation observed in preclinical studies. | Findings: GLP‑1 users had a 17% lower overall cancer incidence (HR 0.83) compared with matched non‑users in the OneFlorida cohort.; Significant risk reductions were observed for endometrial (HR 0.71), ovarian (HR 0.74) and meningioma (HR 0.68) cancers.; In Medicare type 2 diabetes patients, GLP‑1 vs SGLT2 was associated with a 22% increased kidney cancer risk (HR 1.22).; GLP‑1 vs DPP4 showed a borderline 18% increased endometrial cancer risk (HR 1.18) but was not statistically definitive.; Among cancer survivors with diabetes, GLP‑1 exposure improved overall survival (HR 0.78) and breast cancer‑specific survival (HR 0.71) versus DPP4.

metadata.speaker: Zhong Bian
metadata.talk_title: Real‑world evidence of GLP‑1 receptor agonists on cancer risk, incidence, and survivorship

text: Real-world variant-level frequencies in NSCLC from liquid biopsy testing | Speaker: Emma Longshore | Tumors: NSCLC | MOA: Analyzed >350,000 liquid biopsy NGS and ddPCR tests to quantify variant-level prevalence of actionable NSCLC alterations, demonstrating population-level differences from trial-enriched cohorts and highlighting rapid, non‑invasive molecular profiling across diverse ethnic groups. | Findings: Analyzed 350,000 NSCLC liquid biopsy tests from 2015‑2025, representing community practice across 20 self-reported ethnicities.; Technical success rate >90% for both NGS and ddPCR platforms.; KRAS G12C was the most frequent SNV; EGFR L858R and exon 19 deletions were also prevalent.; CCDC6‑RET was the most common fusion; ROS1 and ALK fusions were detected at expected frequencies.; MYC copy‑number gain was the most common CNV among the panel.

metadata.speaker: Emma Longshore
metadata.talk_title: Real-world variant-level frequencies in NSCLC from liquid biopsy testing

text: Histologic landscape and prognostic grading of lung cancer in never smokers | Speaker: Trinh Tran | Tumors: NSCLC | MOA: Characterized histologic patterns of lung cancer in never smokers using the large XELOC Lung cohort and validated the IASLC grading system for non‑mucinous adenocarcinoma, then developed a deep‑learning model on whole‑slide images to predict five‑year overall survival, revealing ancestry‑linked risk patterns. | Findings: In 844 never‑smoker lung cancers, adenocarcinoma and carcinoid were over‑represented, while squamous and SCLC were under‑represented compared with smoker cohorts.; Combined IASLC grades 1 + 2 showed better overall survival than grade 3 (HR 0.38 in all stages; HR 0.31 in stage I‑II).; Deep‑learning model improved AUC for five‑year OS when added to clinical variables and grading (integrative model AUC > clinical‑only model).; Model identified a subset of grade 3 tumors with low risk, enriched in East Asian ancestry.; Web‑based heat‑map tool enables pathologists to visualize high‑risk histologic regions.

metadata.speaker: Trinh Tran
metadata.talk_title: Histologic landscape and prognostic grading of lung cancer in never smokers

text: Real-world outcomes of trastuzumab deruxtecan vs chemotherapy in HER2‑amplified mCRC | Speaker: Zenara Shah | Tumors: metastatic colorectal cancer | MOA: Compared real‑world overall survival of HER2‑amplified microsatellite‑stable metastatic colorectal cancer patients receiving second‑line trastuzumab deruxtecan versus standard chemotherapy, showing a late survival advantage (5‑yr OS 58% vs 49%) despite similar 1‑yr OS and higher rates of ILD and heart failure. | Findings: Propensity‑matched cohort of 1,870 patients per arm achieved covariate balance (SMD <0.1).; Early survival similar (1‑yr OS 83% vs 85%); long‑term survival diverged favoring trastuzumab deruxtecan (5‑yr OS 58% vs 49%).; Adjusted hazard ratio for death with chemotherapy vs T‑DXd = 1.14 (caution due to early curve crossing).; Higher incidence of all‑grade interstitial lung disease (12%) and heart failure (9%) in the T‑DXd group.; Hematologic toxicities comparable; fatigue and vomiting more frequent with T‑DXd, diarrhea more common with chemotherapy.

metadata.speaker: Zenara Shah
metadata.talk_title: Real-world outcomes of trastuzumab deruxtecan vs chemotherapy in HER2‑amplified mCRC

text: Cancer risk with ARB vs ACE inhibitor initiation in US veterans | Speaker: Shivani Himbert | MOA: Emulated a target trial using VHA data to compare cancer incidence and diagnosis‑free mortality between ARB and ACE inhibitor initiators, finding a 20‑25% lower cancer risk with ARBs without differences in overall mortality. | Findings: Cohort of 2.6 M veterans (10% ARB, 90% ACE) followed up to 10 years.; ARB initiation associated with 20‑25% lower overall cancer risk (RR 0.75‑0.80).; No significant difference in diagnosis‑free mortality between groups.; Effect stronger in patients >70 years (≈30% risk reduction).; Consistent risk reduction across major solid‑tumor subtypes.

metadata.speaker: Shivani Himbert
metadata.talk_title: Cancer risk with ARB vs ACE inhibitor initiation in US veterans

text: Assisted reproductive technology and risk of female hormone‑related cancers | Speaker: Emily Peiying Lin | Tumors: breast cancer, ovarian cancer, endometrial cancer | MOA: Nationwide propensity‑matched cohort study in Taiwan linking ART procedures to subsequent incidence of breast, ovarian, and endometrial cancers, revealing modest but statistically significant increased risks for breast (HR ≈ 1.12) and ovarian (HR ≈ 1.46) cancers, with no effect on endometrial cancer. | Findings: Cohort of 105,000 ART users and 105,000 matched non‑ART controls (mean age 47).; Breast cancer events: 1,774 (ART) vs 1,581 (non‑ART).; Ovarian cancer events: 235 (ART) vs 161 (non‑ART).; Endometrial cancer events: 261 (ART) vs 252 (non‑ART).; Adjusted HRs: breast cancer 1.12, ovarian cancer 1.46, endometrial cancer 1.03 (not significant).

metadata.speaker: Emily Peiying Lin
metadata.talk_title: Assisted reproductive technology and risk of female hormone‑related cancers

text: Real‑world clinical genomics platform for under‑represented populations | Speaker: Shubhankur Sood | MOA: Built a scalable, modular real‑world clinical genomics platform that integrates whole‑genome sequencing, transcriptomics, imaging, and AI‑driven decision support, initially linking German precision‑oncology infrastructure with a prospective Indian patient cohort to generate globally representative multi‑omics data. | Findings: German WGS pipeline achieved >85% clinically actionable reporting across 20 tumor types.; Pilot Indian cohort demonstrated feasibility of generating WGS, imaging, and pathology data for under‑represented patients.; AI models trained on German data successfully applied to Indian cases for therapy recommendation and risk stratification.

metadata.speaker: Shubhankur Sood
metadata.talk_title: Real‑world clinical genomics platform for under‑represented populations

text: Pan‑cancer landscape of alternative lengthening of telomeres via machine‑learning on clinical sequencing | Speaker: Harshit Sahe | MOA: Developed an ensemble classifier that leverages off‑target reads from MSK‑IMPACT panels to predict ALT activity, applying it to 78,000 tumors to map pan‑cancer ALT prevalence, uncover novel genetic associations (e.g., RB1, POT1) and tumor‑type specific prognostic impacts. | Findings: Classifier achieved ROC‑AUC >0.85 on held‑out validation using C‑circle assay as ground truth.; ALT prevalence recapitulated known high‑ALT cancers (glioma, sarcoma, osteosarcoma) and identified estimates for >30 additional tumor types.; ATRX/DAXX truncations enriched for ALT but many ALT‑positive tumors lacked these alterations.; Missense mutations in RB1 and POT1 associated with ALT activity in wild‑type ATRX/DAXX tumors.; ALT positivity correlated with better OS in glioma but worse OS in sarcoma and osteosarcoma.

metadata.speaker: Harshit Sahe
metadata.talk_title: Pan‑cancer landscape of alternative lengthening of telomeres via machine‑learning on clinical sequencing

text: Behavioral Insights for Cancer Prevention Messaging and Evaluation of Colorectal Cancer Screening Messages | Speaker: Jeffrey Niederdeppe | MOA: Niederdeppe demonstrated that outcome‑focused, audience‑segmented messaging improves intentions for colorectal cancer screening, especially when messages are tailored to racial subgroups; generic messages increase intent modestly, but race‑congruent messages boost both screening intention and sharing likelihood among Black participants. | Findings: A wiki‑survey of >2,000 Black and White adults identified distinct top‑ranked messages for each racial group.; In a subsequent RCT (≈2,000 participants), all message conditions increased screening intention versus control.; Black‑preferred messages produced the highest mean intention scores among Black participants, outperforming median‑ranked and White‑preferred messages.; White participants showed no significant increase in screening intention across any message condition.; Message sharing intentions aligned with racial preference: Black participants were more likely to share Black‑preferred messages, and White participants were more likely to share White‑preferred messages.

metadata.speaker: Jeffrey Niederdeppe
metadata.session_title: From Risk Awareness to Informed Action Advancing Cancer Communication Across Prevention and Genomic Care
metadata.talk_title: Behavioral Insights for Cancer Prevention Messaging and Evaluation of Colorectal Cancer Screening Messages

text: Commercial Marketing Techniques for Precision Oncology Communication and the GenePilot Decision Support Tool | Speaker: Anita Kinney | Tumors: breast cancer, lung cancer, pan-cancer | MOA: Kinney applied commercial segmentation, perceptual mapping, and vector message modeling to create GenePilot, a web‑based decision aid that tailors content to mistrust levels and delivers personalized messaging, resulting in reduced decisional conflict and increased self‑efficacy for genetic testing among Black cancer patients. | Findings: Segmentation identified high‑ vs low‑mistrust clusters among Black patients, each with distinct messaging needs.; Perceptual mapping revealed that high‑mistrust patients prioritized concerns about privacy, insurance exploitation, and genetic discrimination.; GenePilot incorporated persona‑based modules (Fly, Glide, Soar, Navigate) addressing these concerns.; In the RCT (≈100 Black patients), GenePilot significantly lowered decisional conflict and increased self‑efficacy compared with usual care.; Usage analytics showed mandatory progression through all four modules, ensuring exposure to core content.

metadata.speaker: Anita Kinney
metadata.session_title: From Risk Awareness to Informed Action Advancing Cancer Communication Across Prevention and Genomic Care
metadata.talk_title: Commercial Marketing Techniques for Precision Oncology Communication and the GenePilot Decision Support Tool

text: Pre‑cancer evolution of the upper gastrointestinal tract using organoid and single‑cell models | Speaker: Dr. Leung | Tumors: gastric cancer, gastroesophageal junction cancer | MOA: Deep whole‑genome sequencing of microdissected gastric glands revealed age‑related SNV accumulation and a two‑fold SNV/three‑fold indel increase in intestinal metaplasia glands, indicating clonal expansion from a common ancestor. Single‑cell RNA‑seq of organoids shows a spectrum from hybrid gastric‑intestinal phenotypes to advanced intestinal differentiation, driven by epigenetic reprogramming (hypermethylation of gastric genes, demethylation of colon genes) and fetal signature reversion, with chromosome 20 gain linked to matrix‑independent growth. | Findings: Microdissected metaplastic glands display ~2‑fold higher SNV burden and ~3‑fold higher indel rate than adjacent non‑metaplastic glands.; Mutational signature SBS18 (ROS injury) and increased ID2/ID1 ratio emerge early in metaplasia, resembling MSI tumor signatures.; Single‑cell RNA‑seq defines hybrid gastric‑intestinal cells and a fetal gut signature (TROP2, TACSTD2) in metaplastic organoids.; Chromosome 20 gain is frequent in metaplastic organoids and enables growth without Matrigel, suggesting an early tumor‑initiating event.; Claudin‑18.2 expression declines during metaplastic progression, potentially mediating resistance to CLDN18.2‑targeted therapies.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Leung
metadata.talk_title: Pre‑cancer evolution of the upper gastrointestinal tract using organoid and single‑cell models

text: HER2‑directed bispecific antibody zanidatamab in metastatic gastric/GEJ cancer | Speaker: Dr. Jaffa Ajani | Tumors: gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma | MOA: Zanidatamab is an asymmetric bispecific antibody that simultaneously engages two HER2 epitopes, inducing receptor clustering, cap formation and hexamerization, which markedly enhances FcγR cross‑linking, complement C1q recruitment and thereby drives ADCC, ADCP and complement‑dependent cytotoxicity beyond that achieved by trastuzumab, pertuzumab or their combination. | Findings: Zanidatamab induces HER2 cap formation and hexamerization not observed with trastuzumab, pertuzumab, or their combination.; In the fourth‑line setting, zanidatamab monotherapy produced durable responses absent with standard HER2‑targeted therapy.; Phase II zanidatamab + chemo yielded a median PFS advantage of 4 months over trastuzumab + chemo (HR 0.65, p < 0.001).; Adding tislelizumab to zanidatamab + chemo further improved OS (HR 0.72, ~7‑month gain) compared with trastuzumab + chemo.; Diarrhea was the most common toxicity in the zanidatamab‑chemo arms, requiring proactive management.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Jaffa Ajani
metadata.talk_title: HER2‑directed bispecific antibody zanidatamab in metastatic gastric/GEJ cancer

text: Neoadjuvant chemo‑immunotherapy (FLOT + durvalumab) reshapes curative treatment of resectable gastroesophageal cancer | Speaker: Dr. Yelena Janjigian | Tumors: gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma | MOA: Durvalumab combined with the triplet chemotherapy FLOT delivers sustained neo‑antigen release and checkpoint blockade while the tumor remains in situ, leading to deep tumor regression (MPR/pCR) and enhanced immune priming that enables organ‑preserving strategies in resectable gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma. | Findings: Neoadjuvant durvalumab + FLOT achieved a 19% pCR rate and 19% MPR rate, markedly higher than historic chemotherapy alone.; Patients with pCR had durable disease‑free survival with median follow‑up >4 years.; Clinical complete response was observed in 83% of early‑cohort patients after six cycles of neoadjuvant therapy.; ctDNA clearance correlated with pathologic response but 38% of ctDNA‑negative patients still recurred, highlighting residual risk.; Chromosomal instability (CIN) signatures predicted poorer immunotherapy benefit, suggesting a need for additional biomarkers.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Yelena Janjigian
metadata.talk_title: Neoadjuvant chemo‑immunotherapy (FLOT + durvalumab) reshapes curative treatment of resectable gastroesophageal cancer

text: Distinguishing selection in normal tissues from cancer causation | Speaker: Kamila Axelrod | Tumors: esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, acute myeloid leukemia, breast cancer, pan-cancer | MOA: Axelrod presented a quantitative framework that compares mutation frequencies in cancers (Y) to frequencies in matched normal tissues (X) to compute a carcinogenic effect (odds ratio). Using esophageal SCC, AML and other cancers, she showed that some canonical drivers (e.g., TP53) have high carcinogenic effects, whereas others (e.g., NOTCH1, PIK3CA) appear neutral or even cancer‑inhibiting, indicating that positive selection in normal tissues can distort perceived driver status. | Findings: Carcinogenic effect is calculated as the odds ratio of cancer vs. normal tissue mutation frequencies.; TP53 shows a carcinogenic effect in the thousands in esophageal SCC, confirming strong driver status.; NOTCH1 mutations are more frequent in normal esophagus than in cancer, suggesting a tumor‑inhibiting role.; PIK3CA, FAD1, EP300 show low carcinogenic effects, indicating limited contribution to malignancy.; In AML, classic drivers (e.g., FLT3) have high carcinogenic effects, while TET2/DNMT3A have low effects.

metadata.speaker: Kamila Axelrod
metadata.talk_title: Distinguishing selection in normal tissues from cancer causation

text: Clonal evolution and promotion in mouse skin carcinogenesis | Speaker: Alan Balmain | Tumors: skin squamous cell carcinoma (mouse model) | MOA: Balmain demonstrated that initiating mutations (e.g., DMBA‑induced HRAS Q61L) persist as latent clones for months, but tumor formation requires a promoting inflammatory stimulus (TPA). Promotion drives clonal expansion of specific RAS mutants, with immune cell infiltration (neutrophils, monocytes) being essential; HRAS and KRAS mutants compete for clonal dominance, and HRAS loss reveals KRAS‑driven tumors. | Findings: A single DMBA dose creates ~30,000–50,000 mutations, including HRAS Q61L, which remains latent for up to a year.; TPA promotion induces massive clonal expansion of HRAS Q61L, accounting for >90% of tumors.; Spontaneous KRAS G12D/G13R clones expand with TPA but disappear unless HRAS is knocked out.; HRAS knockout mice develop KRAS‑driven tumors, revealing competitive clonal interactions.; Promotion requires innate immune cells; NSG mice (immune‑deficient) develop few tumors.

metadata.speaker: Alan Balmain
metadata.talk_title: Clonal evolution and promotion in mouse skin carcinogenesis

text: Germline‑somatic associations in cancer using real‑world panel sequencing | Speaker: Jian Carrot Zhang | Tumors: pan-cancer, breast cancer, colorectal cancer, pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer | MOA: Zhang described a pipeline that imputes genome‑wide germline genotypes from off‑target reads of clinical tumor panels, enabling GWAS of germline variants influencing somatic driver acquisition. A germline locus near MDM4 was linked to higher TP53 mutation rates, likely via increased MDM4 expression reducing p53 activity, and this association persisted after adjusting for mutational burden and smoking. | Findings: Off‑target reads from panel sequencing can accurately impute common germline variants (R²>0.8).; Pan‑cancer GWAS identified a 1q32/M​DM4 locus associated with TP53 mutations; replicated in Dana‑Farber and TCGA cohorts.; CRISPR deletion of the implicated enhancer reduced MDM4 expression, confirming functional relevance.; The MDM4 risk allele is enriched in stage IV disease and lung metastasis in breast cancer, independent of TP53 status.; Ancestry‑specific germline variant explains part of the higher ERG fusion frequency in European‑ancestry prostate cancer.

metadata.speaker: Jian Carrot Zhang
metadata.talk_title: Germline‑somatic associations in cancer using real‑world panel sequencing

text: Cancer driver mutations in normal tissues and their relation to cancer risk | Speaker: Nuria López‑Bigas | Tumors: colon cancer, lung cancer, bladder cancer, blood (AML) | MOA: López‑Bigas introduced MutRisk, a model that integrates tissue‑specific mutation rates, trinucleotide signatures, and chromatin context to estimate per‑site mutation probabilities in normal stem cells. Multiplying by stem‑cell pool sizes yields estimates of how many cells harbor specific driver mutations (e.g., ~1.5 million TP53‑mutant lung basal cells in a smoker). The analysis shows that random mutagenesis alone cannot explain observed cancer incidence, highlighting the need for clonal selection driven by promotion and microenvironmental factors. | Findings: MutRisk predicts highly unequal per‑site mutation probabilities; some TP53 codons are orders of magnitude more likely to mutate.; Estimated numbers of TP53‑mutant stem cells range from ~18 000 in colon to ~1.5 million in smoker lung tissue.; Combinations of driver mutations (e.g., APC + APC + KRAS) are exceedingly rare without clonal selection (<1 per million individuals).; Duplex sequencing of normal bladder reveals strong positive selection for RBM10 truncations and TP53 mutations, with higher DN/DS in males.; TERT promoter mutations show strong selection only in smokers, linking exposure to clonal expansion.

metadata.speaker: Nuria López‑Bigas
metadata.talk_title: Cancer driver mutations in normal tissues and their relation to cancer risk

text: Genomic characterization of multiple primary lung cancers in TRACERx | Speaker: Charlotte Grieco | Tumors: NSCLC | MOA: Whole-exome sequencing of multiple primary NSCLC tumors revealed a 10% discordance between clinical and genomic relatedness, indicating many cases are misclassified as metastases or primaries, with no distinct genomic features distinguishing multiple primaries. | Findings: 25% of TRACERx patients have >1 primary tumor, 12% have >1 lung primary; 10% discordance between clinical and genomic relatedness leads to potential mistreatment; Multiple primaries show similar genomic divergence as tumors from different patients; Higher cumulative tobacco exposure associated with multiple lung primaries

metadata.speaker: Charlotte Grieco
metadata.talk_title: Genomic characterization of multiple primary lung cancers in TRACERx

text: Mouse Cancer Cell Line Atlas reveals tissue-specific KRAS dosage evolution | Speaker: Sebastian Mueller | Tumors: pancreatic cancer, lung cancer, intestinal cancer | MOA: Analysis of 590 mouse cancer cell lines shows that KRAS dosage increase (gain of a second mutant allele) is a common event across KRAS-driven tumors, occurring early in pancreatic cancer but later in lung and intestinal cancers, with tissue-specific dependencies on CDKN2A or Wnt pathway alterations. | Findings: Two-thirds of KRAS-driven mouse pancreatic cancers acquire a second mutant KRAS copy early in tumor evolution; KRAS dosage increase occurs late (carcinoma stage) in lung and intestinal KRAS-driven cancers; CDKN2A loss is required for KRAS dosage gain in pancreas but not in intestine or lung; Wnt pathway activation precedes KRAS amplification in intestinal tumors

metadata.speaker: Sebastian Mueller
metadata.talk_title: Mouse Cancer Cell Line Atlas reveals tissue-specific KRAS dosage evolution

text: Allele-specific KRAS mutation signatures in lung adenocarcinoma | Speaker: Colin Lindsay | Tumors: NSCLC | MOA: Signature analysis of 100k whole-genome lung adenocarcinomas shows smoking-associated SBS4 directly causes KRAS G12C, G12V, and G13C mutations, while clock-like signatures drive other KRAS variants, revealing subtype-specific mutational etiologies. | Findings: Smoking signature SBS4 directly implicated in KRAS G12C, G12V, G13C mutations; Clock-like signatures SBS5/40 associated with KRAS G12A, G12D, G13D, Q61H mutations; KRAS mutant tumors show higher smoking signature burden than KRAS-wt; Subtype-specific signature contributions suggest smoking does not drive all KRAS variants

metadata.speaker: Colin Lindsay
metadata.talk_title: Allele-specific KRAS mutation signatures in lung adenocarcinoma

text: Functional consequences of ecDNA versus HSR amplification architecture | Speaker: Elizabeth Brunk | Tumors: breast cancer, other solid tumors | MOA: Single-cell multi-omics of ecDNA- versus HSR-amplified cell lines shows that ecDNA dosage correlates tightly with gene expression and protein levels, with nonlinear transcriptional scaling for specific genes (e.g., PVT1), and that ecDNA heterogeneity is actively maintained through biased inheritance and growth advantage. | Findings: ecDNA-bearing cells display a broad 100‑1000 copy number range per cell, correlating with HER2 protein levels; Gene expression scaling with ecDNA dosage is stronger and more coordinated than in HSR cells; PVT1 transcriptional output and Myc program are highly dependent on ecDNA architecture; Sorted high‑ecDNA and low‑ecDNA populations reconverge to original distribution within 2‑3 generations via biased segregation and growth advantage

metadata.speaker: Elizabeth Brunk
metadata.talk_title: Functional consequences of ecDNA versus HSR amplification architecture

text: Single-cell dissection of lung adenocarcinoma to small cell transformation | Speaker: Joseph Chen | Tumors: lung cancer | MOA: Single-cell RNA and spatial profiling reveal that adenocarcinoma cells transition through a basal, hypoxia‑driven intermediate state before diverging to small‑cell neuroendocrine or squamous lineages, with FOX2B driving neuroendocrine reprogramming and loss of NOTCH signaling. | Findings: Transformed tumors display greater phenotypic diversity than de novo small cell; A basal intermediate state marked by NF‑κB, JAK‑STAT, hypoxia precedes neuroendocrine transformation; FOXF2B overexpression induces neuroendocrine markers and suppresses EGFR signaling; SDK1 and KEAP1 mutations may define a neuroendocrine‑to‑GI plasticity axis in large‑cell neuroendocrine carcinoma

metadata.speaker: Joseph Chen
metadata.talk_title: Single-cell dissection of lung adenocarcinoma to small cell transformation

text: Optical pooled CRISPRi screen identifies regulators of pancreatic cancer plasticity | Speaker: Nick Godzik | Tumors: pancreatic cancer | MOA: Lineage‑resolved optical pooled CRISPRi screening of ~900 perturbations in PDAC cells identifies H3K9 methyltransferases SUV39H1/2 as plasticity regulators that increase epithelial‑mesenchymal transitions via heterochromatin loss, distinct from classic EMT drivers. | Findings: ZEB1 knockdown biases cells toward epithelial state regardless of initial phenotype; GRL2 loss biases toward mesenchymal state; SUV39H1/2 loss enhances bidirectional plasticity, increasing state transitions; Dual‑guide approach enables detection of epistatic interactions (e.g., ZEB1 vs GRL2)

metadata.speaker: Nick Godzik
metadata.talk_title: Optical pooled CRISPRi screen identifies regulators of pancreatic cancer plasticity

text: Joint single-cell methylome and 3D genome profiling of glioma heterogeneity | Speaker: Yue Wu | Tumors: glioma, glioblastoma | MOA: Joint single-cell methylome and chromatin contact profiling of gliomas reveals asynchronous changes where 3D genome reorganization precedes DNA methylation shifts, identifies mismatched OPC‑like/astrocyte‑like states, and shows ecDNA subclones (e.g., EGFRvIII) associate with distinct methylation programs. | Findings: IDH‑mutant gliomas share clonal astrocyte‑like cells with 1p/19q codeletion; Mismatched methylation and 3D genome states suggest early chromatin remodeling during cell‑state transitions; ecDNA (EGFR, CDK4) present only in IDH‑wt GBM, with structural variants correlating with methylation subclones; Oncogene‑specific TF motif enrichment (MAPK for EGFR ecDNA, Hedgehog for GLI1 ecDNA) links ecDNA structure to epigenetic reprogramming

metadata.speaker: Yue Wu
metadata.talk_title: Joint single-cell methylome and 3D genome profiling of glioma heterogeneity

text: Gain-of-function molecular glues targeting transcription factors BCL6 and p53 | Speaker: Nathaniel Gray | Tumors: lymphoma, Ewing sarcoma | MOA: Chemically induced proximity glues recruit BRD4, CDK9, or p300 to transcription factors BCL6 or mutant p53, converting them from repressors to activators and triggering a broad pro‑apoptotic transcriptional program; analogous glues tether EWS‑FLI1 to BCL6 loci to rewire gene expression. | Findings: BCL6‑BRD4 TSIP activates a BCL6‑dependent reporter with EC50 ~5 nM via a hook‑shaped ternary complex.; BRD4 recruitment relocalizes to BCL6 loci, inducing NOXA and other apoptotic genes more potently than BCL6 loss.; In lymphoma xenografts with high BCL6, the TSIP suppresses tumor growth at modest doses, while BCL6‑low models are resistant.; TRAP‑1 (p53‑BRD4 glue) induces p21 and MDM2 expression in p53 Y220C cells, demonstrating gain‑of‑function activation.; dTag‑based glue redirects EWS‑FLI1 to BCL6 sites, upregulating SOX2 and illustrating programmable transcriptional rewiring.

metadata.speaker: Nathaniel Gray
metadata.talk_title: Gain-of-function molecular glues targeting transcription factors BCL6 and p53
