text: Digital pathology models AEON and Paladin for tumor subtyping and molecular alteration inference | Speaker: Kevin Boehm | Tumors: colorectal cancer, pancreatic cancer, urothelial carcinoma, breast cancer, glioma | MOA: AEON uses a knowledge graph–derived representation to infer 124 detailed tumor subtypes directly from H&E whole‑slide images, while Paladin conditions on each subtype to predict the presence of specific molecular alterations, demonstrating that digital pathology can capture phenotype‑genotype relationships for a subset of alterations (~4%). | Findings: AEON achieved an average one‑vs‑rest AUROC of 0.996 across 124 tumor subtypes in the internal MSK test set.; Multimodal integration of AEON with the GDENS genomic classifier improved performance in both primary and metastatic validation cohorts.; Paladin correctly identified 9 of 11 ovarian granulosa cell tumors and outperformed DeepHistology on most molecular alteration predictions.; Only ~4% of examined molecular alterations showed a strong phenotype‑genotype signal on H&E, confirming limited but actionable predictive value.; Digital pathology aided variant‑of‑unknown‑significance annotation, low‑purity sample inference, and phenocopy detection.

metadata.speaker: Kevin Boehm
metadata.talk_title: Digital pathology models AEON and Paladin for tumor subtyping and molecular alteration inference

text: Multi‑omic model for glioblastoma recurrence prediction centered on histopathology | Speaker: Julia Lowe | Tumors: glioblastoma | MOA: A pathology‑foundation model (UniHeal) is fine‑tuned to predict GBM recurrence time from H&E tiles, using MRI radiomics and clinical covariates as inputs, while spatial omics (Xenium, Codex) provide explainability by linking predictive tiles to gene‑program and immune‑cell signatures. | Findings: Preliminary cohort of 19 GBM patients shows that short‑recurrence tumors exhibit disrupted tissue architecture and necrosis, whereas long‑recurrence tumors retain normal segmentation.; UniHeal embeddings cluster tiles into biologically meaningful groups (e.g., necrotic vs. vascular regions).; Spatial alignment of Xenium and Codex data reveals that longer recurrence is associated with enhanced immune activity, while short recurrence shows immunosuppressive signatures.; A K‑means spatial domain analysis identified an oligodendrocyte‑enriched niche (cluster 8) with increased immune engagement in long‑recurrence tumors.

metadata.speaker: Julia Lowe
metadata.talk_title: Multi‑omic model for glioblastoma recurrence prediction centered on histopathology

text: Unified single‑cell and spatial atlas of prostate cancer progression | Speaker: Faming Zhao | Tumors: prostate cancer | MOA: Integration of >700 k single‑cell profiles across localized, metastatic, and neuroendocrine prostate cancer defines epithelial, immune, and stromal state trajectories, revealing SP1‑macrophage and mCAF‑centered immunosuppressive niches that drive progression and correlate with poor survival. | Findings: SP1‑macrophage expansion is associated with lymph‑node and bone metastasis and predicts worse overall survival.; mCAF enrichment co‑localizes with SP1‑macrophage in a stromal niche (CN7) linked to poor outcomes.; Anti‑SP1 treatment in bone‑metastasis mouse models reduced tumor burden, pain, and prolonged survival.; NEPC emergence aligns with specific epithelial lineage‑positive states and distinct transcription factor programs.

metadata.speaker: Faming Zhao
metadata.talk_title: Unified single‑cell and spatial atlas of prostate cancer progression

text: Deep learning profiling of regulatory somatic variants across clonal cancer evolution | Speaker: Ksenia Sokolova | Tumors: pan-cancer | MOA: A sequence‑based deep learning model (SAIE) predicts the regulatory impact of somatic variants by comparing reference and mutant genome embeddings across 40 learned sequence classes, enabling patient‑level regulatory disruption scores that correlate with progression‑free interval independent of mutational burden. | Findings: High regulatory disruption scores are associated with significantly worse progression‑free survival across TCGA pan‑cancer cohorts.; Severity of regulatory impact, not the number of regulatory variants, drives the prognostic signal.; Clonal versus subclonal disruption severity provides complementary prognostic information.; Six patient clusters based on disruption profiles show distinct pathway enrichments (e.g., immune vs. cell‑cycle).

metadata.speaker: Ksenia Sokolova
metadata.talk_title: Deep learning profiling of regulatory somatic variants across clonal cancer evolution

text: Spatial multi‑omics integration to guide glioblastoma surgery and engineered macrophage therapy | Speaker: Chibawanye Ene | Tumors: glioblastoma | MOA: Integrated spatial transcriptomics, proteomics, and mass‑spec imaging of glioblastoma core and edge identifies mesenchymal‑like and AC‑like cell states linked to TGF‑β–driven immunosuppression; engineered macrophages lacking TGF‑β receptors are designed to resist this suppression and improve therapeutic efficacy. | Findings: Mesenchymal‑like cell states are enriched in hypoxic tumor cores, while AC‑like cells produce TGF‑β2 that activates tumor‑associated macrophages.; SP1‑macrophage and mCAF co‑localization defines an immunosuppressive niche associated with poor survival.; MasSpec Pen can detect metabolic signatures of proliferating (Ki‑67+) tumor cells intra‑operatively, potentially guiding resection margins.; CRISPR‑KO of TGF‑β receptors in engineered macrophages reduces tumor burden and pain in a glioblastoma bone‑metastasis mouse model.

metadata.speaker: Chibawanye Ene
metadata.talk_title: Spatial multi‑omics integration to guide glioblastoma surgery and engineered macrophage therapy

text: ADT Norm: non‑parametric batch correction for single‑cell proteomics across technologies | Speaker: Ye Zhang | MOA: ADT Norm identifies negative and positive peaks in antibody‑derived tag (ADT) distributions using functional data analysis and aligns these landmarks across batches, removing technical variation while preserving biological cell‑type signals for downstream integration of CITE‑seq, CyTOF, and other single‑cell proteomics platforms. | Findings: ADT Norm aligns background and signal peaks across heterogeneous CITE‑seq batches, achieving superior batch mixing and cell‑type separation compared with SeR normalization.; The method quantifies antibody staining quality, flagging markers with poor signal‑to‑background separation.; An AI‑agent interface enables natural‑language driven parameter tuning for large‑scale multi‑technology integration.

metadata.speaker: Ye Zhang
metadata.talk_title: ADT Norm: non‑parametric batch correction for single‑cell proteomics across technologies

text: Foundation‑model‑driven MHC‑II peptide binding prediction with data‑efficient graph neural network | Speaker: Kamal Laughal | MOA: AlphaFold3 generates structural representations of peptide‑MHC‑II complexes, ESM2 provides sequence embeddings, and a graph neural network trained on low‑volume PepSeq binding data predicts peptide affinity, achieving state‑of‑the‑art performance with only ~2% of traditional training data. | Findings: The GNN model trained on 2% of the data matches or exceeds NetMHC‑II Pan performance on DRB1 alleles.; Zero‑shot AlphaFold3 scoring (Fisher score) provides moderate predictive power, but the GNN substantially improves AUC.; Orientation errors in AlphaFold3 predictions for HLA‑DP alleles reduce performance, suggesting a need for orientation‑aware modeling.; Training NetMHC‑II Pan on the same limited dataset yields a 10% lower AUC, confirming the data efficiency of the new approach.

metadata.speaker: Kamal Laughal
metadata.talk_title: Foundation‑model‑driven MHC‑II peptide binding prediction with data‑efficient graph neural network

text: Spatial metabolomics and microdevice delivery to map intratumoral drug responses | Speaker: Sean Davidson | Tumors: prostate cancer, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, breast cancer | MOA: Implantable microdevices release drugs locally; MALDI imaging visualizes spatial drug distribution and metabolic changes. In KRAS‑mutant tumors, inhibition of macropinocytosis with EIPA reduces intracellular amino acids, confirming nutrient acquisition via protein uptake. Metabolomic signatures (purine catabolites, lipid profiles) correlate with immune cell neighborhoods, enabling prediction of immune states from metabolites alone. | Findings: EIPA delivery via microdevice decreased tumor amino‑acid levels in KRAS‑mutant xenografts, confirming macropinocytosis‑driven nutrient uptake.; DQ‑BSA fluorescence showed lysosomal processing of extracellular protein in KRAS‑mutant but not KRAS‑wildtype cells.; Spatial metabolomics identified two macrophage metabolic states: purine‑rich (pro‑inflammatory) versus lipid‑rich (pro‑tumor).; Logistic regression on metabolite data predicted immune neighborhoods with ROC AUC >0.85, suggesting metabolites can serve as surrogate immune biomarkers.; Microdevice can co‑deliver diverse agents (small molecules, base editors, antisense oligos, ADCs) with release kinetics tuned by PEG molecular weight.

metadata.speaker: Sean Davidson
metadata.talk_title: Spatial metabolomics and microdevice delivery to map intratumoral drug responses

text: Implantable microdevice platform for intratumoral pharmacodynamics and precision treatment selection | Speaker: Dr. Unknown | Tumors: glioblastoma, cutaneous T‑cell lymphoma, head and neck cancer, prostate cancer, bladder cancer, pan‑cancer (solid tumors) | MOA: The grain‑of‑rice sized implantable microdevice contains ~20 reservoirs delivering micro‑doses of drugs directly into the tumor for 3–5 days. Spatial gradients of drug concentration are measured by MALDI‑MS or fluorescence, while parallel readouts (IHC, spatial transcriptomics, CyTOF) capture pharmacodynamic effects on tumor cells, immune subsets, and signaling pathways, enabling rapid prediction of systemic response and mechanistic biomarker discovery. | Findings: Implantable microdevices were placed in >350 patients across 13 trials with no serious adverse events.; Local drug concentration gradients correlated with apoptosis (cleaved caspase‑3) and proliferation inhibition (PCNA) in GBM xenografts.; Spatial transcriptomics confirmed on‑target pathway inhibition for osimertinib (EGFR), lapatinib (HER2/EGFR), everolimus (mTOR), and abemaciclib (cell‑cycle).; In a pilot GBM cohort, microdevice‑derived biomarkers predicted clinical temozolomide response in 5/5 patients, outperforming MGMT methylation status.; Interferon response programs were strongly associated with high‑efficacy temozolomide zones, suggesting a role for innate immunity in alkylator sensitivity.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Unknown
metadata.talk_title: Implantable microdevice platform for intratumoral pharmacodynamics and precision treatment selection

text: Granulocyte reprogramming in gastric metaplasia and phosphodiesterase inhibition as neoadjuvant therapy | Speaker: Juanita Merchant | Tumors: gastric adenocarcinoma | MOA: Helicobacter infection induces type I interferon production by plasmacytoid dendritic cells, which together with Hedgehog signaling up‑regulates SLFN4 in granulocytic neutrophils, converting them into suppressive MDSCs that consume L‑arginine via arginase‑1 and maintain low cyclic GMP through PDE6 activity. Inhibition of PDE6 with tadalafil or sildenafil raises intracellular cGMP, activates PKG, and triggers apoptosis of these MDSCs, restoring CD8 T‑cell function and enhancing response to standard FLOT chemotherapy. | Findings: Glee1 knockout mice retain normal gastric architecture despite Helicobacter infection, implicating Glee1‑positive myeloid cells in metaplasia.; SLFN4 expression marks granulocytic MDSCs; knockdown of SLFN4 increases apoptosis and reduces T‑cell suppression in vitro.; IL1B overexpression plus MNU yields gastric tumors in 45‑90% of mice; sildenafil treatment reduces tumor size and SLFN4‑positive cell infiltration.; In a human neoadjuvant window trial (n≈14), 2 weeks of tadalafil 20 mg daily decreased SLFN12L‑positive granulocytic MDSC frequency in tumor biopsies.; Subsequent FLOT chemotherapy after tadalafil further eliminated MDSCs and exhausted T‑cells while expanding cytotoxic CD8 T‑cells.

metadata.speaker: Juanita Merchant
metadata.talk_title: Granulocyte reprogramming in gastric metaplasia and phosphodiesterase inhibition as neoadjuvant therapy

text: Mechanistic insights into KRAS activation and novel direct KRAS inhibitors | Speaker: Frank McCormick | Tumors: pan-cancer | MOA: McCormick described a covalent inhibitor that targets a histidine-95 residue unique to KRAS, allowing binding to the GTP‑bound state and shifting the switch‑one region to an inactive state‑one conformation. He also presented a PI3K‑alpha “breaker” that blocks the Ras‑PI3K interaction, increasing affinity from ~20 µM to ~6 nM and preventing downstream signaling. | Findings: SHP2 phosphatase activity is dispensable for RAS activation, indicating a non‑catalytic role in SOS‑mediated signaling.; A covalent inhibitor targeting KRAS histidine‑95 can engage both GDP‑ and GTP‑bound KRAS, overcoming the limitation of off‑state inhibitors.; Binding of the inhibitor to the switch‑two pocket forces switch‑one into an unproductive state‑one conformation, blocking effector interactions.; The PI3K‑alpha breaker increases KRAS‑PI3K binding affinity to low‑nanomolar range, enabling selective disruption of KRAS‑driven PI3K signaling.; Structural studies reveal distinct conformations of RAF activation complexes that may be exploitable for next‑generation RAF inhibitors.

metadata.speaker: Frank McCormick
metadata.talk_title: Mechanistic insights into KRAS activation and novel direct KRAS inhibitors

text: Clinical activity of the KRAS G12D inhibitor 3034 combined with EGFR blockade | Speaker: Cameron Pitt | Tumors: colorectal cancer, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, endometrial cancer, NSCLC | MOA: Pitt presented the allosteric KRAS inhibitor 3034, which binds the switch‑two pocket and forces switch‑one into an inactive conformation, thereby blocking effector signaling of both G12D and G12V mutants. When combined with EGFR inhibition (cetuximab), the regimen suppresses wild‑type KRAS amplification and upstream RTK feedback, leading to deep tumor regressions and >90% ctDNA clearance in KRAS‑mutant colorectal, pancreatic, and endometrial cancers. | Findings: 3034 monotherapy slowed tumor growth in KRAS G12D HPAC xenografts but did not induce regression.; Combination of 3034 with cetuximab produced tumor regressions in the majority of mice and deep partial responses in patients.; ≥90% reduction in KRAS G12D ctDNA correlated with radiographic responses across colorectal, pancreatic, and endometrial cohorts.; No increase in cetuximab‑related rash or Grade ≥3 adverse events observed with the combination.; Acquired resistance manifested as KRAS wild‑type amplification after ~300 days of therapy, highlighting a limitation of the current inhibitor’s coverage of wild‑type KRAS.

metadata.speaker: Cameron Pitt
metadata.talk_title: Clinical activity of the KRAS G12D inhibitor 3034 combined with EGFR blockade

text: Preclinical and early clinical evaluation of a pan‑KRAS on/off state inhibitor (3034) | Speaker: Cameron [last name not provided] | Tumors: endometrial cancer, colorectal cancer, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, NSCLC | MOA: The oral pan‑KRAS inhibitor 3034 binds both the inactive and active states of KRAS, suppressing downstream MAPK signaling and shifting the tumor microenvironment toward immune activation while reducing immunosuppressive signals, leading to tumor growth inhibition and shrinkage that can be enhanced by EGFR blockade. | Findings: Endometrioid endometrial cancer patients showed robust and durable responses despite co‑occurring PI3K pathway alterations.; Combination of 3034 with cetuximab prevented outgrowth observed with monotherapy in preclinical models.; Preclinical mouse studies demonstrated tumor shrinkage at low oral doses (10‑30 mg) with reduced gastrointestinal adverse events compared with earlier KRAS inhibitors.

metadata.speaker: Cameron [last name not provided]
metadata.talk_title: Preclinical and early clinical evaluation of a pan‑KRAS on/off state inhibitor (3034)

text: Clinical development of multi‑selective KRAS tricomplex inhibitors (Deruxon Rasib) and combination strategies | Speaker: Mallika Singh | Tumors: NSCLC, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, colorectal cancer | MOA: Deruxon Rasib forms a tricomplex with cyclophilin A and KRAS, sterically blocking effector binding and stimulating GTP hydrolysis, thereby shutting down MAPK and PI3K signaling across multiple KRAS mutants; this dual mechanism yields tumor regression and induces immune activation without significant liver toxicity. | Findings: Resolute‑302 met its primary and secondary endpoints with a disease control rate of 95% in KRAS mutant patients.; PFS and OS curves showed lower confidence‑interval bounds exceeding those of standard second‑line chemotherapy, supporting a survival benefit.; Preclinical models demonstrated durable tumor regression and prevention of relapse when Deruxon Rasib was combined with covalent KRAS G12C inhibitor (Aleron) or G12D inhibitor (Zoldon).; Combination of Deruxon Rasib with gemcitabine/nab‑paclitaxel improved durability of response in pancreatic cancer models, informing the frontline RESOLUTE‑303 trial design.; Resistance mechanisms identified include amplification of the mutant KRAS allele (≈60% of resistant cases) and non‑genomic adaptations (~40%).

metadata.speaker: Mallika Singh
metadata.talk_title: Clinical development of multi‑selective KRAS tricomplex inhibitors (Deruxon Rasib) and combination strategies

text: KEAP1-NRF2 mediated resistance to KRAS inhibition and glutamine metabolism targeting | Speaker: Wen-Hsun Chang | Tumors: pancreatic cancer, non-small cell lung cancer | MOA: Loss of KEAP1 stabilizes NRF2, reprogramming transcription and glutamine metabolism to confer resistance to KRAS G12D and pan‑RAS inhibitors; co‑inhibition of glutamine metabolism with DRP104 restores sensitivity in vitro and in vivo. | Findings: CRISPR screens identified KEAP1 knockout as a top driver of resistance to KRAS G12D (MRTX1133) and pan‑RAS (RMC7977) inhibitors.; KEAP1 KO cells show NRF2 and NQO1 up‑regulation and reduced sensitivity to KRAS inhibitors in both pancreatic and NSCLC models.; A glutamine antagonist (DRP104) combined with KRAS inhibitors suppresses tumor growth in three resistant in vivo models.; Patient and PDX datasets reveal higher expression of a KEAP1‑deficiency gene signature in KRAS inhibitor‑resistant cases.

metadata.speaker: Wen-Hsun Chang
metadata.talk_title: KEAP1-NRF2 mediated resistance to KRAS inhibition and glutamine metabolism targeting

text: Selective ULK1/2 inhibitor 2088 synergizes with KRAS pathway blockade | Speaker: Bail | Tumors: non-small cell lung cancer, pancreatic cancer, melanoma | MOA: The ULK1/2 inhibitor 2088 blocks autophagy initiation, enhancing the efficacy of KRAS pathway inhibitors (MEK or KRAS G12C inhibitors) by preventing drug‑tolerant persister cell emergence without clonal selection. | Findings: 2088 shows higher cellular affinity than existing ULK1 inhibitors in NanoBRET assays.; Combination of 2088 with trametinib (MEK inhibitor) or sotorasib (KRAS G12C inhibitor) yields strong synergy in NSCLC H2030 cells.; In vivo, 2088 plus sotorasib significantly improves tumor growth inhibition compared to monotherapy in Calu‑1 xenografts.; DNA barcode tracking indicates the combination delays clonal outgrowth and reduces drug‑tolerant persister populations.

metadata.speaker: Bail
metadata.talk_title: Selective ULK1/2 inhibitor 2088 synergizes with KRAS pathway blockade

text: Modeling acquired resistance to pan‑KRAS inhibitor RMC‑6236 in pancreatic cancer | Speaker: Di Zan | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma | MOA: KRAS Y64 mutations disrupt binding of the pan‑KRAS molecular glue RMC‑6236, conferring resistance; resistance can be overcome by MEK inhibition, suggesting downstream MAPK blockade as a viable combination. | Findings: Y64D mutation abolishes RMC‑6236 binding to KRAS and prevents tri‑complex formation with RAF.; KRAS Y64D engineered cell lines show >50‑fold increase in IC50 to RMC‑6236 compared with wild‑type.; In xenografts, Y64D tumors exhibit markedly reduced response to RMC‑6236 at both low and high doses.; MEK inhibitor restores sensitivity in Y64D mutant models, indicating downstream MAPK blockade can bypass resistance.

metadata.speaker: Di Zan
metadata.talk_title: Modeling acquired resistance to pan‑KRAS inhibitor RMC‑6236 in pancreatic cancer

text: Combining RAS inhibitors with ribonucleotide reductase inhibitor BBI 825 to prevent ecDNA‑driven resistance | Speaker: Silvia Polidoro | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: Inhibition of ribonucleotide reductase with BBI 825 limits nucleotide pools, suppressing ecDNA‑driven KRAS amplification and delaying or preventing resistance to KRAS inhibitors in colorectal cancer models. | Findings: Combination of BBI 825 with adagrasib or sotorasib completely prevented resistance emergence in ecDNA‑positive RW7213 cells.; BBI 825 suppressed KRAS amplification in resistant subclones and reduced MEK amplification in deraxurib‑treated cells.; In RW7213 xenografts, BBI 825 plus adagrasib markedly delayed tumor growth and lowered KRAS amplification frequency.; In CLR142 PDX, addition of BBI 825 enhanced efficacy of sotorasib plus cetuximab and reduced c‑MYC expression.

metadata.speaker: Silvia Polidoro
metadata.talk_title: Combining RAS inhibitors with ribonucleotide reductase inhibitor BBI 825 to prevent ecDNA‑driven resistance

text: JAK‑STAT pathway inhibition sensitizes KRAS G12D mutant pancreatic cancer to KRAS inhibitors | Speaker: Yi Zhao | Tumors: pancreatic cancer | MOA: KRKRAS G12D inhibition induces acute STAT3 activation via IL‑6 feedback; STAT3 inhibition restores sensitivity and synergizes with KRAS inhibitors in resistant pancreatic cancer models. | Findings: Acquired KRAS G12D inhibitor‑resistant PDAC cells display up‑regulated JAK1/STAT3 signaling.; An oral STAT3 inhibitor selectively kills KRAS‑resistant cells and synergizes with KRAS G12D inhibitor in vitro.; Combination of KRAS inhibitor and STAT3 inhibitor leads to durable tumor regressions in KPC CDX models, overcoming relapse seen with KRAS inhibitor alone.; JAK1 inhibitor tofacitinib also blocks phospho‑STAT3 and enhances KRAS inhibitor efficacy.

metadata.speaker: Yi Zhao
metadata.talk_title: JAK‑STAT pathway inhibition sensitizes KRAS G12D mutant pancreatic cancer to KRAS inhibitors

text: VEGFR2 blockade overcomes KRAS G12D inhibitor resistance driven by PI3Kγ activation | Speaker: Sung Yun Wong | Tumors: gastrointestinal cancers, pancreatic cancer | MOA: Acquired resistance to KRAS G12D inhibition activates a KRAS‑PI3Kγ‑AKT‑SP1 axis that drives VEGF‑A secretion and autocrine VEGFR2 signaling; VEGFR2 blockade with DC101 restores sensitivity. | Findings: Resistant PDOs show increased VEGF‑A expression and phospho‑VEGFR2 activation.; CRISPR‑mediated VEGFR2 knockout or DC101 treatment sensitizes resistant cells to MRTX1133.; PI3Kγ inhibition reduces VEGF‑A/VEGFR2 signaling and re‑sensitizes resistant models.; Combination of MRTX1133 with DC101 markedly suppresses tumor growth in multiple resistant xenograft models.

metadata.speaker: Sung Yun Wong
metadata.talk_title: VEGFR2 blockade overcomes KRAS G12D inhibitor resistance driven by PI3Kγ activation

text: KRAS G12C inhibition induces chromosomal instability creating a vulnerability to Aurora kinase A inhibition | Speaker: Chendu Li | Tumors: non-small cell lung cancer | MOA: KRAS G12C inhibition induces DNA damage and micronuclei formation in a subset of NSCLC cells, activating ATR/ATM pathways that stabilize cyclin B1; Aurora kinase A inhibition forces mitotic catastrophe in these cells. | Findings: KRAS G12C inhibitor LY3499446 induces variable DNA damage and micronuclei across NSCLC lines.; Aurora kinase A inhibitor LSN3321213 shows the strongest synergy with KRAS G12C inhibition, especially in micronuclei‑high cells.; Combination treatment leads to prolonged G2/M arrest and mitotic catastrophe, markedly reducing colony formation.; In vivo, low‑dose AURKA inhibition combined with KRAS G12C inhibitor produces tumor regression and extends relapse‑free survival.

metadata.speaker: Chendu Li
metadata.talk_title: KRAS G12C inhibition induces chromosomal instability creating a vulnerability to Aurora kinase A inhibition

text: TAP2 downregulation drives immune evasion and can be therapeutically reversed | Speaker: Kurt Sch"alper | Tumors: lung cancer, colorectal cancer, brain metastases | MOA: Downregulation of TAP2 in lung cancer cells reduces antigen presentation modestly (10‑15% peptide loss) but more critically impairs interferon‑γ signaling via upregulation of the inhibitor SOX1 and suppression of chemokines (CXCL10, CCL5, CXCL11), leading to T‑cell exclusion. IL‑4 produced by tumor‑associated myeloid cells epigenetically silences TAP2, an effect reversible by IL‑4R blockade or epigenetic drugs (HDAC inhibitors, taxanes). Restoring TAP2 re‑sensitizes cells to cytokine signaling and tumor‑antigen specific killing. Separately, secreted factors such as PLA2G10 act as active T‑cell excluders, limiting lymphocyte migration and promoting tumor growth; blocking these molecules restores T‑cell infiltration. | Findings: 24% of treatment‑naïve lung cancers show cancer‑cell selective TAP2 downregulation; only 6% show TAP1 loss.; Low TAP2 expression predicts an 80% increased risk of death (HR 1.8) after immunotherapy, with no effect on chemotherapy outcomes.; TAP2 knockout reduces tumor‑antigen specific CD8 T‑cell killing more than TAP1 loss; re‑expression of TAP2 rescues killing.; TAP2 loss leads to a 10‑15% reduction in total HLA‑bound peptides but causes a >50% decrease in interferon‑γ‑induced gene expression (e.g., IDO1, PD‑L1) via SOX1 up‑regulation.; IL‑4 secreted by CD11b+ myeloid cells epigenetically closes the TAP2 promoter, an effect not reversed by exogenous IFN‑γ/TNF‑α.

metadata.speaker: Kurt Sch"alper
metadata.talk_title: TAP2 downregulation drives immune evasion and can be therapeutically reversed

text: Chromatin redistribution of Rb reveals estrogen‑response activation by CDK4/6 inhibition | Speaker: Shyam | Tumors: hormone receptor‑positive breast cancer | MOA: CDK4/6 inhibition dephosphorylates Rb, causing widespread chromatin binding; beyond canonical E2F repression, Rb is recruited to active enhancers of estrogen‑responsive genes, enhancing their expression (including cyclin D1), which can blunt cell‑cycle arrest unless blocked by endocrine therapy. | Findings: CDK4/6 inhibition increases chromatin‑bound Rb at >10,000 sites, 75% at promoters and many at active enhancers.; Rb binding at non‑promoter enhancers is associated with increased H3K27ac and up‑regulation of nearby estrogen‑response genes.; CRISPR disruption of Rb‑bound enhancers attenuates estrogen‑response gene induction and cyclin D1 protein up‑regulation.; Combining CDK4/6 inhibitors with endocrine therapy yields deeper suppression of cell‑cycle genes and prevents cyclin D1‑mediated resistance.

metadata.speaker: Shyam
metadata.talk_title: Chromatin redistribution of Rb reveals estrogen‑response activation by CDK4/6 inhibition

text: Programmable RNA sensors for cancer‑specific fusion targeting | Speaker: Nolan Prettykid | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: ADAR‑mediated RNA editing sensors are programmed to bind cancer‑specific fusion breakpoints; upon editing a stop‑codon in the guide, translation of a downstream cytotoxic payload (e.g., iCaspase9) is enabled, selectively killing fusion‑positive cells. | Findings: Linear and gap RNA sensors selectively activate reporter expression in cells harboring the target fusion RNA.; In MCF7 cells with an endogenous ARFGAP2‑SOX2 fusion, gap sensors drive mNeon fluorescence with >10‑fold specificity over fusion‑negative MCF10A.; Fusion‑targeted sensors coupled to iCaspase9 reduce MCF7 viability to ~80% versus ~100% for non‑targeting controls.; High‑throughput sensor library screening begins to define design rules for effective RNA‑sensor constructs.

metadata.speaker: Nolan Prettykid
metadata.talk_title: Programmable RNA sensors for cancer‑specific fusion targeting

text: Systems design challenges and technology opportunities for clinical trial enrollment | Speaker: Laura Mangravite | MOA: Mangravite described the clinical trial enrollment problem as a two‑sided optimization issue, outlining public and private data‑centric solutions, the $2 billion private investment landscape, and the need for many‑to‑many trial‑patient visibility, buyer‑driven optimization, and vertical integration of platform technologies. | Findings: Only ~7% of cancer patients enroll in trials, whereas ~8% would be needed to fill open slots.; Approximately 50% of trials fail to meet enrollment targets.; Public data sources (e.g., ClinicalTrials.gov, TEFCA) provide trial listings but lack granular inclusion/exclusion criteria.; Private sector investment in trial‑matching technologies exceeds $2 billion, roughly matching public investment.; Current solutions are fragmented (within‑system vs. cross‑system) and often expose patients to only a subset of available trials.

metadata.speaker: Laura Mangravite
metadata.talk_title: Systems design challenges and technology opportunities for clinical trial enrollment

text: Clinical trial matching, nudges, and AI: practical experiences and future directions | Speaker: Debra Schrag | MOA: Schrag presented the evolution of clinical trial matching nudges at MSK—from first‑generation email alerts to second‑generation progression‑timed nudges (which showed modest, non‑significant accrual gains)—and outlined a vision for third‑generation AI‑driven, EHR‑integrated, multi‑modal workflows that combine eligibility prescreening with immediate patient‑facing actions such as video consent and scheduling. | Findings: MSK’s first‑generation nudge system sends daily email alerts about potential trial matches based on genomic profiling.; A randomized trial of progression‑timed nudges showed a small, non‑significant increase in accrual (a few percentage points).; Clinician time and health‑system money were identified as the top barriers to trial accrual.; Patient trust, rather than travel logistics, was highlighted as the primary barrier to enrollment.; Telehealth, video‑informed consent, and home‑based monitoring were proposed as operational solutions to reduce patient burden.

metadata.speaker: Debra Schrag
metadata.talk_title: Clinical trial matching, nudges, and AI: practical experiences and future directions

text: Serial Plasma Comprehensive Genomic Profiling Detects Therapy Resistance and Guides Management of Metastatic Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer | Speaker: William Bowers | Tumors: NSCLC | MOA: Serial plasma comprehensive genomic profiling (PCGP) using Guardant 360 detects actionable and resistance alterations (e.g., EGFR, MET, EGFR T790M, C797S, BRAF) in metastatic NSCLC, enabling genotype‑matched therapy selection and demonstrating that ctDNA detectability correlates with overall survival. | Findings: 37% of NSCLC patients had an actionable alteration on first plasma PCGP.; In treatment‑naive patients, 36% harbored FDA‑approved genotype‑matched alterations.; 22% of treatment‑naive patients started genotype‑matched therapy within 30 days of plasma result.; Undetectable ctDNA was associated with significantly longer overall survival versus detectable ctDNA.; Patients receiving genotype‑matched therapy based on plasma findings had significantly improved overall survival.

metadata.speaker: William Bowers
metadata.talk_title: Serial Plasma Comprehensive Genomic Profiling Detects Therapy Resistance and Guides Management of Metastatic Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer

text: Feasibility of Plasma ctDNA for Detecting Brain Metastasis Specific Alterations in Lung Cancer | Speaker: Dr. Stabile | Tumors: NSCLC | MOA: Plasma ctDNA profiling detects MET amplifications, which are enriched in lung cancer brain metastases; radiation may enhance ctDNA shedding, improving detection of brain‑specific alterations. | Findings: MET amplification is significantly more common in lung cancer brain metastases (16.4%) than in primary tumors (3.7%).; Plasma ctDNA detects MET amplifications in ~10% of patients at progression, but concordance with tissue is limited.; In paired pre‑ and post‑craniotomy samples, only 1 of 2 tissue MET amplifications were captured in plasma.; Radiation therapy appears to increase ctDNA shedding, leading to higher VAF/CNV signals post‑radiation.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Stabile
metadata.talk_title: Feasibility of Plasma ctDNA for Detecting Brain Metastasis Specific Alterations in Lung Cancer

text: AXL mRNA Overexpression in CTCs as a New Potential Liquid Biopsy Biomarker in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer | Speaker: Evi Leonido | Tumors: NSCLC | MOA: AXL mRNA overexpression in size‑enriched circulating tumor cells (CTCs) is detected by RT‑qPCR and rises after osimertinib exposure, suggesting a role in EMT‑mediated resistance and providing a potential biomarker for selecting AXL‑targeted therapies. | Findings: AXL mRNA is overexpressed in CTCs of ~13% of NSCLC patients at baseline and increases after the first osimertinib cycle.; AXL overexpression persists in a subset of patients at disease progression, indicating a possible resistance mechanism.; During anti‑PD‑1 therapy, AXL overexpression emerges in a few patients, suggesting adaptive resistance.; CTC‑derived AXL expression provides complementary information to ctDNA and tissue analyses.

metadata.speaker: Evi Leonido
metadata.talk_title: AXL mRNA Overexpression in CTCs as a New Potential Liquid Biopsy Biomarker in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer

text: Circulating Tumor Cell‑Informed Pipeline for Rapid Personalization of Synergistic Cytokine‑Armed CAR‑NK Cell Therapy in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma | Speaker: Yin Zhu | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma | MOA: CTC enrichment via a microfluidic Labyrinth device identifies mesothelin or MUC4 expression, guiding selection of cytokine‑armed CAR‑NK cells (IL‑12/IL‑15) that synergistically enhance NK activation, granzyme B release, and long‑term tumor killing in PDAC models. | Findings: 87% of PDAC patients had CTCs expressing at least one CAR‑NK target (mesothelin or MUC4).; MUC4‑positive CTCs were enriched in metastatic patients.; IL‑12 and IL‑15 armed CAR‑NK cells achieved near‑complete tumor eradication in 2D killing assays and eliminated spheroids by day 12.; Synergistic cytokine‑armed CAR‑NK cells provided superior tumor suppression and survival benefit in mouse models compared with conventional CAR‑NK.

metadata.speaker: Yin Zhu
metadata.talk_title: Circulating Tumor Cell‑Informed Pipeline for Rapid Personalization of Synergistic Cytokine‑Armed CAR‑NK Cell Therapy in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma

text: ctDNA Clearance Dynamics in MSI‑High Colorectal Cancer Treated with Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors | Speaker: Hannah Robinson | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: Longitudinal tumor‑informed ctDNA monitoring (Signatera) in MSI‑high metastatic colorectal cancer reveals that early and sustained ctDNA clearance after immune checkpoint inhibitor initiation predicts markedly improved overall survival. | Findings: 73% of MSI‑high mCRC patients were ctDNA positive before ICI therapy.; 77% achieved ctDNA clearance at least once after ICI start, median time 96 days.; Early clearance (<4 months) occurred in 44% and correlated with 4‑year OS of 95% vs 81% for ctDNA‑positive patients.; Any clearance conferred a 10‑fold OS advantage (95.5% vs 66.1% 4‑yr OS).; Sustained clearance (≥6 months) was observed in 63% of patients.

metadata.speaker: Hannah Robinson
metadata.talk_title: ctDNA Clearance Dynamics in MSI‑High Colorectal Cancer Treated with Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors

text: Genomic Signatures in Red Blood Cell DNA‑Enabled Early Non‑Invasive Detection of Colorectal Neoplasia | Speaker: Xinyu Yao | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: Red blood cell‑associated DNA fragments, released during erythropoiesis under tumor‑induced genotoxic stress, carry distinct genomic coverage patterns that differ between colorectal cancer patients and healthy controls, enabling a sequencing‑based classifier to detect advanced neoplasia with high accuracy. | Findings: RBC DNA fragments are shorter (avg 4.3 kb) than genomic DNA but longer than cfDNA.; Distinct genome‑wide coverage patterns differentiate CRC patients from healthy donors.; A binary classifier achieved AUC 0.95, 85% sensitivity for advanced adenomas and 95% for CRC at 90% specificity.; Performance remained robust across external validation cohorts and was not confounded by blood counts or lifestyle factors.; In a prospective head‑to‑head comparison, RBC‑DNA testing outperformed FIT for detecting advanced adenomas and Stage 1 CRC.

metadata.speaker: Xinyu Yao
metadata.talk_title: Genomic Signatures in Red Blood Cell DNA‑Enabled Early Non‑Invasive Detection of Colorectal Neoplasia

text: CUPIA 2 collaborative multi-agent LLM for cancer of unknown primary diagnosis | Speaker: Kai Wang | Tumors: pan-cancer | MOA: CUPIA 2 uses a multi-agent large language model ensemble to ingest NGS variant data and generate tissue-of-origin predictions with rationale derived from a 100,000-patient Smart Data database, achieving ~77% top‑1 accuracy internally and ~62% on independent MSK data. | Findings: CUPIA 2 achieved 77% top‑1 accuracy and 93% top‑3 accuracy across 19 cancer types in internal validation.; On independent MSK cohort (12,000 samples) top‑1 accuracy was 62% and top‑3 accuracy 82%.; Model provided rationale linking co‑mutations (e.g., KRAS G12D + TP53 R175H) to predicted tissue origins.; Chairman LLM overwrote 24% of ensemble predictions during training.

metadata.speaker: Kai Wang
metadata.talk_title: CUPIA 2 collaborative multi-agent LLM for cancer of unknown primary diagnosis

text: Deep learning model predicts palbociclib response in ER+ HER2‑ negative advanced breast cancer | Speaker: Akshat Singhal | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: A visible neural network maps genomic alterations to hierarchical protein complexes, enabling prediction of palbociclib sensitivity; the model stratifies patients into sensitive (HR 0.38, median PFS +14 mo) and resistant groups, with specificity for CDK4/6 inhibition versus endocrine therapy alone. | Findings: PalboVNN stratified UCSD patients (n=36) into responders vs non‑responders with HR 0.38 and median PFS benefit of 14 months.; In the larger MSK cohort (n=474) the model retained significance (HR 0.56) with an 18‑month median PFS advantage.; Model performance was specific to palbociclib‑containing regimens and did not stratify letrozole‑only patients.; Interpretation identified 18 protein assemblies (11 shared) driving predictions, including DNA integrity and AKT signaling.; A prospective phase‑II trial has been launched based on these findings.

metadata.speaker: Akshat Singhal
metadata.talk_title: Deep learning model predicts palbociclib response in ER+ HER2‑ negative advanced breast cancer

text: AI‑derived H&E biomarkers predict survival under immunotherapy vs chemotherapy in NEPTUNE NSCLC trial | Speaker: Chintan Parmar | Tumors: non-small cell lung cancer | MOA: PathAI's off‑the‑shelf AI model segments tumor, immune and fibroblast compartments on H&E slides, quantifies densities and spatial relationships, and these features improve survival stratification beyond PD‑L1 and TMB, especially predicting benefit from immunotherapy. | Findings: Fibroblast density was a negative prognostic marker in both IO and chemo arms (high density → worse OS).; Immune cell density showed a predictive interaction: high density correlated with improved OS only in the immunotherapy arm.; Multivariate Cox model adding H&E features to PD‑L1/TMB achieved significant separation (p<0.05) whereas clinical features alone did not.; At 18‑month follow‑up, high‑risk group defined by H&E features had 21% event rate, supporting enrichment potential.

metadata.speaker: Chintan Parmar
metadata.talk_title: AI‑derived H&E biomarkers predict survival under immunotherapy vs chemotherapy in NEPTUNE NSCLC trial

text: Deep learning predicts metabolic pathway activity from routine H&E slides | Speaker: Pahini Pandya | MOA: A ResNet34 encoder‑decoder network is trained on 256 × 256 H&E tiles paired with binary metabolic pathway activity derived from patient‑specific genome‑scale metabolic models (GSMMs) built from TCGA transcriptomics, enabling prediction of pathway enrichment directly from morphology. | Findings: Across 21 cancer types, 87% of 450 pathway‑cancer models achieved AUC > 0.5.; 9% of models (top 10 pathways) reached AUC 0.65–0.85, notably nucleotide metabolism (AUC 0.85 in TGCT) and nuclear transport (AUC 0.79 in COAD).; Metabolic pathways with high predictability clustered in nucleotide synthesis, nuclear/mitochondrial transport, and fatty‑acid β‑oxidation.; Demonstrated feasibility of using H&E morphology to infer functional metabolic states, suggesting utility for trial enrichment.

metadata.speaker: Pahini Pandya
metadata.talk_title: Deep learning predicts metabolic pathway activity from routine H&E slides

text: Longitudinal fusion of low‑dose CT improves lung cancer risk prediction | Speaker: Hanieh Ajami | Tumors: non-small cell lung cancer | MOA: Multiple low‑dose CT scans are processed by the Sybil model to extract encoded and attention features; these are fused via vision and temporal transformers (Hybrid) or concatenated (Bi/ Tri‑fusion) to produce six‑year risk scores, leveraging temporal disease progression for improved discrimination. | Findings: Hybrid architecture achieved near‑perfect AUC (0.99) at year 1 and maintained 0.94 at year 6 on NLST test set.; Hybrid model outperformed Bi‑fusion and Tri‑fusion across all horizons and also generalized to external Moffitt cohort after fine‑tuning.; Statistical tests confirmed significant performance differences (p < 0.05) between hybrid and other models.; Model handles missing time points via attention masking, making it applicable to real‑world screening data.

metadata.speaker: Hanieh Ajami
metadata.talk_title: Longitudinal fusion of low‑dose CT improves lung cancer risk prediction

text: Multimodal deep learning predicts gastric cancer response to first‑line anti‑PD‑1 therapy | Speaker: Jingyuan Wang | Tumors: gastric cancer | MOA: A self‑attention fusion network combines CT‑derived radiomic features, H&E‑derived graph‑based pathomic embeddings, and clinical variables to predict first‑line chemo‑immunotherapy response; high predicted PR status correlates with increased tumor fraction, up‑regulated immune‑activating pathways, and improved survival. | Findings: CRT model achieved AUC 0.97 for response prediction in training set and validated across two external cohorts.; Predicted PR patients had significantly longer PFS and OS (HR ≈ 0.45–0.48) after multivariate adjustment for age, sex, PD‑L1 CPS.; Pathway analysis showed enrichment of immune‑activating signatures (alpha/gamma response) in predicted PR group versus immune‑inhibitory pathways (IL‑10, NF‑κB) in non‑PR group.; Model outperformed PD‑L1 CPS and unimodal radiomics or pathomics models in precision‑recall and confusion matrix metrics.

metadata.speaker: Jingyuan Wang
metadata.talk_title: Multimodal deep learning predicts gastric cancer response to first‑line anti‑PD‑1 therapy

text: Lipid-associated macrophages as therapeutic targets and CAR‑monocyte strategy | Speaker: Jennifer Guerrero | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: PARP inhibition induces cGAS‑STING activation and CD8 T‑cell recruitment but simultaneously expands lipid‑associated, CSF1R‑ and TREM2‑positive macrophages that suppress immunity; anti‑CSF1R synergizes with PARP inhibition to double survival in mice, and a TREM2‑directed CAR‑monocyte platform is designed to phagocytose and eliminate these suppressive macrophages while secreting pro‑inflammatory cytokines. | Findings: Olaparib treatment of BRCA‑deficient mice increased tumor‑infiltrating macrophages expressing PD‑L1, CSF1R, CD36 and TREM2.; Anti‑CSF1R combined with olaparib doubled median overall survival from ~100 to ~200 days in the mouse model, an effect dependent on CD8 T cells.; TREM2‑CAR monocytes specifically phagocytosed TREM2‑positive target cells in vitro, whereas irrelevant CARs did not.; In vivo, a single IV dose of TREM2‑CAR monocytes increased intratumoral CD8 T cells and reduced tumor burden by ~50% in a breast cancer model, further enhanced by anti‑PD‑1.; The AXLAP phase 1b trial (axcitilimab + olaparib) is >50% enrolled in metastatic HER2‑negative, BRCA1/PALB2‑mutated breast cancer, enabling correlative studies of macrophage modulation.

metadata.speaker: Jennifer Guerrero
metadata.talk_title: Lipid-associated macrophages as therapeutic targets and CAR‑monocyte strategy

text: Redefining myeloid states in glioma with CNMF and organoid platforms | Speaker: Tyler Miller | Tumors: glioblastoma, brain tumor | MOA: Consensus non‑negative matrix factorization (CNMF) decomposes glioma single‑cell RNA‑seq into identity and activity programs, revealing four dominant myeloid activity programs (systemic inflammatory, microglial inflammatory, dexamethasone‑driven immunosuppressive, hypoxia‑driven scavenger); the scavenger program predicts poor response to checkpoint blockade and CAR‑T therapy, while the microglial inflammatory program correlates with response. | Findings: CNMF identified 14 myeloid programs across glioma, with four activity programs accounting for >90% of cells.; The scavenger immunosuppressive program (hypoxia‑linked) was enriched in non‑responders to checkpoint blockade and CAR‑T therapy.; Microglial inflammatory program was enriched in responders and associated with improved overall survival.; CAR‑T infusion induced a dose‑dependent surge of the complement immunosuppressive program in CSF myeloid cells across all patients.; Baseline high scavenger program levels in CSF predicted worse overall survival after CAR‑T treatment.

metadata.speaker: Tyler Miller
metadata.talk_title: Redefining myeloid states in glioma with CNMF and organoid platforms

text: Clinical targeting of immunosuppressive macrophages: lessons from IL‑4, IL‑1 and checkpoint combos | Speaker: Thomas Moran | Tumors: non‑small cell lung cancer, colorectal cancer, breast cancer, pan‑cancer | MOA: IL‑4Rα blockade with dupilumab interrupts tumor‑derived type II cytokine signaling that imprints immunosuppressive IL‑4‑responsive macrophages in the bone marrow, restoring anti‑tumor immunity in a subset of PD‑1‑refractory NSCLC patients; combined IL‑1α/β inhibition (anakinra) further disrupts inflammasome‑driven myeloid suppression, enhancing checkpoint efficacy in preclinical models of lung, colorectal and pancreatic cancer. | Findings: Dupilumab added to ongoing PD‑1 blockade induced remission and complete pain relief in a patient with progressive NSCLC.; Approximately one‑third of PD‑1‑refractory NSCLC patients achieved disease control after three dupilumab doses, allowing continuation of checkpoint therapy.; IL‑4 neutralization reduced emergency myelopoiesis and tumor‑associated macrophage accumulation in KRAS‑mutant mouse lung cancer.; Combined IL‑4Rα and PD‑1 blockade synergistically reduced tumor burden in KP1 mouse model compared with either monotherapy.; Dual IL‑1α/β blockade (anakinra) suppressed age‑related inflammasome activation and tumor growth in old mouse models of colorectal and pancreatic cancer.

metadata.speaker: Thomas Moran
metadata.talk_title: Clinical targeting of immunosuppressive macrophages: lessons from IL‑4, IL‑1 and checkpoint combos

text: Engineering next‑generation CAR T cells: membrane, signaling, and armoring strategies | Speaker: Remus | Tumors: multiple myeloma, B‑cell ALL, B‑cell lymphoma, solid tumors | MOA: Remus described engineering of CAR T cells by optimizing membrane residence, hinge, transmembrane, and intracellular signaling domains, and by adding armoring payloads (e.g., cytokine secretion, PD‑1/FAS/CD200 re‑programming) to improve persistence, reduce exhaustion, and modulate the tumor microenvironment. | Findings: Kinase‑inhibitor “metronomic rest” improves CAR T memory phenotype (Ramos et al.).; Self‑clustering of Cilta‑cel‑like CARs drives cytokine release and neurotoxicity in vitro, which can be mitigated by selecting non‑clustering VHH binders.; Bispecific/tandem CARs (e.g., CD19/CD20) show variable efficacy depending on transmembrane and co‑stimulatory domain configuration.; Armoring with IL‑18 or anti‑PD‑1 scFv linked to IL‑12 improves tumor control in murine models.; TGF‑β during manufacturing preserves central‑memory phenotype and enhances in vivo persistence of CAR T cells.

metadata.speaker: Remus
metadata.talk_title: Engineering next‑generation CAR T cells: membrane, signaling, and armoring strategies

text: Innate bridge cell engineering: gamma‑delta T cells for cancer therapy | Speaker: Trent Spencer | Tumors: neuroblastoma, osteosarcoma, glioblastoma, T‑ALL, pediatric AML | MOA: Spencer outlined the use of ex vivo expanded Vδ1 and Vδ2 gamma‑delta T cells, which recognize phosphoantigens (via butyrophilin‑mediated TCR signaling), stress ligands (NKG2D), and mediate ADCC (CD16), and described strategies to enhance memory phenotype (TGF‑β during expansion) and to combine with chemotherapy, zoledronate, and dinutuximab for synergistic tumor killing. | Findings: Allogeneic gamma‑delta T cells can be expanded from donors without causing graft‑versus‑host disease.; Donor fitness (exercise, age) correlates with expansion potential and CD16 expression.; TGF‑β during manufacturing preserves central‑memory phenotype and markedly improves in vivo persistence and osteosarcoma killing.; Triple combination (temozolomide + zoledronate + dinutuximab) with gamma‑delta T cells yields superior neuroblastoma killing in preclinical models.; BiTE or CAR expression in gamma‑delta T cells achieves comparable cytotoxicity to conventional alpha‑beta CAR T cells.

metadata.speaker: Trent Spencer
metadata.talk_title: Innate bridge cell engineering: gamma‑delta T cells for cancer therapy

text: In vivo lentiviral vector CAR delivery platform (VivoVEC) and RACR armoring | Speaker: Ryan Larsen | Tumors: B‑cell lymphoma, CLL, ALL, multiple myeloma, solid tumors (exploratory) | MOA: Larsen presented VivoVEC, a surface‑engineered lentiviral vector displaying a multi‑domain fusion (anti‑CD3 scFv, CD80, CD58) that binds T cells with high avidity, delivers a CAR transgene and a rapamycin‑activated cytokine receptor (RACR) that provides selective IL‑2/IL‑15‑like signaling upon rapamycin administration, enabling in vivo generation, expansion, and functional persistence of CAR T cells without lymphodepletion. | Findings: Multi‑domain fusion particles achieve rapid (≤10 min) high‑avidity binding to human T cells in vitro.; Co‑stimulatory‑enhanced particles generate polyfunctional CAR T cells with superior serial killing versus anti‑CD3‑only particles.; In NSG MHC‑KO humanized mice, particles encoding anti‑CD19 CAR produce durable tumor control at low vector doses.; In cynomolgus macaques, a single IV dose yields ~40% CAR‑positive T cells, peaks at days 7‑10, and induces rapid, complete B‑cell depletion.; Transient low‑grade CRS observed; no severe infusion reactions despite high in vivo transduction.

metadata.speaker: Ryan Larsen
metadata.talk_title: In vivo lentiviral vector CAR delivery platform (VivoVEC) and RACR armoring

text: Spatial omics workflow and challenges for neuroimmune characterization | Speaker: Logan Walsh | MOA: Described the development and benchmarking of cell segmentation tools and hierarchical phenotyping pipelines for spatial transcriptomics and proteomics, emphasizing the importance of accurate nucleus and membrane segmentation to correctly assign immune phenotypes in tumor sections. | Findings: Developed Circle Cell Segmentation Across Scales (CCSAS) tool that outperforms existing segmentation methods qualitatively and quantitatively.; Implemented a ranked hierarchy pixel‑by‑pixel classification approach for immune phenotyping that improves cell type assignment compared with simple dimensionality reduction.; Demonstrated that accurate segmentation dramatically impacts downstream spatial analyses such as pairwise cell interaction and cellular neighborhood quantification.

metadata.speaker: Logan Walsh
metadata.talk_title: Spatial omics workflow and challenges for neuroimmune characterization

text: Spatial transcriptomics of perineural invasion in pancreatic cancer and PDGFD‑PDGFRB functional validation | Speaker: Will Wang | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma | MOA: Spatial transcriptomics identified PDGFD enrichment in cancer cells adjacent to nerves; functional assays showed PDGFD‑PDGFRB signaling promotes perineural invasion by enhancing cancer cell invasiveness, neurite outgrowth, and Schwann‑cell mediated tumor migration, which can be blocked by PDGFRB inhibition. | Findings: A bulk RNA‑derived classifier predicts perineural invasion and uncovered missed PNI cases on histology.; Spatial profiling revealed PDGFD‑PDGFRB as the only ligand‑receptor pair overlapping between sequencing‑based (GeoMx) and imaging‑based (SMI) datasets.; CRISPR activation of PDGFD in PDAC organoids increased 3D neural invasion index, which was dose‑dependently blocked by the PDGFRB inhibitor SU16f.; Recombinant PDGFD stimulates neurite outgrowth from DRG neurons; this effect is abolished by PDGFRB inhibition.; In vivo, PDGFD overexpression augments orthotopic tumor nerve invasion, while PDGFRB inhibition reduces sciatic nerve invasion.

metadata.speaker: Will Wang
metadata.talk_title: Spatial transcriptomics of perineural invasion in pancreatic cancer and PDGFD‑PDGFRB functional validation

text: Integrating spatial neuroimmune signatures with bulk RNA to predict immunotherapy resistance | Speaker: Amit (Dr. Amit) | Tumors: skin cancer, head and neck cancer, pancreatic cancer, melanoma, gastric cancer | MOA: Bulk RNA signatures of nerve injury and neurodegeneration are enriched in tumors that fail anti‑PD‑1 therapy; spatial profiling links these signatures to immunosuppressive microenvironments (e.g., FoxP3+ Tregs, myeloid cells) around injured nerves, suggesting nerve‑mediated resistance mechanisms. | Findings: Half of anti‑PD‑1 non‑responders exhibited histologic perineural invasion, whereas responders had significantly lower rates.; Bulk RNA‑seq of non‑responders showed enrichment of nerve injury pathways (ATF3, C‑JUN) and neurodegeneration GO terms.; Applying neurodegeneration signatures to TCGA head‑and‑neck cohort stratified patients by survival, with high‑signature tumors having worse outcomes.; Spatial profiling demonstrated co‑localization of nerve injury markers with immunosuppressive cells (FoxP3+ Tregs, myeloid cells) but not with effective anti‑tumor immune signatures.; NanoString GeoMx analysis confirmed that nerve‑adjacent regions in non‑responders express higher checkpoint molecules (PD‑L1, CTLA‑4) compared with responders.

metadata.speaker: Amit (Dr. Amit)
metadata.talk_title: Integrating spatial neuroimmune signatures with bulk RNA to predict immunotherapy resistance

text: Targeting Telomeres in Cancer and Aging | Speaker: Maria Blasco | Tumors: NSCLC, glioblastoma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia | MOA: Blasco's work demonstrates that extending telomere length via TERT gene therapy or ultra‑long telomere chimeric mice prolongs lifespan and reduces cancer incidence in mice, while telomere shortening drives fibrosis in lung and kidney. Mutations in the shelterin component POT1 act either as dominant‑negative (causing short telomeres and fibrosis) or gain‑of‑function (producing abnormally long but fragile telomeres that predispose to cancer). Inhibition of the shelterin protein TRF1, whose stability is regulated by PI3K/Akt‑mediated phosphorylation, impairs tumor growth in lung cancer and glioblastoma mouse models without overt toxicity, establishing TRF1 as a druggable telomere‑protective target. | Findings: Mice engineered to carry ultra‑long telomeres live significantly longer and develop 40% fewer spontaneous tumors compared with wild‑type controls.; AAV‑mediated, non‑integrative TERT gene therapy administered at 1 yr or 2 yr of age extends median lifespan by ~15% and markedly reduces progression of bleomycin‑induced pulmonary fibrosis.; POT1 knock‑in mice recapitulate human telomere‑biology disease phenotypes: short telomeres, multi‑telomeric FISH signals, reduced litter size, intestinal and testicular atrophy, and accelerated lung and kidney fibrosis.; Genetic or pharmacologic inhibition of TRF1 reduces tumor burden by ~50% in KRAS‑driven lung cancer and glioblastoma mouse models without increasing normal tissue toxicity.; TRF1 stability is controlled by Akt‑mediated phosphorylation at threonine 330; phospho‑dead (T330A) mice exhibit shorter telomeres, increased DNA damage, and higher papilloma formation after chemical carcinogenesis, whereas phospho‑mimetic (T330E) mice maintain longer telomeres but display rapid telomere attrition in adult tissues.

metadata.speaker: Maria Blasco
metadata.talk_title: Targeting Telomeres in Cancer and Aging

text: Dendritic cell mitochondrial metabolism regulates anti-tumor immunity | Speaker: Hongbo Qi | Tumors: melanoma, lung adenocarcinoma, osteosarcoma, pancreatic cancer | MOA: Qi identified that cDC1 cells in tumors exist in two mitochondrial states; OPA1 drives mitochondrial fusion and high oxidative phosphorylation, enabling superior T cell priming. Loss of OPA1 impairs mitochondrial cristae, reduces oxidative phosphorylation, and diminishes anti‑tumor immunity. NRF1 acts downstream of OPA1 to regulate electron transport chain genes, and its overexpression partially rescues OPA1 deficiency. | Findings: cDC1 cells display mitochondrial high and low populations across multiple tumor models (B16, lung, osteosarcoma, pancreatic).; Mitochondrial‑high cDC1 have higher oxidative phosphorylation, ATP production, and superior ability to prime CD8 T cells in vitro and in vivo.; Tumor progression shifts cDC1 toward the mitochondrial‑low, dysfunctional state, reducing T cell priming capacity.; Adoptive transfer of mitochondrial‑high cDC1 slows tumor growth and synergizes with anti‑PD‑L1, anti‑CTLA‑4, and anti‑PD‑1 therapies, leading to durable immunity upon rechallenge.; OPA1 is up‑regulated in tumor‑infiltrating cDC1; its conditional knockout impairs mitochondrial cristae, oxidative phosphorylation, and anti‑tumor immunity, leading to uncontrolled tumor growth in multiple models.

metadata.speaker: Hongbo Qi
metadata.talk_title: Dendritic cell mitochondrial metabolism regulates anti-tumor immunity

text: BACH1 drives tumor‑intrinsic immune evasion in triple‑negative breast cancer | Speaker: Long Nguyen | Tumors: triple-negative breast cancer | MOA: BACH1 acts as a transcriptional repressor that silences type I interferon genes (e.g., IFI21) in TNBC cells; loss of BACH1 derepresses interferon signaling, increases CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration and activation, reduces lung metastasis, and improves response to checkpoint blockade, whereas BACH1 overexpression promotes immune‑evasive, hypoxia‑driven cell states. | Findings: A transition cell state (20‑30% of tumor cells) links proliferative, invasive, and hypoxic clusters and predicts T‑cell exclusion in TNBC.; BACH1 is identified as a top regulator of this transition state; knockout reduces the transition population, overexpression expands it.; High BACH1 activity signature correlates with poor response to pembrolizumab + chemotherapy and low TILs in I‑SPY and other TNBC cohorts.; BACH1 knockout in mouse TNBC models increases CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration, activation, and reduces lung metastasis; phenotype rescued by BACH1 re‑expression.; Mechanistically, BACH1 directly binds and represses IFI21 (type I IFN) locus; loss of BACH1 elevates type I IFN signaling, enhancing anti‑tumor immunity.

metadata.speaker: Long Nguyen
metadata.talk_title: BACH1 drives tumor‑intrinsic immune evasion in triple‑negative breast cancer

text: Temporal dynamics of PD‑1 blockade reveal drug holidays and CD22 as a co‑inhibitory target | Speaker: John Wherry | MOA: Continuous PD‑1 blockade chronically enhances TCR signaling in progenitor exhausted T cells, eroding their capacity to generate intermediate effector‑like exhausted cells and leading to functional decline. A drug holiday restores this capacity, allowing a second wave of reinvigoration. Long‑term PD‑1 loss induces up‑regulation of CD22 on progenitor exhausted cells, providing an additional negative feedback; blocking CD22 (or using a PD‑1×CD22 bispecific) restores intermediate exhausted cell expansion and improves viral control and tumor suppression. | Findings: Short‑term PD‑1 blockade yields a transient T cell reinvigoration peak; continuous blockade does not improve long‑term outcomes compared with short‑term treatment.; A drug holiday (2‑week treatment, 2‑month washout, re‑treatment) produces a second robust reinvigoration, leading to better viral control in chronic LCMV infection.; Continuous PD‑1 blockade depletes the intermediate exhausted T cell population (CD63⁺) while preserving terminally exhausted cells.; Progenitor exhausted T cells exposed to long‑term PD‑1 blockade up‑regulate CD22, a B‑cell inhibitory receptor that dampens TCR signaling.; Anti‑CD22 antibody or PD‑1×CD22 bispecific restores intermediate exhausted cell expansion and improves disease control in both viral and tumor models.

metadata.speaker: John Wherry
metadata.talk_title: Temporal dynamics of PD‑1 blockade reveal drug holidays and CD22 as a co‑inhibitory target

text: Mechanisms of resistance to direct KRAS inhibitors and combinatorial strategies | Speaker: Kevin Ostrem | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, non-small cell lung cancer, colorectal cancer | MOA: Allele‑specific KRAS G12C covalent inhibitors selectively bind mutant KRAS, sparing wild‑type KRAS and T cells, while checkpoint blockade releases PD‑1 mediated inhibition, together enabling immune recognition of shared neoantigens and leading to durable tumor regressions. | Findings: KRAS G12C covalent inhibitors achieve ~80% disease control in KRAS G12C NSCLC patients but relapses are common.; In mouse models, a minor resistant G12D subpopulation expands under G12C inhibition, limiting response.; Combining a KRAS G12C inhibitor with anti‑PD‑1 therapy increases complete response rate to ~45% versus 7% with inhibitor alone.; Mice achieving complete responses reject rechallenge with 100% G12D tumors, indicating immune memory.

metadata.speaker: Kevin Ostrem
metadata.talk_title: Mechanisms of resistance to direct KRAS inhibitors and combinatorial strategies

text: Intrinsic mechanisms of resistance to KRAS inhibitors and rational combination strategies | Speaker: Chiara Ambrogio | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, colorectal cancer, non-small cell lung cancer | MOA: Allele‑specific KRAS G12C inhibitors bind the mutant cysteine pocket, while upstream SOS1 inhibition or downstream MEK inhibition provides vertical blockade of MAPK signaling, overcoming intrinsic resistance mechanisms such as KEAP1 or SMARCA4 co‑alterations. | Findings: Combination of KRAS G12C inhibitor with SOS1 inhibitor yields superior tumor regression in KRAS G12D mouse models compared with monotherapy.; KRAS G12C plus MEK inhibitor produces the greatest tumor shrinkage among tested combinations.; Preclinical data support ongoing clinical trials testing KRAS inhibitor + SOS1 or MEK inhibitor combinations.

metadata.speaker: Chiara Ambrogio
metadata.talk_title: Intrinsic mechanisms of resistance to KRAS inhibitors and rational combination strategies

text: Hippo‑YAP/TAZ pathway as an adaptive resistance mechanism and therapeutic target | Speaker: Silvio Gutkind | Tumors: uveal melanoma, cutaneous melanoma, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma | MOA: Inhibition of MAPK signaling triggers rapid down‑regulation of RND3, relieving suppression of RhoA and activating FAK‑YAP/TAZ signaling, which drives adaptive resistance; combined FAK inhibition and TEAD disruption synergize with KRAS or MEK inhibitors to suppress tumor growth and restore immune infiltration. | Findings: MEK inhibition leads to loss of RND3 within 24 h, causing rapid YAP target gene up‑regulation.; FAK inhibitor defactinib combined with a TEAD inhibitor produces tumor regressions in uveal melanoma models where each agent alone is cytostatic.; In mouse models, the combination restores CD8+ T‑cell infiltration and improves survival compared with monotherapy.; Hippo‑YAP activation also induces chemokines (CXCL1, CXCL5, CXCL8) that recruit immunosuppressive myeloid cells.

metadata.speaker: Silvio Gutkind
metadata.talk_title: Hippo‑YAP/TAZ pathway as an adaptive resistance mechanism and therapeutic target
tumor_types: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma

text: HA-based biomaterial models reveal ROS and hyaluronidase driven glioblastoma invasion | Speaker: Dr. Sanjay Kumar | Tumors: glioblastoma | MOA: Glioblastoma cells invade hyaluronic acid-rich brain matrix via CD44 engagement; leader cells secrete HYAL2 to locally degrade HA, creating paths for follower cells, and ROS signaling via the transsulfuration pathway supports invasion, which can be limited by targeting this pathway. | Findings: HA-based 3D invasion device enables separation of invasive rim and core GBM cells for comparative analysis.; Invasive GBM cells show enrichment of ROS and transsulfuration pathway genes, matching patient tumor data.; Leader GBM cells deposit a trail of HYAL2, degrading HA and facilitating faster follower cell invasion.; Inhibition of hyaluronidase activity or genetic targeting of the transsulfuration pathway reduces GBM invasion in vitro.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Sanjay Kumar
metadata.talk_title: HA-based biomaterial models reveal ROS and hyaluronidase driven glioblastoma invasion

text: Stiffness-driven Twist nuclear translocation via G3BP2 and TYK2 in triple‑negative breast cancer | Speaker: Dr. Valerie Weaver | Tumors: triple negative breast cancer | MOA: In stiff extracellular matrices, TYK2 dissociates from interferon‑R1 and becomes cytosolic, allowing LIN kinase to phosphorylate Twist1 on a specific tyrosine, releasing Twist from G3BP2 anchoring and driving its nuclear translocation, which triggers EMT and invasion; TYK2 inhibition mimics stiffness loss, promoting invasion even on soft matrices via the same Twist pathway. | Findings: Stiff ECM induces nuclear translocation of Twist1 without changing its protein level.; G3BP2 binds Twist1 in soft ECM, preventing nuclear entry; stiffness‑dependent phosphorylation by LIN releases Twist.; TYK2 membrane localization is lost on stiff matrices, acting as a metastasis suppressor; TYK2 inhibition drives invasion on soft matrices.; TYK2 deletion or inhibition increases lung dissemination of TNBC PDX without affecting primary tumor size.; Twist deletion abrogates the invasive phenotype induced by TYK2 loss, confirming epistatic relationship.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Valerie Weaver
metadata.talk_title: Stiffness-driven Twist nuclear translocation via G3BP2 and TYK2 in triple‑negative breast cancer

text: One Gene at a Time: Metabolic Adaptations Driving Metastatic Growth in Pancreatic Cancer | Speaker: Dr. Matuszewski | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma | MOA: The lab identified metastasis‑specific metabolic genes (GSTT1, SLC30A4, MAT2A) that are up‑regulated in PDAC liver and lung metastases and are required and sufficient for metastatic colonization; GSTT1 drives extracellular matrix remodeling via fibronectin glutathionylation, SLC30A4 mediates serine uptake addiction, and MAT2A translocates to the nucleus to produce SAM for chromatin methylation in metastatic cells. | Findings: GSTT1 is absent in primary PDAC but highly expressed in liver and lung metastases and its knockout abolishes metastatic outgrowth while primary tumor growth is unaffected; GSTT1 overexpression induces ectopic metastases in multiple organs and promotes fibronectin secretion via glutathione conjugation; SLC30A4 is specifically up‑regulated in metastatic lesions, and its loss impairs 3D colony formation and metastatic colonization; overexpression increases serine uptake and rescues growth in serine‑depleted conditions; MAT2A shifts from cytoplasmic to nuclear localization in metastatic cells, supporting nuclear SAM production for histone methylation; nuclear MAT2A is required for metastatic growth

metadata.speaker: Dr. Matuszewski
metadata.talk_title: One Gene at a Time: Metabolic Adaptations Driving Metastatic Growth in Pancreatic Cancer

text: Targeting IMPDH2 and Ferroptosis to Suppress Metastatic Pancreatic Cancer | Speaker: Dr. Pankaj Singh | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma | MOA: IMPDH2 is overexpressed in PDAC metastases and drives purine biosynthesis; chronic mycophenolic acid (MPA) exposure induces resistance via up‑regulation of glutathione metabolism (SLC7A11, GPX4); co‑targeting ferroptosis (RSL3) or cystine uptake (sulfasalazine) restores MPA sensitivity and markedly reduces metastatic burden in mouse models. | Findings: IMPDH2 expression is high in primary and metastatic PDAC and correlates with poor patient survival; Long‑term MPA exposure selects for PDAC cells with increased glutathione metabolism (up‑regulation of SLC7A11, GPX4) and a 20‑fold increase in IC50; Sulfasalazine sensitizes MPA‑resistant cells to MPA in vitro and modestly reduces tumor burden in vivo; Combination of MPA with the ferroptosis inducer RSL3 enhances cell killing and decreases liver metastasis size in mouse splenic injection models

metadata.speaker: Dr. Pankaj Singh
metadata.talk_title: Targeting IMPDH2 and Ferroptosis to Suppress Metastatic Pancreatic Cancer

text: NUDT5‑PPAT Interaction Controls Purine Biosynthesis Switch and Thiopurine Sensitivity | Speaker: Dr. Raul Ramos | MOA: NUDT5 binds PPAT via its R70 residue, promoting PPAT tetramerization and suppressing de novo purine synthesis; loss of NUDT5 or disruption of the NUDT5‑PPAT interaction maintains PPAT in an active dimeric state, rendering cells resistant to thiopurines and de novo pathway inhibitors. | Findings: NUDT5 deficiency confers resistance to 6‑thioguanine and to de novo pathway inhibitors (methotrexate, leflunomide); NUDT5 directly interacts with PPAT; the R70A mutation abolishes binding without affecting catalytic activity; Wild‑type NUDT5 (or catalytic dead) induces PPAT tetramerization and reduces its enzymatic activity by ~80% in vitro; In xenografts, tumors expressing NUDT5‑binding‑defective PPAT remain resistant to 6‑TG, whereas WT NUDT5 restores drug sensitivity

metadata.speaker: Dr. Raul Ramos
metadata.talk_title: NUDT5‑PPAT Interaction Controls Purine Biosynthesis Switch and Thiopurine Sensitivity

text: Targetable Metabolite Increases Neuronal Hyperexcitability in Glioma Microenvironment | Speaker: Khalil Abdullah | Tumors: glioma | MOA: Elevated guanosine acetate (GAA) accumulates in glioma due to AGAT/GAMT imbalance, acts on GABA_A receptors in tumor‑infiltrated brain where KCC2 is downregulated, increasing neuronal hyperexcitability and tumor growth; AGAT knockout reduces GAA secretion and prolongs survival without affecting in‑vitro cell fitness. | Findings: GAA is the most overabundant metabolite in high‑grade glioma compared to normal brain (563 metabolites screened).; AGAT expression correlates with glioma grade; AGAT knockout mice show increased survival despite unchanged tumor growth in flank.; GAA induces neuronal hyperexcitability via GABA_A receptors; effect is blocked by gabazine and KCC2 agonist CLP257.; Dietary ornithine supplementation with arginine restriction lowers tumor GAA and extends survival, mimicking AGAT knockout.; A surgical window trial will enroll 12 patients to test ornithine supplementation and arginine‑restricted diet pre‑operatively.

metadata.speaker: Khalil Abdullah
metadata.talk_title: Targetable Metabolite Increases Neuronal Hyperexcitability in Glioma Microenvironment

text: Targeting Mitochondrial Complex I Overcomes Adaptive Response to Chemotherapy in Advanced Pancreatic Cancer | Speaker: Sergio Attanasio | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma | MOA: Chemotherapy induces mitochondrial fission and OXPHOS up‑regulation in PDAC clones; IM‑156, a potent Complex I inhibitor, blocks this adaptive respiration, increases oxidative stress, impairs clonogenic regrowth, and eradicates relapse‑associated clones when combined with gemcitabine/nab‑paclitaxel. | Findings: Clonal barcoding identified ~12% of PDAC clones driving gemcitabine relapse.; Chemotherapy‑responsive clones upregulate OXPHOS and mitochondrial fission (phospho‑DRP1).; IM‑156 more potent than metformin/phenformin, inhibits OCR at 10 µM without lactic acidosis.; Gemcitabine + IM‑156 prolongs regrowth delay, increases apoptosis, and reduces relapse‑clone frequency in mice.; Phase 1/2 trial (n=18) showed 50% partial responses, 80% disease control, median PFS 6 mo, OS 18 mo, with acceptable safety at 400 mg PO daily.

metadata.speaker: Sergio Attanasio
metadata.talk_title: Targeting Mitochondrial Complex I Overcomes Adaptive Response to Chemotherapy in Advanced Pancreatic Cancer

text: Estrogen Therapy Alleviates Cancer‑Associated Cachexia in Mouse Models | Speaker: Gang Huang | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, melanoma, lung cancer | MOA: LKB1 loss drives HIF‑2α‑mediated cytokine secretion and severe cachexia; HIF‑2α inhibition (rezotibib) rescues fat and muscle but worsens anemia, which can be corrected with EPO. Estrogen (E2) restores mitochondrial TCA activity, suppresses glycolysis, and reverses systemic catabolism, preserving body composition in male cachectic mice. | Findings: KPL mice develop rapid weight loss, fat and muscle wasting, and anemia despite tumor size similar to KP controls.; HIF‑2α inhibition with rezotibib restores body weight, fat, and muscle but induces anemia due to reduced EPO.; E2 pellet treatment in cachectic male mice maintains body weight, fat, and muscle, normalizing serum catabolic metabolites.; Estrogen reprograms peripheral tissues: upregulates OXPHOS/TCA, downregulates proteolysis pathways in muscle and adipose.; Ovariectomy abolishes female protection from cachexia, indicating ovarian hormone dependence.

metadata.speaker: Gang Huang
metadata.talk_title: Estrogen Therapy Alleviates Cancer‑Associated Cachexia in Mouse Models

text: Ketogenic Diet Sensitizes Pancreatic Cancer to Metabolic Therapies | Speaker: Omid Hajihassani | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma | MOA: Ketogenic diet forces glycolytic PDAC cells to rely on TCA cycle and induces hepatic glutamine overproduction; tumors upregulate glutamine transporters and enzymes, becoming glutamine‑addicted; concurrent inhibition of glutamine metabolism (CB‑839 or DON) synergizes with the diet to suppress tumor growth. | Findings: Ketogenic diet slows tumor growth and extends mouse survival but does not eradicate tumors.; Tumors on ketogenic diet show increased TCA cycle metabolites and a 4‑fold rise in intratumoral glutamine.; Isotope tracing shows tumor does not synthesize glutamine de novo; liver produces excess glutamine under low‑protein ketogenic diet.; Glutamine transporter and utilization enzymes are upregulated in ketogenic‑diet tumors.; Combination of ketogenic diet with glutaminase inhibitor CB‑839 or DON yields greater tumor suppression than either alone.

metadata.speaker: Omid Hajihassani
metadata.talk_title: Ketogenic Diet Sensitizes Pancreatic Cancer to Metabolic Therapies

text: Metabolic Changes Associated with Senescence in CAFs Regulate Fibrosis in Pancreatic Cancer | Speaker: Devashi Sen | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma | MOA: Senescent myofibroblasts upregulate mitochondrial αKG production via IDH2/3, providing substrate for collagen prolyl/lysyl hydroxylases, leading to thicker collagen fibers and enhanced fibrosis in PDAC; targeting IDH2/3 may blunt this pro‑fibrotic program. | Findings: Senescent CAFs (P16+ α‑SMA+) increase tumor collagen deposition and fiber thickness.; Senescent CAFs display higher mitochondrial content but lower per‑mitochondrion membrane potential.; Metabolomics shows accumulation of glycolytic intermediates and early TCA metabolites (citrate, αKG) with reduced downstream TCA metabolites.; IDH2 and IDH3 expression is upregulated in senescent CAFs, suggesting enhanced αKG production for collagen hydroxylation.; Depletion of senescent cells (Ink‑Tag model) reduces collagen abundance in PDAC tumors.

metadata.speaker: Devashi Sen
metadata.talk_title: Metabolic Changes Associated with Senescence in CAFs Regulate Fibrosis in Pancreatic Cancer

text: Targeting Metabolism in BRCA‑Deficient Tumors via PKM2 Activation | Speaker: Myra Di Tano | Tumors: breast cancer, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer | MOA: BRCA2 loss induces PKM1 overexpression, creating a high pyruvate kinase state; pharmacologic activation of PKM2 (mitapivat) further drives pyruvate flux, causing mitochondrial oxidative stress, impaired mitophagy, and selective death of BRCA‑deficient cells. | Findings: BRCA2 loss upregulates PKM1 (constitutively active) while PKM2 remains unchanged.; PKM2 activator (dasatinib or mitapivat) selectively kills BRCA2‑KO cells and increases γH2AX.; Overexpression of PKM1 in WT cells sensitizes them to PKM2 activation, confirming PKM1’s role.; In vivo, mitapivat (400 mg PO daily) delays growth of BRCA2‑KO tumors without weight loss or organ toxicity.; PKM activation reduces glucose oxidation in TCA cycle, downregulates ETC complexes, and impairs PINK1‑mediated mitophagy, leading to mitochondrial superoxide accumulation.

metadata.speaker: Myra Di Tano
metadata.talk_title: Targeting Metabolism in BRCA‑Deficient Tumors via PKM2 Activation

text: Stromal microenvironment signatures predict bone metastasis in prostate cancer | Speaker: Massimo Loda | Tumors: prostate cancer, pancreatic cancer, breast cancer | MOA: Loda's group identified a bone‑like stromal gene signature in primary prostate tumors, driven by periostin‑rich cancer‑associated fibroblasts that arise via epithelial‑to‑stromal signaling (loss of AR motifs, gain of AP1 motifs) and promote neuroendocrine differentiation and bone organotropism. | Findings: A stromal osteomimicry signature, including periostin, distinguishes high‑grade prostate tumors that metastasize to bone.; Periostin is enriched in neuroendocrine prostate cancer stroma and colocalizes with αVβ3/αVβ5 integrin signaling.; Mouse models recapitulate human stromal changes; fibroblast clusters acquire AP1 motifs and lose AR/GR motifs.; Co‑culture of periostin‑expressing fibroblasts or recombinant periostin induces neuroendocrine differentiation (FOXA2) in organoids.; Spatial analysis shows reduced distance between periostin‑positive fibroblasts and neuroendocrine cells in bone metastases versus primary tumors.

metadata.speaker: Massimo Loda
metadata.talk_title: Stromal microenvironment signatures predict bone metastasis in prostate cancer
