text: Metabolic dependencies drive organ‑specific metastasis in breast cancer | Speaker: George Poulogiannis | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: Poulogiannis demonstrated that organ‑specific metabolic environments create unique dependencies: brain metastases rely on de novo fatty‑acid synthesis (FASN), lung metastases on pyruvate carboxylase, and bone metastases on glutaminolysis (GLS1), making these enzymes tractable therapeutic targets. | Findings: Metabolic gene signatures predict overall metastatic potential with 86% accuracy; metabolic‑only features improve prediction.; Organ‑specific dependencies identified: FASN in brain, PC in lung, GLS1 in bone metastases.; Bone‑metastatic clones exhibit heightened glutamine uptake, increased GLS1 activity, and sensitivity to GLS1 inhibitor CBA39.; Depleting serine/glycine reduces metastasis in bone, kidney, ovary but not in brain, liver, lung.; Integrated MetaboForm platform infers tumor metabolomes from transcriptomics, revealing distinct metabolic landscapes across metastatic sites.

metadata.speaker: George Poulogiannis
metadata.talk_title: Metabolic dependencies drive organ‑specific metastasis in breast cancer

text: CTC heterogeneity and TMPO as a driver of metastasis in prostate cancer | Speaker: Cory Barret Shen | Tumors: prostate cancer | MOA: Shen showed that TMPO (LAP2) sustains a hypoxia‑driven transcriptional program in large CTC‑derived organoids, promoting survival in circulation and bone colonization; TMPO knockdown shifts cells toward oxidative phosphorylation, reduces organoid size, CTC numbers, and bone metastasis without affecting primary tumor growth. | Findings: CTC burden correlates tightly (R>0.9) with metastatic score in GEM mice.; Single CTCs can be cultured into organoids; organoid size segregates into hypoxic (large) vs. ox‑phos (small) phenotypes.; TMPO knockdown does not affect primary tumor growth but reduces circulating CTCs and bone metastasis in both subcutaneous and intracardiac models.; TMPO activity correlates with hypoxia signatures and organoid size; loss of TMPO shifts metabolism toward oxidative phosphorylation.; Human CRPC CTCs show high nuclear TMPO co‑expressed with lamin, supporting clinical relevance.

metadata.speaker: Cory Barret Shen
metadata.talk_title: CTC heterogeneity and TMPO as a driver of metastasis in prostate cancer

text: Colibactin-producing pks+ E. coli adhesion drives CRC in mouse models | Speaker: Lars Verbeke | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: pks+ E. coli adheres to intestinal epithelium via high‑affinity FimH/FimLH adhesins, positioning the unstable colibactin toxin in close proximity to host DNA where it cross‑links AT‑rich sequences, inducing a SBS88/ID18 mutational signature and driving colorectal tumorigenesis; pharmacologic blockade of FimH (Sibofimlock) reduces bacterial adhesion, colibactin‑induced DNA damage, and tumor development in germ‑free‑derived Zap2 mice. | Findings: Only mice colonized with the CRC isolate 11G5 (pks+, clbQ+) showed severe CRC phenotypes, whereas Nissle 1917 did not despite both being pks+.; Deletion of clbQ abolished the tumor‑promoting effect of 11G5, confirming colibactin dependence.; FimH or FimLH loss in 11G5 eliminated epithelial binding, γ‑H2AX induction, and CRC exacerbation.; High‑affinity 11G5 FimH variants restored binding and genotoxicity when expressed in Nissle, demonstrating variant‑specific adhesion strength.; Sibofimlock, a small‑molecule FimH inhibitor, dose‑dependently reduced bacterial adhesion and colibactin‑driven tumor development in vivo.

metadata.speaker: Lars Verbeke
metadata.talk_title: Colibactin-producing pks+ E. coli adhesion drives CRC in mouse models

text: Sulfur amino‑acid diet, Mucispirillum schaedleri and NKT‑XCL1‑CDC1 axis in colorectal cancer | Speaker: Wendy Garrett | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: A high sulfur‑amino‑acid diet thickens the colonic inner mucus layer, creating a niche for Mucispirillum schaedleri; this bacterium releases phospholipids that activate NKT cells to secrete XCL1, which in turn recruits and activates Batf3‑dependent CDC1 dendritic cells, enhancing CD8⁺ T‑cell cytotoxicity and reducing adenocarcinoma burden in Apc‑driven mouse models. | Findings: High sulfur amino‑acid diet increased inner mucus thickness without increasing goblet cell numbers.; M. schaedleri bloomed in high‑diet mice across three tumor models (MC38, ApcMin, orthotopic organoids).; Diet‑induced tumor protection was lost in Batf3‑KO mice lacking CDC1 dendritic cells.; Neutralizing XCL1 abolished the anti‑tumor benefit of the high diet, implicating NKT‑derived XCL1 as essential.; Conditioned media from M. schaedleri stimulated NKT cells to produce XCL1 in an MR1‑independent manner.

metadata.speaker: Wendy Garrett
metadata.talk_title: Sulfur amino‑acid diet, Mucispirillum schaedleri and NKT‑XCL1‑CDC1 axis in colorectal cancer

text: Intratumoral Fusobacterium nucleatum drives epithelial quiescence and therapy resistance | Speaker: Susan Bowman | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: Intratumoral Fusobacterium nucleatum localizes predominantly extracellularly, where its phospholipid components trigger epithelial MAPK activation and CXCL8 secretion, leading to a dose‑dependent G0/G1 cell‑cycle arrest (quiescence) without increasing proliferation; this quiescent state reduces 5‑FU efficacy and creates an immunosuppressive microenvironment characterized by myeloid infiltration and checkpoint up‑regulation. | Findings: Fusobacterium signals are mainly extracellular; bacterial load correlates with increased inter‑cellular spacing in tumor tissue.; High bacterial density regions show reduced Ki‑67 and a shift toward G0/G1 arrest in cancer cells (MOI ≥10).; In vitro, Fusobacterium exposure induces MAPK (p‑p38, FOSL) activation and CXCL8 secretion in a dose‑dependent manner.; Patients with high intratumoral Fusobacterium have lower major pathological response to neoadjuvant 5‑FU therapy.; Clade 2 (F. animalis sensu stricto) dominates CRC tumors and possesses acid‑resistance (GAD) and ethanolamine utilization genes, suggesting selective fitness.

metadata.speaker: Susan Bowman
metadata.talk_title: Intratumoral Fusobacterium nucleatum drives epithelial quiescence and therapy resistance

text: Neuroinflammatory memory drives gastric tumorigenesis via vagal sensory neurons and ILC2 | Speaker: Yi Zheng | Tumors: gastric cancer | MOA: Vagal sensory neurons retain an inflammatory memory after gastric injury or H. pylori eradication, mediated by IL-13 signaling that epigenetically programs neurons to release CGRP, which together with ILC2-derived IL-5 amplifies epithelial metaplasia and promotes orthotopic gastric tumor progression. | Findings: Prior gastric injury or H. pylori eradication creates a lasting inflammatory memory in vagal sensory neurons lasting >6 months.; Memory-encoded neurons require IL-13 signaling; IL-13 receptor knockout abolishes the memory phenotype.; ILC2-derived IL-5 induces CGRP release from sensory neurons, enhancing epithelial progenitor activation.; Selective vagal denervation or ablation of memory-encoded neurons eliminates accelerated regeneration and tumor promotion.; Transplantation of memory-encoded neurons into Trpv1-deficient recipients restores the tumor-promoting memory.

metadata.speaker: Yi Zheng
metadata.talk_title: Neuroinflammatory memory drives gastric tumorigenesis via vagal sensory neurons and ILC2

text: ILC2-driven T cell exhaustion in MASLD-associated hepatocellular carcinoma | Speaker: Naoko Ohtani | Tumors: hepatocellular carcinoma | MOA: High‑fat diet induces gut gram‑positive bacterial metabolites that activate hepatic ILC2 via TLR2, leading to CXCL9 secretion by LSEC and recruitment of CXCR3+ CD8 T cells that become exhausted through granzyme K‑mediated IL‑1β release, driving MASLD‑associated HCC progression. | Findings: HFD increases gram‑positive bacteria‑derived deoxycholic acid and LTA, activating hepatic ILC2 via TLR2.; ILC2 produce IL‑5 and IL‑13, promoting CXCL9 expression in LSEC, which recruits CXCR3+ T cells.; CXCR3 blockade or CXCL9 knockout markedly reduces HCC development in HFD mice.; Exhausted CD8 T cells in steatotic liver express high Granzyme K, which drives IL‑1β release and tumor promotion.; Granzyme K knockout mice show reduced HCC incidence; overexpression accelerates tumor growth.

metadata.speaker: Naoko Ohtani
metadata.talk_title: ILC2-driven T cell exhaustion in MASLD-associated hepatocellular carcinoma

text: Stress‑induced remodeling of enteric glia promotes colorectal tumor initiation | Speaker: Shuyang He | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: Chronic restraint stress elevates glucocorticoids, activating enteric glial cells that secrete factors promoting ROS, DNA damage and hyperproliferation of intestinal epithelial stem cells, thereby accelerating tumor initiation in ApcMin mice; glial‑derived conditioned medium upregulates tumorigenic genes in organoids. | Findings: Physical restraint stress raises corticosterone levels in mice.; Stressed enteric glia increase ROS and γH2AX DNA damage in gut epithelium.; Glial depletion (Plp1‑CreERT2/DTR) markedly reduces stress‑induced tumor burden in ApcMin mice.; Conditioned medium from glucocorticoid‑treated glia enhances outgrowth and tumorigenic gene expression in pre‑tumor organoids.; Stress‑induced glial activation correlates with early‑stage glial infiltration in mouse polyps, which diminishes in advanced tumors.

metadata.speaker: Shuyang He
metadata.talk_title: Stress‑induced remodeling of enteric glia promotes colorectal tumor initiation

text: Chronic sleep deprivation reshapes microbiota and impairs 5‑FU efficacy in colorectal cancer | Speaker: Maria Hernandez | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: Repeated nocturnal bar disturbance induces circadian disruption (↓BMAL1, ↑Cry1/2) and dysbiosis, leading to reduced intratumoral CD4⁺/CD8⁺ T cells, lower IFN‑γ, and impaired 5‑FU response; fecal microbiota from sleep‑deprived donors recapitulates these effects in recipient mice. | Findings: Sleep‑deprived mice develop larger MC38 tumors and higher tumor weight than controls.; Tumors from SD mice show decreased BMAL1 and increased Cry1/2 expression.; SD reduces intratumoral CD4⁺, CD8⁺, IFN‑γ⁺ T cells and NK cell granzyme A frequency.; 5‑FU efficacy is blunted in SD mice, with higher tumor growth despite chemotherapy.; FMT from SD donors transfers dysbiosis and chemoresistance to antibiotic‑treated recipients.

metadata.speaker: Maria Hernandez
metadata.talk_title: Chronic sleep deprivation reshapes microbiota and impairs 5‑FU efficacy in colorectal cancer

text: Obesity‑induced pre‑adipocyte IGF‑1 signaling drives ovarian cancer metastasis to omentum | Speaker: Sophia Hou | Tumors: ovarian cancer | MOA: Pre‑adipocytes from high‑BMI donors secrete higher IGF‑1 and reduced IGFBPs, activating AKT and NF‑κB (p65) in ovarian cancer cells, promoting SOX2‑driven tumor initiation and fibronectin‑mediated extracellular matrix remodeling, thereby enhancing omental colonization and decreasing survival. | Findings: Co‑injection of high‑BMI pre‑adipocytes accelerates early tumor growth and reduces mouse survival compared to normal‑BMI pre‑adipocytes.; Both normal and high‑BMI pre‑adipocytes increase IGF‑1 secretion; high‑BMI cells have lower IGFBP levels, increasing bioavailable IGF‑1.; IGF‑1 stimulation activates AKT and NF‑κB (p65) in ovarian cancer cells under both nutrient‑replete and -deprived conditions.; High‑BMI pre‑adipocyte co‑culture upregulates ECM genes (fibronectin) and SOX2 expression in cancer cells.; Obese patient omental tissue shows elevated IGF‑1 and activated IGF‑1R signaling.

metadata.speaker: Sophia Hou
metadata.talk_title: Obesity‑induced pre‑adipocyte IGF‑1 signaling drives ovarian cancer metastasis to omentum

text: Hybrid EMT tumor cells and TIMO monocytes drive immunosuppression in head and neck cancer | Speaker: Dichen Lin | Tumors: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma | MOA: A tumor‑enriched monocyte subset (TIMO) co‑localizes with hybrid EMT cancer cells; reciprocal signaling enhances EMT gene expression and monocyte immunosuppressive programs, leading to reduced T cell activation and resistance to cisplatin and ICB. | Findings: TIMO monocytes are enriched in tumors and associate with poor survival across HNSCC cohorts.; Hybrid EMT tumor cells (high ITGB4) are spatially adjacent to TIMO monocytes.; Co‑culture of TIMO monocytes with EMT‑high organoids increases EMT gene expression and monocyte immunosuppressive markers.; EMT‑high organoids recruit more monocytes than EMT‑low counterparts.; Presence of TIMO monocytes diminishes CD69 and granzyme B expression in co‑cultured T cells.

metadata.speaker: Dichen Lin
metadata.talk_title: Hybrid EMT tumor cells and TIMO monocytes drive immunosuppression in head and neck cancer
tumor_types: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma

text: IL‑1β‑high mature neutrophils mediate ICB resistance in prostate cancer bone metastasis | Speaker: Aram Liu | Tumors: prostate cancer | MOA: Bone‑metastatic prostate cancer harbors a mature neutrophil subset expressing high IL‑1β that suppresses CD8⁺ T cell proliferation; IL‑1R blockade restores checkpoint inhibitor efficacy, indicating IL‑1 signaling as a therapeutic target for ICB‑resistant bone disease. | Findings: IL‑1β‑high mature neutrophils are enriched in prostate cancer bone metastases but scarce in soft‑tissue sites.; These neutrophils suppress CD8⁺ T cell proliferation in vitro.; Adoptive transfer of bone‑derived neutrophils confers ICB resistance to subcutaneous tumors.; IL‑1R antagonist combined with anti‑PD‑L1 markedly reduces tumor growth in intra‑osseous models, whereas monotherapies are ineffective.; High neutrophil IL‑1β signature predicts poorer survival and increased immune‑suppressive gene expression in patient cohorts.

metadata.speaker: Aram Liu
metadata.talk_title: IL‑1β‑high mature neutrophils mediate ICB resistance in prostate cancer bone metastasis

text: The Genomic Landscape of Likely Human Pre-cancers | Speaker: Dr. Steele | MOA: Comprehensive genomic profiling of ~1,500 human pre-cancer lesions across 33 tissue types identified high heterogeneity in mutational burden, copy-number alterations, and driver gene alterations, and a random forest model using TMB, ploidy, and genome aberration predicts malignant potential. | Findings: Pre-cancer samples exhibited coding mutation counts ranging from <10 to >3,000 across tissue types.; 43% of pre-cancers lacked detectable driver gene alterations compared with 11% in TCGA cancers.; Tumor mutational burden, ploidy, and percent genome aberrant were the top three features distinguishing cancer-like from precancer-like samples.; In Barrett's esophagus, the cancer-like score correlated with progression to invasive cancer.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Steele
metadata.talk_title: The Genomic Landscape of Likely Human Pre-cancers

text: Mechanisms of Tumor Dormancy Through Immune Niche Formation and Its Impact on Immune Therapeutic Relapse | Speaker: Dr. Ahad | Tumors: triple-negative breast cancer | MOA: Dormant tumor cells up‑regulate CD200, which engages CD200R on NK cells within a monocyte‑neutrophil‑NK cell niche, suppressing NK‑mediated killing; CD200 knockdown reduces dormant lesions, and anti‑CD200 therapy eradicates residual dormant cells after chemotherapy, preventing relapse. | Findings: Dormant lesions (1‑8 cells) were enriched for monocytes, neutrophils, dendritic cells, and NK cells, but lacked T cells.; CD200 expression was high in dormant tumor cells and mediated resistance to NK‑cell killing.; CD200 knockdown reduced dormant lesion burden without affecting proliferative lesions.; Anti‑CD200 antibody combined with cisplatin and anti‑PD‑1 eliminated residual dormant cells and prevented tumor regrowth after therapy withdrawal.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Ahad
metadata.talk_title: Mechanisms of Tumor Dormancy Through Immune Niche Formation and Its Impact on Immune Therapeutic Relapse

text: Ligandable PNT Domain Establishes ERG as a Druggable Oncogenic Driver in Prostate Cancer | Speaker: Dr. Wang | Tumors: prostate cancer | MOA: Pbite‑1 binds the PNT domain of ERG with ~28 µM affinity, stabilizing the protein and disrupting PNT‑mediated protein‑protein interactions, leading to down‑regulation of ERG target genes, induction of apoptosis, and inhibition of invasion in ERG‑positive prostate cancer models. | Findings: Pbite‑1 stabilizes ERG PNT domain in vitro (DSF) and in cells (CETSA) with KD ~28 µM.; Biotinylated Pbite‑1 pulls down full‑length ERG but not PNT‑deleted fragments, confirming domain specificity.; Pbite‑1 selectively reduces viability and induces apoptosis in ERG‑positive cell lines and organoids, sparing ERG‑negative controls.; Treatment suppresses ERG‑regulated transcriptional programs (MYC, AR, etc.) and inhibits invasion in ERG‑overexpressing models.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Wang
metadata.talk_title: Ligandable PNT Domain Establishes ERG as a Druggable Oncogenic Driver in Prostate Cancer

text: Novel Brain‑Penetrant BRAF Inhibitor HSK42360 for BRAF‑Mutant Glioma | Speaker: Dr. Xidong Gao | Tumors: glioma | MOA: HSK42360 induces an external rotation of the αC‑helix of BRAF, preventing RAF dimerization and thus avoiding paradoxical MAPK activation; it penetrates the brain (Kp,uu = 1.1) and shows potent inhibition of class I‑III BRAF mutants in vitro and tumor regression in intracranial glioma models. | Findings: HSK42360 does not cause paradoxical MAPK activation in HCT116 cells.; In vitro IC50s against class II (G469A) and class III (G466V) BRAF mutants ranged from 7.6 nM to 101 nM, outperforming dabrafenib.; Brain penetration Kp,uu = 1.1 exceeds the 0.3 threshold for CNS drugs.; In intracranial A375 CDX mice, HSK42360 significantly prolonged survival.; In a clinical cohort (n=23), ORR was 42.1% (high‑grade) and 50% (low‑grade) with durable responses and reduced BRAF‑inhibitor toxicities.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Xidong Gao
metadata.talk_title: Novel Brain‑Penetrant BRAF Inhibitor HSK42360 for BRAF‑Mutant Glioma

text: Active RAS Inhibition Intercepts Pancreas Cancer in Mice | Speaker: Dr. Tan | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma | MOA: RAS inhibitors induce apoptosis of KRAS‑mutant PanIN lesions, reducing their number and delaying tumor onset; intermittent metronomic dosing further prolongs latency, demonstrating that early interception of pre‑malignant KRAS‑driven lesions can extend survival independent of adaptive T‑cell immunity. | Findings: 10‑day RAS inhibition reduced PanIN lesions from ~400 to significantly fewer in 9‑week‑old KPC mice.; RAS inhibition increased cleaved caspase‑3 in PanIN cells, indicating apoptosis without transdifferentiation.; Four weeks of RAS inhibition delayed tumor onset and improved overall survival in KPC mice.; T‑cell depletion did not affect the interception benefit, suggesting a T‑cell‑independent mechanism.; Metronomic weekly RAS inhibition (1 week on/1 week off) delayed tumor onset by >200 days and extended survival by >1 year.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Tan
metadata.talk_title: Active RAS Inhibition Intercepts Pancreas Cancer in Mice

text: Phase 1/2 Study of Deruxnaratib with Gemcitabine and Nab‑Paclitaxel in First‑Line Metastatic Pancreatic Cancer | Speaker: Dr. Wolpin | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma | MOA: Deruxnaratib binds cyclophilin A and forms a complex that sterically blocks effector binding to GTP‑bound KRAS (codons 12,13,61 and WT), suppressing MAPK signaling; combined with gemcitabine/nab‑paclitaxel, it yields high response rates and deep ctDNA reductions in KRAS‑mutant PDAC. | Findings: Confirmed ORR of 58% and DCR of 90% in 40 first‑line PDAC patients receiving deruxnaratib + gemcitabine/nab‑paclitaxel.; Six‑month landmark PFS and OS were 84% and 90%, respectively, exceeding historical chemotherapy benchmarks.; 96% of evaluable patients achieved ≥50% reduction in KRAS ctDNA; 61% cleared detectable KRAS mutation.; Grade ≥3 rash occurred in ~10‑15% of patients; overall safety profile was manageable with dose reductions.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Wolpin
metadata.talk_title: Phase 1/2 Study of Deruxnaratib with Gemcitabine and Nab‑Paclitaxel in First‑Line Metastatic Pancreatic Cancer

text: Gapless But Not Global: Ancestry-Enriched Functional Sequence Missing from Human Reference Genomes | Speaker: Naisha Chambu | MOA: The study aligns African ancestry-enriched contigs (~300 Mb) to gapless T2T-CHM13 and HPRC pangenome assemblies, revealing that many unmapped sequences map to centromeric, HLA, and CpG island regions, contain predicted coding and regulatory elements, and are transcriptionally active in normal and cancer RNA‑seq datasets, highlighting reference bias that can miss clinically relevant variants. | Findings: 40% of African ancestry-enriched contigs map nearly perfectly to T2T‑CHM13; ~80% map reasonably well.; 94% of mapped contigs overlap centromeric or satellite repeat regions, with notable enrichment in the HLA locus.; Gene set enrichment shows over‑representation of MHC complex proteins and neuronal signaling genes.; 92% of contigs align to at least one HPRC assembly, with significant enrichment to African and admixed American references.; 10.5 Mb of non‑repeat sequence shows transcriptional activity in 1000 Genomes cell lines, TCGA cancer cohorts, and Davis lab datasets.

metadata.speaker: Naisha Chambu
metadata.talk_title: Gapless But Not Global: Ancestry-Enriched Functional Sequence Missing from Human Reference Genomes

text: Epigenetics, Ancestry, and Cancer Disparity: Nature and Nurture Interplay | Speaker: King Jordan | Tumors: breast cancer, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, kidney cancer, skin cancer | MOA: Genetic ancestry correlates more strongly than self‑identified race with breast cancer survival disparities; differential expression of PAQR6, driven by promoter hypomethylation in African ancestry tumors, mediates increased mortality, illustrating that epigenetic regulation links ancestry‑related environmental exposures to clinical outcomes. | Findings: Genetic ancestry provides higher resolution than self‑identified race for modeling survival disparities in four cancers (breast, HNSCC, kidney, skin).; Somatic mutation profiles showed no ancestry‑specific driver mutations or survival interactions.; Differential expression analysis identified seven genes whose ancestry‑specific expression interacts with survival; five are in breast cancer, including PAQR6.; PAQR6 is up‑regulated in African ancestry breast tumors and its promoter is hypomethylated, linking epigenetic activation to poorer outcomes.; Multivariable Cox models using continuous ancestry metrics detect more significant survival associations than categorical self‑identified race.

metadata.speaker: King Jordan
metadata.talk_title: Epigenetics, Ancestry, and Cancer Disparity: Nature and Nurture Interplay
tumor_types: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma

text: Translating Genomic Equity: Infrastructure for Global Precision Oncology | Speaker: Clayton Yates | Tumors: prostate cancer | MOA: Integrating ancestry‑informed serum proteomics, single‑cell immune profiling, and spatial transcriptomics reveals an inflammation‑driven, myeloid‑rich tumor microenvironment in African ancestry prostate cancers; a TNFRSF9/PTEN signature predicts lethal disease, and deep‑learning pathology (CODA) links histologic patterns to immune infiltration, enabling ancestry‑specific risk stratification. | Findings: Serum cytokine profiling shows elevated CXCL1, CXCL5, and macrophage recruitment proteins in African ancestry individuals.; A two‑gene signature (TNFRSF9, PTEN) predicts lethal prostate cancer in African ancestry patients with 78.2% accuracy; combined with NCCN risk score reaches 90% accuracy.; Neighborhood deprivation index (NDI) correlates with heightened inflammatory cytokines, linking social determinants to molecular risk.; Single‑cell PBMC analysis identifies expanded CD16+ monocytes and exhausted CD8+ TEM cells (LAG‑3+) in African ancestry subjects.; Tumor deconvolution and spatial profiling reveal increased myeloid‑derived suppressor cells and M1/M2 macrophage polarization in African ancestry tumors.

metadata.speaker: Clayton Yates
metadata.talk_title: Translating Genomic Equity: Infrastructure for Global Precision Oncology

text: Neuronal mitochondria transfer drives breast cancer metastasis | Speaker: Simon | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: Neuronal cells secrete axon guidance molecules such as SEMA4F, inducing cancer neurogenesis; neuronal mitochondria are transferred to mesenchymal breast cancer cells via tunneling nanotubes, increasing their oxidative phosphorylation and conferring resistance to oxidative and shear stress, which enriches for metastatic outgrowth. | Findings: Dominant‑negative TGF‑β receptor expression blocked plasticity and reduced metastasis without changing primary tumor weight.; Denervation of the mammary fat pad with Botox decreased tumor mitochondrial content and reduced metastatic burden by ~35% in mouse models.; Co‑culture of neurons with cancer cells increased cancer cell respiration and mitochondrial mass (≈30% increase).; Mitochondrial transfer from neurons to cancer cells occurred in 10‑15% of tumor cells in vivo; denervation reduced this transfer by 35%.; Green (mitochondria‑receiving) cancer cells were enriched in lung and brain metastases despite no increase in in‑vitro invasion.

metadata.speaker: Simon
metadata.talk_title: Neuronal mitochondria transfer drives breast cancer metastasis

text: Tumor‑derived mitochondrial DNA transfer impairs T‑cell function and reprograms macrophages | Speaker: Yosuke Togashi | Tumors: melanoma, non‑small cell lung cancer | MOA: Tumor cells harbor high‑frequency mtDNA mutations and transfer these dysfunctional mitochondria to T cells via tunneling nanotubes and extracellular vesicles; USP30‑mediated mitophagy resistance allows mutant mitochondria to persist in T cells, impairing OXPHOS, glycolytic balance, memory formation and response to PD‑1 blockade. Parallel transfer to macrophages drives pro‑angiogenic, immature phenotypes that sensitize tumors to VEGF inhibition. | Findings: 40% of patient T cells shared mtDNA mutations with autologous tumor cells, confirming in‑vivo mitochondrial transfer.; In vitro co‑culture showed MitoDSRed‑positive T cells after 2‑3 days, confirming functional transfer.; In vivo, MitoDSRed‑positive TILs increased over time (day 21‑42) and displayed heteroplasmy/homoplasmy of tumor mtDNA mutations.; Blocking cell‑cell contact, tunneling nanotubes, or EV release reduced mitochondrial transfer, indicating multiple routes.; USP30 is overexpressed in cancer cells; mutant mitochondria resistant to mitophagy are preferentially transferred to T cells.

metadata.speaker: Yosuke Togashi
metadata.talk_title: Tumor‑derived mitochondrial DNA transfer impairs T‑cell function and reprograms macrophages

text: Engineering mitochondrial transfer to supercharge adoptive T‑cell therapy | Speaker: Luca | Tumors: melanoma, acute lymphoblastic leukemia | MOA: Bone‑marrow mesenchymal stromal cells donate functional mitochondria to activated CD8 T cells via tunneling nanotubes; transferred mitochondria increase mtDNA content (~30%), boost oxidative phosphorylation and spare respiratory capacity, leading to enhanced engraftment, deeper tumor infiltration, and prolonged anti‑tumor activity of adoptively transferred T cells. | Findings: Co‑culture of activated CD8 T cells with MSCs achieved ~10% mitochondrial transfer rate.; Mito‑positive T cells contained ~30% more mitochondrial DNA than mito‑negative controls.; Functional mitochondria (MSC‑derived) increased basal respiration and spare respiratory capacity in recipient T cells; EtBr‑treated dysfunctional mitochondria did not.; In B16 melanoma, mito‑positive Pmel‑1 cells controlled tumor growth for >42 days, whereas mito‑negative cells relapsed after ~21 days; survival was significantly extended.; Mito‑positive T cells showed higher frequencies in spleen and tumor, and penetrated deeper into tumor tissue.

metadata.speaker: Luca
metadata.talk_title: Engineering mitochondrial transfer to supercharge adoptive T‑cell therapy

text: AI-augmented workflow tools for clinical trial operations | Speaker: Umut Topaloglu | MOA: Developed a suite of AI-augmented tools—including semi‑automatic common data element annotation, a fair data workbench, and eligibility‑criteria structuring—where AI generates candidate mappings or drafts and expert humans review, accept, or reject outputs, preserving oversight while accelerating data harmonization and trial matching. | Findings: Semi‑automatic semantic matching of new data elements to existing CDEs provides confidence scores and side‑by‑side comparisons, with human reviewers intervening on low‑confidence matches.; The fair data workbench pipelines standardize heterogeneous trial data, enabling cross‑trial analyses that were previously blocked by format inconsistencies.; LLM‑assisted structuring of eligibility criteria and patient EHR data creates a basis for deterministic patient‑matching engines like MatchBox, with two mandatory human verification steps.; Integration with USCDI‑Plus standards and FHIR data‑quality ontologies allows quantitative assessment of EHR data completeness.

metadata.speaker: Umut Topaloglu
metadata.talk_title: AI-augmented workflow tools for clinical trial operations

text: AI‑generated consent documents and multilingual translation for trial enrollment | Speaker: Tana Nelson | MOA: Implemented AI pipelines that ingest full protocol documents to auto‑generate first‑draft consent forms at an eighth‑grade reading level, embed structured risk tables, and produce lay‑person summaries; coupled with AI‑assisted multilingual translation (initially Spanish) that halves translation time while retaining human expert review for regulatory certification. | Findings: AI‑generated consent draft can be produced in ~4 minutes versus up to two weeks for manual medical‑writer preparation.; Initial AI translation of a 10,000‑word consent reduces turnaround from five days to approximately 2.5 days before human post‑editing.; Human‑in‑the‑loop review flags sections where AI performance is weak (e.g., specimen storage language), ensuring regulatory compliance.; Prototype lay‑person one‑page study summaries improve patient comprehension by presenting key study elements in plain language.

metadata.speaker: Tana Nelson
metadata.talk_title: AI‑generated consent documents and multilingual translation for trial enrollment

text: Reducing Animal Testing in Oncology Non-Clinical Development | Speaker: Michael Manning | MOA: Weight-of-evidence risk assessments integrate non‑clinical, clinical, and literature data to replace routine three‑month GLP toxicology studies for CD3 bispecific T‑cell engagers and antibody‑drug conjugates, focusing on target‑specific toxicities and leveraging NAMs where appropriate. | Findings: Analysis of IND and BLA submissions showed that three‑month general toxicology studies are often unnecessary for CD3 bispecific T‑cell engagers because target binding is absent in animals and chronic exposure cannot be achieved.; For antibody‑drug conjugates, toxicity was attributed to the small‑molecule payload rather than the antibody, indicating that three‑month non‑human primate studies add little value and can be limited to rodent studies.; Weight‑of‑evidence approaches, incorporating literature, clinical data, and NAMs, can replace embryo‑fetal developmental and chronic toxicity studies without compromising patient safety.

metadata.speaker: Michael Manning
metadata.talk_title: Reducing Animal Testing in Oncology Non-Clinical Development

text: Incorporating New Approach Methodologies, or NAMs, in Oncology Drug Development | Speaker: Natalie Simpson | MOA: NAMs—including hiPSC‑cardiomyocytes, organoid/spheroid cultures, and organ‑on‑chip systems—are used as human‑relevant in‑vitro platforms to replace or supplement animal toxicology studies, particularly for QT prolongation, organ‑specific toxicities, and reproductive toxicity assessments in oncology INDs. | Findings: A total of 139 hiPSC‑CM studies were submitted to the FDA from 2012‑2025, representing only ~1% of commercial IND submissions per year.; 301 organoid/spheroid studies were identified across divisions (2008‑2025); 91% of organoid and 86% of spheroid submissions in oncology were for pharmacology, with only 6‑9% submitted as safety NAMs.; Organ‑on‑chip models were successfully used in a bispecific antibody case to replace animal studies for first‑in‑human dosing, supporting safety and starting dose selection.; Complex NAMs were identified in only eight INDs, with four proposing replacement of animal studies, indicating early but growing adoption.

metadata.speaker: Natalie Simpson
metadata.talk_title: Incorporating New Approach Methodologies, or NAMs, in Oncology Drug Development

text: A Glimpse into the Future in Bioinformatics | Speaker: Matthew Thompson | MOA: A curated FDA oncology IND database integrates mechanisms, targets, and product classes to enable rapid weight‑of‑evidence assessments, inform starting dose strategies, and evaluate the necessity of repeat‑dose toxicology studies, supporting potential reductions in animal use. | Findings: The FDA bioinformatics team has compiled a searchable database of over 8,000 commercial oncology INDs, cataloguing mechanisms, targets, and modality classes.; Analysis shows a steady increase in oncology IND submissions since 2010, with both biologics and small molecules contributing to the rise.; Retrospective studies are planned to compare one‑month versus three‑month repeat‑dose toxicology results with clinical safety outcomes to identify when non‑rodent studies may be omitted.

metadata.speaker: Matthew Thompson
metadata.talk_title: A Glimpse into the Future in Bioinformatics

text: Bone Repair External State Program Drives Cancer Cell Dedifferentiation and Immune Invasion in Melanoma | Speaker: Jackson Weir | Tumors: melanoma | MOA: Spatial profiling identified anti‑inflammatory hubs enriched for SPP1⁺ macrophages and POSTN⁺ fibroblasts that exclude CD8⁺ T cells, induce a dysfunctional T‑cell state, and via secreted tissue‑repair ligands drive melanoma dedifferentiation to a neural‑crest‑like state and protect tumor cells from cytokine‑mediated killing. | Findings: Identified an anti‑inflammatory hub composed of SPP1⁺ macrophages and POSTN⁺ fibroblasts that is largely T‑cell excluded.; T cells within the anti‑inflammatory hub are dysfunctional singleton clonotypes lacking expansion.; Ligand program from the hub (SPP1, POSTN) induces melanoma cells to dedifferentiate from a melanocytic to a neural‑crest‑like state in vitro.; SPP1 pretreatment protects neural‑crest‑state melanoma cells from killing by IFN‑γ, TNF‑α and other cytotoxic cytokines.; Spatial correlation shows anti‑inflammatory hubs predict higher neural‑crest trajectory scores, linking niche composition to tumor dedifferentiation and immune evasion.

metadata.speaker: Jackson Weir
metadata.talk_title: Bone Repair External State Program Drives Cancer Cell Dedifferentiation and Immune Invasion in Melanoma

text: Tumor‑Specific Antibodies Elicited by Engineered Bacteria Promote Bladder Cancer Immunotherapy | Speaker: Matthew Ruane | Tumors: bladder cancer | MOA: Engineered probiotic E. coli Nissle with a synchronized lysis circuit secretes CXCL13 within bladder tumors, recruits B and T cells to form tertiary lymphoid structures in draining lymph nodes, generates tumor‑specific IgG antibodies, and synergizes with PD‑1 blockade to double the cure rate in mice. | Findings: Engineered E. coli Nissle selectively colonizes bladder tumors without spreading to normal tissue.; Intravesical delivery of CXCL13‑producing bacteria induces TLS formation in draining lymph nodes and increases tumor‑specific IgG antibodies.; Combination of CXCL13‑bacteria with anti‑PD‑1 cures 50% of mice versus 25% with anti‑PD‑1 alone.; Efficacy requires T follicular helper cells; depletion of these cells abolishes therapeutic benefit.; Treatment is well tolerated with no weight loss or systemic toxicity compared with controls.

metadata.speaker: Matthew Ruane
metadata.talk_title: Tumor‑Specific Antibodies Elicited by Engineered Bacteria Promote Bladder Cancer Immunotherapy

text: Integrating Single‑Cell and Spatial Transcriptomics with Mouse Models to Understand How Tumor‑Associated Macrophages Suppress Antitumor Immunity | Speaker: Rosandra Tonia | Tumors: melanoma, breast cancer | MOA: Host‑derived GPNMB deficiency reprograms tumor‑associated macrophages toward an interferon‑driven pro‑inflammatory phenotype, expands CXCL10⁺ macrophages, enhances CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration and activation, and markedly improves tumor control; the effect requires tissue‑resident (LysM‑Cre) but not bone‑marrow‑derived macrophages. | Findings: Gpnmb‑/- mice exhibit significantly reduced tumor growth and increased survival in melanoma, breast, and lung metastasis models.; Knockout tumors show higher CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration, activation (PD‑1⁺, TIM‑3⁺) and increased memory phenotypes.; scRNA‑seq reveals expansion of CXCL10⁺ pro‑inflammatory macrophages and contraction of mitochondrial‑rich, immunosuppressive macrophages.; GPNMB loss decreases fatty‑acid uptake in both pro‑ and anti‑inflammatory tumor macrophages.; Tumor control is abolished after systemic T‑cell depletion and only partially reduced after CD8⁺ depletion, indicating dependence on T cells.

metadata.speaker: Rosandra Tonia
metadata.talk_title: Integrating Single‑Cell and Spatial Transcriptomics with Mouse Models to Understand How Tumor‑Associated Macrophages Suppress Antitumor Immunity

text: Vaccine Stimulation of Bystander T Cells in the Lymph Node Unexpectedly Promotes Tumor‑Specific Host Immunity to Regress Solid Tumors | Speaker: Liam Ma | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, melanoma, breast cancer | MOA: An amphiphile vaccine targeting a generic FITC‑CAR on adoptively transferred T cells triggers rapid IFN‑γ release, transiently degrades the fibrotic PDAC capsule, up‑regulates MHC I/II on tumor cells, and activates endogenous CD8⁺ T cells, leading to swift tumor regression even when the CAR does not recognize tumor antigen; efficacy is IFN‑γ dependent and enhanced by anti‑PD‑L1 blockade. | Findings: Vaccine boosting of tumor‑irrelevant CAR T cells induces >50% tumor regression within 24 h across PDAC, melanoma, and breast cancer models.; Efficacy is abolished by IFN‑γ neutralization, demonstrating cytokine dependence.; Tumor regression persists after CAR T depletion at 3 days, indicating reliance on endogenous immunity.; Serum IFN‑γ and CCL2 spike transiently after vaccination, coinciding with rapid degradation of the PDAC fibrotic capsule.; MHC I up‑regulation on tumor cells and activation of host CD8⁺ T cells are essential; B2m‑KO tumors are resistant.

metadata.speaker: Liam Ma
metadata.talk_title: Vaccine Stimulation of Bystander T Cells in the Lymph Node Unexpectedly Promotes Tumor‑Specific Host Immunity to Regress Solid Tumors

text: IL‑18‑secreting CAR T cells uncover divergent immune mechanisms of antigen‑heterogeneous solid tumor clearance | Speaker: Audrey May | Tumors: melanoma, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, breast cancer | MOA: IL‑18‑secreting CD19 CAR T cells, despite low persistence, remodel the myeloid compartment by expanding activated neutrophils and macrophages with IFN‑γ‑responsive gene signatures, leading to rapid clearance of antigen‑heterogeneous tumors independent of adaptive CD8⁺ T‑cell priming, while Rag1‑KO mice retain efficacy, indicating a dominant innate mechanism. | Findings: IL‑18 CAR T cells achieve superior heterogeneous tumor control compared with IL‑36, FLT3‑L, or CAR‑only controls.; IL‑18 CAR T cells show low persistence in tumor and lymph nodes but accumulate in the spleen.; Endogenous CD8⁺ T cells display an effector‑memory phenotype but reduced tumor‑reactive ELISpot responses.; Myeloid cells, especially neutrophils and macrophages, are markedly expanded and exhibit IFN‑γ‑responsive and antigen‑presentation gene signatures.; Neutrophil depletion does not impair IL‑18 CAR efficacy, suggesting macrophages are the critical mediators.

metadata.speaker: Audrey May
metadata.talk_title: IL‑18‑secreting CAR T cells uncover divergent immune mechanisms of antigen‑heterogeneous solid tumor clearance

text: Gut Microeukaryotes, Endogenous Viruses, and Cancer | Speaker: Dr. Long Nguyen | MOA: Nguyen described population-scale analyses linking gut microeukaryote Blastocystis prevalence to plant-based diets, favorable cardiometabolic markers, lower adiposity, and reduced odds of colorectal cancer, and presented trans-kingdom dysbiosis in MASLD driven by oral bacteria, acylcarnitine metabolites, and endogenous viruses that may modulate bacterial communities via predator-prey dynamics. | Findings: Blastocystis prevalence exceeds 40% in several under‑studied regions (e.g., Tanzania, Fiji) and is higher in adults than children, suggesting non‑vertical transmission.; Higher adherence to plant‑based diets correlates with increased Blastocystis carriage (median AUC ~0.85 for bacterial composition predicting Blastocystis).; Blastocystis‑positive individuals show improved fasting/postprandial triglycerides, higher HDL, lower GlicA, and a 6% decrease in odds of carriage per BMI point increase.; Case‑control analysis shows a 29% lower odds of Blastocystis in colorectal cancer and IBD samples versus healthy controls.; In a 1,100‑person dietary RCT, Blastocystis prevalence modestly expanded in participants achieving weight‑loss goals on high‑quality diets.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Long Nguyen
metadata.talk_title: Gut Microeukaryotes, Endogenous Viruses, and Cancer

text: Population‑scale EBV Persistence and Host Genetics | Speaker: Dr. Caleb La Roe | Tumors: lymphoma, lung cancer, nasopharyngeal carcinoma | MOA: La Roe demonstrated that latent EBV DNA can be quantified from existing whole‑genome sequencing data, identified a high‑EBV‑load subpopulation (~10%) and linked host genetic variation at 45 loci—many in antigen presentation and B‑cell pathways—to persistence, which in turn associates with autoimmune, respiratory, and cancer phenotypes, and provided preliminary evidence of geographic strain variation. | Findings: Approximately 10% of individuals in UK Biobank and All of Us have high EBV DNA levels detectable in blood WGS, despite ~90% seropositivity.; Masking low‑complexity repetitive EBV regions is essential; otherwise 40% of samples would be mis‑classified.; GWAS of 400,000 European‑ancestry participants identified 45 independent loci (antigen presentation, B‑cell transcription factors) associated with EBV persistence.; Genetic risk for EBV persistence overlaps with risk loci for systemic lupus, type 1 diabetes, and rheumatoid arthritis.; High‑EBV carriers show increased incidence of HIV infection, rheumatoid arthritis, COPD, lung cancer, and lymphomas across health‑record ICD‑10 data.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Caleb La Roe
metadata.talk_title: Population‑scale EBV Persistence and Host Genetics

text: Cancer Mycobiome: Truth, Myth, and Current Data | Speaker: Dr. Iliyan Iliev | Tumors: colorectal cancer, stomach cancer, head and neck cancer, esophageal cancer, lung cancer | MOA: Iliev highlighted that tumor‑associated fungi, especially Candida albicans, are present in the mucosal layer of gastrointestinal tumors, where strain‑specific production of the peptide toxin candidalysin induces IL‑17/IL‑1 inflammation and promotes tumorigenesis; antifungal fluconazole clears gut Candida and restores beneficial bacterial diversity and butyrate production, suggesting a causal role for the mycobiome in cancer progression. | Findings: Fungal DNA (Candida albicans) is detectable in multiple GI cancers (CRC, stomach, esophageal, head‑and‑neck) but not in brain tumors.; Strain‑level analysis shows diverse C. albicans isolates with variable hyphal formation and candidalysin production.; In AOM/DSS mouse models, C. albicans colonization aggravates tumor development, whereas C. glabrata does not.; Fluconazole treatment clears both oral and gut Candida, whereas oral nystatin only clears oral colonization.; Systemic antifungal therapy restores bacterial diversity, notably increasing butyrate‑producing Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia intestinalis, and raises fecal butyrate levels.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Iliyan Iliev
metadata.talk_title: Cancer Mycobiome: Truth, Myth, and Current Data

text: LINE1 ORF1p as a pan‑cancer biomarker and ultra‑sensitive single‑molecule detection assay | Speaker: Martin Taylor | Tumors: colorectal cancer, gastric cancer, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, esophageal cancer, gastroesophageal cancer, colon adenoma, STIC lesions, breast cancer | MOA: LINE1 ORF1p is de‑repressed in cancer and high‑risk precursors, producing a tumor‑specific protein detectable in plasma via ultra‑sensitive single‑molecule sandwich assays; assay sensitivity improves with custom nanobody pairs and bar‑coded Mosaic detection, enabling early‑stage cancer detection and real‑time monitoring of treatment response. | Findings: LINE1 ORF1p is expressed in >99% of examined carcinomas and high‑risk precursors across organ systems.; First‑generation single‑molecule assay detected ORF1p in 50% of cancer plasma samples while remaining undetectable in 402/406 healthy controls.; Second‑generation nanobody‑based assays increased early‑stage ovarian cancer sensitivity to 83% without loss of specificity.; Adding ORF1p to a CA125+HE4 panel raised AUC from 0.94 to 0.98 in a pilot ovarian cancer cohort.; Serial ORF1p levels perfectly segregated responders from non‑responders in a gastroesophageal cancer monitoring cohort (p<0.001).

metadata.speaker: Martin Taylor
metadata.talk_title: LINE1 ORF1p as a pan‑cancer biomarker and ultra‑sensitive single‑molecule detection assay
tumor_types: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma

text: Naturally occurring antibodies as biomarkers for early cancer detection and outcome prediction | Speaker: Qi Dang | Tumors: lung cancer, pancreatic cancer, ovarian cancer, melanoma, renal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma | MOA: Naturally occurring autoantibodies arise against tumor‑associated antigens (e.g., NY‑ESO‑1, p53, MMP14, LINE1 ORF1p) and viral antigens; high‑throughput protein arrays and PhIP‑seq identify antibody signatures that can differentiate cancer patients from controls, predict early disease, and correlate with immunotherapy outcomes. | Findings: Single autoantibody markers show modest AUCs; panels of multiple antibodies substantially improve diagnostic performance.; p53 autoantibodies combined with CA125 outperform CA125 alone for ovarian cancer detection.; Anti‑interferon antibodies are enriched in responders to checkpoint inhibition across several tumor types, suggesting a predictive biomarker.; A viral exposure antibody signature predicts poorer survival in HCC patients receiving immunotherapy and rises longitudinally before HCC diagnosis.; IgG deposition is abundant on tumor cells in tissue sections, and cloned autoantibodies (e.g., against MMP14) can enhance phagocytosis and NK‑cell ADCC.

metadata.speaker: Qi Dang
metadata.talk_title: Naturally occurring antibodies as biomarkers for early cancer detection and outcome prediction

text: Unbiased autoantibody atlas for early cancer detection | Speaker: Dr. Dang | Tumors: hepatocellular carcinoma, cirrhosis, hepatitis | MOA: The study builds a large-scale atlas of autoantibodies by profiling serum from liver disease cohorts using human protein arrays and FIP‑seq, revealing distinct autoantibody signatures that separate HCC from cirrhosis/hepatitis and identifying antibodies that correlate with clinical outcomes. | Findings: Principal component analysis of autoantibody profiles segregates HCC patients from cirrhosis and hepatitis cohorts.; Heat‑map clustering shows a distinct blue cluster of HCC samples versus red cluster of non‑cancer liver disease.; Autoantibodies against a PD‑L1 chaperone protein are enriched in HCC patients with longer overall survival.; The planned CRUK Grand Challenge atlas will expand to >16,000 individuals across high‑risk groups (genetic predisposition, heavy smokers, obese, centenarians, twins).; Baseline autoantibody patterns are being evaluated as predictors of response to checkpoint inhibitor neoadjuvant therapy.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Dang
metadata.talk_title: Unbiased autoantibody atlas for early cancer detection

text: Multi-Cancer Early Detection: Where Are We and Where Do We Want to Go? | Speaker: Peter Sasieni | Tumors: pan-cancer | MOA: Peter reviewed the landscape of multi‑cancer early detection (MCED) tests, highlighting that current commercial assays (cfDNA methylation, protein‑mutation panels, fragmentomics, CTC immunocytochemistry, electrical properties) achieve high specificity (≥96.4%) but variable sensitivity (20‑70%) that depends on cancer type and stage. He discussed trial outcomes, notably the NHS Galleri RCT which failed to meet its primary stage‑3/4 reduction endpoint but showed a trend toward fewer stage‑4 diagnoses and increased early‑stage detection, and PATHFINDER 2 which demonstrated a 62% PPV and 74% episode sensitivity for 12 cancers. | Findings: All five commercial MCED tests have specificities ≥96.4%, but a specificity of 99.6% would reduce false positives nine‑fold compared with 96.4%.; Reported sensitivities vary widely (20‑70%) and are lower for early‑stage cancers, making stage‑specific performance a critical limitation.; Galleri’s NHS RCT did not achieve a statistically significant reduction in stage 3/4 cancers, though a reduction in stage 4 disease was observed.; PATHFINDER 2 reported a PPV of 62% and an episode sensitivity of 74% for 12 targeted cancers in an asymptomatic cohort.; Overall detection rate of cancers with current MCED tests is approximately 1 in 200 screened, with >50% of positive tests leading to a cancer diagnosis.

metadata.speaker: Peter Sasieni
metadata.talk_title: Multi-Cancer Early Detection: Where Are We and Where Do We Want to Go?

text: Navigating from Hype to Hope in Multi-Cancer Early Detection | Speaker: Ruth Etzioni | Tumors: pan-cancer | MOA: Ruth dissected the conceptual gap between diagnostic performance and clinical benefit, emphasizing that PPV and sensitivity are often conflated, that early‑stage sensitivity is hard to ascertain, and that down‑staging (stage 3/4 reduction) may not reliably predict mortality benefit without robust modeling of sojourn times and incidence patterns. | Findings: PPV and sensitivity are distinct metrics; confusion between them fuels hype around MCED performance.; Early‑stage sensitivity cannot be directly measured in most diagnostic studies and must be inferred from stage‑specific incidence data.; Late‑stage (stage 3/4) reduction, as used in the Galleri trial, does not consistently correlate with mortality benefit across cancer types.; Modeling of sojourn times shows that cancers with very short early‑stage windows (e.g., ovarian) may not benefit from high‑sensitivity tests.

metadata.speaker: Ruth Etzioni
metadata.talk_title: Navigating from Hype to Hope in Multi-Cancer Early Detection

text: NCI Director's Address: Funding, Policy, and Future Priorities | Speaker: Anthony Lattai | MOA: Dr. Lattai outlined the NCI's funding landscape, highlighting a 34% decline in US cancer death rates since 1991, a $128 M budget increase to $7.3 B for FY2026, and a shift to multi‑year and Select Pay funding mechanisms that maintain scientific merit while providing flexibility. He emphasized new priorities such as functional precision medicine, cancer vaccine trials, prevention and screening initiatives, and efforts to accelerate clinical trial activation. | Findings: US cancer death rates have fallen 34% since 1991, reflecting improved screening, prevention, and therapies.; NCI FY2026 budget increased by $128 M to a total of $7.3 B, representing a record level of extramural funding.; Approximately 200 new competing and 1,500 non‑competing extramural grants have been processed for FY2026.; Projected R01 success rate for FY2026 is ~11%, with a target of ~120 Early Stage Investigator awards.; NCI will fund three new therapeutic cancer vaccine trials over the next three years through a public‑private partnership with FNIH.

metadata.speaker: Anthony Lattai
metadata.talk_title: NCI Director's Address: Funding, Policy, and Future Priorities

text: Stepping Stones program overview and resource support | Speaker: Morgan O'Hare | MOA: The Stepping Stones program provides gap‑filling, IND‑enabling services (toxicology, PK, formulation, synthetic route optimization, ADME/DMPK) for NCI‑funded small‑molecule projects, aiming to de‑risk leads and improve eligibility for subsequent funding such as NExT, SBIR, or venture capital. | Findings: Six rounds of the Stepping Stones program have been completed, supporting 17 distinct projects across various malignancies and a chemotherapy‑induced peripheral neuropathy indication.; Supported activities have included formulation work (e.g., salt screens, oral suspensions), synthetic route scale‑up, mouse and rat PK studies, ADME/DMPK profiling (metabolic stability, CYP, HERG), and biomarker assay development.; Several investigators who received Stepping Stones support subsequently secured SBIR/STTR funding, while others refined chemistry or advanced compounds toward startup formation.

metadata.speaker: Morgan O'Hare
metadata.talk_title: Stepping Stones program overview and resource support

text: Ceramide-based colorectal cancer risk score and DES1 inhibitor studies | Speaker: Mary Playdon | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: The consortium developed a ceramide-based risk score for colorectal cancer by integrating prospective cohort lipidomics with genetic analyses of ceramide pathway genes. In parallel, DES1 knockout and pharmacologic inhibition of DES1 in obese mouse models reduced ceramide production and delayed colorectal tumor development, supporting a causal role for ceramides in obesity-driven colorectal carcinogenesis. | Findings: A ceramide-based risk score predicts colorectal cancer risk in prospective human cohorts.; DES1 knockout mice exhibit lower tissue ceramide levels and reduced colorectal tumor burden under high‑fat diet conditions.; A first‑in‑class DES1 small‑molecule inhibitor lowers ceramide production and recapitulates the protective phenotype of the knockout in obese mouse models.

metadata.speaker: Mary Playdon
metadata.talk_title: Ceramide-based colorectal cancer risk score and DES1 inhibitor studies

text: AFABP as circulating biomarker and immunotherapy target in high‑risk breast cancer | Speaker: Bing Li | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: AFABP (FABP4) mediates fatty‑acid transport and signaling in adipose tissue; its overexpression in obesity creates a lipid‑rich microenvironment that promotes breast tumor growth. Anti‑AFABP antibodies block this signaling, reducing tumor progression in both FABP4‑deficient mice and human breast cancer PDX models, suggesting AFABP as a circulating biomarker and immunotherapy target. | Findings: Circulating AFABP levels are significantly higher in women with high‑risk breast cancer compared with controls.; Anti‑AFABP antibodies demonstrate therapeutic efficacy, reducing tumor volume by ~45% in PDX models.; Conditional knockout of FABP4 in mice attenuates high‑fat diet‑induced breast tumor promotion.

metadata.speaker: Bing Li
metadata.talk_title: AFABP as circulating biomarker and immunotherapy target in high‑risk breast cancer

text: Visceral fat‑induced inflammation inflammatype for colorectal and liver cancer risk | Speaker: Ed Giovannucci | Tumors: colorectal cancer, liver cancer | MOA: Using cohorts with direct visceral adiposity measurements (DEXA) and comprehensive plasma inflammatory profiling, the team identified a multi‑protein “inflammatype” that reflects visceral fat‑driven inflammation. This signature is associated with higher risk of colorectal and liver cancers, providing a blood‑based biomarker to capture obesity‑related inflammatory pathways beyond BMI. | Findings: An inflammatype derived from visceral fat‑associated proteins predicts colorectal cancer risk (hazard ratio ~1.6 in top quartile).; The same signature is linked to increased liver cancer incidence, independent of BMI.; Visceral fat measured by DEXA correlates more strongly with the inflammatype than BMI (r=0.48 vs 0.22).

metadata.speaker: Ed Giovannucci
metadata.talk_title: Visceral fat‑induced inflammation inflammatype for colorectal and liver cancer risk

text: Biospecimen science funding opportunities and Moonshot Biobank overview | Speaker: Lokesh Agrawal | MOA: Dr. Agrawal described the NCI biospecimen science infrastructure that standardizes pre‑analytical processes, provides curated specimen banks (NCCN, CHTN, Moonshot), and funds multidisciplinary U01 projects to generate reproducible, clinically annotated biospecimens for assay validation across solid and hematologic cancers. | Findings: The U01 biospecimen science program has funded 24 grants covering a broad range of cancer types.; From 2022‑2024, the CHTN network served 618 unique researchers, distributing 117 specimens and supporting 122 publications.; The Cancer Moonshot Biobank enrolled ~1,300 patients, with 1,020 having longitudinal biospecimens, including ~300 with multiple blood draws and ~150 with paired tissue collections.; Diversity metrics of the Moonshot cohort show 18% Black/African American and 8% Hispanic participants, exceeding typical US trial representation.

metadata.speaker: Lokesh Agrawal
metadata.talk_title: Biospecimen science funding opportunities and Moonshot Biobank overview

text: Acetylcholine signaling by T and B cells modulates tumor and liver regeneration | Speaker: Tak | Tumors: pancreatic cancer, liver cancer, breast cancer | MOA: T cell-derived acetylcholine promotes vascular dilation and immune cell trafficking, while B cell-derived acetylcholine is essential for liver regeneration after partial hepatectomy; loss of acetylcholine in T cells reduces tumor growth and alters immune phenotypes. | Findings: B cell-specific deletion of Chat leads to lethality after 70% partial hepatectomy, indicating essential role in liver regeneration; T cell-specific Chat deletion reduces tumor growth and alters vascular density in mouse models; Serum choline levels correlate with patient prognosis across multiple cancer types

metadata.speaker: Tak
metadata.talk_title: Acetylcholine signaling by T and B cells modulates tumor and liver regeneration

text: Profiling and targeting innervating peripheral neurons in pancreatic cancer | Speaker: Andreas Trump | Tumors: pancreatic cancer | MOA: Fast‑Blue retrograde tracing identifies pancreas‑innervating sympathetic and sensory neurons; denervation with 6‑OHDA or nab‑paclitaxel reduces neuronal density, reprograms CAFs to a pro‑inflammatory state, enhances CD8 T‑cell infiltration, and synergizes with PD‑1 blockade to suppress tumor growth. | Findings: Fast‑Blue tracing reveals identical numbers of neurons innervating normal pancreas and PDAC, but PDAC shows massive axonal sprouting; Denervation with 6‑OHDA (sympathetic) or nab‑paclitaxel (sensory) individually slows tumor growth; combined denervation nearly abolishes tumor progression in mouse models; Denervation converts immunosuppressive CAFs to pro‑inflammatory phenotype and increases CD8 T‑cell infiltration; Preclinical data support a phase I/II trial (SYNERGY) combining celiac ganglion radiotherapy, nab‑paclitaxel/gemcitabine, and PD‑1 inhibition

metadata.speaker: Andreas Trump
metadata.talk_title: Profiling and targeting innervating peripheral neurons in pancreatic cancer

text: Nociceptor neurons drive CD8 T‑cell exhaustion via CGRP in melanoma | Speaker: Sebastien Talbot | Tumors: melanoma | MOA: Melanoma activates nociceptor neurons to release CGRP, which binds RAMP1 on CD8 T cells, driving an exhausted phenotype (↑PD‑1, LAG‑3, TIM‑3, ↓IFN‑γ); genetic or pharmacologic blockade of CGRP‑RAMP1 signaling restores T‑cell function and reduces tumor growth. | Findings: Ablation of TRPV1+ nociceptors reduces melanoma growth and increases IFN‑γ+ CD8 T cells in tumors; Co‑culture of DRG neurons with melanoma up‑regulates CGRP expression in neurons; Exogenous CGRP induces PD‑1, LAG‑3, TIM‑3 up‑regulation and IFN‑γ loss in CD8 T cells; effect absent in RAMP1‑KO T cells; RAMP1‑deficient CD8 T cells show reduced exhaustion and slower tumor growth when transferred into melanoma‑bearing mice; High RAMP1 expression in melanoma patients associates with worse survival and reduced response to checkpoint blockade

metadata.speaker: Sebastien Talbot
metadata.talk_title: Nociceptor neurons drive CD8 T‑cell exhaustion via CGRP in melanoma

text: Engineering biparatopic antibodies for FGFR2 fusion targeting and ADC development | Speaker: Bill Sellers | Tumors: intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, gastric cancer, breast cancer, colon cancer | MOA: Biparatopic antibodies BC and BD simultaneously engage two distinct epitopes on the extracellular domain of FGFR2 fusions, increasing avidity, promoting receptor internalization and lysosomal degradation, and retaining activity against kinase‑domain resistance mutations; when conjugated to ADC payloads they induce tumor regression in FGFR2‑amplified models. | Findings: Biparatopic antibodies BC and BD showed >2‑fold higher solution affinity and avidity compared with parental antibodies.; BC and BD blocked colony formation of FGFR2‑driven BaF3 cells more effectively than parental antibodies.; In FGFR2‑OPTN PDX, BC and BD inhibited tumor growth (~20% regression) whereas small‑molecule FGFR2 inhibitor achieved ~20% regression, demonstrating comparable efficacy.; Tumors treated with BC/BD showed near‑complete loss of surface FGFR2, indicating receptor down‑regulation via internalization.; BC and BD retained internalization and anti‑proliferative activity against FGFR2 kinase‑domain resistance mutants.

metadata.speaker: Bill Sellers
metadata.talk_title: Engineering biparatopic antibodies for FGFR2 fusion targeting and ADC development

text: Zenitatamab (ZAN) bi‑paratopic HER2 antibody: unique CDC activity and clinical benefit | Speaker: Nina Weiser | Tumors: biliary tract cancer, gastric cancer, breast cancer, HER2‑positive solid tumors | MOA: Zenitatamab binds HER2 ECD2 and ECD4 on adjacent HER2 molecules (trans bi‑paratopic binding), clustering receptors into large caps that trigger rapid complement activation (CDC) and enhanced internalization, leading to superior tumor cell killing compared with the trastuzumab + pertuzumab combination. | Findings: Zenitatamab shows 1.5‑fold higher cell‑surface saturation than trastuzumab or pertuzumab alone, indicating trans bi‑paratopic binding.; Super‑resolution microscopy revealed larger HER2 clusters (caps) with ZAN versus microclusters with the antibody combination.; ZAN mediates potent CDC, achieving near‑100% cytotoxicity within 15 min, whereas trastuzumab + pertuzumab show no CDC.; In HER2‑positive biliary tract PDX, ZAN induced complete tumor regression at doses equal or lower than the trastuzumab + pertuzumab combination.; Phase III HORIZON‑GEA101 demonstrated significant PFS (12.4 mo vs 8.0 mo) and a trend toward OS benefit (24.4 mo vs 19.2 mo) for ZAN + chemo, independent of PD‑L1 status.

metadata.speaker: Nina Weiser
metadata.talk_title: Zenitatamab (ZAN) bi‑paratopic HER2 antibody: unique CDC activity and clinical benefit

text: Two‑plus‑one bispecific platform for EMPP3‑targeted CD3 T‑cell engagers and CD28 costimulation | Speaker: John Desjarlais | Tumors: clear cell renal cell carcinoma, colorectal cancer, prostate cancer, lung adenocarcinoma | MOA: A 2+1 bispecific format places two EMPP3‑binding VHHs in tandem to achieve avidity‑driven selectivity for high‑density EMPP3 tumors, while a monovalent CD3 arm provides T‑cell activation; co‑targeting CD28 with a separate bispecific further amplifies T‑cell signaling, overcoming exhaustion and enhancing tumor killing. | Findings: The 2+1 EMPP3‑CD3 bispecific shows potent cytotoxicity against EMPP3‑high RCC cells while sparing low‑expressing normal cells, demonstrating an avidity‑driven therapeutic window.; In the Phase I study (n=20), 5 patients achieved partial responses and >50% tumor reduction was observed in >50% of patients despite heavy pretreatment.; CRS occurred in 70% of patients but was mostly grade 1‑2; grade 3 occurred in <5% and no grade 4 events were reported.; Two best responders lacked detectable EMPP3 by IHC, suggesting possible bystander killing or assay sensitivity issues.; Combination of EMPP3‑CD3 with EMPP3‑CD28 bispecific restored T‑cell activity in chronic stimulation assays, indicating potential to overcome T‑cell exhaustion.

metadata.speaker: John Desjarlais
metadata.talk_title: Two‑plus‑one bispecific platform for EMPP3‑targeted CD3 T‑cell engagers and CD28 costimulation

text: Development of NEO811, a molecular glue degrader of ARNT (HIF-1β) for clear cell renal cell carcinoma | Speaker: Phil Chamberlain | Tumors: clear cell renal cell carcinoma | MOA: NEO811 is a cereblon‑recruiting molecular glue that induces ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of the transcription factor ARNT, disrupting the obligate HIF‑α/ARNT dimer and shutting down pan‑HIF transcriptional programs in VHL‑deficient ccRCC, leading to tumor regression even in models resistant to HIF‑2α inhibitors. | Findings: NEO811 degrades ARNT with >log‑unit selectivity over other NEO substrates in whole‑cell proteomics.; Oral NEO811 induces potent tumor regression in ccRCC xenografts at low doses with no body‑weight loss.; In HIF‑2α G323E mutant and HIF‑2α‑low PDX models, NEO811 retains activity whereas belzutifan loses efficacy.; Systemic ARNT degradation in mice is well tolerated, indicating a potentially safe therapeutic window.

metadata.speaker: Phil Chamberlain
metadata.talk_title: Development of NEO811, a molecular glue degrader of ARNT (HIF-1β) for clear cell renal cell carcinoma

text: AZD8359, a CD8‑biased T‑cell engager targeting STEAP2 for metastatic castration‑resistant prostate cancer | Speaker: Suzanne Sitnikova | Tumors: prostate cancer | MOA: AZD8359 is a bivalent bispecific antibody that binds STEAP2 on prostate tumor cells and a CD8‑binding arm to preferentially engage CD8+ T cells, delivering cytotoxic signals while limiting CD4‑driven cytokine release, thereby achieving potent tumor regression with a wider therapeutic index. | Findings: STEAP2 is highly and homogeneously expressed in >95% of metastatic castration‑resistant prostate cancer lesions with minimal normal tissue expression.; AZD8359 mediates STEAP2‑dependent tumor cell killing in vitro; killing is abolished in STEAP2‑KO cells.; CD8‑biased format increases potency compared with a non‑CD8‑guided TCE while reducing CD4 activation and cytokine release.; In humanized mouse flank and bone‑metastasis models, AZD8359 achieves complete tumor clearance with no activity from isotype control.; Therapeutic index (cytotoxic vs cytokine release) is markedly expanded versus conventional 2+1 TCEs both in vitro and in vivo.

metadata.speaker: Suzanne Sitnikova
metadata.talk_title: AZD8359, a CD8‑biased T‑cell engager targeting STEAP2 for metastatic castration‑resistant prostate cancer

text: TNG961, an oral HBS1L molecular glue degrader for FOCAD‑deleted cancers | Speaker: Hillary Nicholson | Tumors: pancreatic cancer, non‑small cell lung cancer, FOCAD‑deleted cancers | MOA: TNG961 is a cereblon‑recruiting molecular glue that induces selective proteasomal degradation of HBS1L, a key component of the HBS1L‑PELO ribosome rescue complex; loss of HBS1L in FOCAD‑deficient tumors triggers ER stress and the unfolded protein response, leading to selective tumor cell death. | Findings: TNG961 degrades HBS1L with picomolar potency while sparing GSPT1 and other NEO substrates.; In FOCAD‑negative isogenic cell lines, TNG961 shows >100‑fold selectivity for loss of viability compared with FOCAD‑positive counterparts.; Oral dosing leads to dose‑proportional exposure and robust HBS1L degradation in tumor PD tissues.; Complete tumor regressions observed in multiple FOCAD‑deleted CDX/PDX models of pancreatic cancer and NSCLC.; Non‑overlapping sensitivity with MTAP‑cooperative PRMT5 inhibitors; sequential or combined therapy yields enhanced tumor control.

metadata.speaker: Hillary Nicholson
metadata.talk_title: TNG961, an oral HBS1L molecular glue degrader for FOCAD‑deleted cancers

text: EPI-326, a bispecific EGFR degrader (EpiTac) targeting integrin β6 for EGFR‑driven solid tumors | Speaker: Shirah Garde | Tumors: non‑small cell lung cancer, head and neck cancer, colorectal cancer | MOA: EPI-326 is a bispecific IgG1 antibody that binds EGFR on tumor cells and integrin β6 as a degrading receptor; the ternary complex drives lysosomal internalization and degradation of EGFR, removing both its kinase activity and scaffolding functions while sparing normal tissues lacking integrin β6, resulting in durable tumor regressions. | Findings: Integrin β6 is highly expressed and co‑localized with EGFR in NSCLC, head‑and‑neck, and CRC, but limited in normal skin and colon.; EPI-326 degrades EGFR across wild‑type, activating, and resistance mutations, achieving complete tumor regressions where blocking antibodies only induce stasis.; Single dose yields >90% EGFR loss lasting >7 days, indicating catalytic degradation.; Preclinical safety in cynomolgus monkeys shows no EGFR‑related toxicities up to 204 mg/kg, supporting a wide therapeutic index.; Combination with osimertinib (NSCLC) or KRAS inhibitor (CRC) yields deeper and more durable responses.

metadata.speaker: Shirah Garde
metadata.talk_title: EPI-326, a bispecific EGFR degrader (EpiTac) targeting integrin β6 for EGFR‑driven solid tumors

text: First-in-class B7-H3 targeted sialidase for boosting innate and adaptive anti-tumor immunity | Speaker: James Broderick | Tumors: ovarian cancer, non-small cell lung cancer, prostate cancer, colorectal cancer, head and neck cancer | MOA: The next‑generation B7‑H3‑targeted sialidase binds tumor cells via a B7‑H3 antibody arm and delivers a high‑Km human sialidase that removes surface sialic acids, exposing neoantigens and reducing CD163+ M2 macrophages, thereby enhancing both innate and adaptive immune responses. The targeting arm adds Fc‑mediated ADCC/ADCP and prolongs desialylation to >7 days, overcoming the short‑lived effect of the first‑gen construct. | Findings: Targeted sialidase achieved markedly deeper and more durable tumor desialylation than untargeted enzyme (PNA signal sustained for up to 7 days).; In a humanized A375 xenograft, targeted sialidase outperformed PD‑1 blockade in tumor control.; Paired patient biopsies showed 80‑90% reduction of CD163+ macrophages after treatment.; First‑gen molecule demonstrated safety and proof‑of‑mechanism but only modest clinical activity due to transient desialylation.; B7‑H3 and hypersialylation co‑occur in >50% of ovarian, lung, and prostate cancers, supporting patient selection.

metadata.speaker: James Broderick
metadata.talk_title: First-in-class B7-H3 targeted sialidase for boosting innate and adaptive anti-tumor immunity

text: Discovery of ECI‑830, a potent and selective CDK2 inhibitor for HR‑positive breast cancer and CCNE1‑amplified tumors | Speaker: Sunib Jagani | Tumors: HR-positive breast cancer, ovarian cancer, non-small cell lung cancer | MOA: ECI‑830 is a type‑I ATP‑competitive inhibitor that binds the CDK2 ATP pocket, exploiting unique lower‑hinge residues (His84, Gln85) to achieve >100‑fold selectivity over CDK1. Inhibition of CDK2 blocks cyclin‑E1‑driven Rb phosphorylation, leading to deeper G1 arrest and enhanced suppression of E2F‑driven transcription, especially when combined with the CDK4/6 inhibitor ribociclib. | Findings: ECI‑830 shows >100‑fold selectivity for CDK2 over CDK1 and other CDKs.; In cyclin‑E1 amplified models, single‑agent ECI‑830 produces dose‑dependent tumor growth inhibition with corresponding p‑Rb suppression.; Combination of ECI‑830 with ribociclib yields greater tumor regression than ribociclib alone in multiple HR‑positive breast cancer xenografts.; RNA‑seq confirms that the combination more profoundly down‑regulates E2F target pathways than ribociclib monotherapy.; Steady‑state unbound plasma concentrations above the phospho‑Rb AC50 are required for efficacy.

metadata.speaker: Sunib Jagani
metadata.talk_title: Discovery of ECI‑830, a potent and selective CDK2 inhibitor for HR‑positive breast cancer and CCNE1‑amplified tumors

text: TRI‑611, a CNS‑penetrant ALK molecular glue degrader for ALK‑fusion positive NSCLC | Speaker: Vito Palomba | Tumors: ALK‑positive non‑small cell lung cancer | MOA: TRI‑611 is a cereblon‑recruiting molecular glue that binds a distal site on the ALK kinase domain, inducing a ternary complex with CRBN and a novel helical degron on ALK. This leads to poly‑ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of EML4‑ALK, including all tested TKI‑resistance mutations, while sparing other kinases and cereblon neosubstrates. | Findings: TRI‑611 induces selective degradation of EML4‑ALK with >90% loss in tumor tissue after oral dosing.; Degradation is cereblon‑dependent; CRBN knockout abrogates activity.; Potent anti‑tumor activity against a panel of ALK TKI‑resistance mutations, including double and triple mutants.; In lorlatinib‑resistant xenografts, TRI‑611 alone drives tumor regression, whereas lorlatinib is ineffective.; Oral administration achieves brain concentrations comparable to lorlatinib and regresses intracranial ALK‑positive tumors.

metadata.speaker: Vito Palomba
metadata.talk_title: TRI‑611, a CNS‑penetrant ALK molecular glue degrader for ALK‑fusion positive NSCLC

text: Discovery and development of a CD30 dual‑payload ADC combining MMAE and TOP1 inhibitor | Speaker: Megan Rice | Tumors: Hodgkin lymphoma, anaplastic large cell lymphoma | MOA: The ADC uses a site‑specific non‑natural amino acid to attach two MMAE molecules (DAR2) and native cysteines to attach eight topoisomerase‑I inhibitor molecules (DAR8). CD30 binding triggers internalization; the MMAE component kills microtubules while the TOP1 inhibitor induces DNA damage, providing complementary mechanisms that overcome P‑gp‑mediated resistance and enable robust tumor regression at sub‑optimal doses. | Findings: Dual‑payload ADC achieves tumor regression in both parental and P‑gp‑overexpressing ALCL models, whereas MMAE‑only ADC fails in the resistant line.; At a sub‑optimal dose (0.6 mg/kg), the dual‑payload ADC induces robust tumor regression, while single‑payload ADCs show minimal effect.; Rat tolerability study shows MTD of 60 mg/kg for the dual‑payload ADC, substantially higher than brentuximab vedotin (10 mg/kg).; Pharmacokinetics reveal a longer half‑life and stable linker‑payload integrity compared with conventional stochastic conjugates.; Preliminary non‑human primate data (not disclosed) indicate favorable safety at clinically relevant exposures.

metadata.speaker: Megan Rice
metadata.talk_title: Discovery and development of a CD30 dual‑payload ADC combining MMAE and TOP1 inhibitor

text: First-in-class oral macrocycle Cyclin AB RXL inhibitor CID-078 | Speaker: Marie Evangelista | Tumors: solid tumors | MOA: CID-078 is an oral macrocyclic inhibitor that binds the hydrophobic RXL pocket of cyclin A and cyclin B, preventing their interaction with E2F and Mit1, respectively. This sustains E2F activity and forces cyclin B‑Cdk complexes into premature mitosis, causing replication stress, mitotic catastrophe and apoptosis preferentially in RB‑deficient or E2F‑high tumor cells. | Findings: CID-078 achieves sub‑nanomolar potency against cyclin A/B in biochemical assays.; Oral bioavailability improved from 2% to 25% in preclinical species.; RB loss or biallelic RB1 inactivation correlates with >2‑fold increased sensitivity in cell line screens.; E2F‑high transcriptional signature predicts sensitivity across a broad panel of cancer cell lines.; In vivo, CID-078 induces tumor regression in RB‑deficient PDX models, with responses correlating with E2F expression.

metadata.speaker: Marie Evangelista
metadata.talk_title: First-in-class oral macrocycle Cyclin AB RXL inhibitor CID-078

text: Oral BRD9 degrader AMX883 for AML | Speaker: Martin Pass | Tumors: AML | MOA: AMX883 is an oral, covalent reversible PROTAC that binds BRD9 and recruits the E3 ligase DCAF16 via a cyanoacrylamide warhead, forming a ternary complex that leads to ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of BRD9, thereby releasing the differentiation block in AML blasts and inducing myeloid differentiation and apoptosis. | Findings: AMX883 degrades BRD9 with DC90 of 0.3 nM and high selectivity over other bromodomain proteins.; BRD9 degradation induces myeloid differentiation markers (CD11B, CD86) in AML cell lines.; In MV411 xenografts, AMX883 achieves sustained BRD9 degradation beyond plasma PK.; In two AML PDX models, AMX883 monotherapy leads to complete tumor regression and significant survival benefit versus venetoclax or vehicle.; Combination of AMX883 with venetoclax prevents emergence of venetoclax resistance and shows synergistic tumor control in vivo.

metadata.speaker: Martin Pass
metadata.talk_title: Oral BRD9 degrader AMX883 for AML

text: ENPP3‑targeted ADC JNJ‑2175 for solid tumors | Speaker: Smruthi Vijayaraghavan | Tumors: renal cell carcinoma, non-small cell lung cancer, colorectal cancer, endometrial cancer | MOA: JNJ‑2175 is a site‑specifically conjugated ADC comprising a high‑affinity ENPP3 antibody linked via a branched linker to the AFHPA auristatin‑derived payload; upon internalization in ENPP3‑positive tumor cells, the payload is metabolized to a non‑bystander auristatin, delivering potent microtubule inhibition while controlled bystander activity is achieved through the initial cell‑permeable intermediate. | Findings: JNJ‑2175 binds dose‑dependently to ENPP3‑positive cells with no off‑target binding to ENPP1/2.; Rapid internalization observed in ENPP3‑positive cell lines.; Potent cytotoxicity against ENPP3‑positive lines; no activity in ENPP3‑negative or knockout cells.; Co‑culture assays demonstrate bystander killing of ENPP3‑negative cells only when mixed with ENPP3‑positive cells.; In three ENPP3‑positive PDX models (NSCLC, RCC), JNJ‑2175 produces dose‑dependent tumor regressions with complete responses.

metadata.speaker: Smruthi Vijayaraghavan
metadata.talk_title: ENPP3‑targeted ADC JNJ‑2175 for solid tumors

text: Dual Vbeta6/Vbeta10 T‑cell agonist IPN‑1203 | Speaker: Stefan Pleiss | Tumors: solid tumors | MOA: IPN‑1203 is a trispecific bispecific construct that simultaneously binds Vbeta6 and Vbeta10 TCR domains on a subset of T cells and delivers a wild‑type IL‑15/IL‑15Rα fusion, providing potent, selective activation and proliferation of these T cells with enhanced STAT5 signaling, leading to central‑memory differentiation, reduced exhaustion, and durable antitumor immunity. | Findings: IPN‑1203 binds selectively to ~6% of peripheral T cells (Vbeta6/Vbeta10) with high affinity (1.9 nM).; Rapid STAT5 activation via IL‑15 component without direct TCR phosphorylation.; Five‑day PBMC cultures show >50‑fold expansion of Vbeta‑positive T cells (EC50 ~50 pM).; In mouse surrogate model, IPN‑1203 induces complete tumor regressions dependent on CD8 and Vbeta13 T cells.; Single‑cell RNA‑seq reveals >5‑fold increase in central memory CD8 T cells and >50% reduction in exhausted T cells.

metadata.speaker: Stefan Pleiss
