text: Tumor intrinsic and extrinsic mechanisms of ADC resistance in bladder cancer | Speaker: Dr. Jonathan Chou | Tumors: bladder cancer, urothelial carcinoma | MOA: Enfortumab vedotin targets NECTIN4, is internalized and releases MMAE; resistance mechanisms include low or heterogeneous NECTIN4 expression, payload efflux, and altered endosomal trafficking. NECTIN4 expression can be pharmacologically up‑regulated via PPARγ agonists (rosiglitazone) or retinoic‑acid signaling (ATRA/Bexarotene), enhancing ADC efficacy. | Findings: NECTIN4 high tumors (H‑score >225) achieve median OS of 31.5 months versus 18.4 months in low expressors.; Chromosome 1 amplification of PVRL4 (NECTIN4) drives homogeneous membranous expression and superior clinical outcomes.; Rosiglitazone induces NECTIN4 surface expression in low‑expressing bladder cancer cells without affecting normal urothelium, sensitizing them to EV.; Retinoic‑acid agonists (ATRA, Bexarotene) similarly up‑regulate NECTIN4 via STRA6‑RXR signaling.; EV‑resistant models retain or increase NECTIN4 but show reduced ADC internalization due to altered lysosomal trafficking.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Jonathan Chou
metadata.talk_title: Tumor intrinsic and extrinsic mechanisms of ADC resistance in bladder cancer

text: HER2 ADC resistance mechanisms and combination strategies | Speaker: Dr. Unknown | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: Trastuzumab deruxtecan binds HER2, is internalized, and releases a topoisomerase‑I inhibitor; resistance occurs via HER2 point mutations that impair antibody binding, reduced HER2 surface density, and heterodimerization with EGFR that limits internalization. EGFR blockade or activation can modulate HER2 internalization and restore sensitivity. | Findings: HER2 binding‑site mutations prevent T‑DXd internalization and confer resistance in vitro.; Doxycycline‑induced HER2 down‑regulation reduces ADC internalization and increases IC50 by ~800‑fold.; EGFR overexpression decreases HER2 homodimers, reducing T‑DXd efficacy; EGFR knockdown or cetuximab treatment restores HER2 internalization.; Combining cetuximab with T‑DXd improves tumor responses in HER2‑high/EGFR‑high models in vivo.; CAR‑T targeting HER2 remains effective against EV‑resistant cells that retain HER2 expression.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Unknown
metadata.talk_title: HER2 ADC resistance mechanisms and combination strategies

text: ZC3H18 truncating mutations drive ERV accumulation and melanomagenesis | Speaker: Megan Inscho | Tumors: melanoma, colon cancer, uterine cancer, pan-cancer | MOA: Truncating mutations in the RNA‑surveillance factor ZC3H18 act in a dominant‑negative manner, losing interaction with the NEXT complex while retaining RNA‑binding capacity, leading to cytoplasmic sequestration and stabilization of endogenous retroviral RNAs; these ERV transcripts are necessary and sufficient to accelerate melanomagenesis in zebrafish and human models. | Findings: 35% of melanoma patients harbor mono‑ or biallelic loss of ZC3H18, and ~30% of all solid tumors show focal deletions of the locus.; ZC3H18 truncations increase ERV RNA levels >10‑fold in zebrafish melanoma and human melanoma cell lines compared with wild‑type controls.; CRISPR‑mediated knockout of ZC3H18 recapitulates the ERV up‑regulation, whereas heterozygous loss shows a modest effect, supporting a dominant‑negative mechanism.; Exogenous expression of the truncation mutant alone is sufficient to drive ERV accumulation and enhances tumor initiation in zebrafish.; Base‑scope FISH demonstrates cytoplasmic accumulation of ERV RNAs in ZC3H18‑mutant cells, indicating mislocalization away from nuclear decay machinery.

metadata.speaker: Megan Inscho
metadata.talk_title: ZC3H18 truncating mutations drive ERV accumulation and melanomagenesis

text: Splicing‑regulated LAG‑3 intron removal enables conditional FOXO1 and IL‑12 expression to overcome T‑cell exhaustion | Speaker: Omar Abdelwahab | Tumors: melanoma | MOA: Exhausted CD8+ T cells splice out a retained intron in LAG3, enabling full‑length LAG‑3 protein; this splicing switch is harnessed by inserting a therapeutic cassette downstream of the intron, so that FOXO1 or IL‑12 is expressed only after intron removal in chronically stimulated T cells, thereby reprogramming exhausted T cells to a less exhausted, more cytotoxic phenotype and improving anti‑tumor activity. | Findings: A previously unannotated intron in LAG3 is retained in acutely stimulated CD8+ T cells but efficiently removed in exhausted tumor‑infiltrating T cells, correlating with a 4‑fold increase in LAG‑3 mRNA and protein.; Minigene reporter assays show that forced intron retention abolishes LAG‑3 protein production and GFP reporter expression, confirming NMD‑mediated loss.; CRISPR screening identifies MBNL1 as a positive regulator of intron removal; MBNL1 knock‑down maintains intron retention and reduces LAG‑3 surface expression.; Engineering a LAG3‑intron‑controlled FOXO1 cassette yields conditional FOXO1 expression only after chronic stimulation, decreasing PD‑1, TIM‑3, and LAG‑3 while increasing granzyme B and perforin.; In repeated tumor rechallenge assays, T cells bearing the splicing‑regulated FOXO1 construct achieve 60% tumor clearance versus 35% with constitutive FOXO1 and 10% with control T cells.

metadata.speaker: Omar Abdelwahab
metadata.talk_title: Splicing‑regulated LAG‑3 intron removal enables conditional FOXO1 and IL‑12 expression to overcome T‑cell exhaustion

text: Impact of the intestinal microbiome on CAR T cell therapy | Speaker: Melody Smith | Tumors: B-cell lymphoma, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, multiple myeloma | MOA: Antibiotic exposure, especially anaerobe‑targeting agents (piperacillin‑tazobactam, meropenem), disrupts gut microbiota, reducing beneficial taxa such as Akkermansia and Enterococcus‑derived SagA activity, leading to lower CAR T cell expansion, increased neurotoxicity, and shortened PFS/OS. Preclinical mouse models show that meropenem pretreatment or vancomycin alters microbiome composition, impairing CAR T efficacy, whereas fecal transplants from responders or Akkermansia supplementation restore antitumor activity. | Findings: Antibiotic exposure within 4‑6 weeks before CAR T therapy is independently associated with reduced OS and PFS across five retrospective cohorts (n≈1,000 total).; Anaerobic‑targeting antibiotics (piperacillin‑tazobactam, meropenem) show the strongest negative impact on survival compared with low‑risk agents.; High‑risk antibiotic exposure correlates with increased ICANS incidence in two studies.; Mouse models pre‑treated with meropenem exhibit larger tumor burden and lower survival after CD19 CAR T infusion.; Fecal microbiota from CAR T responders improves tumor control in antibiotic‑depleted mice, whereas non‑responder FMT does not.

metadata.speaker: Melody Smith
metadata.talk_title: Impact of the intestinal microbiome on CAR T cell therapy

text: CAR T response rates: harnessing the microbiome | Speaker: City of Hope speaker | Tumors: B-cell lymphoma, multiple myeloma | MOA: Antibiotic exposure (especially high‑risk anaerobic agents) selects for resistant Enterococcus strains lacking SagA activity and reduces beneficial taxa such as Akkermansia, leading to impaired CAR T expansion and higher progression rates. Reintroduction of Akkermansia or SagA‑expressing bacteria restores immune activation via AhR or NOD2 pathways, improving CAR T efficacy. | Findings: Antibiotic exposure prior to CAR T is linked to reduced PFS and OS in both US and German cohorts.; Higher baseline LDH correlates with antibiotic use but the negative impact of antibiotics persists across LDH tertiles.; Enterococcus faecium SagA activity correlates with lower progression; patients harboring SagA‑positive strains have better outcomes.; Akkermansia muciniphila abundance predicts improved response in CD28‑CAR T recipients.; Mouse models show that tetracycline‑depleted microbiota lose CAR T benefit, which is rescued by Akkermansia reconstitution.

metadata.speaker: City of Hope speaker
metadata.talk_title: CAR T response rates: harnessing the microbiome

text: Enterococcus SagA and NOD2 signaling modulate immunotherapy | Speaker: Howard Hang | Tumors: melanoma, lung cancer | MOA: Enterococcus faecium expresses the cell‑wall hydrolase SagA, which cleaves peptidoglycan into muramyl dipeptides that activate host NOD2 signaling. NOD2 activation enhances dendritic cell maturation and CD8⁺ T‑cell cytotoxicity, thereby potentiating checkpoint blockade and CAR T efficacy. SagA deletion abolishes this effect, while engineered SagA‑expressing Lactococcus lactis restores it. | Findings: SagA‑expressing Enterococcus faecium synergizes with CTLA‑4 and PD‑L1 blockade in antibiotic‑treated mice, whereas SagA‑null strains do not.; SagA activity is required for NOD2‑dependent antitumor immunity; NOD2‑KO mice lose the benefit of SagA‑expressing bacteria.; Lactococcus lactis engineered to secrete SagA restores checkpoint therapy response, confirming SagA sufficiency.; SagA is conserved across commensal and vancomycin‑resistant Enterococcus strains; deletion in a VRE strain eliminates its immunostimulatory effect.; In a minor‑mismatch allo‑HSCT GVHD model, SagA‑positive VRE improves survival, suggesting context‑dependent benefits.

metadata.speaker: Howard Hang
metadata.talk_title: Enterococcus SagA and NOD2 signaling modulate immunotherapy

text: AI‑assisted storytelling and GIS mapping to reduce cervical and colorectal cancer disparities | Speaker: Dr. Lourdes Vizconde-Gabinati | Tumors: cervical cancer, colorectal cancer, breast cancer, lung cancer | MOA: The speaker described a GIS‑based mapping workflow that visualizes cancer incidence trends over time and an AI‑assisted storytelling pipeline that generates low‑health‑literacy scripts, storyboards, and digital assets (videos, fotonovelas, social‑media clips). By pairing community‑derived narratives with AI‑generated content, the program achieved a 45% rise in cervical‑screening appointments and produced 13 peer‑reviewed articles, demonstrating that culturally tailored, AI‑accelerated communication can translate epidemiologic data into measurable community‑level screening improvements. | Findings: Implementation of GIS mapping identified high‑burden zip codes for cervical and colorectal cancer, guiding targeted outreach.; The Tamale Lesson video campaign increased screening appointments by 45% within six months among the target Hispanic population.; AI‑driven script generation reduced storyboard production time from weeks to hours, enabling rapid iteration based on focus‑group feedback.; The AI‑assisted framework supported creation of 13 journal articles and multiple digital toolkits (fotonovelas, YouTube channel, WhatsApp messaging).; Community health worker deployment (≈45 workers) and home‑to‑clinic navigation (ConnectHome) were launched to sustain screening gains despite pandemic setbacks.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Lourdes Vizconde-Gabinati
metadata.talk_title: AI‑assisted storytelling and GIS mapping to reduce cervical and colorectal cancer disparities

text: Markey Cancer Network: capacity building and research integration across Kentucky | Speaker: Dr. Pamela Hull | Tumors: lung cancer, colorectal cancer, breast cancer | MOA: The presentation outlined a hybrid care and research network that builds capacity in 20 independent Kentucky community hospitals, achieving 18 CoC accreditations, increasing referral volume (~1,000/year) and patient accruals (1,400), while embedding patient‑advocate scientists into basic and clinical projects to align research priorities with community needs. | Findings: Eighteen of twenty network hospitals achieved CoC accreditation within three years of joining the Markey Cancer Network.; Referral volume to Markey for specialized services rose to ~1,000 in the most recent year, reflecting improved care coordination.; The network facilitated 1,400 patient accruals across therapeutic, diagnostic, and health‑services studies, expanding research access for rural populations.; Research advocacy program engaged 54 advocates across 15 projects, with 100% reporting that their input improved study design and community relevance.; Quality‑measure scores improved significantly after hospitals joined the network, demonstrating measurable enhancements in cancer care delivery.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Pamela Hull
metadata.talk_title: Markey Cancer Network: capacity building and research integration across Kentucky

text: Sustainability models for community engagement: Be Well initiative and AI‑driven outreach | Speaker: Dr. Lorna McNeill | MOA: The speaker presented a place‑based sustainability framework that couples AI‑generated, culturally tailored communication tools with community‑led implementation (e.g., gardens, sun shades, food distribution). By transferring ownership to local organizations after 2–3 years, the model achieves >90% program continuation without ongoing grant support. | Findings: The Be Well initiative delivered 21 million pounds of healthy food and installed 82 sun shades, impacting 676 000 residents across four neighborhoods.; 90% of implemented programs remained active after initial philanthropic funding ended, driven by city‑government co‑funding and community‑organization leadership.; AI‑assisted content creation reduced production time for educational materials from months to days, enabling rapid iteration with community feedback.; Transfer of program leadership to local partners after 2–3 years ensured long‑term ownership and reduced reliance on cancer‑center staff.; Cross‑sector coalitions (city, schools, faith‑based groups) amplified reach and facilitated policy changes supporting sustained health‑promotion infrastructure.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Lorna McNeill
metadata.talk_title: Sustainability models for community engagement: Be Well initiative and AI‑driven outreach

text: Defining senescence, senotypes and implications for cancer | Speaker: Jennifer Elisseeff | MOA: The talk described how senescent cells adopt distinct senotypes in different tissue niches, identified via p16-Cre reporter mice and single-cell RNA‑seq, and how these senotypes influence wound healing, fibrosis, and tumor immune microenvironment, including vascular remodeling and T‑cell infiltration. | Findings: Senescent cells in fibrosis models are primarily stromal (CD29+ CD45-), with distinct vascular and fibroblastic senotypes identified by bulk and single‑cell sequencing.; Arthritic (ACL) injury before B16 tumor implantation reduces tumor growth and markedly increases response to checkpoint blockade, associated with increased CD8+ T‑cell infiltration and enhanced vascular P‑selectin expression.; Genetic ablation of p16‑positive senescent cells (Incakat model) abolishes the vascular and T‑cell infiltration phenotype and eliminates the immunotherapy benefit, indicating senescent cells are necessary for the observed anti‑tumor effect.

metadata.speaker: Jennifer Elisseeff
metadata.talk_title: Defining senescence, senotypes and implications for cancer

text: Redox‑based pan‑senolytic Senlytic and its preclinical cancer prevention potential | Speaker: Clemens Schmidt | Tumors: melanoma, lymphoma, RAS‑driven cancers | MOA: Senlytic is a redox‑activated pro‑drug that exploits the elevated NADH/low GSH ratio and labile iron in senescent cells to generate hydroxyl radicals via Fenton chemistry, inducing ferroptosis and apoptosis selectively in p53‑competent senescent cells across multiple senescence inducers. | Findings: Senlytic shows >10‑fold senolytic index over proliferating cells across replicative, oncogene‑induced, therapy‑induced, and virus‑induced senescence models.; In vivo, Senlytic clears p16‑positive senescent cells in aged mouse lungs, reducing collagen cuff formation without measurable toxicity.; Senlytic administered after chemotherapy eliminates therapy‑induced senescent lymphoma cells, extending mouse survival, but is ineffective in p53‑deficient tumors.; In a BRAF‑nevus mouse model, Senlytic reduces nevi and delays melanoma onset, demonstrating cancer‑preventive potential by targeting OIS lesions.; Senlytic prevents NMU‑induced RAS‑driven T‑cell lymphomagenesis in wild‑type mice, indicating that removal of incipient senescent lesions blocks tumor formation.

metadata.speaker: Clemens Schmidt
metadata.talk_title: Redox‑based pan‑senolytic Senlytic and its preclinical cancer prevention potential

text: Foundation models in pathology: data requirements, performance and robustness | Speaker: Jeroen van der Laak | Tumors: prostate cancer, breast cancer, pan-cancer | MOA: Foundation models are trained with self‑supervised learning on large, diverse pathology image collections to produce high‑dimensional embeddings that capture generic visual features; these embeddings enable few‑shot downstream tasks such as cancer grading, mutation prediction, and survival modeling with reduced data requirements. | Findings: Training on 12,000 prostate biopsies and 5,600 pathologist reviews yielded a quadratic weighted Kappa of up to 0.93, matching expert performance.; Foundation models achieved comparable performance with as little as 1% of the training data, whereas task‑specific models required >30% of data to reach similar accuracy.; Generalizability of foundation models was superior on out‑of‑distribution cohorts but depended on the diversity of the pre‑training data.; Foundation models consumed 35 times more energy than task‑specific models, highlighting a trade‑off between data efficiency and computational cost.

metadata.speaker: Jeroen van der Laak
metadata.talk_title: Foundation models in pathology: data requirements, performance and robustness

text: Benchmarking foundation models for survival prediction and the SURFER prognostic model | Speaker: Jana Lipkova | Tumors: bladder cancer, colorectal cancer, brain cancer, pan-cancer | MOA: SURFER extends a vision‑language foundation model (Titan) with SoftCLIP, a weighted contrastive loss that incorporates patient survival times into the embedding space, enabling the model to learn prognostic features directly from whole‑slide images and associated outcome text. | Findings: Patch‑level foundation models outperform slide‑level models for survival prediction across 13 cancer types.; Multimodal models (image + text) do not significantly improve survival prediction over unimodal models when prognostic information is absent from the text.; The SURFER model, trained with SoftCLIP on ~15,000 slides, yields a clear gradient of risk groups in UMAP space and improves downstream survival C‑index compared with the baseline Titan model.; Pan‑cancer training slightly outperforms cancer‑specific models, demonstrating feasibility of a single prognostic model for diverse tumor types.

metadata.speaker: Jana Lipkova
metadata.talk_title: Benchmarking foundation models for survival prediction and the SURFER prognostic model

text: Clinical applications of pathology foundation models and future AI agents | Speaker: Jakob Kater | Tumors: lung cancer, prostate cancer, breast cancer, pan-cancer | MOA: Foundation models generate generic image embeddings that can be fine‑tuned for specific clinical tasks; when combined with large language model agents, they enable multimodal reasoning across pathology, radiology, genomics and clinical records to support tumor board decision‑making and trial matching. | Findings: AI models trained on H&E slides can predict EGFR mutation status, allowing a 43% reduction in rapid molecular testing without loss of diagnostic accuracy.; Foundation models accelerate development of downstream tasks (e.g., molecular alteration inference, survival prediction) by requiring far fewer labeled examples.; Multimodal agents that integrate foundation model embeddings with language models can replicate tumor board reasoning and achieve performance comparable to human oncologists in benchmark studies.

metadata.speaker: Jakob Kater
metadata.talk_title: Clinical applications of pathology foundation models and future AI agents

text: New insights into SHP2 signaling to RAS and its catalytic domain functions | Speaker: Ben | Tumors: leukemia, solid tumors | MOA: Catalytic cysteine mutations in SHP2 (C459D) retain signaling to RAS/ERK despite being phosphatase-dead, acting as an adapter that directly binds the DH/PH domain of SOS1 to promote sustained Ras activation, while phosphatase activity serves as a negative feedback. | Findings: RMZ-4550 allosteric SHP2 inhibitor blocks EGF-induced RAS activation in 3T3 cells, rescued by SHP2 TMQL mutant expression.; Catalytic cysteine-to-aspartate (C459D) mutant restores RAS activation and sustains ERK/AKT signaling despite being >20,000‑fold phosphatase dead.; C459D mice are viable with mild phenotype, whereas C459E is embryonic lethal, indicating functional divergence of catalytic mutants.; Zebrafish shp2 C/D mutant rescues cardiac defects, confirming functional signaling across species.; Structural studies reveal direct binding of SHP2 catalytic domain to SOS1 DH/PH domain; mutations disrupting this interface abrogate signaling while preserving phosphatase activity.

metadata.speaker: Ben
metadata.talk_title: New insights into SHP2 signaling to RAS and its catalytic domain functions

text: Omega‑6 fatty acids activate mTORC1 via FABP5 and promote aggressive triple‑negative breast cancer | Speaker: John Planas | Tumors: triple-negative breast cancer, hormone receptor positive breast cancer | MOA: Omega‑6 fatty acids bind FABP5, inducing a conformational change that enables FABP5 to dock Raptor and assemble active mTORC1, driving proliferation of FABP5‑high triple‑negative breast cancer; omega‑3 promotes FABP5 degradation and induces microbiome‑derived lithocholic acid, which activates AMPK and suppresses mTOR signaling. | Findings: FABP5 directly binds omega‑6 fatty acids, exposing a docking site for Raptor and activating mTORC1 in TNBC cells.; FABP5 knockdown abolishes omega‑6‑induced mTOR activation and proliferation in TNBC cell lines.; TNBC PDX tumors and patient serum show elevated FABP5; omega‑6‑fed mice exhibit higher tumor FABP5 and mTOR signaling than omega‑3‑fed controls.; Visceral adipocyte‑derived extracellular vesicle FABP5 is taken up via macropinocytosis, sensitizing otherwise FABP5‑low cells to omega‑6‑driven mTOR activation.; Omega‑3 fatty acids accelerate FABP5 proteasomal degradation (half‑life 2‑4 h vs 24 h with omega‑6).

metadata.speaker: John Planas
metadata.talk_title: Omega‑6 fatty acids activate mTORC1 via FABP5 and promote aggressive triple‑negative breast cancer

text: Structural and regulatory mechanisms of BRAF and CRAF activation and dimerization | Speaker: Debbie Morrison | Tumors: cancer (RAS/RAF driven) | MOA: BRAF and CRAF are held in an auto‑inhibited state by 14‑3‑3 and the cysteine‑rich domain; oncogenic mutations or RAS‑GTP binding destabilize this interface, allowing the CRD to release, BC heterodimer formation, and activation of MEK/ERK. Distinct N‑terminal acidic regions confer KRAS selectivity for BRAF, while CRAF relies more on 14‑3‑3 interactions. | Findings: BRAF possesses a constitutive acidic N‑terminal segment that drives selective binding to KRAS polybasic region.; Disruption of the BC dimer interface abolishes EGF‑stimulated kinase activity of both BRAF and CRAF.; Class II/III BRAF mutants require BC heterodimerization for MAPK signaling, explaining paradoxical activation by first‑generation RAF inhibitors.; Cryo‑EM of auto‑inhibited BRAF shows the cysteine‑rich domain cradled by 14‑3‑3, occluding the dimer interface; mutations in this region release the inhibition.; In vitro KRAS‑GTP nanodisc assays demonstrate concentration‑dependent activation of BRAF that is dimer‑dependent and enhanced by membrane context.

metadata.speaker: Debbie Morrison
metadata.talk_title: Structural and regulatory mechanisms of BRAF and CRAF activation and dimerization

text: Autocrine LIF signaling drives myeloid immunosuppression and plasticity in ALK‑mutant lung adenocarcinoma | Speaker: Ray Palay | Tumors: lung adenocarcinoma (ALK‑mutant, LKB1/ALK) | MOA: Loss of LKB1 in ALK‑mutant lung adenocarcinoma upregulates leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF), which acts in an autocrine manner via LIFR/STAT3 to maintain dedifferentiated, SOX17‑high tumor cell states that secrete chemokines (CCL2, CXCL1/5/7) recruiting immunosuppressive ARG1⁺ interstitial macrophages and cyclic‑high neutrophils, thereby suppressing T‑cell function; blockade of LIF signaling genetically or with an anti‑LIF antibody reverses myeloid suppression and restores anti‑tumor immunity. | Findings: LIF is transcriptionally up‑regulated in ALK‑mutant/LKB1‑deficient tumors and correlates with phospho‑STAT3 positivity in mouse and human samples.; Genetic deletion of LIF or LIFR markedly reduces tumor burden and diminishes immunosuppressive neutrophil (cyclic‑high) and ARG1⁺ interstitial macrophage populations.; T‑cell functional cytokine production (IFN‑γ, TNF‑α) is restored in LIFR‑deleted tumors; T‑cell depletion abrogates the tumor‑growth advantage conferred by LIF signaling.; LIF‑driven tumors harbor distinct dedifferentiated tumor cell clusters (high SOX17, PROM1/CD133) that are depleted upon LIF blockade.; Anti‑LIF antibody treatment recapitulates genetic deletion effects, reducing tumor size and myeloid immunosuppression in established tumors.

metadata.speaker: Ray Palay
metadata.talk_title: Autocrine LIF signaling drives myeloid immunosuppression and plasticity in ALK‑mutant lung adenocarcinoma

text: Molecular and cellular alterations associated with malignant progression in the pancreas | Speaker: Laura Wood | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma | MOA: The work maps genomic and microenvironmental alterations across pancreatic precancerous lesions (IPMN, PanIN) showing that KRAS mutations are present early, while progression to invasive cancer is sometimes driven by additional alterations such as SMAD4 loss and distinct fibroblast and immune cell niche remodeling. | Findings: IPMNs originate polyclonally with multiple KRAS or VGR2 clones, but high-grade IPMNs become clonal.; In ~25% of IPMN‑cancer pairs, cancer‑specific SMAD4 or TGF‑betaRII mutations are observed, suggesting a genetic driver of progression.; Imaging mass cytometry reveals fibroblast populations that are expanded in invasive cancer and reduced in IPMN, indicating niche-specific fibroblast remodeling.; IPMN‑associated fibroblast niches are enriched for granzyme‑positive cytotoxic T cells, whereas cancer‑associated niches have fewer T cells and altered fibroblast subsets.

metadata.speaker: Laura Wood
metadata.talk_title: Molecular and cellular alterations associated with malignant progression in the pancreas

text: Evolution of pancreatic cancer microenvironment focusing on PanIN lesions | Speaker: Marina Pasca di Mangliano | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma | MOA: Spatial transcriptomics and single‑cell integration of donor pancreas samples reveal distinct epithelial and stromal domains in PanIN lesions, with IL6/JAK‑STAT3 signaling up‑regulated in poorly differentiated tumor areas and fibroblast subsets (ACTA2+, LRC15+, LEF1+) uniquely enriched around tumor, while plasma cells are enriched near PanIN and macrophages around tumor. | Findings: PanIN lesions are present in >50% of organ donors, including young individuals, indicating high prevalence of silent precancers.; Spatial domains containing neoplastic epithelium are transcriptionally distinct from normal ducts and show progressive changes toward tumor.; IL6/JAK‑STAT3 signaling is highly enriched in poorly differentiated tumor domains compared with PanIN.; Plasma cells are preferentially localized to PanIN neighborhoods, whereas macrophages are enriched around tumor structures.; Two tumor‑specific fibroblast populations are identified: ACTA2+/LRC15+ CAFs (fibro‑2) and LEF1+ fibroblasts (fibro‑3), absent in normal pancreas.

metadata.speaker: Marina Pasca di Mangliano
metadata.talk_title: Evolution of pancreatic cancer microenvironment focusing on PanIN lesions

text: Stromal targeting strategies for interception of pancreatic cancer | Speaker: Hatti (Fox Chase Cancer Center) | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma | MOA: The lab isolates patient‑derived fibroblasts, characterizes a composite 'host factor' metric of stromal protumorigenicity, and screens antibodies (e.g., anti‑NETRIN G1) and peptide inhibitors to normalize fibroblast function, testing them in vitro, in orthotopic co‑injection models, and in a pulse‑dose radiation clinical trial (PLDR) aimed at reducing stromal activation. | Findings: A quantitative 'host factor' integrates multiple stromal biomarkers to distinguish protumorigenic from tumor‑suppressive fibroblast states.; Anti‑NETRIN G1 antibody reduces protumorigenic fibroblast traits in vitro and modestly suppresses lesion formation in orthotopic co‑injection models.; Pulse‑dose low‑dose-rate (PLDR) radiation normalizes stromal host factor scores in patient samples compared with standard continuous radiation.; Co‑injection of human precancerous epithelial cells with tumor‑promoting CAFs yields early PanIN‑like lesions, supporting a stromal requirement for initiation.

metadata.speaker: Hatti (Fox Chase Cancer Center)
metadata.talk_title: Stromal targeting strategies for interception of pancreatic cancer

text: ARCH-DR multimodal single-cell profiling of esophageal adenocarcinoma | Speaker: Nick Navin | Tumors: esophageal adenocarcinoma | MOA: ARCH-DR is a high‑throughput archival DNA‑RNA co‑sequencing chemistry that simultaneously captures copy‑number alterations, somatic mutations and full‑length transcriptomes from thousands of single cells in fresh, frozen or FFPE esophageal adenocarcinoma specimens, enabling reconstruction of genetic lineages and phenotypic plasticity. | Findings: Analyzed 12 EAC patients (≈34,000 cells) with ARCH‑DR, revealing patient‑specific transcriptional clusters driven by copy‑number dosage effects.; Identified three epithelial lineages (esophageal, gastric, intestinal) within individual tumors, with most subclones displaying mixed lineage phenotypes, indicating high cellular plasticity.; Detected ecDNA amplifications of EGFR and ERBB2 that segregated with distinct genetic subclones and showed expression saturation at ~20 copies.; Found that ~51% of genes exhibit dosage‑sensitive expression correlating with copy‑number changes, while the remainder are dosage‑insensitive.; Observed that ~20% of somatic mutations are associated with altered gene expression, highlighting mutation‑driven transcriptional effects.

metadata.speaker: Nick Navin
metadata.talk_title: ARCH-DR multimodal single-cell profiling of esophageal adenocarcinoma

text: PTA enables uniform single‑cell genome amplification and reveals hidden mutational diversity in pediatric leukemia | Speaker: Charles Gewirtz | Tumors: acute myeloid leukemia | MOA: Primary Template-directed Amplification (PTA) adds irreversible terminators to a Phi29‑based whole‑genome amplification, producing uniformly covered single‑cell genomes that retain accurate allele frequencies, enabling high‑sensitivity SNV and copy‑number detection, which was applied to pediatric leukemia to uncover a hidden mutational burden and clonal drug‑resistance mechanisms. | Findings: PTA achieves ~90% detection of known germline variants with allele‑frequency distribution centered at 50%, outperforming MDA and PCR‑based methods.; Single‑cell sequencing of pediatric leukemia revealed 2,000–4,000 mutations per cell, far exceeding the <1,000 mutations observed in bulk sequencing.; De‑novo mutational signatures (SBS2/13 APOBEC) were identified at the single‑cell level, showing heterogeneous signature activity across clones.; Post‑treatment MRD analysis uncovered JAK2‑mutant subclones that were undetectable in bulk but expanded after chemotherapy, suggesting a genetic basis for resistance.; Integration of surface‑marker index sorting with PTA enabled mapping of phenotypic (surface protein) and genotypic (SNV/CNV) traits onto phylogenetic trees.

metadata.speaker: Charles Gewirtz
metadata.talk_title: PTA enables uniform single‑cell genome amplification and reveals hidden mutational diversity in pediatric leukemia

text: SKY‑Met: high‑throughput single‑cell DNA methylation and multi‑omic profiling | Speaker: Andrew Addy | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, acute myeloid leukemia | MOA: SKY‑Met combines combinatorial indexing with nucleosome disruption to achieve genome‑wide bisulfite‑free single‑cell DNA methylation profiling at high throughput; the platform also supports simultaneous ATAC‑seq or whole‑genome sequencing, enabling multi‑omic interrogation of epigenetic state, chromatin accessibility and copy‑number in thousands of cells from frozen or fixed tissues. | Findings: Generated a 140,000‑cell methylome atlas of the human cerebral cortex, revealing cell‑type‑specific CpG methylation patterns and non‑CG methylation dynamics in neuronal subtypes.; Applied SKY‑Met to pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, achieving >90% CpG coverage per cell and enabling copy‑number profiling from frozen tumor specimens.; Demonstrated a joint methylome‑ATAC co‑assay on ~8% of 140,000 bone‑marrow cells, providing concordant cell‑type clustering from both modalities.; Detected a balanced translocation in a PDAC subclone using combined single‑cell genome + Hi‑C reads, illustrating the ability to capture structural variants alongside epigenetic information.

metadata.speaker: Andrew Addy
metadata.talk_title: SKY‑Met: high‑throughput single‑cell DNA methylation and multi‑omic profiling

text: Precision medicine in childhood CNS tumors and high‑risk brain tumors | Speaker: David Ziegler | Tumors: brain tumors, low-grade glioma, diffuse midline glioma, sarcoma | MOA: Ziegler described a national whole‑genome and methylation profiling program that identifies actionable alterations (e.g., NTRK fusions, MYC amplification) in high‑risk pediatric brain tumors; matched targeted agents such as larotrectinib produce disease stabilization or objective responses, and patients receiving precision‑guided therapy show significantly improved progression‑free and overall survival compared with unguided treatment. | Findings: 71% of high‑risk CNS tumor patients harbored a therapeutic target; 5% had a diagnostic revision based on genomics.; Precision‑guided therapy conferred a 44% reduction in hazard of death (HR 0.56, 95% CI 0.38‑0.82) versus unguided therapy.; Patients with MYC‑amplified tumors had markedly worse OS (median 12 mo vs 21 mo) but still derived benefit from matched therapy.; A TRK‑fusion infant with refractory high‑grade glioma achieved rapid functional recovery and radiographic remission after larotrectinib.

metadata.speaker: David Ziegler
metadata.talk_title: Precision medicine in childhood CNS tumors and high‑risk brain tumors

text: Precision medicine in childhood bone sarcomas: osteosarcoma and Ewing sarcoma subtyping | Speaker: Catherine Janeway | Tumors: osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma | MOA: Janeway identified MYC amplification (and high MYC protein) as a high‑risk biomarker in osteosarcoma, correlating with markedly reduced overall survival, and demonstrated that STAG2 mutations predict relapse in Ewing sarcoma, establishing biologic subtypes that can guide risk‑adapted therapy and future targeted approaches. | Findings: MYC amplification occurs in ~10% of osteosarcoma and predicts significantly worse OS (median 1.5 yr vs 5.4 yr).; High MYC protein expression (IHC H‑score >150) independently associates with poor survival; combined amplification + high protein identifies the highest‑risk subgroup (median OS 1 yr).; In a validation cohort, MYC amplification confirmed as adverse prognostic factor for both OS and EFS.; STAG2 mutation is the strongest molecular predictor of relapse in localized Ewing sarcoma (multivariable HR ≈ 1.5).; Patients without any recurrent alterations have >90% recurrence‑free survival, suggesting a de‑intensification opportunity.

metadata.speaker: Catherine Janeway
metadata.talk_title: Precision medicine in childhood bone sarcomas: osteosarcoma and Ewing sarcoma subtyping

text: Molecular subtyping of osteosarcoma and Ewing sarcoma for outcome prediction | Speaker: Jane Wei | Tumors: osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma | MOA: Wei integrated targeted sequencing and IHC data to define biologic subtypes in osteosarcoma (MYC amplification + high protein) and Ewing sarcoma (STAG2 mutation), demonstrating that these molecular alterations independently predict poorer survival and can be used to stratify patients for risk‑adapted therapy. | Findings: MYC amplification occurs in ~10% of osteosarcoma and predicts markedly inferior OS (median 1.5 yr).; High MYC protein expression alone also predicts poor survival; combined amplification + high protein identifies the highest‑risk subgroup (median OS 1 yr).; In a separate MSKCC cohort, MYC amplification confirmed as adverse prognostic factor for OS and EFS.; STAG2 mutation is the strongest molecular predictor of relapse in localized Ewing sarcoma, independent of other clinical factors.; Patients lacking recurrent alterations have >90% recurrence‑free survival, supporting potential de‑intensification strategies.

metadata.speaker: Jane Wei
metadata.talk_title: Molecular subtyping of osteosarcoma and Ewing sarcoma for outcome prediction

text: Slide Tags spatial transcriptomics and lineage tracing in tumor ecosystems | Speaker: Unnamed Broad presenter | Tumors: melanoma, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, lung cancer | MOA: Slide Tags uses photo-cleavable DNA barcodes on spatial arrays to label nuclei, providing true single-cell resolution spatial transcriptomics; combined with lineage barcoding and CNV detection to map tumor clone spatial niches and infer expansion dynamics. | Findings: Slide Tags achieves true single-cell resolution with median >3,000 UMIs per cell, outperforming Visium HD in melanoma specimens.; Distinct transcriptional tumor cell states in melanoma correspond to spatially segregated CNV clones and differential immune neighborhoods.; Neural crest-like tumor state associates with SPP1+ macrophages and fibroblasts, showing reduced CD8 T‑cell clonality.; Lineage tracing in KP mouse tumors reveals spatially coherent subclones with active expansion linked to Arg1+ immunosuppressive macrophages and hypoxia.; Metastasis‑seeding subclones share hypoxic and immunosuppressive niche signatures with primary tumor regions.

metadata.speaker: Unnamed Broad presenter
metadata.talk_title: Slide Tags spatial transcriptomics and lineage tracing in tumor ecosystems

text: Decoding tissue architecture in pancreatic cancer using SEGER and Wormhole | Speaker: Dana Pe'er | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma | MOA: SEGER assigns transcripts to nuclei using AI‑driven graph embeddings, eliminating segmentation errors; Wormhole transforms high‑dimensional niche matrices into a scalable latent space, enabling trajectory and interaction analysis of spatial neighborhoods. | Findings: SEGER improves transcript‑to‑cell assignment over geometric methods, preserving continuous cell‑state manifolds.; Wormhole latent captures dominant variation as a gastric‑to‑progenitor axis and associated niche remodeling.; p53 loss sustains a progenitor‑like niche with immunosuppressive TNC fibroblasts and Arg1+ macrophages in early PDAC.; Ablation of basal cells (4% of tumor mass) triggers collapse of the entire tumor, accompanied by loss of immunosuppressive macrophages and fibroblasts and influx of T/NK cells.; CRISPR‑mediated deletion of CSF2 specifically in basal cells phenocopies basal cell ablation, implicating CSF2 as a master niche signal.

metadata.speaker: Dana Pe'er
metadata.talk_title: Decoding tissue architecture in pancreatic cancer using SEGER and Wormhole

text: Spatial transcriptomics and proteomics reveal organization of glioma and head‑and‑neck cancer | Speaker: Itay Tirosh | Tumors: glioblastoma, IDH‑mutant glioma, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma | MOA: Combines Visium spatial transcriptomics (55 µm spots) with CODEX multiplexed protein imaging to map cancer cell states and microenvironmental interactions, revealing spatial coherence, hypoxia‑driven layering in glioma and microenvironment‑dependent partial EMT patterns in head‑and‑neck cancer. | Findings: In GBM, mesenchymal‑hypoxia tumor cells form spatially coherent patches; high hypoxia correlates with structured tissue organization.; GBM spatial layers: necrotic/hypoxic core → mesenchymal/hypoxia → inflammatory macrophages → vascular repair → neurodevelopmental tumor cells → normal brain parenchyma.; IDH‑mutant gliomas show less structure overall; low‑grade tumors retain normal white‑gray matter boundaries that act as barriers to malignant cell infiltration.; In head‑and‑neck cancer, partial EMT programs are either edge‑enriched (fibroblast‑derived TGF‑β) or core‑enriched (myeloid‑derived oncostatin M), influencing immune infiltration.; Oncostatin M and TGF‑β both induce partial EMT genes in vitro, but spatial context determines dominant driver in vivo.

metadata.speaker: Itay Tirosh
metadata.talk_title: Spatial transcriptomics and proteomics reveal organization of glioma and head‑and‑neck cancer
tumor_types: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma

text: Spatial Transcriptomics Profiling of Colorectal Cancer Tumors in Alaska Native People: Discovery of Prognostic Biomarkers | Speaker: Geryk Cheng | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: This study utilized spatial transcriptomics (GeoMix) to profile colorectal cancer tumors in Alaska Native people, identifying prognostic biomarkers associated with mortality. Key findings include differential gene expression (SPINK4, MUQ2, HBA2) and pathway enrichment (interferon response, EMT) in tumor and stromal compartments, as well as altered cell type abundance (plasma cells, mast cells), correlating with patient survival outcomes. | Findings: Identified spatially specific markers tied to colorectal cancer-specific mortality in Alaska Native people.; In the tumor center epithelial compartment, downregulation of MILK2 and SPINK4, and interferon alpha and gamma pathways were associated with not dying from colorectal cancer.; In the tumor center, a decrease in plasma cells and an increase in mast cells were observed in patients who did not die from colorectal cancer.; In the invasive margin epithelial compartment, an increase in HBA2 expression was observed in patients who died from colorectal cancer.; Epithelial-mesenchymal transition pathways were enriched in the invasive margin (epithelial and stromal compartments) in patients who died from colorectal cancer.

metadata.speaker: Geryk Cheng
metadata.talk_title: Spatial Transcriptomics Profiling of Colorectal Cancer Tumors in Alaska Native People: Discovery of Prognostic Biomarkers

text: Highly Multiplexed Immunoassays Enable Discovery of Multi-Marker EV Surface Signatures as Novel Biomarkers | Speaker: David Routtenberg | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: This presentation introduces a novel combinatorial immunosequencing platform for highly multiplexed profiling of extracellular vesicle (EV) surface signatures. The technology enables the discovery of multi-marker combinations that can distinguish cell origins and provide prognostic information, demonstrating improved sensitivity over single markers and showing consistent findings across multiple colorectal cancer cohorts. | Findings: Soluble CEA was undetectable in 16% of stage IV CRC patients, while the same molecule on EV surfaces was detectable.; The combinatorial immunosequencing platform can detect rare EV subpopulations (1 in 10 million) with high sensitivity and a four-log dynamic range.; Three-marker combinations consistently discriminated between epithelial and stromal cell origins in CRC EVs across three independent cohorts.; Several multi-marker EV surface signatures showed FDR significant prognostic value in longitudinal CRC cohorts.; CD73, CD13, and CEA were identified as recurrent components in CRC-secreted EVs with prognostic potential.

metadata.speaker: David Routtenberg
metadata.talk_title: Highly Multiplexed Immunoassays Enable Discovery of Multi-Marker EV Surface Signatures as Novel Biomarkers

text: Differences in Survival Outcomes Among Metastatic Colorectal Cancer Patients Across Fibroblast Growth Factor Receptor Two and Three Expression Levels | Speaker: Steve Soto | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: This study investigated the prognostic and predictive value of FGFR2 and FGFR3 gene expression and FGFR2 SNPs in metastatic colorectal cancer patients from the CALGB SWOG 80405 trial. FGFR2 high expression was associated with worse survival overall and specifically in the cetuximab arm, while FGFR3 high expression and a specific FGFR2 SNP (RS-3135718) were associated with improved survival in the cetuximab arm, suggesting differential roles in response to EGFR inhibition. | Findings: FGFR2 high expression was prognostic for worse overall survival in mCRC patients (HR 1.28).; FGFR2 high expression was predictive of worse overall survival in the cetuximab arm (HR 1.56).; FGFR3 high expression was predictive of improved overall survival in the cetuximab arm (HR 0.59).; FGFR2 SNP RS-3135718 variant allele was predictive of improved PFS and OS in the cetuximab arm.; FGFR2 inhibition decreased cell viability in CRC cell lines, reiterating its criticality for cell survival.

metadata.speaker: Steve Soto
metadata.talk_title: Differences in Survival Outcomes Among Metastatic Colorectal Cancer Patients Across Fibroblast Growth Factor Receptor Two and Three Expression Levels

text: Mapping of Spatial Organization of B Cells and Immune Signaling in Triple Negative Breast Cancer to Characterize Response to Immunotherapy | Speaker: Lubna Ahmad | Tumors: triple negative breast cancer | MOA: This study investigated the role of B cells and cytokine signaling in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) response to immunotherapy using imaging mass cytometry (IMC). Findings indicate that B cell densities, specific B cell niches (e.g., B activated niche), and their interactions with other immune cells are significantly associated with immunotherapy response. The spatial organization of B cells and cytokine enrichment within niches appear to be key drivers of treatment efficacy. | Findings: Several B cell populations (germinal center B, plasma memory, naive B) are associated with immunotherapy response on-treatment.; Specific B cell niches (germinal center, B activated, plasma-rich, plasma-maturing) were identified.; The B activated niche and its interactions with other immune cells are predictive of immunotherapy response.; B cells are more significantly impacted post-immunotherapy compared to other TME cells.; Cytokine enrichment within niches is a persistent feature in immunotherapy responders across treatment time points.

metadata.speaker: Lubna Ahmad
metadata.talk_title: Mapping of Spatial Organization of B Cells and Immune Signaling in Triple Negative Breast Cancer to Characterize Response to Immunotherapy

text: AI-Powered Deep Visual Proteomics (DVP) Links Pancreatic Precursor Biology to PDAC Survival Phenotypes | Speaker: Andreas Mand | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, pancreatic precursor lesions | MOA: This study applied AI-powered Deep Visual Proteomics (DVP) to analyze pancreatic precursor lesions and PDAC. By integrating high-resolution microscopy with mass spectrometry-based spatial proteomics, the researchers identified early molecular changes in normal ducts associated with cancer development, including immune editing and metabolic reprogramming. The technology also enabled the detection of KRAS mutations directly from proteomic data, linking genotype to phenotype and revealing insights into immune evasion in high-grade PANA. | Findings: Cancer-associated normal ducts show distinct proteomic profiles compared to incidental normal ducts, including oxidative stress, metabolic reprogramming, and immune editing.; Inflammation and antigen presentation pathways are upregulated early in pancreatic precursor lesions but drop sharply in high-grade PANA, indicating immune evasion.; KRAS hotspot mutations can be identified from proteomic data, enabling genotype-phenotype correlation in precursor lesions.; The study identified a 'cancer field effect' where normal ducts near tumors acquire immune signatures.; DVP identified distinct proteomic differences between spatially adjacent regions within tumors, highlighting tumor heterogeneity.

metadata.speaker: Andreas Mand
metadata.talk_title: AI-Powered Deep Visual Proteomics (DVP) Links Pancreatic Precursor Biology to PDAC Survival Phenotypes

text: Spatial Immune Multiomics Refines Prognostication in Early-Stage Estrogen Receptor-Positive Breast Cancer | Speaker: Zach Kinsella | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: This study utilized spatial multiomics (IHC, spatial transcriptomics, spatial proteomics) on early-stage ER+ breast cancer patients from the TAILORx trial to refine prognostication in the intermediate recurrence score group. Findings reveal that inflamed immune microenvironments are associated with dysfunctional responses, including upregulation of checkpoints and downregulation of ER signaling. High stromal CD8 density was identified as a predictive marker of chemo inferiority, suggesting that immune infiltration patterns can refine treatment decisions. | Findings: Four TME types and three epithelial types were identified, with immune types not significantly captured by Oncotype DX Recurrence Score.; Inflamed epithelia were characterized by downregulation of ESR1 and suppression of DNA repair pathways.; Inflamed TME and epithelia were prognostic in the intermediate recurrence score group, with chemotherapy showing poorer outcomes.; High stromal CD8 density was a predictive marker of chemo inferiority in the intermediate recurrence score group.; Increasing CD8 density conferred poorer outcome on chemotherapy, adding prognostic information to clinical variables.

metadata.speaker: Zach Kinsella
metadata.talk_title: Spatial Immune Multiomics Refines Prognostication in Early-Stage Estrogen Receptor-Positive Breast Cancer

text: Unbiased Phenotyping of CRISPR Edited Tumors with Preserved Map and Subcellular Imaging of the Mouse Whole Transcriptome, 22,000 Plex | Speaker: Maxime Deynaud | Tumors: lung cancer | MOA: This presentation describes the PertiMap platform, which uses CRISPR-edited, barcoded tumors in mice to generate large-scale in vivo perturbation data. This data is then 'humanized' using the MAIRS model, which projects human biology onto mouse H&E images, enabling the discovery of novel therapeutic targets and combinations. The approach allows for unbiased phenotyping of genetic perturbations and identification of drivers of tumor biology and response to therapy. | Findings: The PertiMap platform enables scaled in vivo genetic perturbation and multimodal tissue profiling.; The MAIRS model can project human biology onto mouse H&E images, effectively 'humanizing' preclinical models.; MAIRS identified tumors with high predicted human CCAM6 expression in mouse models, correlating with specific histological changes.; The embedding space of perturbations revealed distinct phenotypic clusters associated with immune infiltration, fibrosis, and metabolic signatures.; VEGFR1 knockout tumors treated with PD1 showed a shift towards a hot TME, suggesting a rationale for combination therapy.

metadata.speaker: Maxime Deynaud
metadata.talk_title: Unbiased Phenotyping of CRISPR Edited Tumors with Preserved Map and Subcellular Imaging of the Mouse Whole Transcriptome, 22,000 Plex

text: Pragmatic trial of mailed FIT versus FIT-DNA outreach in community health centers | Speaker: Jennifer Haas | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: Mailed outreach using either annual FIT kits or triennial FIT‑DNA kits, combined with text reminders and manufacturer‑provided navigation, modestly increased colorectal cancer screening uptake (28% vs 23% at 90 days) in underserved community health centers, though follow‑up colonoscopy rates remained suboptimal. | Findings: FIT‑DNA arm achieved 28% screening completion at 90 days versus 23% for FIT (p<0.05).; The modest advantage persisted at 180 days (≈27% vs 22%).; Higher screening rates were observed in Los Angeles sites for FIT‑DNA, driven by lower baseline screening.; Hispanic and Medicaid/uninsured participants showed greater uptake of FIT‑DNA, likely reflecting clinic‑level differences.; Colonoscopic follow‑up after abnormal results was low across all sites, with Boston showing the highest rates.

metadata.speaker: Jennifer Haas
metadata.talk_title: Pragmatic trial of mailed FIT versus FIT-DNA outreach in community health centers

text: DISRUPT: AI‑driven patient‑trial matching to improve equity in cancer trial enrollment | Speaker: Nina Bachael | Tumors: breast cancer, lung cancer, liver cancer | MOA: An EMR‑based algorithm identifies patients at treatment decision points, matches them to open trials, and delivers bilingual trial summaries to clinicians and patients before the decision visit, resulting in higher minority enrollment (58%) and a 27% enrollment rate among eligible patients, surpassing historical benchmarks. | Findings: Enrolled 579 patients, of whom 58% self‑identified as minority, reversing typical under‑representation.; Eligibility filtering reduced manual chart review workload by 35%.; Among eligible patients, 27% enrolled in a trial, compared with ~22% at NCI centers.; No racial/ethnic differences were observed in patient attitudes toward trials or in physician‑reported trial discussions.; High refusal rate due to emotional burden at decision points limited overall enrollment.

metadata.speaker: Nina Bachael
metadata.talk_title: DISRUPT: AI‑driven patient‑trial matching to improve equity in cancer trial enrollment

text: Multimodal navigation to increase lung cancer screening in the I‑95 corridor | Speaker: Robert Winn | Tumors: lung cancer | MOA: A multimodal, multilevel navigation system—combining community activators, certified community health workers, and clinical nurse navigators—was deployed to identify, engage, and guide African‑American adults in the I‑95 corridor through low‑dose CT lung‑cancer screening, resulting in enrollment of 220 participants and collection of >5,000 biospecimens. | Findings: Identified 675 African‑American individuals eligible for lung‑cancer screening; 220 (≈33%) enrolled after navigation.; Collected >5,000 biospecimens and contacted >3,000 community members, demonstrating feasibility of large‑scale outreach.; Multimodal navigation (community activators + CHWs + nurse navigators) improved screening uptake compared with prior single‑navigator models.; Rural sites required intensive door‑to‑door outreach; lack of mobile screening vans limited reach in remote areas.; Financial‑toxicity navigation was planned but not fully implemented due to resource constraints.

metadata.speaker: Robert Winn
metadata.talk_title: Multimodal navigation to increase lung cancer screening in the I‑95 corridor

text: Survey of US Oncology Trial Site Activation Timelines | Speaker: Mark Stewart | MOA: Mark Stewart presented analysis of a multi‑company survey of registrational oncology trials (2020‑2024) showing that US sites open the first site quickly (~150 days) but lag substantially in scaling to 75% of planned sites (>300 days) and in enrolling the first patient (~80 days). He linked these delays to cumulative protocol amendments, each adding 30‑60 days, and highlighted systemic bottlenecks across regulatory review, IRB processes, contracting, and site readiness. | Findings: US first site activation median 150 days, faster than Europe and China.; Time to activate 75% of planned US sites exceeds 300 days, whereas South Korea achieves ~45 days and other regions 100‑125 days.; First patient in US takes ~80 days versus 40‑50 days in non‑US regions.; Each additional protocol amendment version adds approximately 30‑60 days to overall study start time.; Trials with three or more protocol versions experience an extra 70‑80 days delay compared with the original version.

metadata.speaker: Mark Stewart
metadata.session_title: Strengthening the Oncology Trial Ecosystem through Operational and Regulatory Innovation
metadata.talk_title: Survey of US Oncology Trial Site Activation Timelines

text: Stress and mutation dependency reshape CAF heterogeneity via HSF1 and oxidative stress pathways | Speaker: Ruth Shoresh-Jal | Tumors: breast cancer, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, ovarian cancer, prostate cancer | MOA: Cancer cell BRCA mutations drive upregulation of stress‑responsive transcription factors (HSF1, NRF2, ATF4, XBP1) in adjacent stromal fibroblasts, reprogramming them toward an immune‑regulatory iCAF phenotype that suppresses NK‑cell cytotoxicity and promotes tumor progression. | Findings: BRCA‑mutated tumors exhibit higher stromal HSF1, ATF4, and XBP1 expression compared with BRCA‑wild‑type tumors.; HSF1‑dependent signaling converts fibroblasts to iCAFs that down‑regulate NK‑cell activating receptors (NKG2D, DNAM1).; CAF‑mediated internalization of NK‑cell ligands (CD155, ULBP1) impairs NK‑cell cytotoxicity in ex vivo co‑culture assays.; In vivo NK‑cell depletion or CAF enrichment increases stromal content and reduces metastasis control in mouse models.; High nectin‑2 expression on CAFs correlates with poorer overall survival in breast cancer tissue microarrays.

metadata.speaker: Ruth Shoresh-Jal
metadata.talk_title: Stress and mutation dependency reshape CAF heterogeneity via HSF1 and oxidative stress pathways

text: Chronic stress, glucocorticoids, and neutrophil NETs promote metastatic outgrowth | Speaker: Speaker Unknown | Tumors: breast cancer, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma | MOA: Chronic stress elevates glucocorticoids, which activate the glucocorticoid receptor in neutrophils, driving excessive NET formation that remodels the lung microenvironment, expands ECM, suppresses T‑cell infiltration, and creates a permissive niche for dormant disseminated tumor cells to proliferate and form metastases. | Findings: Restraint stress increased circulating corticosterone and produced a ~4‑fold rise in lung metastases.; Chronic unpredictable mild stress also elevated corticosterone and enhanced metastatic burden despite milder hormone rise.; Stressed lungs showed increased ECM (fibronectin), reduced T‑cell infiltration, and expanded neutrophils.; Neutrophils from stressed mice formed markedly more NETs ex vivo; this required neutrophil‑intrinsic glucocorticoid receptor signaling.; DNase treatment abolished NET DNA, reduced ECM deposition, and returned metastatic burden to baseline levels in stressed mice.

metadata.speaker: Speaker Unknown
metadata.talk_title: Chronic stress, glucocorticoids, and neutrophil NETs promote metastatic outgrowth

text: Social stressors associate with accelerated epigenetic aging in Black breast cancer survivors | Speaker: Jesse Plaschak | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: Chronic exposure to socioeconomic and built‑environment stressors (low income, neighborhood disinvestment) correlates with accelerated DNA‑methylation aging (DunedinPACE) in breast cancer survivors, suggesting that systemic stress pathways may hasten biological aging and potentially influence cancer outcomes. | Findings: Mean DunedinPACE was 1.3 (accelerated aging) two years after breast cancer diagnosis.; Lower income‑to‑poverty ratio, higher perceived physical disorder, and greater objective neighborhood disinvestment correlated positively with epigenetic age acceleration (p≤0.1).; BMI and current smoking showed the strongest independent associations with accelerated aging (smoking largest effect size).; Repeated measures in 38 participants showed a modest overall deceleration of epigenetic age over time, but the effect of social stressors attenuated at the later time point.; Chemotherapy receipt also influenced epigenetic age acceleration, suggesting treatment may mediate stress‑related aging effects.

metadata.speaker: Jesse Plaschak
metadata.talk_title: Social stressors associate with accelerated epigenetic aging in Black breast cancer survivors

text: Accelerating Molecular Glue Degrader Discovery and Selective Chemical Probe Development | Speaker: Eric Fischer | Tumors: acute myeloid leukemia | MOA: Fischer described a high‑throughput degradomics pipeline that couples data‑independent acquisition mass spectrometry with affinity‑purification MS to identify molecular glue degraders. Structural biology (cryo‑EM) and predictive algorithms enable rapid (≈6 weeks) discovery of selective degraders, exemplified by a cereblon‑recruited KAT2A degrader that shows no off‑target degradation and induces loss of KAT2A and H3K9ac in AML PDX models. | Findings: Cost per molecule for degradomics dropped from >$20,000 in 2012 to < $500 using DIA‑MS and automation.; Discovery timeline from initial screen to high‑resolution cryo‑EM structure reduced to ~6 weeks.; A selective KAT2A degrader was identified that does not degrade the paralog KAT2B or off‑target GSPD1/2.; In an aggressive AML PDX model, treatment with the KAT2A degrader caused complete loss of KAT2A protein and H3K9 acetylation, confirming on‑target activity.; Structural analysis revealed a unique tyrosine‑mediated interface on cereblon that confers selectivity for KAT2A over KAT2B.

metadata.speaker: Eric Fischer
metadata.talk_title: Accelerating Molecular Glue Degrader Discovery and Selective Chemical Probe Development

text: Structural Basis of PI3‑Kinase Activation by Membrane Recruitment, RAS, and Multivalent RTK Scaffolds | Speaker: Natalia Dzura | Tumors: breast cancer, acute myeloid leukemia | MOA: Dzura showed that membrane recruitment of PI3K via farnesylated KRAS and phospho‑RTK tails drives stepwise displacement of autoinhibitory domains, exposing a previously unseen C‑terminal SH2 domain that initially blocks full activation. Inclusion of PIP2 in the nanodisc induces a conformational swing of helix‑12, enabling substrate capture. The common oncogenic H1047R mutation likely destabilizes the helix‑12 hinge, favoring the active conformation. Multivalent HER3 phospho‑tails further promote dimerization of the holoenzyme, creating a highly active, membrane‑anchored state resistant to re‑autoinhibition. | Findings: Cryo‑EM of PI3K bound to farnesylated KRAS on nanodiscs revealed progressive loss of regulatory domains (auto‑inhibitory N‑SH2 and iSH2) across three structural classes.; A previously unobserved C‑terminal SH2 domain contacts the membrane and acts as an additional checkpoint before full activation.; Inclusion of PIP2 in the nanodisc reorients the holoenzyme, forming a true helix‑12 that swings 180° and directly engages substrate PIP2 in the active site – the first such observation.; The H1047R oncogenic mutation likely disrupts a hinge interaction (His1047‑Trp1051), facilitating helix‑12 swing and membrane association, explaining its activating effect.; Multivalent HER3 phospho‑tails induce a dimeric PI3K configuration at the nanodisc edge, preventing re‑assembly of the auto‑inhibited state and representing a fully active dimeric species.

metadata.speaker: Natalia Dzura
metadata.talk_title: Structural Basis of PI3‑Kinase Activation by Membrane Recruitment, RAS, and Multivalent RTK Scaffolds

text: Conformational Landscapes of Protein Kinases Reveal Low‑Populated States for Selective Inhibition | Speaker: Babis Kalodimos | MOA: Kalodimos demonstrated that protein kinases sample multiple low‑populated conformational states in solution. Using high‑field NMR, three states were characterized for ABL (active, inactive‑1, inactive‑2) and for Src (active, fully inactive, and a novel intermediate). The intermediate state exhibits steric clashes with ADP, explaining its role in rapid ADP release and processive phosphorylation. Gleevec’s selectivity arises from binding the rare inactive‑2 state of ABL, and resistance mutations destabilize this state. Structural insight into these invisible states enables rational design of highly selective inhibitors via virtual docking of billions of compounds or experimental DEL screening. | Findings: ABL kinase populates three conformations: a ground active state and two low‑populated inactive states (~5% each).; Gleevec binds selectively to the inactive‑2 state, explaining its high specificity and the mechanism of many resistance mutations that destabilize this state.; Src family kinases also sample an intermediate conformation (~5%) that has markedly reduced ADP affinity, identifying it as the key state for rapid ADP release during processive phosphorylation.; Mutations that destabilize the intermediate state abolish processive phosphorylation by Src and Lck, confirming its functional relevance.; VirtualFlow docking of >70 billion compounds against the inactive‑2 ABL structure yielded nanomolar inhibitors with promising selectivity profiles.

metadata.speaker: Babis Kalodimos
metadata.talk_title: Conformational Landscapes of Protein Kinases Reveal Low‑Populated States for Selective Inhibition

text: CAR T‑cell consolidation therapy for older ALL patients and BAFF‑R CAR for CD19‑negative relapse | Speaker: Steve Forman | Tumors: acute lymphoblastic leukemia, lymphoma | MOA: CD19 CAR T cells with a naive‑phenotype enrichment expand, contract, and persist for 4–5 months, trafficking to CSF and providing durable remission in older ALL patients when given in first remission; BAFF‑R CAR T cells target an essential B‑cell survival receptor, showing expansion, low neurotoxicity, and clinical activity in CD19‑negative relapsed B‑cell malignancies. | Findings: In a cohort of 48 older ALL patients, CD19 CAR achieved 90% complete remission with no dose‑limiting toxicities and markedly reduced grade ≥2 CRS (17% vs 80% in relapse setting).; CAR T cells were detectable in CSF of every treated patient, indicating CNS trafficking and no observed CNS relapses.; Two molecular relapses were identified by ClonoSEQ; both patients were successfully retreated and proceeded to allogeneic transplant.; First‑in‑human BAFF‑R CAR demonstrated expansion comparable to CD19 CAR, grade 1 toxicities only, and ≥70% objective responses in lymphoma patients.; BAFF‑R expression persisted in ~66% of CD19‑negative ALL relapses, supporting its role as a salvage target.

metadata.speaker: Steve Forman
metadata.talk_title: CAR T‑cell consolidation therapy for older ALL patients and BAFF‑R CAR for CD19‑negative relapse

text: Engineering TCR‑engineered T cells to overcome TGF‑β–driven dysfunction in solid tumors | Speaker: Phil Greenberg | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, melanoma, breast cancer, lung cancer, glioblastoma | MOA: Engineered TCR T cells targeting mesothelin or KRAS G12V infiltrate pancreatic tumors but acquire a TGF‑β–driven, mitigated exhaustion program; CRISPR knockout of the TGF‑β‑responsive transcription factor IKZF3 (Aeolus) reduces both TGF‑β and exhaustion signatures but induces apoptosis, which can be rescued by synthetic fusion proteins delivering pro‑survival signals. HIT CARs replace the scFv with antibody heavy/light chains to create HLA‑independent, ultra‑sensitive receptors that eradicate low‑density CD70‑expressing tumors in PDX models, outperforming conventional CARs. | Findings: Mesothelin‑specific TCR T cells showed tumor infiltration but displayed a dominant TGF‑β–driven exhaustion signature distinct from blood T cells.; IKZF3 (Aeolus) knockout eliminated the TGF‑β signature and mitigated exhaustion but caused activation‑induced cell death, which was rescued by engineered fusion proteins delivering IL‑2 or FasL‑derived survival signals.; HIT CD70 CARs demonstrated superior sensitivity, achieving tumor eradication in renal cell carcinoma PDXs with low CD70 expression where conventional CARs failed.; KRAS G12V‑specific TCRs engineered with CD8αβ and CD28 co‑stimulation induced durable tumor regressions and biomarker (CEA, ctDNA) declines in 3 of 4 patients.; Spatial analysis revealed that exhausted engineered T cells reside in tumor cores surrounded by TGF‑β, whereas functional T cells localize to tertiary lymphoid structures near vasculature.

metadata.speaker: Phil Greenberg
metadata.talk_title: Engineering TCR‑engineered T cells to overcome TGF‑β–driven dysfunction in solid tumors

text: Evolution of PARP inhibitors and lessons for synthetic lethality development | Speaker: Mark O'Connor | Tumors: ovarian cancer, breast cancer, prostate cancer, pancreatic cancer, NSCLC, colorectal cancer | MOA: PARP inhibitors trap PARP1 on DNA, preventing repair of single-strand breaks that convert to double-strand breaks during replication; in HR-deficient tumors (e.g., BRCA1/2 loss) this leads to lethal genomic instability, while normal cells retain homologous recombination capacity, providing a therapeutic window. Trapping potency, dose intensity, and duration of target inhibition dictate clinical efficacy. | Findings: PARP1 trapping, not just catalytic inhibition, is essential for monotherapy activity; talazoparib and sarucaparib show stronger trapping and greater efficacy than rucaparib.; Complete (>90%) PARP inhibition is required for tumor regression; sub‑therapeutic dosing leads to tumor escape and resistance.; BRCA1/2 mutation type influences response; hypomorphic C61G BRCA1 mutants confer reduced sensitivity compared to null alleles.; Acquired resistance is driven by HR re‑activation, evidenced by RAD51 foci re‑appearance in >90% of resistant models.; Dose‑intensity correlates with long‑term tumor control; continuous high‑dose olaparib prevents escape, whereas intermittent dosing increases residual tumor burden.

metadata.speaker: Mark O'Connor
metadata.talk_title: Evolution of PARP inhibitors and lessons for synthetic lethality development

text: Targeting ARID1A/ARID1B synthetic lethality and SMARCA2/SMARCA4 paralog dependencies | Speaker: Steve Ballen | Tumors: ovarian cancer, lung cancer, endometrial cancer | MOA: Selective degradation of ARID1B via VHL or cereblon-recruited PROTACs eliminates the compensatory paralog in ARID1A-deficient cancers, leading to loss of BAF complex function and tumor cell death, while sparing normal cells that retain ARID1A. Similarly, inhibition of SMARCA2 in SMARCA4-mutant tumors exploits paralog synthetic lethality, causing chromatin remodeling failure and tumor regression, with enhanced anti‑tumor immunity when combined with PD‑1 blockade. | Findings: ARID1B degraders achieve nanomolar potency and >10‑fold selectivity over ARID1A in biochemical and cellular assays.; Cereblon‑based ARID1B degraders show superior potency and no off‑target neo‑substrate activity across the proteome.; Ternary complex crystal structures reveal a ligand twist that enhances cooperativity, informing SAR for both VHL and CRBN series.; SMARCA2 inhibitor LY4050784 (909) combined with anti‑PD‑1 yields 6/6 complete responses in a BRG1‑knockout syngeneic mouse model and induces durable immune memory.; Combination of SMARCA2 inhibition with PD‑1 blockade is well tolerated (no weight loss) and produces sustained tumor control.

metadata.speaker: Steve Ballen
metadata.talk_title: Targeting ARID1A/ARID1B synthetic lethality and SMARCA2/SMARCA4 paralog dependencies

text: Quantitative molecular imaging to enable personalized radiopharmaceutical therapy | Speaker: Dr. Delphine Chen | Tumors: neuroendocrine tumors, prostate cancer | MOA: Quantitative PET/SPECT imaging of SSTR and PSMA ligands enables patient selection and dosimetry for beta‑emitting radiopharmaceuticals; higher tumor uptake (SUV) predicts better outcomes, while FDG metabolic burden inversely correlates with response, supporting personalized dosing and treatment planning. | Findings: Post‑hoc NETTER‑1/2 analyses showed similar survival benefit across low, intermediate, and high somatostatin receptor uptake levels.; VISION trial post‑hoc quartile analysis demonstrated that patients in the highest PSMA PET SUV quartile had the best radiographic PFS and OS.; Low FDG metabolic tumor volume predicted superior response to lutetium‑PSMA therapy, independent of PSMA uptake intensity.; Single‑time‑point dosimetry at ~24 h can estimate tumor absorbed dose, but lesion doses decrease with successive cycles.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Delphine Chen
metadata.talk_title: Quantitative molecular imaging to enable personalized radiopharmaceutical therapy

text: Clinical advances and opportunities in prostate cancer using alpha and beta emitting radiopharmaceuticals | Speaker: Dr. Neil Tonk | Tumors: prostate cancer | MOA: Beta‑emitting lutetium‑177 PSMA‑617 delivers cross‑fire radiation to PSMA‑positive prostate cancer lesions, improving OS and PFS; alpha‑emitting actinium‑225 PSMA provides high‑LET, short‑range DNA double‑strand breaks, achieving deep PSA responses but with high salivary gland toxicity. Combination strategies aim to exploit complementary mechanisms and overcome resistance. | Findings: VISION trial showed a 4‑month OS benefit (median 11 mo vs 7 mo) for lutetium‑177 PSMA‑617 in APMR.; Approximately 30% of patients were non‑responders, linked to low PSMA uptake, FDG‑PSMA discordance, or TP53 mutations.; Actinium‑225 PSMA therapy yielded median OS 16 mo in heavily pretreated patients, with 70% experiencing xerostomia after one cycle.; Early‑line trials (PSMA‑4, PSMA‑ADDITION) improve radiographic PFS but have not yet shown OS advantage, likely due to crossover.; Alpha emitters may overcome radioresistance in high‑grade disease and micrometastases, while beta emitters are suited for bulk disease.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Neil Tonk
metadata.talk_title: Clinical advances and opportunities in prostate cancer using alpha and beta emitting radiopharmaceuticals

text: Preclinical and translational strategies to combine radiopharmaceuticals with other cancer therapies | Speaker: Dr. Zach Morris | Tumors: head and neck cancer, medulloblastoma, solid tumors (various) | MOA: NM‑600 incorporates into tumor cell membranes, delivering Y‑90 beta radiation; when combined with checkpoint blockade, sub‑maximal tumor doses preserve immune cells and enhance systemic anti‑tumor immunity. Astatine‑211 PARP‑targeted alpha therapy induces DNA double‑strand breaks and up‑regulates PARP1, creating a positive feedback loop that increases tumor uptake and promotes immune priming. | Findings: Personalized dosimetry using NM‑600 allowed subtraction of radiopharmaceutical dose from external beam plans, enabling safe delivery of combined therapy in head‑and‑neck cancer.; Low‑to‑moderate Y‑90 NM‑600 doses synergized with anti‑CTLA‑4, enhancing local and systemic tumor control and generating immune memory.; Alpha‑emitting actinium showed superior immune priming (increased TCR clonality) in poorly immunogenic tumors compared with beta emitters.; Heterogeneous intratumoral dose distribution (mixed high/low uptake) activated multiple immune pathways (type‑I IFN, MHC up‑regulation) and improved survival in mouse models, an effect lost with homogeneous dosing.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Zach Morris
metadata.talk_title: Preclinical and translational strategies to combine radiopharmaceuticals with other cancer therapies

text: Non-enzymatic HDAC-mediated repression reveals selective stress adaptive mechanisms for cancer therapy | Speaker: Olivia Debnath | Tumors: neuroblastoma, multiple myeloma | MOA: This talk describes the discovery and characterization of E6R, a non-enzymatic inhibitor of the Sin3-Rpd3L (HDAC1/2) complex in yeast and neuroblastoma cells. Unlike traditional HDAC inhibitors, E6R disrupts protein-protein interfaces, leading to a distinct transcriptomic signature. In neuroblastoma, E6R induces cell cycle arrest via p53/E2F signaling and integrated stress response, achieving therapeutic effects without the broad cytotoxicity of enzymatic HDAC inhibitors. | Findings: E6R is a non-enzymatic inhibitor of the Sin3-Rpd3L complex, identified through a yeast-based reporter assay screening 52,000 compounds.; E6R exhibits a distinct transcriptomic signature compared to enzymatic HDAC inhibitors (TSA) and complex knockouts (Rpd3, Sin3).; In neuroblastoma cells, E6R reduces invasion without significant cytotoxicity, unlike TSA.; E6R affects 14x fewer genes than TSA in neuroblastoma cells, indicating higher transcriptional selectivity.; E6R induces cell cycle arrest via p53/E2F signaling and repression of G2M checkpoint genes.

metadata.speaker: Olivia Debnath
metadata.talk_title: Non-enzymatic HDAC-mediated repression reveals selective stress adaptive mechanisms for cancer therapy

text: Molecular Glue Degrader of the ARNT Protein | Speaker: Jake Fachman | Tumors: clear cell renal cell carcinoma | MOA: NEO811 is a potent and selective molecular glue degrader of ARNT (HIF1 beta) for clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC). ARNT is central to HIF signaling, angiogenesis, proliferation, and immune suppression. NEO811 demonstrates dose-dependent tumor growth inhibition as a single agent, shows synergistic effects with belzutifan, and retains activity in models of acquired and intrinsic resistance to HIF-2 alpha inhibitors, supporting its clinical development. | Findings: ARNT knockdown in A498 cells leads to tumor growth regression, validating ARNT as a target in ccRCC.; NEO811 is a potent ARNT degrader with low nanomolar activity, dependent on cereblon, and shows a favorable selectivity window.; NEO811 demonstrates dose-dependent tumor growth inhibition in the 7860 xenograft model, with >50% regression at 3 mg/kg.; NEO811 shows synergistic tumor growth regression when combined with belzutifan.; NEO811 retains activity in a model of acquired resistance to HIF-2 alpha inhibitors (G323E mutation).

metadata.speaker: Jake Fachman
metadata.talk_title: Molecular Glue Degrader of the ARNT Protein

text: Molecular Glue Degrader Targeting the CCNE1 Protein | Speaker: Ralf Tiedje | Tumors: ovarian cancer, endometrial cancer, gastric cancer, breast cancer, colorectal cancer | MOA: MRT55811 is a first-in-class molecular glue degrader targeting CCNE1, an oncogene amplified in various cancers. It induces co-degradation of CCNE1 and CDK2, leading to Rb dephosphorylation, cell cycle arrest, and anti-proliferative effects specifically in CCNE1-amplified cancers. This mechanism differentiates it from CDK2 inhibitors and suggests a favorable therapeutic window. | Findings: MRT55811 is a potent and selective CCNE1 degrader, exclusively active in CCNE1 amplified cell lines.; MRT55811 induces co-degradation of CCNE1 and CDK2, leading to Rb dephosphorylation and S-phase arrest.; The degrader forms a quaternary complex involving CRBN, glue, CCNE1, and CDK2.; MRT55811 shows potent anti-proliferative activity in CCNE1 amplified cell lines, with GI50s in the nanomolar range.; MRT55811 demonstrates tumor regression in xenograft models of CCNE1 amplified gastric, ovarian, and breast cancers.

metadata.speaker: Ralf Tiedje
metadata.talk_title: Molecular Glue Degrader Targeting the CCNE1 Protein

text: Molecular Glue Degrader of the RNA Binding Protein HuR | Speaker: Zhang Yang | Tumors: colorectal cancer, solid tumors | MOA: Degron Therapeutics has developed DG6498, a potent and selective molecular glue degrader of the RNA-binding protein HuR, targeting BRAF-mutant colorectal cancer. HuR is an undruggable oncogenic driver. DG6498 induces CRBN-dependent degradation of HuR, showing efficacy in BRAF-mutant CRC models and overcoming resistance to BRAF inhibitors.
