The compound has favorable PK/PD properties and is currently in Phase 1 clinical development. | Findings: A molecular glue degrader of HuR was identified through proteomic screening of a proprietary compound library.; HUR degrader two exhibits potent HuR degradation (DC50 = 3.8 nM, 96% max degradation) dependent on CRBN and the proteasome.; Cryo-EM structure reveals the ternary complex formation between CRBN, MGD, and HuR.; HuR dependency is strongly correlated with BRAF mutation status, making BRAF-mutant CRC a key indication.; The HuR degrader selectively reduces cell viability in BRAF-mutant CRC cell lines.

metadata.speaker: Zhang Yang
metadata.talk_title: Molecular Glue Degrader of the RNA Binding Protein HuR

text: BBO10203, a RAS PI3 Breaker, Inhibits Phospho-AKT Signaling in HER2-Amplified Models Through Inhibition of Non-Canonical RAS Signaling | Speaker: James Theis | Tumors: esophageal cancer, lung cancer, colorectal cancer, pancreatic cancer, breast cancer | MOA: BBO10203 is a covalent inhibitor that breaks the RAS-PI3K interaction, specifically targeting HER2-amplified cancers. It potently suppresses phospho-AKT signaling by inhibiting non-canonical RAS isoforms (RS2) and canonical RAS signaling. BBO10203 demonstrates strong monotherapy efficacy and combination potential with HER2-targeted agents, offering a new therapeutic strategy for HER2-amplified tumors. | Findings: HER2-amplified cell lines are particularly sensitive to disruption of the RAS-PI3K interaction by BBO10203.; BBO10203 achieves potent single-digit nanomolar suppression of phospho-AKT in HER2-amplified lines.; Non-canonical RAS isoforms, particularly RS2, play a significant role in driving phospho-AKT signaling in HER2-amplified cells.; BBO10203 inhibits both non-canonical and canonical RAS signaling pathways.; BBO10203 shows strong monotherapy tumor regression in HER2-amplified KYSC esophageal CDX model.

metadata.speaker: James Theis
metadata.talk_title: BBO10203, a RAS PI3 Breaker, Inhibits Phospho-AKT Signaling in HER2-Amplified Models Through Inhibition of Non-Canonical RAS Signaling

text: Catalytic Inhibitors of the KAT2A/B Protein in Multiple Myeloma | Speaker: Christine Jensen-Paggacas | Tumors: multiple myeloma, AML | MOA: Pfizer has developed KAT2I, a first-in-class catalytic inhibitor of KAT2A/B, targeting multiple myeloma. KAT2A/B are key components of the SAGA complex, driving oncogenic transcription. KAT2I treatment leads to downregulation of MYC and E2F targets, and upregulates interferon responses, sensitizing myeloma cells to immune killing. The compound shows robust efficacy as monotherapy and in combination with standard of care agents and T-cell engagers. | Findings: Multiple myeloma cells show a strong dependency on the SAGA complex and KAT2A/B.; KAT2I is a potent, selective, and orally bioavailable catalytic inhibitor of KAT2A/B.; KAT2I treatment leads to dose-dependent reduction of H3K9 acetylation, mimicking genetic loss of KAT2A/B.; KAT2I shows broad activity across a panel of multiple myeloma cell lines.; KAT2I downregulates MYC and E2F target genes, contributing to tumor-intrinsic response.

metadata.speaker: Christine Jensen-Paggacas
metadata.talk_title: Catalytic Inhibitors of the KAT2A/B Protein in Multiple Myeloma

text: Discovery of a New Class of Mutant-Targeted Catalytic RAS Oncogene Inhibitors | Speaker: Jacqueline Smith | Tumors: pancreatic cancer, lung cancer, colorectal cancer | MOA: RMO-55 is a novel catalytic RAS inhibitor that mimics natural GAPs by stimulating GTP hydrolysis of oncogenic RAS G12 mutants, restoring them to the GDP state. This mechanism leads to potent inhibition of RAS signaling and cell proliferation, with a wider therapeutic window than steric inhibitors. RMO-55 demonstrates deep and durable tumor regressions in preclinical models and shows activity in settings of acquired resistance, supporting its clinical development. | Findings: RMO-55 is a new class of mutant-targeted catalytic RAS inhibitor that stimulates GTP hydrolysis of G12 mutant RAS.; RMO-55 produces rapid and near-complete reduction in G12V GTP levels biochemically.; RMO-55 causes potent and near complete reduction in cellular RAS GTP levels and phospho-ERK.; RMO-55 robustly inhibits proliferation in G12 mutant cell lines, with greater efficacy than deraxasip.; RMO-55 shows a reduced effect on wild-type cell lines compared to deraxasip.

metadata.speaker: Jacqueline Smith
metadata.talk_title: Discovery of a New Class of Mutant-Targeted Catalytic RAS Oncogene Inhibitors

text: CQ0736 polysaccharide‑based KRAS‑targeted therapy via macropinocytosis | Speaker: Jinhua Hu | Tumors: pan-KRAS tumors | MOA: CQ0736 is a dextran‑based conjugate bearing docetaxel and gamma‑linolenic acid that exploits enhanced macropinocytosis in KRAS‑driven tumors for selective tumor accumulation; the conjugate releases docetaxel intracellularly, inducing apoptosis while avoiding P‑gp efflux, resulting in durable tumor regression across KRAS G12C, G12D and wild‑type models. | Findings: CQ0736 achieved sustained intratumoral docetaxel exposure for 96 h versus free DTX.; In KRAS G12C lung CDX, weekly CQ0736 reduced tumor volume 3.6‑fold vs RMC and 5.2‑fold vs adagrasib at day 28.; CQ0736 showed durable tumor control without resistance in KRAS G12C PDX (16.5‑fold reduction vs RMC at day 49).; No significant body‑weight loss or hematologic toxicity observed across CDX/PDX studies.

metadata.speaker: Jinhua Hu
metadata.talk_title: CQ0736 polysaccharide‑based KRAS‑targeted therapy via macropinocytosis

text: Orally bioavailable small‑molecule MYC translation inhibitors (WDC‑623) | Speaker: Michelle Kriner | Tumors: solid tumors | MOA: WDC‑623 binds to a regulatory element in the MYC 5'‑UTR, stabilizing an inhibitory RNA structure that blocks translation initiation; rapid loss of MYC protein (half‑life ~30 min) leads to selective repression of MYC‑driven transcriptional programs while sparing non‑MYC short‑half‑life proteins. | Findings: Structure‑guided hit‑to‑lead improved potency >100‑fold to single‑digit nM (WDC‑623).; WDC‑623 reduced c‑MYC protein within 30 min without affecting MYC mRNA levels.; Proteomics showed c‑MYC and its direct targets CDC25A/B were the most repressed proteins after 2 h treatment.; Oral BID dosing (5 mg/kg) produced significant tumor growth inhibition in SCLC CDX and 125 % TGI in PDAC xenograft with no weight loss.; Compound activity is nutrient‑dependent; high nutrient levels (normal plasma) blunt MYC repression, suggesting tumor‑selective activity.

metadata.speaker: Michelle Kriner
metadata.talk_title: Orally bioavailable small‑molecule MYC translation inhibitors (WDC‑623)

text: Intramolecular glue Cbl‑B inhibitors (NX‑1607) advancing to Phase 1 | Speaker: Frederick Cohen | Tumors: colorectal cancer, triple‑negative breast cancer, B‑cell lymphoma | MOA: NX‑1607 binds to the closed conformation pocket at the interface of Cbl‑B’s three domains, acting as an intramolecular glue that locks Cbl‑B in an inactive state, thereby releasing the brake on T‑cell and NK‑cell activation; the resulting immune activation synergizes with anti‑PD‑1 therapy to produce tumor regression. | Findings: High‑throughput screen of 250 k compounds yielded a single Cbl‑B hit (NRX‑001) with 30 µM potency.; Enantiomeric resolution identified the active S‑enantiomer; crystal structure revealed binding to a buried pocket near Tyr363.; Medicinal chemistry optimization produced NX‑1607 with sub‑nanomolar Kd (0.4 nM) and excellent oral bioavailability.; NX‑1607 monotherapy achieved tumor regression at 10–30 mg/kg daily in colorectal, TNBC, and B‑cell lymphoma models.; Combination with anti‑PD‑1 showed synergistic survival benefit across multiple syngeneic models.

metadata.speaker: Frederick Cohen
metadata.talk_title: Intramolecular glue Cbl‑B inhibitors (NX‑1607) advancing to Phase 1

text: NEO811, a first‑in‑class ARNT molecular glue degrader for clear cell RCC | Speaker: Jennifer Griffin | Tumors: clear cell renal cell carcinoma | MOA: NEO811 binds cereblon and creates a neo‑substrate interface that recruits ARNT, inducing a conformational rearrangement that enables ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation; loss of ARNT disrupts HIF‑α heterodimer transcription, leading to potent anti‑tumor activity in VHL‑deficient RCC. | Findings: Structure‑guided design converted initial hit (compound A) into selective ARNT degrader (compound C) with reduced off‑target cereblon neo‑substrate degradation.; NEO811 demonstrated >80 % ARNT degradation at low nanomolar concentrations in cellular assays.; In vivo, once‑daily oral dosing for 21 days produced marked tumor regression in ccRCC xenografts with good tolerability.; NEO811 showed superior potency to FDA‑approved HIF‑2α inhibitor belzutifan in HIF transcriptional inhibition assays.

metadata.speaker: Jennifer Griffin
metadata.talk_title: NEO811, a first‑in‑class ARNT molecular glue degrader for clear cell RCC

text: DNA‑templated spatially controlled degraders (DTAG) for CDK4/6‑Cyclin D1 | Speaker: Rong Zeng | Tumors: glioblastoma | MOA: DTAG‑v1 uses a 20‑bp double‑stranded DNA scaffold to position a CDK4/6 inhibitor and an E3 ligase recruiter at defined distances; the optimal geometry (ligand on major groove) enables formation of a productive ternary complex that simultaneously degrades CDK4, CDK6 and the undruggable Cyclin D1, demonstrating that spatial programming via DNA can control target selectivity. | Findings: Four DNA‑templated PROTAC geometries showed distinct degradation profiles; version 1 (major‑groove placement) degraded CDK4, CDK6 and Cyclin D1.; Molecular dynamics revealed that productive ternary complexes correlated with negative ΔG values and close proximity of CDK4/6 to the E3 ligase.; In vivo, DTAG‑v1 achieved robust tumor regression in U251 xenografts with no significant body‑weight loss.; The platform is modular: swapping the CDK4/6 ligand for CDK9 or CDK2 inhibitors generated degraders for other cyclin‑CDK complexes without re‑synthesizing the DNA scaffold.

metadata.speaker: Rong Zeng
metadata.talk_title: DNA‑templated spatially controlled degraders (DTAG) for CDK4/6‑Cyclin D1

text: BH‑501284, a pseudo‑irreversible pan‑KRAS switch‑II inhibitor | Speaker: Jin Cui | Tumors: non‑small cell lung cancer, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, colorectal cancer | MOA: BH‑501284 binds the KRAS switch‑II pocket in both GDP‑ and GTP‑bound states with picomolar affinity and a residence time >54 h, rigidifying KRAS and preventing RAF interaction; the pseudo‑irreversible kinetic profile yields sustained pathway inhibition after drug washout. | Findings: SPR showed picomolar Kd and >54 h residence time on GDP‑bound KRAS G12D, outperforming AMG 410 (1.4 h).; Washout experiments demonstrated >90 % p‑ERK inhibition retained 24 h after removal, comparable to covalent G12C inhibitor.; Potent activity across KRAS G12V, G12D, G12C (IC50 <3 nM) and KRAS‑amplified lines (IC50 ~1.5 nM); inactive on NRAS/HRAS mutants.; Oral BID dosing as low as 5 mg/kg achieved deep tumor regressions in multiple KRAS mutant CDX models.; Only ~2‑fold shift in IC50 when EGFR ligand added, and synergistic with cetuximab in long‑term growth assays.

metadata.speaker: Jin Cui
metadata.talk_title: BH‑501284, a pseudo‑irreversible pan‑KRAS switch‑II inhibitor

text: Proteomics‑guided discovery of TRIM21‑mediated multimeric degradation (ACE compounds) | Speaker: Aihuan Yu | MOA: ACE compounds act as molecular glues that convert the E3 ligase TRIM21 into a degrader of nuclear pore complex proteins; binding is NUP98‑dependent, leading to ordered degradation of inner‑ring NPC subunits followed by outer‑ring components, demonstrating that multimeric assembly state governs TRIM21‑mediated proteasomal clearance. | Findings: Phenotypic screen identified three ACE compounds that cause IFN‑γ‑dependent cell death.; CRISPR screen highlighted TRIM21 as essential for ACE activity.; Proteomics revealed selective degradation of inner‑ring NPC proteins, reversible by proteasome inhibition.; Time‑course proteomics showed hierarchical degradation: inner‑ring NPC subunits degraded within 4 h, outer‑ring later, nuclear basket unchanged at 12 h.; BioID proximity labeling demonstrated ACE‑dependent recruitment of TRIM21 to NPC complexes via NUP98; NUP98 knockout abolished recruitment.

metadata.speaker: Aihuan Yu
metadata.talk_title: Proteomics‑guided discovery of TRIM21‑mediated multimeric degradation (ACE compounds)

text: MUTA tetravalent antibody platform for next-generation ADCs | Speaker: Dr. Juntala | Tumors: solid tumors | MOA: The MUTA platform creates a tetravalent, multi-epitope antibody that simultaneously binds two tumor antigens (e.g., MUC16 and NaPi2b) to improve internalization, efficacy, and safety of ADCs, with site-specific conjugation and a hydrophilic linker to enhance plasma stability and therapeutic window. | Findings: MUDA tetravalent ADCs outperformed monospecific ADCs in lung, colon, head and neck xenograft models, showing greater tumor regression.; PK in monkeys demonstrated stable plasma exposure up to 9 mg/kg with reversible reticulocyte decrease only at the highest dose, indicating an improved safety margin.; AquaLink hydrophilic linker maintained ADC stability without increasing hydrophobicity, improving plasma stability and bystander activity.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Juntala
metadata.talk_title: MUTA tetravalent antibody platform for next-generation ADCs

text: High-throughput drug screening and single-cell network analysis for IDH mutant glioma | Speaker: Dr. Patrick Kerwin | Tumors: glioma | MOA: Single-cell regulatory network analysis identifies state-specific master regulator programs in IDH mutant glioma; high-throughput drug screening (OncoTreat) predicts compounds that invert these programs (e.g., cisplatin for AC-like, DS‑651b for NPC-like, micofenolate for OC-like), enabling rational combination strategies validated in patient-derived slice explants. | Findings: Three conserved malignant cell states (AC-like, NPC-like, OC-like) were defined across oligodendroglioma and astrocytoma with distinct master regulator programs.; OncoTreat identified state-specific drug vulnerabilities: DNA damage repair inhibitors for AC-like, MAPK pathway inhibitors for NPC-like, and purine synthesis inhibitors for OC-like.; Preliminary ex vivo slice experiments suggest serum biomarkers can detect early state shifts, supporting translational potential.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Patrick Kerwin
metadata.talk_title: High-throughput drug screening and single-cell network analysis for IDH mutant glioma

text: Serum hyaluronic acid as a predictive biomarker for T‑DXD‑induced interstitial lung disease | Speaker: Dr. Peng Guo | Tumors: solid tumors | MOA: Age‑dependent accumulation of T‑DXD in adult lungs leads to alveolar macrophage activation, endothelial HYAL2 up‑regulation, extracellular matrix remodeling and release of hyaluronic acid fragments into serum, which serve as an early non‑invasive biomarker for ADC‑induced interstitial lung disease. | Findings: Adult mice develop T‑DXD‑induced ILD (40%) whereas young mice are protected (0%).; Adult lungs show higher T‑DXD accumulation, increased mature alveolar macrophages, elevated CTSB and SPP1 expression, and endothelial HYAL2 up‑regulation.; Serum HA levels rise significantly in adult mice with ILD and predict ILD in a pilot clinical cohort (AUC 74% alone, 93% with fibrosis panel).; Early HA elevation precedes radiographic ILD, suggesting utility for pre‑emptive monitoring.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Peng Guo
metadata.talk_title: Serum hyaluronic acid as a predictive biomarker for T‑DXD‑induced interstitial lung disease

text: Co‑clinical trial of datopotamab deruxtecan in patient‑derived xenografts | Speaker: Dr. Dhruv Chachad | Tumors: breast cancer, head and neck SCC, bladder carcinoma, pancreatic adenocarcinoma | MOA: Datopotamab deruxtecan (ADC targeting Trop‑2) delivers a topoisomerase‑1 inhibitor payload; co‑clinical PDX models recapitulate patient responses and reveal synergistic antitumor activity when combined with gemcitabine, likely via enhanced DNA damage in Trop‑2‑positive tumors. | Findings: Dato induced tumor regression and prolonged time to doubling across multiple PDX models, mirroring patient outcomes (78.6% concordance).; Gemcitabine synergized with Dato in PDXs derived from patients with progressive disease, leading to greater tumor control than either agent alone.; Biopsy take rate was 47% overall, demonstrating feasibility of generating co‑clinical PDXs from basket trial specimens.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Dhruv Chachad
metadata.talk_title: Co‑clinical trial of datopotamab deruxtecan in patient‑derived xenografts

text: Inducer‑amplifier strategy targeting p53‑mutant cancers | Speaker: Dr. Bakin | Tumors: pancreatic cancer, colon cancer, breast cancer | MOA: A two‑step inducer‑amplifier approach: TAS‑102 induces DNA damage that accumulates in p53‑mutant cells; PARP inhibition blocks single‑strand break repair, enhancing damage; subsequent WEE1 inhibition forces G2‑arrested cells into mitotic catastrophe, achieving selective tumor cell death with low toxicity. | Findings: TAS‑102 plus PARP inhibitor synergistically kills p53‑mutant cells in vitro and reduces tumor growth in PDX models.; Adding WEE1 inhibitor after the inducer‑amplifier increases cell death from 30% to ~80% specifically in p53‑mutant cells.; The sequential regimen is well tolerated in preclinical models and shows early signs of efficacy in a phase‑1 trial.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Bakin
metadata.talk_title: Inducer‑amplifier strategy targeting p53‑mutant cancers

text: KBD‑1111: a selective, long‑acting, brain‑penetrant PARP‑1 inhibitor | Speaker: Dr. Liu | Tumors: BRCA‑deficient cancers, brain metastases | MOA: KBD‑1111 is a highly selective PARP‑1 inhibitor (9,000‑fold over PARP‑2) that traps PARP‑1, exhibits long half‑life, penetrates the CNS (CSF AUC 38.6 ng·h/mL, Kpu 0.26), and demonstrates potent antitumor activity with reduced hematologic toxicity, supporting Q2W dosing. | Findings: KBD‑1111 shows IC50 0.36 nM against PARP‑1 and >9,000‑fold selectivity over PARP‑2.; In BRCA‑deficient xenografts, 10 mg/kg Q2W achieved near‑complete tumor inhibition, superior to AZD5305.; Brain penetration (Kpu 0.26) enabled tumor regression in intracranial models with weekly dosing.; Hematologic toxicity was markedly reduced compared to olaparib, especially with QW dosing.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Liu
metadata.talk_title: KBD‑1111: a selective, long‑acting, brain‑penetrant PARP‑1 inhibitor

text: Comparative analysis of TEAD palmitoylation inhibitor vs PPI in KRAS‑mutant cancers | Speaker: Dr. Sanchez | Tumors: NSCLC, colorectal cancer, pancreatic cancer | MOA: TEAD central‑pocket palmitoylation inhibitors (CPI) block TEAD palmitoylation, while TEAD‑YAP/TAZ PPI inhibitors directly disrupt the protein‑protein interaction; both suppress TEAD‑driven transcription, but PPI achieves greater YAP eviction and target gene repression, leading to more durable synergy with KRAS inhibitors in vitro, though in vivo both modalities show comparable tumor control. | Findings: PPI (IAG 933) combined with KRAS G12C inhibitor delayed resistance and resensitized resistant cells more effectively than CPI (AZD0751) in vitro.; Both TEAD inhibitors suppressed KRAS‑induced TEAD target gene up‑regulation, but PPI achieved greater YAP chromatin eviction.; In NSCLC xenografts, both CPI and PPI enhanced tumor regression with KRAS inhibition, but no additive benefit was observed in KRAS G12D pancreatic models.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Sanchez
metadata.talk_title: Comparative analysis of TEAD palmitoylation inhibitor vs PPI in KRAS‑mutant cancers

text: Targeting RAS and RAF in MSS Metastatic Colorectal Cancer | Speaker: Scott Kopetz | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: Encouraging BRAF V600E inhibition in MSS colorectal cancer requires concurrent EGFR blockade to prevent feedback re‑activation of MAPK signaling; adding chemotherapy (FOLFOX) further suppresses emergent resistant clones and reduces ctDNA‑detectable resistance mutations, leading to higher response rates and prolonged PFS/OS. Parallel KRAS allele‑specific inhibitors (G12C, G12D) show modest activity alone, which is markedly enhanced when combined with EGFR antibodies, reflecting the same feedback loop. Emerging degraders and pan‑RAS approaches aim to overcome subclonal resistance mechanisms such as MET amplification, KRAS/NRAS secondary mutations, and YAP/TEAD activation. | Findings: BreakWater first‑line BRAF V600E + EGFR inhibition plus FOLFOX achieved ORR 67% vs 37% with standard chemotherapy (HR for PFS 0.53, HR for OS 0.49).; Median OS doubled from 15.1 months (control) to 30.3 months with EC+FOLFOX in BRAF V600E MSS colorectal cancer.; ctDNA clearance of the BRAF V600E clone at 6 weeks increased from 35% (control) to 45% (EC) and 67% (EC+FOLFOX), correlating with improved outcomes.; Acquired resistance mutations (KRAS, NRAS, MAP2K1, MET amplification) were subclonal and more frequent after EC alone than after EC+FOLFOX.; KRAS G12C inhibitor adagrasib combined with cetuximab yielded ORR 34% and PFS 6.9 months; elacestrant monotherapy gave ORR 47% (up to 62% with EGFR inhibitor).

metadata.speaker: Scott Kopetz
metadata.talk_title: Targeting RAS and RAF in MSS Metastatic Colorectal Cancer

text: Epidemiology and clinical impact of chemosensory dysfunction in cancer patients | Speaker: Valentina Parma | MOA: Epidemiologic analyses of large population cohorts reveal that chemosensory dysfunction is highly prevalent in cancer patients (≈60% smell, 93% taste) and is associated with substantial reductions in quality of life, increased frailty, malnutrition, and higher risk of comorbidities such as heart failure and cognitive decline. | Findings: Approximately 60% of cancer patients report smell dysfunction and 93% report taste dysfunction.; NHANES data show 14% prevalence of taste dysfunction, 22% smell dysfunction, and 10% both in the general US adult population.; Smell dysfunction reduces odds of a satisfying life by 40%; taste dysfunction reduces it by 60% (NHANES).; During chemotherapy cycles, taste dysfunction peaks at days 4‑7 and improves by the end of the cycle.; Clinician awareness is low: only ~15% can distinguish taste from flavor, yet 44% of clinicians consider taste changes very important to patients.

metadata.speaker: Valentina Parma
metadata.talk_title: Epidemiology and clinical impact of chemosensory dysfunction in cancer patients

text: Molecular mechanisms of targeted therapy‑induced taste dysfunction and development of taste organoid platforms | Speaker: Linda Barlow | MOA: Targeted cancer therapies disrupt taste homeostasis via distinct pathways: Wnt/β‑catenin activation skews progenitor output toward type I cells and reduces sweet perception; Hedgehog inhibition blocks progenitor differentiation causing loss of taste buds; KIT inhibition by anti‑angiogenic TKIs impairs sweet cell fate and promotes bitter differentiation, leading to dysgeusia. | Findings: Wnt/β‑catenin signaling is required for taste progenitor proliferation; hyperactivation increases type I cells and modestly type II cells without affecting sour cells.; Loss of Wnt signaling leads to progressive loss of taste buds, especially in anterior tongue, correlating with reduced sweet behavior in mice.; Smoothened antagonism (Hedgehog inhibition) eliminates taste buds and diminishes gustatory nerve responses, but does not affect progenitor proliferation.; Overexpression of SHH drives excess taste bud formation, indicating Hedgehog promotes differentiation rather than proliferation.; Cabozantinib treatment reduces sweet‑cell markers and increases bitter‑cell markers in mouse taste organoids and in vivo, phenocopying KIT deletion in type II precursors.

metadata.speaker: Linda Barlow
metadata.talk_title: Molecular mechanisms of targeted therapy‑induced taste dysfunction and development of taste organoid platforms

text: Implementation of the Genie Data Model at Providence Cancer Institute | Speaker: Jake Van Kampen | MOA: The GP3 pipeline programmatically extracts source attributes from Providence's Snowflake clinical data warehouse, maps them to the Genie Data Model (GDM) via SQL transformations, validates and stages the data, and exports it for downstream use, dramatically reducing manual abstraction time and improving data quality. | Findings: Programmatic extraction reduced case abstraction time from ~8 hours per case to minutes for thousands of patients.; Automated schema validation and record-level consistency checks identified implausible values (e.g., out-of-range weights) for rapid correction.; Lineage parsing of SQL code automatically documented source provenance for each GDM attribute, facilitating reproducibility.; AI-assisted coding (GitHub Copilot) accelerated development of mapping scripts and improved code quality.; The pipeline achieved near‑real‑time generation of GDM‑aligned tables, enabling rapid data sharing across sites.

metadata.speaker: Jake Van Kampen
metadata.talk_title: Implementation of the Genie Data Model at Providence Cancer Institute

text: Senescent fibroblast SASP drives chemotherapy‑induced peripheral neuropathy and can be reversed by senolytics or MK2 inhibition | Speaker: Dr. Limoli | MOA: Chemotherapy (paclitaxel) induces p16‑positive senescent fibroblasts in peripheral skin; these cells secrete a SASP regulated by MK2 kinase that causes epidermal denervation and behavioral neuropathy. Genetic ablation of p16‑positive cells or pharmacologic senolysis (dasatinib + quercetin) or MK2 inhibition eliminates the SASP, restores innervation and reverses numbness/pain in mice. | Findings: Paclitaxel treatment increased p16 mRNA and protein in peripheral skin but not in dorsal root ganglia or sciatic nerve.; Senescent fibroblasts (p16‑positive, SA‑β‑gal+) accumulated in the skin and were eliminated by inducible suicide gene activation.; Elimination of senescent cells prevented paclitaxel‑induced epidermal denervation and restored normal Von Frey thresholds.; Senolytic treatment (dasatinib + quercetin) after neuropathy onset re‑innervated epidermis and normalized paw thresholds, reversing pain.; Fibroblast‑specific MK2 knockout abolished the neuropathic phenotype despite persistence of senescent cells, implicating MK2‑driven SASP as the effector.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Limoli
metadata.talk_title: Senescent fibroblast SASP drives chemotherapy‑induced peripheral neuropathy and can be reversed by senolytics or MK2 inhibition

text: Long‑term morbidity and mortality in childhood cancer survivors: prevalence, frailty, and socioeconomic impacts | Speaker: Melissa Hudson | MOA: Large‑scale survivorship cohort analyses reveal that treatment‑related exposures (radiation, alkylators, surgery) and socioeconomic deprivation synergistically drive multimorbidity, frailty, and excess mortality in adult survivors of childhood cancer, with genetic predisposition (pathogenic germline variants) further increasing risk of subsequent neoplasms. | Findings: By age 40, childhood cancer survivors have a 25% excess mortality relative to the US population.; More than 90% of survivors develop at least one chronic health condition; 85% of those are serious, disabling, or life‑threatening.; Survivors accrue an average of 17 chronic conditions by age 50, including ~5 severe conditions.; Frailty prevalence in survivors aged 18‑50 matches that of general adults >65 yr; frailty confers a 2.6‑fold higher risk of early death.; Whole‑genome sequencing identified pathogenic germline variants in 6% of survivors, associated with increased risk of second neoplasms.

metadata.speaker: Melissa Hudson
metadata.talk_title: Long‑term morbidity and mortality in childhood cancer survivors: prevalence, frailty, and socioeconomic impacts

text: Functional significance of YTHDF m6A readers in AML and multiple myeloma | Speaker: Kamil Krance | Tumors: acute myeloid leukemia, multiple myeloma | MOA: YTHDF2 and YTHDF3 are cytosolic m6A readers that promote decay of methylated transcripts such as TNFRSF1B; genetic deletion stabilizes these transcripts, leading to heightened TNF‑mediated apoptosis and loss of leukemic stem cell activity in AML. Parallel loss of YTHDF3 impairs ribosomal biogenesis and translation of M6A‑modified mRNAs, reducing leukemic proliferation and sensitizing cells to cytarabine. Normal hematopoiesis remains largely intact, indicating a therapeutic window for targeting these readers. | Findings: YTHDF2 is overexpressed in AML across sub‑genetic subtypes and correlates with leukemic stem cell activity.; YTHDF2 knockout or knockdown abolishes colony formation of AML cells in vitro and markedly extends latency in mouse transplantation models.; Loss of YTHDF2 stabilizes TNFRSF1B mRNA, increasing surface TNFR2 and rendering AML cells highly sensitive to exogenous TNF (apoptosis observed).; YTHDF3 deletion reduces leukemic stem cell frequency in limiting‑dilution assays and impairs engraftment of THP‑1 cells in liver PDX models.; YTHDF3 knockdown sensitizes AML cells to Ara‑C, decreasing the Ara‑C IC50 (exact values not disclosed).

metadata.speaker: Kamil Krance
metadata.talk_title: Functional significance of YTHDF m6A readers in AML and multiple myeloma

text: YTHDF2 and YTHDC1 in tumor immunity and chromatin regulation of plastic cancers | Speaker: Chuan He | Tumors: neuroendocrine prostate cancer, small cell lung cancer, acute myeloid leukemia | MOA: YTHDF2 promotes decay of M6A‑modified transcripts in myeloid‑derived suppressor cells, enhancing their immunosuppressive function after radiation; its loss stabilizes anti‑inflammatory RNAs, reduces MDSC migration, and synergizes with radiation and anti‑PD‑L1 to boost CD8⁺ T‑cell activity. YTHDC1 binds M6A‑modified promoter and enhancer RNAs (including LTR elements) in solid tumors, recruiting SETD1A/YY1 to open chromatin and drive transcription of lineage‑plastic, proliferative programs; inhibition of YTHDC1 collapses this transcriptional program and depletes cycling tumor cells. | Findings: YTHDF2 knockout in MDSCs diminishes their suppressive capacity, reduces IL‑10 production, and enhances CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration after irradiation.; Combining YTHDF2 loss with radiation and anti‑PD‑L1 yields synergistic tumor control in mouse models, dependent on CD8⁺ T cells.; YTHDC1 inhibition (tool compound) markedly reduces viability of neuroendocrine prostate and small‑cell lung cancer cells in vitro and suppresses tumor growth in PDX models.; Loss of YTHDC1 leads to global chromatin closing (reduced DNase I signal, lower H3K27ac/H3K4me3) and down‑regulation of ~6,000 genes linked to LTR‑derived promoter RNAs.; Proteomics identifies SETD1A and YY1 as YTHDC1 interactors mediating transcriptional activation at open chromatin sites.

metadata.speaker: Chuan He
metadata.talk_title: YTHDF2 and YTHDC1 in tumor immunity and chromatin regulation of plastic cancers

text: Precision diets targeting serine/glycine metabolism and combination with PHGDH inhibition | Speaker: Karen Valston | Tumors: lung cancer, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, breast cancer, colorectal cancer | MOA: Limiting dietary serine and glycine reduces circulating one‑carbon metabolites, impairing nucleotide synthesis and antioxidant capacity in tumor cells, which slows growth in serine‑dependent GEM and organoid models. Tumors that up‑regulate de novo serine synthesis via PHGDH become resistant, but combined PHGDH inhibition restores sensitivity, especially when paired with radiotherapy that induces ROS. | Findings: Serine/glycine‑free diet reduced tumor growth and metastasis in KRAS/LKB1 lung and KRAS/p53 pancreatic GEM models (p<0.01).; Combination of serine/glycine restriction with radiotherapy markedly increased tumor cell death compared with either modality alone (p<0.001).; PHGDH‑amplified tumors were resistant to dietary serine depletion, but addition of a PHGDH inhibitor restored tumor growth inhibition (tumor volume reduction 45%, p<0.01).; CRISPR dropout identified folate transporter as a synthetic lethal partner with serine/glycine depletion; knockdown abolished growth of resistant organoids.; Mice on serine/glycine‑free diet showed transient weight loss but no organ toxicity; cachexia markers GDF15 and IL6 were significantly lower (GDF15 ↓30%, IL6 ↓25%).

metadata.speaker: Karen Valston
metadata.talk_title: Precision diets targeting serine/glycine metabolism and combination with PHGDH inhibition

text: Exercise‑derived extracellular vesicles suppress breast cancer metastasis via MTSS1 and NME2 | Speaker: Mark Fabreo | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: Voluntary exercise increases the number and protein cargo of circulating small extracellular vesicles. Proteomic profiling identified MTSS1 and NME2 as enriched in exercise EVs; these proteins suppress EMT‑associated pathways, reducing breast cancer cell migration and metastasis when delivered via EVs, recapitulating the anti‑tumor effect of physical activity. | Findings: Mice with voluntary wheel access ran ~7 km/night and showed ~35% reduction in primary tumor volume compared with locked‑wheel controls (p<0.01).; Metastatic lesions were reduced by >70% in running mice; mice running >6.5 km/day had the greatest metastasis‑free survival (p<0.001).; Exercise‑derived EVs injected into non‑running tumor‑bearing mice reproduced the tumor‑suppressive effect (tumor volume ↓30%, p<0.01).; Proteomic analysis identified 322 proteins significantly up‑regulated in exercise EVs; MTSS1 and NME2 were selected as anti‑metastatic candidates.; Overexpression of MTSS1 or NME2 in 41.2 cells inhibited migration in scratch assays by 50%–60% (p<0.001).

metadata.speaker: Mark Fabreo
metadata.talk_title: Exercise‑derived extracellular vesicles suppress breast cancer metastasis via MTSS1 and NME2

text: Diet‑microbiome interactions in colorectal cancer prevention and the coffee‑microbiome trial | Speaker: Minyang Song | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: Diet shapes gut microbial composition; unhealthy diets enrich CRC‑associated taxa (Fusobacterium, Bacteroides) while healthy diets promote butyrate‑producing microbes. Coffee consumption strongly enriches Lawsonia intracellularis, altering microbial metabolites and plasma metabolome, which is associated with improved survival in CRC patients. | Findings: Microbiome changes are modest in incident polyps (AUC 0.52) but become pronounced in prevalent polyps (AUC 0.67) and strongest in established CRC (AUC 0.85).; A CRC‑microbial diet score derived from CRC‑associated microbes correlates positively with Western diet (r=0.62) and inversely with prudent diet (r=‑0.58).; Higher CRC‑microbial diet score is associated with increased colon cancer risk after multivariable adjustment (HR 1.34 per SD, p=0.004).; Coffee intake after CRC diagnosis is linked to a 30% reduction in mortality (HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.55‑0.89) independent of caffeine content.; Coffee consumption is the strongest single dietary factor predicting a distinct microbiome signature, driven by enrichment of Lawsonia intracellularis.

metadata.speaker: Minyang Song
metadata.talk_title: Diet‑microbiome interactions in colorectal cancer prevention and the coffee‑microbiome trial

text: Mutational signatures reveal hidden mutagenic and promoter exposures across cancers | Speaker: Sir Mike Stratton | Tumors: esophageal squamous carcinoma, renal clear cell cancer, colorectal cancer | MOA: Stratton described how whole-genome sequencing enables extraction of mutational signatures that act as permanent footprints of past carcinogen exposures, revealing both known mutagens (tobacco, aristolochic acids, colibactin) and many silent promoter agents that drive clonal expansion without increasing point mutation burden. | Findings: Esophageal squamous carcinoma shows 10-20-fold geographic incidence variation but no distinct mutational signature, suggesting non‑mutagenic promoters drive risk.; Renal clear cell cancer in SE Europe harbors SBS22A/B signatures linked to aristolochic acid exposure in ~70% of cases.; A novel SBS12 signature is found exclusively in Japan, cause unknown.; Colorectal cancer early‑onset cases have >30% prevalence of SBS88 (colibactin) signature, present in normal colon of ~40% of UK children.; Only 3 of 20 tested carcinogens produced mutational signatures in mouse tumors; the rest act as promoters/selectogens.

metadata.speaker: Sir Mike Stratton
metadata.talk_title: Mutational signatures reveal hidden mutagenic and promoter exposures across cancers

text: Promotion and selectogen mechanisms in tumor initiation and clonal competition | Speaker: Alan Balmain | Tumors: skin papilloma (mouse model) | MOA: Balmain demonstrated that a single mutagenic initiation event (DMBA‑induced HRAS Q61L) remains dormant for months, and promotion by TPA selects specific mutant clones (HRAS Q61L) to expand into tumors, while many spontaneous RAS mutations expand transiently but are eliminated unless HRAS is absent, highlighting clonal competition and promoter selectivity. | Findings: DMBA induces a permanent HRAS Q61L initiation mutation that can remain silent for a year before promotion triggers rapid tumor formation.; Only HRAS Q61L clones persist and give tumors after TPA promotion; other RAS mutants expand transiently then disappear.; In HRAS knockout mice, KRAS G13R clones, normally non‑tumorigenic, give rise to tumors under TPA promotion.; Promoter agents can act without increasing point‑mutation burden, supporting the selectogen concept.

metadata.speaker: Alan Balmain
metadata.talk_title: Promotion and selectogen mechanisms in tumor initiation and clonal competition

text: Epigenetic‑oncogenic cooperation reveals tissue‑specific therapeutic vulnerabilities | Speaker: Karen Kochowski | Tumors: triple-negative breast cancer, colorectal cancer, prostate cancer, HER2‑positive breast cancer | MOA: Kochowski showed that simultaneous inhibition of EZH2 (PRC2) and oncogenic signaling (AKT, KRAS, PTEN, HER2) forces tumor cells into a differentiated, luminal‑like state via GATA3 induction and triggers an involution‑like apoptotic program mediated by JAK1‑STAT3‑BMF, leading to robust tumor regression in multiple tissue contexts. | Findings: EZH2 + AKT inhibition kills ~60% of TNBC models synergistically, with no single‑agent activity.; Combination induces GATA3, shifts cells to mature luminal phenotype, and suppresses basal/stem markers.; BMF is the top up‑regulated pro‑apoptotic gene; its knockout blocks tumor regression.; Predictive transcriptional signature (basal vs mesenchymal) separates sensitive from resistant TNBC lines.; Similar EZH2‑RAS or EZH2‑AKT combos are effective in KRAS‑mutant colorectal, PTEN‑null prostate, and HER2‑positive breast cancers, each exploiting tissue‑specific differentiation pathways.

metadata.speaker: Karen Kochowski
metadata.talk_title: Epigenetic‑oncogenic cooperation reveals tissue‑specific therapeutic vulnerabilities

text: Mechanistic dissection of cancer cachexia: brain‑tumor communication and metabolic drivers | Speaker: Eileen White | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, lung cancer, colorectal cancer, breast cancer | MOA: White described how tumor‑derived cytokines (IL‑6, GDF15) act on distinct brain circuits to suppress appetite and induce apathy, while metabolic reprogramming in cachectic mice diverts tryptophan toward the kynurenine pathway, lowering serotonin and driving depression; pharmacologic restoration of serotonin improves mood but does not reverse muscle/fat wasting, indicating separable mechanisms. | Findings: High‑fat diet worsens cachexia in mouse models via tumor‑derived prostaglandin E2 signaling through the vagus nerve.; Cachectic mice exhibit low serotonin and high kynurenine; SSRI treatment restores serotonin and improves depressive‑like behavior without affecting weight loss.; Two cachexia subtypes identified in patients: inflamed (high GDF15, IL‑6, severe symptoms, poorer survival) vs non‑inflamed (weight loss without systemic inflammation).; Longitudinal patient data reveal dynamic weight trajectories; some patients cycle between loss and stabilization.; Brain‑tumor communication pathways (GDF15‑GFRA1, IL‑6‑dopamine suppression) are key drivers of appetite loss and apathy.

metadata.speaker: Eileen White
metadata.talk_title: Mechanistic dissection of cancer cachexia: brain‑tumor communication and metabolic drivers

text: Neutrophil extracellular traps drive tumor necrosis and metastasis | Speaker: Jose Drover | Tumors: lung cancer, breast cancer, colorectal cancer | MOA: Tumor-derived signals induce a myeloid skew producing LY6C-low vascular-restricted neutrophils that aggregate in tumor vessels, form NETs, occlude perfusion, create downstream hypoxia and necrosis, and promote perinecrotic tumor cell EMT and metastasis. | Findings: Tumors induce LY6C‑low neutrophils that are restricted to the vasculature and form abundant NETs.; Neutrophil aggregates block vessel perfusion, leading to downstream hypoxia and necrosis in mouse tumor models.; Genetic or pharmacologic inhibition of NET formation (disulfiram, DNase I, platelet‑neutrophil interaction blockade) reduces tumor necrosis and lung metastasis.; Perinecrotic tumor cells upregulate hypoxia, EMT, and TGF‑β pathways, enhancing metastatic traits.

metadata.speaker: Jose Drover
metadata.talk_title: Neutrophil extracellular traps drive tumor necrosis and metastasis

text: Ischemic tumor regions reprogram macrophage metabolism to suppress T‑cell killing | Speaker: Carlos Camona Fontaine | Tumors: melanoma | MOA: In ischemic tumor regions, macrophages upregulate arginase‑1, diverting ornithine into polyamine synthesis; excess polyamines are secreted as N1‑acetylspermidine, which tumor cells convert via PAOX to a metabolite that impairs antigen‑specific T‑cell cytotoxicity without altering MHC‑I expression. | Findings: Ischemic macrophages express high ARG1 and secrete N1‑acetylspermidine.; N1‑acetylspermidine suppresses antigen‑specific T‑cell killing of tumor cells in vitro.; PAOX in tumor cells is required for the immunosuppressive effect; PAOX knockout restores T‑cell killing.; Adoptive transfer of antigen‑specific T cells dramatically reduces growth of PAOX‑deficient tumors.

metadata.speaker: Carlos Camona Fontaine
metadata.talk_title: Ischemic tumor regions reprogram macrophage metabolism to suppress T‑cell killing

text: Tumor‑derived angiopoietin‑like 7 drives necrotic core formation and metastatic dissemination | Speaker: Kevin Chung | Tumors: breast cancer, triple‑negative breast cancer, rat 4T1 model | MOA: Tumor cells upregulate ANGPTL7 in necrotic cores, promoting dilated intratumoral vessels, neutrophil NET formation, and TGF‑β enrichment, which together facilitate perinecrotic tumor cell EMT and release of CTC clusters. | Findings: Necrotic core size in rat 4T1 tumors spikes between days 22‑27 and correlates with acute CTC surge.; Tumor‑derived ANGPTL7 is highly expressed in necrotic cores; knockdown reduces necrosis, dilated vessels, CTC clusters, and lung metastasis.; ANGPTL7 knockout lowers total TGF‑β and pSMAD signaling in tumors, shifting macrophage polarization toward inflammatory phenotype.; Human breast cancer analysis shows reparative necrosis changes (distinct from coagulative necrosis) predict poor survival, especially with lymphovascular invasion.

metadata.speaker: Kevin Chung
metadata.talk_title: Tumor‑derived angiopoietin‑like 7 drives necrotic core formation and metastatic dissemination

text: Translational rheostat driven by 4E‑BP1 regulates cancer metastasis | Speaker: Ivan Topisirovic | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: Loss of 4E‑BP1 suppresses breast cancer metastasis by reducing translation of weak mRNAs such as pannexin‑1; paradoxically, 4E‑BP1 activation promotes early metastatic steps (invasion, anoikis resistance) through a Goldilocks level of mTORC1 signaling that selectively up‑regulates translation of long 5'‑UTR, uORF‑rich transcripts. | Findings: 4E‑BP1 double knockout mice crossed with polyoma middle T breast cancer showed larger primary tumors but dramatically reduced lung metastases compared with wild‑type controls.; Re‑expression of 4E‑BP1 rescued metastatic potential, whereas a constitutively active 4E‑BP1‑4A mutant failed to do so, indicating that precise mTORC1‑mediated tuning of 4E‑BP1 is required.; 4E‑BP1‑proficient cells displayed increased invasion and anoikis resistance in vitro, while tail‑vein injection showed no difference in outgrowth, pinpointing early metastatic steps as the affected stage.; Translatome analysis revealed that 4E‑BP1‑dependent up‑regulated mRNAs have longer 5'‑UTRs and more upstream open reading frames, exemplified by pannexin‑1 protein increase without RNA level change.; Serum‑dose and mTOR inhibitor titration experiments demonstrated a biphasic “Goldilocks” response where intermediate mTORC1 activity maximized pannexin‑1 translation, whereas strong inhibition reduced invasion.

metadata.speaker: Ivan Topisirovic
metadata.talk_title: Translational rheostat driven by 4E‑BP1 regulates cancer metastasis

text: tRNA U34 modification by ELP3 shapes cancer proteome via dicodon regulation | Speaker: Olle Larsson | Tumors: breast cancer, prostate cancer | MOA: ELP3‑mediated U34 modification of a subset of tRNAs enhances elongation of codons requiring these modified tRNAs; loss of ELP3 causes ribosome stalling on dicodons that pair a U34‑dependent codon with a neighboring codon, leading to reduced protein output of cell‑cycle genes despite increased polysome association. | Findings: CRISPR‑mediated loss of ELP3 reduces U34 tRNA modification and impairs proliferation of transformed but not non‑transformed cells.; Proteomics showed down‑regulation of many proteins despite higher polysome association, indicating elongation blockade.; Dicodon analysis (PosNet) explained ~30% of translational regulation, double the ~15% explained by single‑codon usage alone.; Six specific dicodons containing a U34‑dependent codon were enriched in down‑regulated proteins; closer spacing of dicodons correlated with stronger repression.; mRNAs enriched for these dicodons also possessed longer 5'‑UTRs and lower initiation efficiency, linking initiation and elongation control.

metadata.speaker: Olle Larsson
metadata.talk_title: tRNA U34 modification by ELP3 shapes cancer proteome via dicodon regulation

text: Selective translation of CaMK2D drives drug tolerance and metastasis in ER‑positive breast cancer | Speaker: Davide Ruggiero | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: ERα binds the 3'‑UTR of CaMK2D mRNA while eIF4A engages a structured 5'‑UTR G‑quadruplex; this looping enhances translation of CaMK2D during drug‑tolerant states, driving calcium‑dependent survival, invasion and metastasis, which can be blocked by calcium channel inhibition (verapamil) or eIF4A inhibition (zotatifin). | Findings: Therapy‑surviving cells (TSC) exposed to high‑dose fulvestrant up‑regulate translation of CaMK2D without changes in mRNA levels, as shown by ribosome profiling and proteomics.; CaMK2D protein, but not its mRNA, correlates with poor prognosis in a 400‑patient ER‑positive breast cancer cohort.; ERα directly binds the 3'‑UTR of CaMK2D; loss of this RNA‑binding activity reduces TSC formation, which can be rescued by CaMK2D overexpression.; eIF4A interacts more strongly with ERα in tamoxifen‑resistant cells; eIF4A inhibition by zotatifin suppresses CaMK2D translation and eliminates TSCs in vitro and in PDX models.; Combination of fulvestrant with verapamil or zotatifin markedly delays tumor regrowth and prevents metastasis to liver and brain in mouse models, whereas single agents show modest effects.

metadata.speaker: Davide Ruggiero
metadata.talk_title: Selective translation of CaMK2D drives drug tolerance and metastasis in ER‑positive breast cancer

text: Phase 1 trial of trastuzumab deruxtecan (DS-8201A) plus olaparib in HER2‑expressing advanced solid tumors | Speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Lee | Tumors: endometrial cancer, ovarian cancer | MOA: Trastuzumab deruxtecan delivers a potent exatecan TOP1‑inhibitor payload to HER2‑expressing tumor cells; concurrent PARP inhibition with olaparib blocks repair of TOP1‑DNA cleavage complexes, enhancing DNA damage and tumor cell death while staggered dosing reduces systemic hematologic toxicity. | Findings: Objective response rate of 54% (confirmed ORR 46%) observed in 28 heavily pre‑treated HER2‑positive endometrial and ovarian cancer patients.; Clinical benefit rate reached 67% with median duration of response 11.2 months.; Staggered (gap) olaparib schedule (days 8‑14) was feasible and reduced Grade 3‑4 hematologic toxicities compared with continuous olaparib dosing.; Six‑month PFS estimated at 88.2% and median PFS 15.2 months despite median of 3.5 prior therapy lines.; Pneumonitis occurred in 7 patients (all low‑grade) and was not dose‑dependent.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Lee
metadata.talk_title: Phase 1 trial of trastuzumab deruxtecan (DS-8201A) plus olaparib in HER2‑expressing advanced solid tumors

text: First‑in‑human study of SOS 6010, an EGFR‑targeted ADC, in advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma | Speaker: Dr. Jian | Tumors: nasopharyngeal carcinoma | MOA: SOS 6010 is a humanized IgG1 ADC that binds EGFR, is internalized, and releases a high‑potency, membrane‑permeable TOP1‑inhibitor payload (GS1) via a cleavable linker, causing DNA damage and tumor cell death, with a by‑stander effect in EGFR‑negative cells. | Findings: Overall ORR of 31.5% in heavily pre‑treated NPC, with higher response at the 4.8 mg/kg dose (36.6%).; Median PFS of 7.5 months and median OS of 14.9 months (4.2 mg/kg cohort; OS not reached at 4.8 mg/kg).; Grade 3+ hematologic toxicities were the most common adverse events, but treatment discontinuation was low.; No clear correlation between baseline EGFR expression level and response, suggesting a possible by‑stander effect.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Jian
metadata.talk_title: First‑in‑human study of SOS 6010, an EGFR‑targeted ADC, in advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma

text: First‑in‑human Phase 1 study of QLS‑5132, a claudin‑6‑targeting ADC, in platinum‑resistant ovarian cancer | Speaker: Dr. Tao Zhu | Tumors: ovarian cancer | MOA: QLS‑5132 couples a humanized anti‑claudin‑6 antibody to a TOP1‑inhibitor payload via a stable hydrazone linker (DAR 8); selective binding to claudin‑6‑positive tumor cells leads to internalization and release of the payload, causing DNA damage and tumor regression with a therapeutic window due to minimal normal tissue expression of claudin‑6. | Findings: Confirmed ORR of 55.6% at the 4.8 mg/kg dose in platinum‑resistant ovarian cancer.; Median relative dose intensity 99.8% and PK exposure increased proportionally from 1.6 to 6.4 mg/kg.; Grade 3+ adverse events occurred in 32.1% of patients; most were mild/moderate GI or hematologic toxicities.; Responses were observed even in two patients with undetectable CLDN6 expression, suggesting possible by‑stander effect.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Tao Zhu
metadata.talk_title: First‑in‑human Phase 1 study of QLS‑5132, a claudin‑6‑targeting ADC, in platinum‑resistant ovarian cancer

text: ARTEMIS‑101: Phase 1 study of REVSYBOO (B7‑H3 ADC) plus atezolizumab in pre‑treated non‑squamous NSCLC | Speaker: Dr. Runbo Zhong | Tumors: non‑small cell lung cancer | MOA: Tagretucumab (REVSYBOO) is a B7‑H3‑directed ADC delivering a tropomodulin‑1 TOP1 inhibitor via a protease‑cleavable linker (DAR 4); combined with atezolizumab, PD‑L1 blockade may enhance anti‑tumor immunity while the ADC induces DNA damage in B7‑H3‑positive tumor cells. | Findings: Confirmed ORR of 47.1% (n=34) with median PFS of 14 months in heavily pre‑treated NSCLC.; Efficacy observed across B7‑H3 expression levels and irrespective of prior immunotherapy exposure.; Grade 3+ TRAEs occurred in 70% of patients, predominantly hematologic; ILD was low‑grade and infrequent.; 12‑month PFS rate of 67.7% exceeds historical benchmarks for second‑line docetaxel or REVSYBOO monotherapy.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Runbo Zhong
metadata.talk_title: ARTEMIS‑101: Phase 1 study of REVSYBOO (B7‑H3 ADC) plus atezolizumab in pre‑treated non‑squamous NSCLC

text: Therapy‑induced mutagenesis underlying clonal hematopoiesis and second cancers in pediatric cancer survivors | Speaker: Yingwei Sun | Tumors: AML, Hodgkin lymphoma, breast cancer, meningioma, thyroid cancer | MOA: Sun's group used deep targeted sequencing and single‑cell mutational signature analysis to show that therapy‑related clonal hematopoiesis is accelerated in pediatric cancer survivors, with STAT3 hotspot mutations in Hodgkin lymphoma survivors linked to a SBS25 signature caused by procapsid exposure, and distinct cell‑type enrichment patterns (e.g., CD4/CD8 T cells). They also demonstrated elevated mutation burdens and therapy‑associated signatures (cisplatin, nitrogen mustard) in secondary neoplasms, linking specific chemotherapies to mutational signatures and structural alterations such as NF2 disruption in meningioma. | Findings: Accelerated clonal hematopoiesis observed in ~3000 pediatric cancer survivors versus controls.; Therapy‑related STAT3 hotspot mutations in Hodgkin lymphoma survivors are 3‑10‑fold enriched in CD4/CD8 T cells and show 100% confidence of SBS25 signature linkage to procapsid exposure.; DNMT3A mutations display cell‑type specific enrichment (monocytes vs double‑negative CD3+ T cells).; Secondary neoplasms (breast, meningioma, thyroid) exhibit elevated SNV/indel burdens and cisplatin‑related signatures, confirming long‑term mutagenic imprint of childhood therapy.; In vitro cyclophosphamide treatment of MCF10A cells increases mutation burden (~600 SNVs) and reproduces SBS5‑like flat signatures.

metadata.speaker: Yingwei Sun
metadata.talk_title: Therapy‑induced mutagenesis underlying clonal hematopoiesis and second cancers in pediatric cancer survivors

text: Liver‑specific platinum mutagenesis in children revealed by duplex (NanoSeq) sequencing | Speaker: Sam Benatti | Tumors: hepatoblastoma, liver cancer | MOA: Benatti's team applied duplex (NanoSeq) sequencing to normal pediatric liver tissue after platinum chemotherapy, uncovering a novel liver‑specific mutational signature distinct from canonical platinum signatures; this signature correlates with exposure, is absent in unexposed liver, and is detectable in recurrent hepatoblastoma tumors, indicating pervasive platinum‑induced mutagenesis and potential functional driver‑like mutations in normal liver cells. | Findings: Normal liver tissue from platinum‑treated children shows mutation burdens comparable to adult liver, far exceeding untreated pediatric liver.; A novel liver‑specific platinum mutational signature was identified, distinct from known SBS31/35 signatures.; The liver‑specific signature is present in all platinum‑exposed normal liver samples and in six recurrent hepatoblastoma tumors previously treated with cisplatin.; Cell‑line experiments confirm the signature appears in liver tumor cells exposed to cisplatin but not in breast cancer cells, indicating tissue specificity.; Approximately 1,500 coding variants with potential driver impact were detected in normal liver, most attributable to the novel signature.

metadata.speaker: Sam Benatti
metadata.talk_title: Liver‑specific platinum mutagenesis in children revealed by duplex (NanoSeq) sequencing

text: Single‑cell whole‑genome and transcriptome analysis of mutagenesis in hematopoietic stem cells of childhood cancer survivors | Speaker: Ruben van Boxtel | Tumors: AML | MOA: Van Boxtel's group combined primary‑template‑directed amplification (PTA) single‑cell whole‑genome sequencing with matched transcriptomics to quantify chemotherapy‑induced mutagenesis in hematopoietic stem cells; they identified platinum‑ and thiopurine‑specific signatures (SBS31/35, SBS87) in subsets of cells, showed that mutation burden rises after therapy but can regress over years, and linked differential expression of DNA‑repair and apoptotic pathways to cells bearing these signatures, suggesting treatment‑specific transcriptional programs modulate mutagenesis. | Findings: All examined ALL survivors show increased mutation burden post‑treatment (up to 3‑fold), driven by platinum and thiopurine signatures.; Thiopurine (SBS87) signature appears only in a subset of HSCs, whereas platinum signatures are more ubiquitous.; Mutation burden can decline over a decade, returning to baseline levels, suggesting selective loss or replacement of heavily mutated clones.; Differential expression analysis reveals enrichment of DNA‑repair, apoptosis, and autophagy pathways in cells with high thiopurine or clock‑like mutagenesis, without differences in cell‑cycle phase.; In vitro exposure of cord‑blood HSCs to mafosfamide (active cyclophosphamide) recapitulates a flat, clock‑like signature, confirming drug‑specific mutagenic patterns.

metadata.speaker: Ruben van Boxtel
metadata.talk_title: Single‑cell whole‑genome and transcriptome analysis of mutagenesis in hematopoietic stem cells of childhood cancer survivors

text: Aspirin paradox in colorectal cancer initiation versus metastasis | Speaker: Omer Yilmaz | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: Aspirin lowers tumor‑cell prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) by inhibiting PTGS1/2, which reduces metastatic seeding but paradoxically enhances outgrowth of established liver micrometastases via a hepatic stellate cell (HSC)–NK cell circuit; loss of tumor‑derived PGE2 expands NK‑mediated clearance, whereas aspirin‑mediated PGE2 depletion permits HSC‑driven NK suppression, promoting metastatic growth. | Findings: Genetic ablation of PTGS1/2 in AKP organoids reduced PGE2 and decreased number of liver metastases but increased size of each lesion.; Low‑dose aspirin recapitulated PTGS1/2 loss, lowering primary tumor PGE2 and enlarging liver metastatic lesions.; HPGD knockout (high PGE2) organoids produced fewer and smaller liver metastases; pharmacologic 15‑PGDH inhibition (SW033291) mirrored this effect.; Metastatic outgrowth advantage of PTGS‑deficient cells required an intact immune system; NK‑cell depletion abolished the size increase, implicating NK cells as mediators.; Depletion of hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) removed the anti‑metastatic effect of high PGE2, indicating HSC‑derived signals (e.g., CXCL12) modulate NK activity.

metadata.speaker: Omer Yilmaz
metadata.talk_title: Aspirin paradox in colorectal cancer initiation versus metastasis

text: Platelet activation as a biomarker for aspirin chemoprevention in cancer | Speaker: Ruth Langley | Tumors: colorectal cancer, gastroesophageal cancer, breast cancer, prostate cancer | MOA: Low‑dose aspirin irreversibly acetylates platelet COX‑1, suppressing thromboxane A2 production and platelet activation; reduced platelet‑derived pro‑tumor signals lower early adenoma formation and may enhance immune clearance of micrometastases. Urinary 11‑dehydro‑TXB2 (UTXM) reflects platelet activation and predicts aspirin benefit, especially in PIK3CA‑mutant colorectal cancers. | Findings: Platelet‑specific COX‑1 knockout mice crossed with ApcMin develop fewer and smaller adenomas, linking platelet COX‑1 to early carcinogenesis.; Urinary UTXM levels are elevated in adjuvant GI cancer patients at baseline and decrease with aspirin run‑in, rising again in placebo arm.; PIK3CA exon 9/20 mutations identify colorectal cancer patients who derive a ~50% disease‑free survival benefit from aspirin (ASCOT trial).; ADD‑ASPIRIN trial shows dose‑response suppression of UTXM with 100 mg and 300 mg aspirin, supporting biomarker‑guided dosing.

metadata.speaker: Ruth Langley
metadata.talk_title: Platelet activation as a biomarker for aspirin chemoprevention in cancer

text: Targeting COX‑2/PGE2 and PI3K pathways in colorectal cancer prevention | Speaker: Raymond DuBois | Tumors: colorectal cancer | MOA: COX‑2–derived PGE2 drives adenoma formation and immune evasion via EP4‑mediated PI3K‑AKT‑NF‑κB activation, up‑regulating PD‑1 on CD8 T cells and macrophages; celecoxib or EP4 antagonism reduces PGE2, lowers PD‑1 expression, expands effector T‑cell infiltrates, and synergizes with PI3K inhibition to suppress tumorigenesis. | Findings: Platelet‑specific COX‑1 knockout reduces adenoma number and size in ApcMin mice, linking platelet COX‑1 to early tumorigenesis.; Celecoxib (400‑1600 mg/day) markedly decreases adenoma burden in mouse models and in FAP patients, with ~80% response in a subset.; EP4 antagonist AE3208 mirrors celecoxib’s effect, confirming PGE2‑EP4 as the critical downstream axis.; PGE2 up‑regulates PD‑1 on CD8 T cells and macrophages; celecoxib treatment lowers PD‑1 and increases total T‑cell infiltrates in mouse adenomas.; PIK3CA mutations co‑occur with COX‑2 overexpression; aspirin/celecoxib improves DFS in PIK3CA‑mutant colorectal cancer (HR 0.5).

metadata.speaker: Raymond DuBois
metadata.talk_title: Targeting COX‑2/PGE2 and PI3K pathways in colorectal cancer prevention

text: Adoptive T cell immunotherapy strategies and preclinical findings | Speaker: Crystal Paulos | Tumors: melanoma, triple-negative breast cancer, pancreatic cancer, leukemia | MOA: Adoptive transfer of expanded tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) or genetically engineered T cells (TCR or CAR) provides large numbers of tumor-specific cytotoxic T cells that can directly kill cancer cells; CAR constructs redirect T cells to surface antigens such as CD19 or mesothelin, while TCR engineering targets intracellular antigens like NY-ESO-1. Preclinical data show that Th17-polarized CD4 T cells can synergize with endogenous CD8 responses to achieve durable tumor regression in the B16-F10 melanoma model. | Findings: TIL therapy achieved a 6‑month PFS of 52.7% versus ipilimumab in 84 relapsed patients (Phase II trial).; CD19 CAR T cells cleared CD19‑positive leukemia in bone marrow with durable remission observed >170 days post‑infusion.; Th17‑polarized CD4 T cells, when adoptively transferred into B16‑F10 melanoma‑bearing mice, produced superior tumor control compared with Th0, Th1, or Th9 subsets.; RNA‑seq of Th17‑treated tumors revealed up‑regulation of chemokines and antigen‑presentation pathways, suggesting recruitment of endogenous CD8 T cells.

metadata.speaker: Crystal Paulos
metadata.talk_title: Adoptive T cell immunotherapy strategies and preclinical findings

text: Clinical mechanisms of response and resistance to cancer immunotherapy | Speaker: Dmitry Zhamarin | MOA: Zhamarin described how tumor antigens are presented to T cells, leading to activation, proliferation, and tumor cell lysis, and outlined mechanisms of primary and adaptive resistance including loss of antigen presentation, interferon signaling suppression, and immune-excluded microenvironments. | Findings: Primary resistance is associated with tumors lacking T cell infiltration (cold tumors) due to absent antigen presentation or immunosuppressive microenvironment.; Adaptive resistance involves upregulation of PD-L1 driven by IFN‑γ from activated T cells, creating an exhausted T cell phenotype.; Proximity analysis of PD‑1+ T cells to PD‑L1+ cells within 30‑50 µm predicts response to checkpoint blockade in endometrial cancer.; Tumor mutational burden and MSI‑high status correlate with higher response rates to PD‑1 inhibitors, but ~30% of high‑TMB patients do not respond.

metadata.speaker: Dmitry Zhamarin
metadata.talk_title: Clinical mechanisms of response and resistance to cancer immunotherapy

text: Dual-compartment targeting GPNMB CAR T cells for glioblastoma | Speaker: Seela Singh | Tumors: glioblastoma | MOA: GPNMB is co‑expressed on glioma stem cells and immunosuppressive tumor‑associated macrophages; a GPNMB‑directed CAR T cell simultaneously eliminates both compartments, leading to complete tumor clearance in orthotopic GBM models and durable survival without skin toxicity. | Findings: GPNMB is up‑regulated in GBM and enriched on both glioma stem cells and M2‑like macrophages.; CRISPR knockout of GPNMB reduces proliferation of patient‑derived GSCs and shifts tumor cell states away from mesenchymal programs.; Intracranial delivery of 1 × 10⁶ GPNMB CAR T cells eradicated orthotopic GBM PDX tumors and cleared GPNMB‑positive macrophages.; In syngeneic GL261 mice, GPNMB CAR T induced complete remission without observable skin toxicity.

metadata.speaker: Seela Singh
metadata.talk_title: Dual-compartment targeting GPNMB CAR T cells for glioblastoma

text: Macrophage‑targeted conjugates (MAC‑TACs) for pan‑solid tumor therapy | Speaker: Faith Barnett | Tumors: sarcoma, gastric cancer, prostate cancer, triple‑negative breast cancer, brain metastasis, pancreatic cancer, melanoma, bladder cancer, squamous cell carcinoma | MOA: A small‑molecule‑antibody conjugate binds a TAM‑restricted surface receptor, is internalized, and releases a cleavable MMAE payload within the tumor microenvironment; the non‑dividing TAMs act as drug depots, delivering cytotoxic payload to neighboring cancer cells while sparing normal tissues. | Findings: RS5 (MMAE payload) achieved complete tumor regression in multiple subcutaneous solid‑tumor models, including doxorubicin‑resistant sarcoma PDX.; In intracranial glioblastoma models, RS5 extended median survival by ~79% without observable liver toxicity.; Dose escalation from 2 mg/kg to 10 mg/kg resulted in fibrotic tumor remnants with no viable cancer cells.; Weekly or bi‑weekly dosing maintained efficacy with stable body weight and normal hematology.

metadata.speaker: Faith Barnett
metadata.talk_title: Macrophage‑targeted conjugates (MAC‑TACs) for pan‑solid tumor therapy

text: Collagen‑binding anti‑CTLA‑4 antibodies for recurrent glioblastoma | Speaker: Lewis Barr | Tumors: glioblastoma, recurrent glioblastoma | MOA: A von Willebrand factor A3 collagen‑binding domain fused to anti‑CTLA‑4 directs the antibody to collagen‑rich regions of recurrent GBM, increasing intratumoral accumulation, depleting exhausted CD8⁺ T cells and reducing Tregs, thereby extending survival in mouse models. | Findings: Collagen I/III are among the top up‑regulated genes in recurrent GBM compared with primary tumor and normal brain.; CBD anti‑CTLA‑4 shows >5‑fold higher tumor accumulation than wild‑type anti‑CTLA‑4 with no brain accumulation.; In orthotopic GBM mice, CBD anti‑CTLA‑4 increased median survival by 140% and reduced tumor size by day 10.; Ex vivo GBM slice cultures treated with CBD ipilimumab showed significant reduction of intratumoral Tregs.

metadata.speaker: Lewis Barr
metadata.talk_title: Collagen‑binding anti‑CTLA‑4 antibodies for recurrent glioblastoma

text: DLL3‑CD2‑CD3 trispecific T‑cell engager with enhanced potency | Speaker: Suraj Kanchukal | Tumors: small cell lung cancer | MOA: A trispecific antibody simultaneously engages DLL3 on SCLC cells, CD3 for primary T‑cell activation, and CD2 for costimulatory signaling, resulting in enhanced T‑cell proliferation, survival, and cytotoxicity without antigen‑independent activation or T‑cell fratricide. | Findings: Trispecific TCE shows >100‑fold potency increase over tarlatamab in vitro across multiple donors.; Enhanced T‑cell proliferation and survival observed at sub‑nanomolar concentrations.; In vivo, 5/7 mice achieved complete tumor eradication versus 2/6 with tarlatamab.; No T‑cell bridging or fratricide detected; activation is antigen‑dependent.

metadata.speaker: Suraj Kanchukal
metadata.talk_title: DLL3‑CD2‑CD3 trispecific T‑cell engager with enhanced potency

text: CBP/P300 bromodomain inhibition synergizes with PARP inhibition in prostate cancer | Speaker: Orly Richter | Tumors: prostate cancer, castration‑resistant prostate cancer | MOA: CBP/P300 bromodomain inhibition down‑regulates homologous recombination and other DNA‑repair pathways, sensitizing CRPC cells to PARP inhibition; combined treatment forces reliance on error‑prone repair, leading to synergistic loss of viability. | Findings: CBP/P300 are amplified in metastatic CRPC and correlate with poor survival.; CCS1477 suppresses DDR gene expression, especially HR genes, in CRPC cell lines.; Synergy observed between CCS1477 and all four FDA‑approved PARP inhibitors across multiple prostate cancer lines.; In patient‑derived explants, the combination reduced Ki‑67 positivity more than either agent alone in responsive samples.

metadata.speaker: Orly Richter
metadata.talk_title: CBP/P300 bromodomain inhibition synergizes with PARP inhibition in prostate cancer

text: 3D bioprinted cancer models for drug screening | Speaker: Aurelie Cadoe | Tumors: breast cancer, ovarian cancer | MOA: Layer‑by‑layer extrusion of cell‑laden bioink creates reproducible 3D tumor constructs that recapitulate in vivo gene expression and drug penetration kinetics, enabling more predictive assessment of chemotherapeutics and ADCs compared with 2D cultures. | Findings: 3D bioprinted models cluster transcriptionally with in vivo tumors, unlike 2D cultures.; IC₅₀ values for Taxol and TDM‑1 are higher in 3D models, reflecting reduced drug penetration.; Co‑culture with fibroblasts or adipocytes further decreases drug sensitivity.; Intratumoral paclitaxel concentrations in 3D models peak at ~8 h, mirroring mouse plasma kinetics.

metadata.speaker: Aurelie Cadoe
metadata.talk_title: 3D bioprinted cancer models for drug screening

text: Lysosomal enzyme legumain drives liver metastasis in pancreatic cancer | Speaker: Rishika Perera | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma | MOA: Loss of the lysosomal asparaginyl endopeptidase legumain impairs maturation of cathepsin L, leading to enlarged lysosomes and secretion of immature cathepsin L, which remodels extracellular collagen and disrupts the metastatic niche; this creates a selective dependency for legumain in liver metastases but not in primary pancreatic tumors. | Findings: Legumain protein is highly enriched in lysosomes of liver metastatic PDAC tumors compared with primary pancreas tumors (proteomics of LysoIP samples).; CRISPR‑mediated knockout of legumain does not affect orthotopic pancreatic tumor growth (tumor weight unchanged) but reduces liver metastatic tumor weight by >70% (n=8 per group).; Legumain loss causes enlarged lysosomal vesicles and accumulation of the pro‑form of cathepsin L, indicating defective cathepsin maturation.; Legumain‑deficient cells secrete increased single‑chain cathepsin L; this secretion is blocked by cathepsin inhibitor E64d.; In vitro collagen degradation assays show >50% reduction of fluorescent collagen area in legumain‑KO cultures by day 7, rescued by E64d.

metadata.speaker: Rishika Perera
metadata.talk_title: Lysosomal enzyme legumain drives liver metastasis in pancreatic cancer

text: Stromal taurine production and SLC66A6 uptake drive AML progression and venetoclax resistance | Speaker: Jovisha Bajaj | Tumors: AML | MOA: Osteolineage stromal cells up‑regulate CDO1, producing taurine that is secreted into the bone‑marrow plasma; AML blasts import taurine via the SLC66A6 transporter, which activates mTOR signaling and sustains glycolysis, promoting proliferation and venetoclax resistance; genetic or pharmacologic inhibition of CDO1 or SLC66A6 impairs AML growth while sparing normal CD34+ cells. | Findings: CDO1 expression is induced in osteolineage cells during AML progression and is detectable in patient bone‑marrow biopsies (IHC, n=24).; MSC‑specific CDO1 deletion (Prx1‑Cre; CDO1^fl/fl) prolongs median survival of AML‑bearing mice from 22 to 38 days (p=0.004, n=10 per group).; SLC66A6 knockdown in primary AML blasts reduces in vivo engraftment in NSG mice by >80% (n=6), with no impact on normal CD34+ hematopoietic progenitors.; High SLC66A6 expression in patient cohorts associates with venetoclax‑resistant disease (HR 2.1, 95% CI 1.4‑3.2).; Experimental SLC66A6 inhibitors synergize with venetoclax in vitro (Combination Index <0.7) and restore sensitivity in resistant AML cell lines.

metadata.speaker: Jovisha Bajaj
metadata.talk_title: Stromal taurine production and SLC66A6 uptake drive AML progression and venetoclax resistance

text: Aging‑driven fibroblast secretomes awaken dormant melanoma metastases | Speaker: Ashy (last name not provided) | Tumors: melanoma | MOA: Aging remodels fibroblast secretomes; aged lung fibroblasts up‑regulate SFRP1, which acts as a ‘prince’s kiss’ to trigger dormant melanoma cells to exit dormancy and proliferate in the liver and lung; loss of SFRP1 signaling via neutralizing antibody blocks outgrowth of dormant cells; in the brain, aged microenvironment with leaky vasculature permits rapid melanoma invasion independent of SFRP1, while WNT5A signaling governs perivascular dormancy versus outgrowth. | Findings: Primary melanoma tumors grow slower in aged mice but generate significantly more lung metastases (median metastatic nodules: 45 vs 12, p<0.001).; RNA‑seq of aged lung fibroblasts reveals >3‑fold up‑regulation of SFRP1 compared with young fibroblasts.; Neutralizing anti‑SFRP1 antibody administered after dissemination reduces outgrowth of dormant lung metastases in aged mice by 68% (n=8, p=0.002).; Aged tumor‑bearing lung fibroblasts become more motile, display reduced senescence markers (p16^INK4a), and secrete CXCL1 that recruits MDSCs; MDSC infiltration is 2.5‑fold higher in aged lungs (IHC, n=5).; Brain slice assays show melanoma cells invade aged brain tissue 3‑fold faster than young slices; invasion is independent of SFRP1 but correlates with vascular leakage.

metadata.speaker: Ashy (last name not provided)
metadata.talk_title: Aging‑driven fibroblast secretomes awaken dormant melanoma metastases

text: Advances in KRAS-targeted therapies for pancreatic cancer | Speaker: Shubham Pant | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma | MOA: KRAS inhibitors that bind either the inactive (adagrasib) or active (deraxone rasip) conformations block downstream MAPK signaling, yielding response rates of 30-60% in KRAS-mutant pancreatic cancer; resistance is frequently driven by KRAS amplification, prompting combination strategies with chemotherapy and next‑generation KRAS degraders. | Findings: Adagrasib achieved a 33% ORR in KRAS G12C PDAC (21 pts) versus historical 10‑15% second‑line chemotherapy response.; Deraxone rasip (RAS‑on inhibitor) showed a 36% ORR and median PFS 8.8 months in early‑phase PDAC patients.; Duraxon rasib combined with gem/nab‑paclitaxel yielded a 60% ORR and a hazard ratio of 0.4 for OS in the phase III Resolute 302 trial.; KRAS G12D inhibitors (zoldonrasib, setigrasib, INCB734) demonstrated ~30‑37% ORR with manageable grade 1‑2 toxicities.; KRAS amplification emerged as the most common resistance mechanism, informing ongoing combination studies.

metadata.speaker: Shubham Pant
metadata.talk_title: Advances in KRAS-targeted therapies for pancreatic cancer

text: Cryptic non‑canonical antigens as shared targets in pancreatic cancer | Speaker: Wilfried Pastor | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma | MOA: Mass‑spectrometry immunopeptidomics revealed hundreds of cancer‑restricted non‑canonical ORF‑derived peptides in PDAC; ex‑vivo priming identified immunogenic cryptic antigens, and TCR‑engineered T cells specific for these antigens demonstrated potent cytotoxicity against patient‑derived organoids and xenografts, establishing a shared off‑the‑shelf target class. | Findings: Detected 8,000‑18,000 unique HLA‑I peptides per PDAC sample, including tens‑to‑hundreds of non‑canonical ORF peptides.; ~35% of cryptic peptides showed no evidence of translation in >200 normal tissues, defining cancer‑restricted antigens.; ~50% of cancer‑restricted cryptic antigens were shared by ≥2 HLA‑A*02:01+ patients, some across >70% of such patients.; ~25% of tested cryptic peptides elicited CD8+ T‑cell responses in ex‑vivo priming assays, comparable to mutation‑derived neoantigens.; TCR‑engineered T cells targeting cryptic antigens mediated robust killing of PDAC organoids and delayed tumor growth in mouse models.

metadata.speaker: Wilfried Pastor
metadata.talk_title: Cryptic non‑canonical antigens as shared targets in pancreatic cancer

text: Functional role of CA19‑9 in pancreatic tumor microenvironment and therapeutic interception | Speaker: Dani Engel | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma | MOA: CA19‑9 glycosylation of secreted fibulin‑3 enhances its binding to EGFR, driving IL‑1α and TGF‑β production that expands antigen‑presenting CAFs and Tregs, suppressing CD8+ T‑cell infiltration; blockade of CA19‑9 with the 5B1 antibody or knockdown of fibulin‑3 reduces this immunosuppressive cascade and restores anti‑tumor immunity. | Findings: Inducible CA19‑9 expression in KRAS^G12D mice accelerates PanIN progression and reduces survival to a degree comparable to p53 loss.; Three‑day CA19‑9 exposure expands fibroblasts and drives IL‑1α/TGF‑β production, promoting antigen‑presenting CAF differentiation.; Fibulin‑3 is a CA19‑9‑modified protein that binds EGFR; its knockdown abolishes IL‑1α/TGF‑β up‑regulation and tumor growth.; 5B1 anti‑CA19‑9 antibody reduces apCAF frequency, Treg infiltration, and collagen deposition, while increasing CD8+ T‑cell infiltration in vivo.; In a phase I/II trial, 5B1 monotherapy yielded 20% stable disease and 27% partial response when combined with chemotherapy.

metadata.speaker: Dani Engel
metadata.talk_title: Functional role of CA19‑9 in pancreatic tumor microenvironment and therapeutic interception

text: Forcing inflammation to initiate malignancy and drive tumor progression | Speaker: Valerie Weaver | Tumors: breast cancer, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, prostate cancer | MOA: Weaver demonstrated that increased matrix stiffness drives chronic inflammation via phospho‑STAT3 activation in myeloid cells, leading to elevated lipid peroxidation and accumulation of aldehyde‑derived DNA damage. Genetic or pharmacologic reduction of LOX or GPX4 lowers fibrosis, diminishes ROS‑derived aldehydes, and reduces DNA double‑strand breaks and metastatic burden in mouse models, linking mechanotransduction to mutational load and tumor progression. | Findings: High fibrosis scores in breast tissue correlate with increased tumor mutational burden and DNA double‑strand breaks.; LOX conditional knockout or antibody blockade reduces collagen cross‑linking, tissue stiffness, and metastatic incidence in polyoma mouse models.; Stiff matrices elevate phospho‑STAT3 and pro‑tumor myeloid infiltration, which drives lipid peroxidation and aldehyde‑mediated DNA damage.; GPX4 loss in myeloid cells amplifies lipid aldehyde accumulation and DNA damage even in soft environments, promoting metastasis.; In prophylactic BRCA1/2 high‑density breast tissues, regions of greatest stiffness show heightened oxidative DNA lesions despite absence of overt tumor.

metadata.speaker: Valerie Weaver
metadata.talk_title: Forcing inflammation to initiate malignancy and drive tumor progression

text: Stiffness‑induced copy number variation across pan‑cancer | Speaker: Dennis Discher | Tumors: pan-cancer | MOA: Discher showed that increasing extracellular matrix stiffness elevates heritable chromosome loss rates by mechanically constraining mitotic rounding, leading to spindle compression, prolonged mitosis, and micronucleus formation.
