This mechanotransduction‑driven mitotic error produces copy‑number losses (and later gains) that scale with collagen‑I‑driven tissue stiffness across multiple cancer types. | Findings: Across TCGA, tumor collagen I transcript levels strongly correlate with total copy‑number variation burden.; In 3D spheroids, mutation (chromosome loss) rate per division increases ~10‑fold when stiffness rises from 0 to 30 kPa.; Stiff agarose gels suppress proliferation but increase per‑division mutation frequency, yielding a super‑Poisson variance pattern.; Myosin II knockdown exacerbates mutation rates in stiff environments, implicating contractile rounding forces in genome stability.; Micronuclei frequency is higher in stiff spheroids and in the cores of tumors, linking mechanical confinement to missegregation.

metadata.speaker: Dennis Discher
metadata.talk_title: Stiffness‑induced copy number variation across pan‑cancer

text: Spatial ecosystem analysis reveals mechanobiology‑driven relapse niches in breast cancer | Speaker: Christina Curtis | Tumors: breast cancer | MOA: Curtis integrated multi‑modal spatial data (MIBI proteomics, CosMX transcriptomics, AFM‑derived stiffness maps, and glycomics) to define a tumor‑dense niche (niche zero) where cancer cells co‑localize with perivascular‑like cells and fibroblasts within a stiff, collagen‑rich microenvironment. This spatial ecosystem predicts poor long‑term outcomes independent of genomic risk classifiers, suggesting that mechanobiology‑driven ECM remodeling creates vascular niches that bypass VEGF signaling and foster relapse. | Findings: Spatial niche zero (high cancer cell density) is a strong independent predictor of 20‑year relapse in ER+ HER2‑ breast cancer.; Perivascular‑like cells and fibroblasts co‑localize within niche zero, forming collagen‑rich vascular niches associated with relapse.; Stiffness measured by AFM‑CNN correlates with niche zero prevalence and doubles relapse risk in the top 20% stiffness group.; Integrative analysis shows that genomic high‑risk subtypes (focal CN amplifications) acquire distinct microenvironmental signatures, refining risk stratification.; Spatial glycomics reveals enrichment of COL6A1, COL3A1, COL1A2 in tumor‑dense regions, linking specific collagen isoforms to aggressive niches.

metadata.speaker: Christina Curtis
metadata.talk_title: Spatial ecosystem analysis reveals mechanobiology‑driven relapse niches in breast cancer

text: Historical context and biological implications of extrachromosomal DNA in cancer | Speaker: Paul Michiel | Tumors: glioblastoma, NSCLC, esophageal adenocarcinoma, lung squamous cell carcinoma, pan-cancer | MOA: Michiel described how extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA) forms via double-strand breaks or chromothripsis, lacks centromeres leading to random segregation, creates high copy-number heterogeneity, and drives rapid oncogene amplification, transcriptional hyperactivity, and therapeutic resistance. | Findings: ecDNA particles are large (1–5 Mb), chromatinized but highly accessible, and absent in normal tissues.; ecDNA amplifies oncogenes (e.g., EGFR, MYC) leading to rapid copy-number changes upon drug treatment and withdrawal.; ecDNA formation is linked to p53 loss and can arise during high-grade dysplasia, predicting progression to invasive cancer.

metadata.speaker: Paul Michiel
metadata.talk_title: Historical context and biological implications of extrachromosomal DNA in cancer

text: Computational tools for ecDNA detection and structural reconstruction | Speaker: Vineet Bafna | Tumors: pan-cancer | MOA: Bafna presented AmpliconSuite, a graph‑based pipeline that parses whole‑genome sequencing to identify focal high‑copy amplifications, classify them as ecDNA cycles, breakage‑fusion‑bridge events, or linear amplicons, and reconstruct possible ecDNA structures using long‑read and short‑read data. | Findings: AmpliconSuite has processed >60,000 WGS samples, providing first‑level ecDNA classification.; In lung cancer cohorts, ~20% of patients harbor computationally confident ecDNA, matching prior pan‑cancer estimates.; Long‑read data resolve ambiguous cycles, enabling validation of complex ecDNA structures (e.g., PC3DM, Polo3.20).; Experimental CRISPR‑Cas cuts and multi‑FISH confirm predicted ecDNA structures in cell lines.

metadata.speaker: Vineet Bafna
metadata.talk_title: Computational tools for ecDNA detection and structural reconstruction

text: Longitudinal whole‑genome analysis of ecDNA in TRACERx lung cancer cohort | Speaker: Myall‑Ghanayem | Tumors: NSCLC | MOA: Ghanayem showed that ecDNA, identified via AmpliconArchitect in longitudinal whole‑genome data, is frequently truncal in NSCLC, often harbors oncogenes (e.g., ERBB2) or immune‑modulatory genes, correlates with aggressive clinical phenotypes, rapid metastatic growth, and resistance to EGFR‑TKI therapy. | Findings: ~20% of early‑stage NSCLC tumors contain ecDNA; prevalence rises to ~30% in metastatic lesions.; ecDNA is predominantly truncal, present across all sampled regions, and usually carries at least one oncogene.; Patients with ecDNA have worse overall survival, higher rates of extra‑thoracic metastasis, and faster lesion growth on imaging.; In a case of EGFR‑mutant NSCLC, ERBB2 ecDNA emerged at progression and was present in all resistant metastases, suggesting a role in TKI resistance.; Unichromosomal ecDNA dominate, but multi‑chromosomal ecDNA also occur, often co‑amplifying immune‑related genes.

metadata.speaker: Myall‑Ghanayem
metadata.talk_title: Longitudinal whole‑genome analysis of ecDNA in TRACERx lung cancer cohort

text: GV20-0251 anti-IGSF8 antibody phase 1/2 study in melanoma | Speaker: Dr. Memi | Tumors: melanoma | MOA: GV20-0251 is an IgG4 anti-IGSF8 antibody that blocks IGSF8, enhancing NK cell cytotoxicity and dendritic cell antigen presentation, leading to tumor regression especially in IGSF8-high, PD-L1-negative melanoma. | Findings: GV20-0251 monotherapy yielded an ORR of 33.3% and DCR of 77.8% in primary ICI‑resistant melanoma (n=9).; Responses were observed in patients with high tumor IGSF8 expression and low PD‑L1.; The antibody showed a favorable safety profile with no dose‑limiting toxicities and a 26‑day half‑life.; Pharmacodynamics demonstrated full target occupancy on circulating T cells at >3 mg/kg and increased intratumoral NK and CD8 T‑cell infiltration.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Memi
metadata.talk_title: GV20-0251 anti-IGSF8 antibody phase 1/2 study in melanoma

text: First-in-human Phase 1 study of PLN101-095 dual integrin inhibitor with pembrolizumab | Speaker: Dr. Timothy Yap | Tumors: non-small cell lung cancer, cholangiocarcinoma, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, renal cell carcinoma | MOA: PLN101-095 blocks integrin αVβ8/αVβ1, preventing local activation of TGF‑β in the tumor microenvironment, thereby reducing immunosuppression and enhancing IFN‑γ–driven anti‑tumor immunity, especially when combined with pembrolizumab. | Findings: Overall ORR was 19% (4/16) with disease control rate of 56% in the dose‑escalation cohort.; In patients with secondary ICI resistance, ORR increased to 30% and DCR to 60%.; Responses included a complete response in cholangiocarcinoma and partial responses in NSCLC and melanoma.; Pharmacodynamics showed dose‑proportional exposure and >24‑hour IC75 coverage at ≥1000 mg BID.; Elevated plasma IFN‑γ and PD‑L1 after 14 days correlated with clinical responses.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Timothy Yap
metadata.talk_title: First-in-human Phase 1 study of PLN101-095 dual integrin inhibitor with pembrolizumab
tumor_types: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma

text: Phase I study of AMG 355 anti‑CCR8 antibody alone and with pembrolizumab | Speaker: Dr. Marwan Fakhry | Tumors: melanoma, gastric cancer, colorectal cancer | MOA: AMG 355 is an afucosylated IgG1 anti‑CCR8 antibody engineered for enhanced FcγRIIIa binding, depleting CCR8‑positive intratumoral Tregs via ADCC, thereby reducing immunosuppression. | Findings: AMG 355 monotherapy yielded a single partial response (melanoma) and limited activity overall.; Combination with pembrolizumab produced one complete response (gastric) and modest disease control (33%).; Pharmacodynamic analyses showed robust CCR8+ cell depletion in tumor biopsies across dose levels.; Safety profile was favorable with ≤5% grade 3 toxicities; infusion reactions were common but mild.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Marwan Fakhry
metadata.talk_title: Phase I study of AMG 355 anti‑CCR8 antibody alone and with pembrolizumab

text: Safety of prolonged atezolizumab exposure in alveolar soft part sarcoma | Speaker: Dr. Alice Chen | Tumors: alveolar soft part sarcoma | MOA: Atezolizumab, an anti‑PD‑L1 antibody, provides durable checkpoint inhibition in ASPS, with long‑term treatment (>2 years) showing low incidence of new grade 2‑3 immune‑related adverse events. | Findings: Extended atezolizumab treatment (>2 years) was feasible with only 3 of 17 patients developing new grade 2‑3 toxicities.; No grade 4‑5 immune‑related events were observed after prolonged exposure.; Median treatment duration reached 124 cycles in the longest‑treated patient.; Overall response rate remained at 37% consistent with earlier reports.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Alice Chen
metadata.talk_title: Safety of prolonged atezolizumab exposure in alveolar soft part sarcoma

text: Phase I study of DKY709 IKZF2 degrader alone and with PDR001 | Speaker: Dr. Giralda | Tumors: non-small cell lung cancer, melanoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma | MOA: DKY709 is a cereblon‑recruiting molecular glue that selectively degrades IKZF2 (Helios) in regulatory T cells, reducing their suppressive function and enhancing effector T‑cell activity; combined with PD‑1 blockade (PDR001) to further potentiate anti‑tumor immunity. | Findings: Robust IKZF2 degradation (>90%) observed in peripheral Tregs at doses ≥6 mg.; Monotherapy yielded 2 confirmed PRs and 1 CR in melanoma; combination added 3 PRs across tumor types.; Peripheral neuropathy was dose‑dependent, occurring mainly >10 mg but reversible with dose adjustments.; Recommended Phase 2 dose established at 6 mg QD for both monotherapy and combination.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Giralda
metadata.talk_title: Phase I study of DKY709 IKZF2 degrader alone and with PDR001

text: Phase 2 trial of tislelizumab with anti‑TIM‑3 and anti‑LAG‑3 in recurrent/metastatic HNSCC | Speaker: Dr. Hyeryoun Kim | Tumors: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma | MOA: Tislelizumab blocks PD‑1, while cirgelicimab and LBA‑007 inhibit TIM‑3 and LAG‑3 respectively, aiming to overcome adaptive resistance by targeting multiple immune checkpoints in HNSCC. | Findings: Overall ORR was similar across all arms (25‑27.5%).; Complete responses were observed only in LAG‑3‑containing arms (3 CRs).; In PD‑L1 low (CPS 1‑19) subgroup, combination arms showed numerically longer median PFS (5.4 mo) than monotherapy (1.4 mo).; Safety was comparable; most AEs were grade 1‑2 with no additive toxicity in combinations.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Hyeryoun Kim
metadata.talk_title: Phase 2 trial of tislelizumab with anti‑TIM‑3 and anti‑LAG‑3 in recurrent/metastatic HNSCC
tumor_types: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma

text: 10‑year survival and cfDNA methylation in melanoma brain metastases treated with ipilimumab + nivolumab | Speaker: Dr. Di Giacomo | Tumors: melanoma | MOA: Combined CTLA‑4 and PD‑1 blockade synergistically activates T‑cells, leading to durable intracranial and systemic responses in melanoma brain metastases; cfDNA tumor fraction and methylation scores serve as surrogate biomarkers of long‑term survival. | Findings: 10‑year OS was 32% with ipilimumab + nivolumab versus 30% with fuio‑mustine and 7% with ipilimumab + fuio‑mustine.; Melanoma‑specific 10‑yr OS reached 36% in the combination arm.; Low baseline tumor fraction and t‑methylation scores predicted superior survival.; Decreases in TF and t‑methylation at week 12 correlated with longer overall survival.

metadata.speaker: Dr. Di Giacomo
metadata.talk_title: 10‑year survival and cfDNA methylation in melanoma brain metastases treated with ipilimumab + nivolumab

text: Digital Tissue Twins: AI‑Powered Prediction of Single‑Cell Spatial Omics from H&E Slides | Speaker: Mingyao Li | Tumors: lung adenocarcinoma, pan-cancer | MOA: Li's group developed AI models (iSTAR, iSCALE, AURORA) that learn the relationship between H&E morphology and spatial gene expression, using bulk RNA‑seq as a dynamic‑range constraint to predict single‑cell resolution transcriptomic maps and cell‑type annotations across whole‑slide images. | Findings: AURORA achieved the highest Pearson correlation and lowest false‑positive rate among competing methods when predicting gene expression on held‑out LUAD samples (5 patients).; Virtual prediction of 4,000 TCGA LUAD slides reproduced known tumor pathology patterns (e.g., KRT8 expression).; Mature TLS area quantified by AURORA correlated with improved patient survival in TCGA LUAD.; Higher tumor‑TLS co‑localization was associated with better cancer survival.; Spatial cuff structures identified by AURORA predicted poorer survival, recapitulating findings from Wang et al. Cancer Cell.

metadata.speaker: Mingyao Li
metadata.talk_title: Digital Tissue Twins: AI‑Powered Prediction of Single‑Cell Spatial Omics from H&E Slides

text: Rosie: Generative AI for In‑Silico Spatial Proteomics from H&E Slides | Speaker: James Zou | Tumors: pan-cancer | MOA: Rosie trains a hierarchical deep‑learning model on paired H&E and CODEX images to impute multiplex protein expression at 8 µm resolution, enabling rapid, low‑cost generation of in‑silico spatial proteomics maps. | Findings: Rosie generates in‑silico CODEX images for up to 50 protein markers in minutes for <$1 cost, matching key structures seen in experimental CODEX.; Performance across external validation sites remained robust, with Pearson correlations ranging from high (99th percentile) to moderate (25th percentile).; Imputed proteomic maps enable accurate segmentation of tissue structures (stroma, tumor epithelium, endothelium) comparable to ground‑truth CODEX.

metadata.speaker: James Zou
metadata.talk_title: Rosie: Generative AI for In‑Silico Spatial Proteomics from H&E Slides

text: Virtual Biotech and AI‑Driven Spatial Omics for Therapeutic Strategy Design | Speaker: Unnamed Session Chair | Tumors: lung cancer, pan-cancer | MOA: The virtual biotech platform uses AI agents to integrate multi‑omic and clinical data, identifying CD276 (B7H3) as a fibroblast‑derived immune checkpoint; agents propose an ADC (CD276‑DXd) strategy, later validated by an FDA breakthrough designation for a similar ADC. | Findings: AI agents identified CD276 highly expressed in tumor‑associated fibroblasts in lung cancer.; Spatial analysis showed CD276‑high fibroblast neighborhoods depleted of immune cells.; High CD276 expression correlated with poorer overall and disease‑specific survival.; Agents independently designed a CD276‑DXd ADC strategy, later mirrored by Merck's FDA‑breakthrough ADC.

metadata.speaker: Unnamed Session Chair
metadata.talk_title: Virtual Biotech and AI‑Driven Spatial Omics for Therapeutic Strategy Design

text: Multiplexed functional assay of BRCA2 missense variants in HAP1 cells | Speaker: Faris | Tumors: breast cancer, ovarian cancer | MOA: A multiplexed assay of variant effects (MAVE) was performed in haploid HAP1 cells where BRCA2 missense variants were introduced at the endogenous locus; cells were cultured and viability ratios (day 5 vs day 14) were sequenced to generate functional scores that distinguish loss‑of‑function (pathogenic strong) from benign variants, enabling calibration to ACMG classification and risk association. | Findings: 502 missense variants (≈10‑11% of all missense) were classified as pathogenic strong, far exceeding the 30‑50 pathogenic missense in ClinVar.; Sensitivity and specificity of the BRCA2 MAVE against known standards were 93‑95% across multiple metrics.; Integration of functional scores with ACMG criteria reduced VUS from ~7,000 to 608 variants (≈90% reclassification).; Combined analysis of two independent BRCA2 MAVEs (HAP1 and mouse ESC) using an integrated VarCall model captured ~95% of variants and further reduced VUS to 396.; Case‑control analysis of pathogenic‑strong missense variants yielded an odds ratio of 4.5 for breast/ovarian cancer risk, comparable to truncating mutations (OR ~5.5).

metadata.speaker: Faris
metadata.talk_title: Multiplexed functional assay of BRCA2 missense variants in HAP1 cells

text: Saturation MAVE of Lynch syndrome mismatch‑repair genes and clinical risk integration | Speaker: Jacob Kitzman | Tumors: colorectal cancer, endometrial cancer | MOA: Saturation MAVE libraries covering >73,000 missense variants across the four Lynch‑syndrome mismatch‑repair genes were introduced into haploid cells; 6‑thioguanine treatment selects for loss‑of‑function variants, and deep sequencing quantifies variant depletion, producing functional scores that correlate with clinical pathogenicity and cancer risk. | Findings: Generated functional maps for >73,000 missense variants across MSH2, MLH1, MSH6, and PMS2.; Proline substitution patterns validated assay performance, showing expected loss‑of‑function in ordered protein regions.; 47 of 48 clinically classified missense variants (independent of functional evidence) were concordant with MAVE results, providing strong evidence for assay reliability.; Retrospective reclassification of 10 individuals in Ambry Genetics database as Lynch syndrome carriers based on MAVE data.; Population‑scale analysis linked loss‑of‑function missense scores to increased colorectal cancer risk, recapitulating known penetrance differences (high for MLH1/MSH2, lower for MSH6/PMS2).

metadata.speaker: Jacob Kitzman
metadata.talk_title: Saturation MAVE of Lynch syndrome mismatch‑repair genes and clinical risk integration

text: Inducing viral mimicry to turn cold small cell lung cancer hot via DHX9, TREX1 and spliceosome inhibition | Speaker: Israel Cañadas | Tumors: small cell lung cancer | MOA: Inhibition or genetic loss of DHX9, TREX1, or spliceosome components leads to accumulation of dsRNA, DNA‑RNA hybrids and crRNA, activating MDA5/MAVS and cGAS‑STING pathways, inducing type I interferon, cytokine production and necroptosis, which remodels the tumor microenvironment, increases CD8+ T‑cell infiltration and sensitizes small cell lung cancer to anti‑PD‑1 therapy. | Findings: DHX9 knockdown in small cell lung cancer cells increases dsRNA and DNA‑RNA hybrids, activating STING and MDA5 pathways.; DHX9 loss reduces tumor growth and enhances CD8+ T‑cell infiltration in immunocompetent mice.; Combination of DHX9 knockdown with anti‑PD‑1 dramatically improves tumor control and survival versus anti‑PD‑1 alone.; Spliceosome inhibition (Pladienolide B) induces crRNA accumulation, ZBP1‑dependent necroptosis, and tumor regression.; Spliceosome inhibitor plus anti‑PD‑1 shows synergistic tumor suppression; effect is lost in CBP1‑deficient mice.

metadata.speaker: Israel Cañadas
metadata.talk_title: Inducing viral mimicry to turn cold small cell lung cancer hot via DHX9, TREX1 and spliceosome inhibition

text: Epigenetic regulation of viral mimicry and its impact on immunotherapy response | Speaker: Catherine Chapinelli | Tumors: melanoma, ovarian cancer, NKT cell lymphoma, high-grade serous ovarian cancer | MOA: DNMT and HDAC inhibition demethylates and opens chromatin, reactivating transposable element transcription that forms dsRNA or DNA‑RNA hybrids, which are sensed by MDA5/MAVS and cGAS‑STING pathways, driving type I interferon signaling, upregulating antigen presentation and PD‑L1, and reshaping the tumor microenvironment to enhance checkpoint blockade efficacy; ADAR1 editing dampens this response, and TP53 status modulates TE expression and drug responsiveness. | Findings: DNMT inhibitors reactivate endogenous retroviruses, generating dsRNA that triggers innate immunity.; Combining DNMTi with HDACi amplifies TE transcription and interferon responses.; ADAR1 knockdown synergizes with DNMTi to improve survival and shift macrophage polarization in ovarian cancer models.; Wild‑type TP53 binds to LTRs and enhances TE transcription upon DNMTi; TP53 loss reduces DNA methylation globally, increasing TE expression.; TP53‑null cells show the strongest interferon response to DNMTi, whereas R175H mutants are less responsive.

metadata.speaker: Catherine Chapinelli
metadata.talk_title: Epigenetic regulation of viral mimicry and its impact on immunotherapy response

text: Viral mimicry enhances cancer vaccine efficacy via interferon‑dependent tumor remodeling | Speaker: Nicolas Verret | Tumors: melanoma, colon carcinoma, lymphoma, MC38 colon cancer | MOA: Azacitidine demethylates tumor DNA, reactivating transposable elements that generate dsRNA and DNA‑RNA hybrids, activating MDA5/MAVS and cGAS‑STING pathways, leading to type I interferon production, upregulation of MHC‑I and PD‑L1, and remodeling of myeloid populations; this creates a permissive microenvironment for vaccine‑elicited T cells to infiltrate, expand, and mediate tumor control, an effect lost when MAVS or STING are knocked out in tumor cells. | Findings: Azacitidine strongly induces transposable element transcription and a type I interferon response in B16 melanoma, dependent on MAVS and STING.; Vaccination alone fails therapeutically, but combined with azacitidine leads to tumor control and improved survival across multiple tumor models.; The combination increases tumor cell MHC‑I expression and expands vaccine‑specific CD8+ T‑cell clones within the TME.; MAVS/STING knockout tumors do not respond to the combination, confirming the necessity of tumor‑intrinsic viral mimicry.; Single‑cell analysis reveals increased cDC1 dendritic cells and reduced immunosuppressive Arg1+ macrophages only when viral mimicry is intact.

metadata.speaker: Nicolas Verret
metadata.talk_title: Viral mimicry enhances cancer vaccine efficacy via interferon‑dependent tumor remodeling

text: Clinical advances and patient experiences with KRAS inhibitors | Speaker: Ignacio Garrido Laguna | Tumors: pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, colorectal cancer, non-small cell lung cancer, gastroesophageal cancer, cholangiocarcinoma | MOA: KRAS inhibitors bind either the GDP‑bound or GTP‑bound conformations of mutant KRAS, blocking downstream MAPK signaling and inducing tumor regression. Pan‑KRAS agents target multiple KRAS alleles, while allele‑specific inhibitors (e.g., QTX‑3034) selectively inhibit G12D. Tricomplex inhibitors form a ternary complex with KRAS and an adaptor, achieving potent inhibition across alleles. Early clinical data show high response and disease‑control rates in KRAS‑driven pancreatic, colorectal, and gastro‑esophageal cancers. | Findings: A patient with metastatic KRAS‑mutant pancreatic cancer achieved a complete response after enrollment in the FMC6236 first‑in‑human study (Nov 2022) and remains in remission.; Early‑phase KRAS inhibitor trials report overall response rates around 30% and disease‑control rates of 80‑90% in pancreatic cancer, markedly exceeding historical chemotherapy control rates.; Pan‑KRAS inhibitors show activity in KRAS‑amplified gastro‑esophageal cancers but face pharmacokinetic challenges and limited efficacy against GTP‑bound KRAS.; Allele‑specific G12D inhibitor QTX‑3034 demonstrated a signal in a small endometrial cancer cohort, highlighting the need for mutation‑focused development.; Resistance mechanisms such as KRAS amplification can be detected by ctDNA, suggesting adaptive dosing or combination strategies.

metadata.speaker: Ignacio Garrido Laguna
metadata.session_title: Where Expected Pathways, Innovation, Safety, and Patient Access Collide
metadata.talk_title: Clinical advances and patient experiences with KRAS inhibitors
